title: Trump blames nationwide grounding of planes on old technology, Biden administration
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump bristled Monday at suggestions he’s been too focused on White House building projects, and that they might have distracted him during the nationwide grounding of all planes, even insisting, “You don’t see me on a scaffold.”
Speaking publicly for the first time about last week’s air traffic snarls caused by a router issue in the aging air traffic control system, Trump got defensive during a lengthy — sometimes testy — exchange with reporters as he left the White House for his trip to Asia,
He faulted old technology and Democrats for the incident that caused upheaval at the country’s airports — especially his predecessor, President Joe Biden. “I don’t take any responsibility” for Friday’s ground stop, Trump said, explaining his Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was in charge.
“What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” the president said. He later noted: “Incredibly, everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing.” Referring to his administration’s efforts to make improvements, he added, “the only responsibility should be, for 40 years they should have done this.”
Trump was silent on the chaos until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking Congress for more money to cover the cost of system improvements.
His blame-shifting and the congressional Democratic finger-pointing follow a familiar pattern of Trump seeking to say others were a fault during major crises — and underscore political divisions that could widen when Democrats take control of Congress in January, with scrutiny of his administration accelerating.
The problems with aging equipment at the Federal Aviation Administration date back decades, well before even the first Trump administration, and past efforts to modernize the system have come up short. The last major effort to overhaul air traffic control, called NextGen, started in 2003 and consumed more than $15 billion over the years.
Airline passengers suffered more woes Monday when United Airlines said it was experiencing a systemwide outage that was affecting departing flights. The airline resolved the issue about 1 1/2 hours after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers.
Trump says he spends ‘very little time’ on White House overhaul
On Monday, when pressed about his priorities, the president spent far more time defending his extensive efforts to mold the White House to his own, often gold and gilded, tastes than he did talking about his administration’s response to the ground stop.
“I spend very little time” on building projects Trump said, adding, “You don’t see me on a scaffold.”
He said the large granite helicopter landing pad he had built on the South Lawn had received “great reviews” and had replaced broken stone walkways and common areas. He also defended the sprawling ballroom being erected, which is larger than the rest of the White House, saying it “fits like a glove.”
“See this stone? Get your cameras on it,” he commanded of reporters on the South Lawn. “This stone was badly broken.”
Pressed further, he told a reporter, “You’re so pathetic,” then continued that he had “a responsibility to make sure the symbol of our country is in decent shape.”
The president suggested that the White House had previously had broken windows and columns that were “in horrible condition,” even though the extensive damage he described wasn’t visible before he ordered so many building projects.
Asked further about who was funding so much work, Trump responded: “This doesn’t cost money. This is peanuts.” The full extent of the costs of his many projects is unknown.
Trump also sought to justify the unusually personal role he’s taken in the parade of building projects at the White House, telling a reporter: “This is called talent. You don’t have talent.”
The Trump administration is seeking additional funding
Duffy, who made the decision Friday to ground the planes, has also pushed Congress for billions more dollars to upgrade a system he said had been neglected for decades.
Duffy said the problem began when a federal contractor was replacing a section of old copper wire with new fiber wire, causing the system to overload.
The Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds,” the agency said.
Duffy said Sunday that billions of dollars are needed to build new architecture for the network and said companies — including AT&T, Verizon and Lumen — are ready to deploy it as soon as the money is there.
Upgrading the nation’s air transportation system is an effort that Congress has dedicated significant sums to in recent years.
Under Biden, Congress approved a massive infrastructure bill that included $25 billion over five years for airport and air traffic control infrastructure improvements. Much of that money went to airport projects like new runways and taxiways and updated terminals.
After Trump returned to the White House in 2025, a Republican-led Congress approved $12.5 billion in 2025 to modernize the FAA’s air traffic system.
The Trump administration said the money would provide critical updates to outdated radar systems and traffic control centers, some dating back to the 1960s. Republicans used the same bill to allocate $170 billion for Trump’s immigration crackdown, for more border security and immigration enforcement.
___
Catalini reported from Morrisville, Pa.

title: Housing crunch weighs on employers' ability to hire, Boston Fed chief says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing shortages and rising home prices are making it increasingly difficult for businesses across northern New England and other parts of the country to attract and retain employees, according to the head of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston.
“A lack of available and affordable housing [for workers] can prevent local businesses from expanding,” Collins said Friday at the Fed’s annual economic conference in Boston.
She cited physicians, skilled mechanics, research scientists and hospitality workers who have declined job offers because of limited housing availability and high costs.
“Increasingly, I also hear about housing projects slowing or stalling due to a lack of skilled construction workers,” she added.
Collins noted that housing policy, zoning decisions and related government spending fall outside the Federal Reserve’s authority. However, she said that central banks can contribute empirical research and economic insights to discussions about housing challenges, which play a significant role in the broader economy.
Keeping inflation in check
As far as monetary policy is concerned, she echoed market expectations that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to tame inflation. The Federal Open Market Committee is widely expected to raise rates for a second time this year at its December meeting. Central bankers are scheduled to meet Dec. 8-9.
“In the near term, the higher interest rates sometimes needed to cool the economy and keep inflation in check can make homes more expensive to buy and to build,” Collins said. “But over the longer run, stable prices create predictable economic conditions that are good for housing.”
While Collins is a non-voting member of the FOMC this year, she participates in policy discussions.
Underscoring the lack of a “silver bullet” to solve today’s housing challenges, Collins urged constructive collaboration among many parties.
“Building a shared understanding of the complexities of the housing market is essential — and a fundamental reason for conferences like this,” she said. “Rigorous research can help inform better decisions and identify potential solutions.”

title: Cornell to examine future of Greek life after report of gang rape at a fraternity house
text:
Cornell University will launch a sweeping review of its Greek system and its future on campus after a report of a gang rape at a fraternity house in 2024, the university’s president said Monday.
The review will focus on the Greek system’s relationship to housing and residential life, President Michael Kotlikoff said in a letter to the Cornell community. Details will be announced in the coming weeks, he said.
The announcement marks the university’s latest response to outrage over its handling of a woman’s report that she was drugged and sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house. The woman, identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, sued Cornell and seven men in September.
Cornell expelled or suspended several students after an internal investigation and barred the fraternity chapter from campus. The accused men have denied wrongdoing, and none has been criminally charged.
Kotlikoff has faced criticism for his handling of the case, including his acknowledgment that he never read the campus police report and did not follow up on the outcome of the investigations. He has defended the university’s disciplinary process and said administrators were prohibited from interfering in criminal investigations.
Cornell previously suspended parties at fraternities and announced additional measures to prevent sexual violence on campus.
“To prevent sexual assault, we must reshape the social environments, interactions, and physical spaces that can contribute to increased risk,” Kotlikoff wrote Monday.
He also outlined plans to expand sexual assault prevention education, create more late-night social opportunities outside residential spaces and establish an academic center dedicated to researching campus sexual violence. The university said it is exploring ways to revitalize businesses and develop public gathering places in Collegetown, a neighborhood near campus where many students live and socialize.
Jane Doe’s lawyers, Thomas Giuffra and Whitney Seals, said in a statement that while they welcomed action by Cornell’s administrators to address sexual assault on campus, “words, task forces, and prospective reviews cannot erase years of institutional inaction.”
“Jane Doe welcomes any genuine effort that prevents another student from enduring what she suffered. However, meaningful reform requires full transparency into how past reports of sexual violence were mishandled, real consequences for those responsible, and a permanent end to a culture that prioritizes institutional reputation over student safety,” they said.
The announcement comes just over a week after Cornell’s Faculty Senate passed a vote of no confidence in the university administration’s ability to address sexual assault on campus.
In his letter Monday, Kotlikoff directly acknowledged the loss of confidence in Cornell’s administration.
“I know many in our community have lost confidence in the Cornell administration’s ability to prevent and respond to sexual violence,” he wrote. “You have raised necessary questions about what the administration is doing to keep our students safe and where we have fallen short.”
Kotlikoff pledged more regular communication about the university’s efforts, including a new public accountability dashboard tracking its progress.
Meanwhile, an independent review led by former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates is underway. Kotlikoff said its findings would guide longer-term changes to how Cornell investigates and adjudicates allegations of sexual misconduct.

title: Nepalese Student Alliance reflects on climate change impacts in Nepal
text:
As Nepal continues to grapple with the impacts of climate change following devastating floods beginning in August 2026 that drew international attention, members of the University of Maine Nepalese Student Association (NSA) gathered on Nov. 13 to celebrate their culture and find a sense of community during a period of uncertainty back home.
Since the 1970s, the International Student Alliance has remained one of the most active student groups at UMaine and has worked to emphasize the presence of the international community. On Fridays, the organization hosts a coffee hour featuring a different country each week, with students sharing their culture through food and presentations.
On Friday, Nov. 13, the coffee hour began with a slideshow presentation that highlighted key aspects of Nepali culture and emphasized how the country, despite its small size, is filled with many different traditions.
After the presentation, attendees were encouraged to enjoy traditional Nepali cuisine. During this time, the Maine Campus spoke to Urgen Lama, a first-year student from Nepal who described his experience in NSA so far. Lama mentioned that he found out about NSA at Culturefest and was not previously aware that there was a big Nepali presence at UMaine, but has since found comfort in the community.
Throughout the event, people were sharing traditional meals from Nepal and chatter filled the room, highlighting the vibrant culture.
“It definitely gives you a place that reminds you of home,” said Lama.
While the coffee hour focused on celebrating Nepali culture, the importance of maintaining connections to home has become especially apparent as students process the impacts of the flooding events in Nepal.
The president of NSA, Aayush Ojha, is pursuing his PhD in chemistry and joined the organization in 2023. In an interview, he spoke about the recent climate change impacts that Nepal is experiencing and said that “climate change has been real since I was a child.”
In a 2022 international finance corporation report, the World Bank Group attributed floods and landslides as the most frequent climate events in the past 40 years, especially with increases in global warming. According to a United Nations article, the recent flooding in August of 2026 was a result of a mountain of glacier ice melting and washing away homes and bridges. This climate catastrophe has killed 1,400 people, including 84 children, with about 5,300 people still missing.
Ojha stated that their only source of communication for a while was through news media outlets where they were only able to see the videos of massive floods. He added that the main struggle was communication and the uncertainty of not knowing what was happening. When asked if the flooding had impacted his family, Ojha said that his immediate family in the capital was not affected but that his extended family in rural areas were. Although Ojha was able to make contact with his family, he mentioned that many members of NSA were unable to contact their loved ones for up to weeks while others were more impacted by losses.
To help alleviate the feeling of uncertainty, Ojha mentioned that when circumstances like this impact their country, organizing these events becomes more valuable.
“The warmth and sense of belonging is what makes NSA truly special for Nepali people here,” said Ojha.
Regarding climate change, Ojha believes that oftentimes in America, climate change can be seen as a new idea or not a serious issue because its impacts aren’t as visible. However, he mentioned that for countries like Nepal, they bear the burden of what developed countries are emitting, making them more vulnerable to climate changes. He calls for both sides to see how they are affecting each other.
“It is important for people from the other side of the world to know that climate change has real impact on people in Nepal,” said Ojha.
Similarly, Lama believes that Americans should become more informed about how climate change impacts other communities around the world and recognize how reducing greenhouse gas emissions could help countries like Nepal.
Ojha encourages people to come to NSA and believes that by coming to these chats, it’s a way to become informed and learn new things. The Nepali people of the UMaine community see this as an opportunity to share the culture of Nepal and celebrate their roots. The members welcomed all attendees from different backgrounds and greeted them with smiles. They ended their presentation by saying dhanyabad, meaning thank you, to those who showed up.

title: Gunman found dead after 2 public safety officers are shot at New York City apartment complex
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Two public safety officers were shot Monday at a New York City apartment complex, police said. Their injuries were not believed to be life-threatening.
The suspected gunman was found dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound after barricading himself in an apartment at the massive Co-op City complex in the Bronx, police said.
The New York Police Department confirmed that the two victims were officers with the Co-op City Department of Public Safety, a private security force for the complex. They were taken to a hospital for treatment.
Police revised the number of victims after initially saying three people has been wounded.
Co-op City, built as middle-income housing in the 1960s and ’70s, has more than 15,300 cooperative apartments in high-rises and townhomes, 50,000 residents and its own ZIP code.
The complex’s emergency dispatchers said they had no information. A message was left for the property’s management.

title: Aging Untold: Meet founder of the ‘We Do Not Care Club’ started; Cut sodium without giving up flavor
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we break down simple ways to cut back on sodium without sacrificing flavor to protect your heart health and blood pressure.
Plus, we sit down with digital creator Melani Sanders, founder of the viral “We Do Not Care Club,” to talk about midlife, menopause and finding freedom in speaking your mind.
Finally, we share the inspiring story of a father who ran alongside his son to help him recover from a traumatic brain injury.
If you need to watch the amount of sodium you take in, giving up added salt does not mean giving up flavor, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Amy O’Rourke said she reads labels because bread, pastries, processed foods and canned goods can contain a lot of sodium.
Rogers said other spices can bring out the natural flavor of food, and she also gives tips on reading nutritional labels.
Melani Sanders created the popular “We Do Not Care Club.”
It started with one social media post announcing the club and asking if anyone wanted to join her.
Millions did and they have created a sisterhood.
Sanders spoke with Aging Untold about opening up on social media, menopause and what the online community supporting her means to her.
Most people know Melani Sanders for the humor in her videos, but one post that has resonated with a lot of people is one in which she opened up during a vulnerable moment.
She shared what led her to hit record and share another side of herself.
Doctors said that James McGinnis would never walk after a high school football injury.
Eleven years ago, McGinnis was a senior football player at Olathe East in high school when he was hit during a game and collapsed.
He suffered a traumatic brain bleed and doctors gave him less than a 7% chance to survive.
They also said that McGinnis would never walk again.
He not only learned to walk but he runs with his dad and together they ran a marathon 11 years after that frightening injury.

title: Kickoff times announced for Maine H.S. football state championship games
text:
MPA announces kickoff times for Maine high school football state championship games
The Maine Principals' Association has announced the kickoff times for Saturday's high school football state championship games, which are being played in Portland and Lewiston.
Fitzpatrick Stadium in Portland is hosting the Class A and Class B state championship games, while Lewiston High School's Don Roux Field will host the Class C and Class D title games.

title: Handwritten draft of MLK's 'I Have a Dream' speech to go on display before it's sold at auction
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — Words scrawled in blue pen — and others scratched out — give an intimate peek into the writing of what would become the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.’s most famous speech.
Delivered Aug. 28, 1963, from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, the “I Have a Dream” speech reflects on the shameful legacy of slavery, segregation and discrimination and looks forward with hope to future equality for the country’s Black citizens. A handwritten draft of that speech goes on display in King’s hometown Monday before it is sold to the highest bidder at auction in January.
The words that became most famous do not appear in the seven pages from a pad of yellow, lined paper. The “I have a dream” refrain was added by King on the spot as he stood before a crowd of tens of thousands of people gathered on the National Mall for the March on Washington.
But other key parts of the speech are there in the civil rights icon’s own handwriting, including the opening lines and the powerful finish invoking an African American spiritual.
King completed the handwritten draft in his hotel room in the wee hours of the morning, less than 12 hours before it was delivered, according to Christie’s, which will handle the sale of the manuscript. It was then given to assistants to be typed and sent to the media, the auction house said in a news release.
Speechwriter Edward Clayton was among the multiple advisers who helped King hash out the content of the speech. His wife, Xernona Clayton, who worked alongside him in the civil rights movement, discovered the draft in the late 1990s, three decades after her husband’s death. It was in a drawer of his desk, tucked inside an envelope labeled “speech.”
“The two of them gelled with writing and words,” Xernona Clayton said in the Christie’s news release. “They would go back and forth and there was such respect. Dr. King, who was a great thinker, said Ed was so good at getting his words on paper and putting them in the right place at the right time.”
Clayton knew the document was important but didn’t realize it was the only remaining handwritten draft and stuck it back in the drawer, finding it there again just two years ago.
Clayton, who established the Still Marching Irrevocable Charitable Unitrust to advance causes important to her, decided after consultation with trusted advisers to sell the draft to support charities that advance her own legacy and that of King. Christie’s expects the draft to fetch more than $10 million. The organizations that will benefit include the Xernona Clayton Foundation and the King Center in Atlanta.
“I am so grateful for the opportunity to give this amazing speech new life, and to give new life to people who are in need,” Clayton said. “And we cannot wait to give that first gift.”
King’s two remaining living children, the Rev. Bernice King and Martin Luther King III, said in the Christie’s release that they are grateful the sale will support the legacy of the movement their father helped build.
“It is poetic that the past will protect the future,” Martin Luther King III said. “We are grateful that this treasure was preserved over decades by the Clayton family. It is a remarkable piece of history that shines a light on our father’s process as he prepared to make a speech that so profoundly affected the course of the Civil Rights movement and our nation. Now, for the first time, the public will have the opportunity to be inspired by this document.”
The draft will be publicly displayed for the first time at the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta from Monday through Sunday. It will be on view in Chicago at a date to be determined and will be shown at Christie’s in New York from Jan. 15, King’s birthday, through Jan. 21 before being offered for auction on Jan. 22.

title: Augusta’s largest indoor flea market creates opportunity for local artists
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Augusta’s largest indoor flea market returned this weekend at the Augusta Civic Center for its third year in a row.
Vendors from across the state set up tables and booths to sell artwork, vintage clothing, antiques, jewelry, and so much more.
Booth reservations for vendors sold out this year. A testament to the event’s growing popularity.
For many, the flea market is an opportunity to dip their toes in the small-business world.
Some local artists displayed their original work at the event, allowing their art to be seen by a variety of potential customers.
One vendor explained how interacting with potential buyers gave her the confidence to keep with her small business.
“It was the thing that actually gave me the confidence to start selling my work proper,” said Jessica Morton, a vendor at the August Flea Market selling her original paintings.
“I’m very happy with how this year’s been, how the previous years have been, and I’m expanding to other craft fairs and markets in the future because of this flea market,” she said.
For up-to-date information about next year’s flea market, visit augustafleamarket.com.

title: Pastor, wife hit and killed by car walking to grandson’s wedding reception
text:
TYLER, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) — A Texas church is mourning the death of its founding pastor and his wife, who were struck and killed by a car Saturday while walking to their grandson’s wedding reception.
Caleb Hawley, lead pastor of LifeSource Community Church, confirmed the deaths of senior teaching pastor John Offutt and his wife, Carla Offutt, during a livestream of Sunday’s service.
“For those of you who don’t know, pastor John and his beautiful wife, Carla, were struck by a car last night walking across the road to their grandson’s reception after the wedding and were hit by a car and killed instantly,” Hawley said, fighting back tears from the pulpit.
Crash details
According to the Texas Department of Public Safety, the incident occurred around 6:15 p.m. Saturday.
Crash investigators said a vehicle traveling westbound on Farm-to-Market Road 515 struck the couple, who were pronounced dead at the scene.
The driver, identified as Ruth Rohrbach, 46, of Winnsboro, was taken to CHRISTUS Winnsboro for treatment, according to the Texas Department of Public Safety.
No charges have been filed against Rohrbach.
Executive pastor Sean Graver said John Offutt had officiated his grandson’s wedding and was walking with his wife to a reception at the Coke Schoolhouse in Como when a vehicle struck them as they crossed the highway.
Church leaders speak after deaths
Hawley said John Offutt was his father-in-law, mentor and friend. The two had worked together to lead LifeSource for nearly 12 years, he said.
“John and I have planned together, dreamed together, led this church together, and I honestly thought I had a lot more years, more conversations, more opportunities to learn from his depth of wisdom, more time to grow together,” Hawley said.
Hawley said the loss had changed the family’s world and urged those grieving not to hide their emotions.
“It’s OK not to be OK,” he said. “We don’t have to pretend this morning. We don’t have to hold back tears. We don’t have to have the right words.”
A church representative said details about arrangements would be shared as they become available.

title: Scam selling tickets to a fake Noah Kahan event now disabled
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FREEPORT, Maine (WMTW) - A scam listing selling tickets to a fake Noah Kahan event in Freeport has now been disabled.
The fake event was posted to the ticketing website Eventbrite and was promoted as an evening concert with singer-songwriter Noah Kahan set for June 12, 2027 at the L.L Bean Flagship store.
Jason Sultham, Manager of Public Affairs at L.L Bean told Maine’s Total Coverage that the store has no affiliation with the listing and that “no such event ever existed.”
He adds that once the scam was discovered, L.L. Bean immediately notified Eventbrite and disabled the listing.
Tickets for Noah Kahan’s, now sold out, “The Last of The Bugs World Tour” went on sale on Thursday. Since then, many fans took to social media advising that scammers were trying to sell fake tickets to those who couldn’t secure any.
The “Sticks Season” singer will kickstart his “The Last of The Bugs World Tour” April 24, 2027 at Sanford Stadium in Athens, Georgia.
Kahan will also be performing for six nights at Fenway Park in Boston, MA with opening acts Buffalo Traffic Jam and Tiny Habits.

title: Maine town uses mystery $55K found in woods to help families pay heating bills
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FALMOUTH, Maine (WGME) — A mysterious stash of tens of thousands of dollars found in a safe in the Maine woods several years ago will now help families pay their heating bills.
Police said $55,000 was found, but a question remains: Where did the money come from?
“We’re surmising that it was there for pickup and something else was going to get dropped off, um, but yeah, we don’t know,” Falmouth Police Chief John Kilbride said.
Falmouth police traced the cash to a bank in New Hampshire and confirmed the money was not stolen. Police said they followed protocol, contacted several law enforcement agencies and advertised that they had a large sum of unclaimed cash, but they could not crack the case.
“It was an intriguing way of getting funds. It’s, you know, this was not taxpayer money,” Falmouth Town Council Chair Bryce Hawke explained. “This was not something that was a product of any really even, um, thoughtful policy. This is just literally a find in the woods.”
Under state law, the unclaimed money had to be used for a charitable purpose.
The Falmouth Town Council voted to direct the funds to the low-income home energy assistance program, or LIHEAP.
Hawke said the decision was a no-brainer. Going into peak heating season, the council believes it could go a long way in helping Mainers in a pinch.
“Knowing how needed these funds are for heating right now, knowing how expensive fuel is for heating, and knowing that we’re going right into the winter. This was a true, a true gift for our community and one that literally fell on our lap,” Hawke said.
The money is expected to be available starting in January.

title: What to know before using gamified credit card rewards
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Some new “gamified” credit cards turn every swipe into a spin of the wheel, with random cashback amounts and surprise payoffs.
Sara Rathner of NerdWallet looked at the trend and said some of these cards now encourage cardholders to take certain actions.
Rathner said the effect depends on what the card asks cardholders to do.
“It could be positive. It could be nudging you to contribute every month to your savings account or pay your bills on time. It could be educational, completing financial literacy courses to unlock certain prizes. And it could also encourage you to spend just to try to game the system and earn just a little bit more rewards. And that’s a slippery slope,” Rathner said.
Rathner said cardholders could end up overspending just to try for a small chance of winning a prize. She also found that the average payout can be much lower than first advertised, and that in some cases the rules can change hour by hour.
“There are lots of examples of gamification that are good, but it’s when you introduce uncertainty and sweepstakes and the potential to win, but you have to spend, spend, spend to up your odds of winning. That’s when it gets dangerous,” Rathner said.
Rathner said anyone using gamification with a financial product should stick to games that are educational and positive and that encourage more saving, not more spending. She said cardholders should not have to engage in something risky just to benefit.

title: Fire guts Maine home
text:
A fire gutted a North Yarmouth home early Saturday morning.
The Royal Road home’s two occupants awoke to smoke alarms about 3:09 a.m. and escaped from the second floor and called 911, according to Maj. Aaron Turcotte, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
When firefighters arrived, they found heavy flames on the first floor of the two-story Cape Cod-style home, Turcotte said Monday morning.
The home sustained substantial structural damage from the fire, with much of the roof and second floor collapsing into the first floor.
Investigators determined the interior of the home was too unstable for anyone to enter, hampering their ability to conduct a complete investigation.
The fire remains under investigation but is believed to be accidental.

title: Virginia state Sen. Louise Lucas pleads not guilty in marijuana-related case
text:
State Sen. L. Louise Lucas, a powerful Virginia Democrat, pleaded not guilty Monday to federal racketeering, drug, money laundering and other charges.
Federal prosecutors have accused Lucas of leading a criminal enterprise that they say acquired and sold large quantities of marijuana and laundered the proceeds. At a news conference and in charging documents, authorities have said Lucas used her political power to insulate the operation from scrutiny and sought to influence Virginia marijuana legislation to financially benefit the alleged marijuana enterprise.
Lucas also faces a charge of conspiracy to commit honest services fraud and of maintaining a drug-involved premises. A jury trial was set for mid-September, according to court records that also reflected her not guilty plea.
One of her attorneys, Anthony Capozzolo, said by email that Lucas “looks forward to litigating this matter in the future” and declined further comment.
Later Monday, supporters of Lucas planned to hold a tele-town hall to discuss the case.
The charges against Lucas were announced after the FBI searched her hometown office and a cannabis shop she owns in May.
Since 2021, marijuana has been legal to possess in Virginia, and many shops across the state have sold cannabis-derived products, but full recreational marijuana sales will not be allowed until July 2027.
A vocal critic of President Donald Trump, Lucas has served in the state Senate — where she’s currently the president pro tempore — since 1992. Before Monday, Lucas made clear she intended to contest the charges and has characterized the Justice Department’s work in the case as an effort to intimidate her.
Lucas has also told reporters she will not resign nor will she step down from her leadership role chairing the powerful Senate finance committee while the case plays out. Since her indictment, she’s carried on with her official duties, participating in committee hearings while the Legislature is out of session.
Lucas, 82, told The Virginian-Pilot for a story published Sunday that she will seek reelection next year.
On Sunday, Lucas’ legal team filed a motion arguing that Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and First Assistant U.S. Attorney Theophani Stamos of the Eastern District of Virginia violated a court rule dealing with the press and fair trials in statements they made at a news conference announcing the indictment. The court should impose “appropriate sanctions for those violations,” Lucas’ team wrote.
Scottie Howell, a spokesperson for the Eastern District of Virginia U.S. Attorney’s Office, declined to comment on the motion. Audrey Cook, a Justice Department spokesperson, said by email that the department “remains confident in its case and will not comment further on pending litigation.”

title: Piper Mountain prepares to welcome early bird Christmas tree customers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEWBURGH, Maine (WABI) - Piper Mountain Christmas Tree Farm will welcome its first customers of the season this weekend, offering cut-your-own and precut balsam fir trees.
Molly and Jesse Jimerson are entering their fifth Christmas season at the helm of the Newburgh farm. While they respect the farm’s history and what it means to Mainers, their family has also started traditions of their own.
“I don’t even know that we were fully aware of how special Piper Mountain was when we first got here,” Molly Jimerson said.
Early bird weekend
The farm’s early bird weekend begins Saturday at 9 a.m. Molly said the couple started it after finding that some customers wanted their Christmas trees up for Thanksgiving.
“Most Christmas tree farms, the tradition is to open the day after Thanksgiving. It’s the biggest day of the year for Christmas trees in Maine,” Jimerson said. “And we found that a lot of people love to have their Christmas tree up for Thanksgiving. So, we started the early bird weekend.”
Customers can choose from precut trees or cut their own on the farm’s 30 acres of trees. The farm provides a saw to customers who want to cut their own, Jimerson said.
Jimerson said keeping a tree watered is key to helping it last through the holidays. The farm will put a fresh cut on trees before customers leave, she said.
“When you get home, you should put your tree straight into a bucket of water. Even if you’re just grabbing ornaments and stuff, because the sap seal can start really early,” she said. “And then get it immediately into the tree stand and then just keep it full of water.”
Cider doughnuts and hours
Piper Mountain is making its own cider doughnuts on-site for the first time. Jimerson said the farm made the change after finding that doughnuts were a favorite among customers but that it was easy to run out or not have them fresh enough.
“We realized to solve that problem, we had to make them right here in house,” she said. “We have perfected the recipe.”
The farm is open Saturday and Sunday from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. It will reopen on Black Friday for the season, with regular hours Thursday through Sunday from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

title: Man charged after allegedly sending peanut butter-covered mail to woman with severe allergy
text:
PLANTATION, Fla. (Gray News) — A Florida man is facing criminal charges after allegedly sending mail smeared with peanut butter to a person who has a life-threatening allergy to peanuts.
Victim reported card
The Plantation Police Department said a victim called officers Aug. 14, 2025, after receiving a peanut butter-covered greeting card in the mail.
The woman has a severe peanut allergy and tried to remove the peanut butter from her hands right after realizing it was on the card, the police department said. She still reacted and experienced hives, itching and tingling in her arms.
Detectives identify sender
Detectives determined that Joseph Gerard Cancellare Jr., 68, of Plantation, sent the envelope.
According to police, Cancellare and the victim knew each other personally, and he was aware of her severe allergy. Investigators did not provide a motive.
Arrest and charges
Cancellare was arrested Nov. 13, 2026, and taken to the Broward County Jail on charges of aggravated battery and culpable negligence.
“This case reminds us that actions intended to harm others can have serious, potentially life-threatening consequences,” Plantation police said.

title: What Mainers should expect from Troy Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
OPINION: On Nov. 4, Troy Jackson was elected to the U.S. Senate, marking an important change in Maine’s longtime leadership in Washington by replacing Susan Collins. Jackson is set to take office on Jan. 3, 2027, which begs the question: What changes will we see in Maine? And more importantly, are we as Mainers going to be better or worse off from this switch?
Jackson famously ran his campaign on a working-class movement, which was one of the reasons he was so successful in this year’s election. Jackson gained immense support from the middle class and centered many of his political views around supporting everyday Mainers.
In Washington, Jackson seeks to pass Medicare for All, lower taxes for middle-class families and abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), all of which should sound enticing to Mainers.
As a state, we have dealt with our fair share of issues regarding ICE, health care cuts and, much like at the national level, class division, all of which Jackson’s opponent, former Sen. Susan Collins, arguably played a role in backing. What Jackson seeks to provide for Maine should sound like a breath of fresh air because it is. The only question is, is it actually feasible?
The answer is yes. Jackson has outlined a plan to co-sponsor and support a “Medicare for All Act,” which builds on legislation from U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders. In his outline, Jackson plans to establish a government-sponsored health care system that ensures Americans, and in turn Mainers, are provided necessary health care at no individual cost. Jackson recognizes that this plan may take a while to go completely into effect and plans on rolling it out in stages, starting with lowering the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55.
Furthermore, Jackson seeks to lower taxes for working-class Mainers by doubling Maine’s earned income tax credit. Additionally, when running for governor, Jackson sought to propose a bill that would create an additional 4% surtax on income over $1 million. This is something I would not be surprised to see come up again when Jackson takes over as senator and is something that would help address wealth inequality in Maine, where the top 20% of households earned 48% of all personal income.
If there were a time to abolish ICE, it would be now, after President Donald Trump reportedly stated his deportation policy was “too tough.” Jackson has been open about his opinion that ICE has been detrimental to the freedoms of this nation and suggests that we should take ICE funding and “put that money into Customs and Border Patrol. They have training, they’re law enforcement, people respect them, [and] we don’t respect ICE.”
While Jackson’s promises to deliver on Medicare, taxes and ICE are great, they are simply a few examples of some much-needed change Jackson plans on bringing. Mainers across the state should be excited for what the next few years have to offer and should have a lot to look forward to, as they appear to be in much better hands after this election cycle.

title: Remembering the Bangor Mall
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In 1977, Morris A. Kravitz broke ground on a fertile stretch of land just north of Bangor’s central shopping district. In previous years, a dairy farm operated here, but as American society learned to embrace the homogeneity of free market enterprise and corporate consumerism began to spread rapidly, this land turned into the ideal location for the Bangor Mall.
Upon its unveiling in 1978, standing at 653,000 sq. feet, the Bangor Mall was not the decaying structure that stands on the corner of Stillwater Ave today. It was a symbol, a grand stamp in the history of Bangor, which has struggled to meet the great metropolitan expectations the city garnered in the turn of the 20th century.
This mall was a symbol of hope for the citizens of Bangor. The mall showed that there were still great things to come for the third largest city in Maine. In a 1990 issue of the Bangor Daily News, journalist Simon Varney describes the mall in almost unbelievable grandeur:
“The shopping center features more than 80 shops. When the mall turned three years old, stores exhibited displays from all over the world. On the mall’s sixth birthday, in ‘84, a shopper won a $10,000 spending spree. Last year, 100 shoppers entered the “money machine” and tried to catch as much money as they could in 60 seconds. The winner received a Caribbean cruise, and got to keep the money.”
This romantic image of the now-condemned shopping center is still prevalent in the memory of many long-time Bangor residents. I spoke with Tom Lynch, who works in the golf section of Dick’s Sporting Goods. At 75 years old, he has lived his whole life in the greater Bangor area and has a sincere fondness for the mall.
“They had a huge fountain in the center of the mall. Especially at Christmas they used to deck it out like you wouldn’t believe,” said Lynch. “When my kids were little, coming to the mall was a really big deal. Even when I lived in Calais, we did a huge amount of our shopping at the mall.”
Since retiring from public education, Lynch has been coming to the mall for work these last five years, and he has watched the once beloved staple of Bangor slip into ruin.
“I’ve just watched business after business leave. I feel terrible for the places that got shut down, coming into the Christmas season and the city decides, ‘okay we’re closing it.’ I feel so bad. I mean, there used to be a York steak house in the food court, it’s sad to see what’s happened to it,” said Lynch.
While working on this story, I spent several hours walking the perimeter of the mall. I peered past city placards into the mirth, mildew and dripping ceilings. There was something about this place I found morbidly alluring.
In the parking lots, freight trucks sink with flat tires as they wait to be auctioned off, holding coffee cups still sitting half full in the cupholders. Within the only two operating stores, Dick’s and JCPenney, employees seem frozen in a wasteland of discounted kitchen appliances and Black Friday deals, diligently manning their stations.
I felt, as I treaded past the empty storefronts, that this was a foregone conclusion in the race of consumption. The gentle slope that has led the American consumer into the embrace of convenience, the desire for accumulation, for that momentary satisfaction tenderly exchanged. It was this journey which led Kravitz to spend millions of dollars turning thirteen acres of fertile earth into a concrete sarcophagus, haunted by the glory of days gone past.
The times change. Amazon and online retail offer an immediacy and convenience no shopping center could compete with. As I stand before this monument, I find myself hoping that we learn from the wound which aches in our city. Hoping this generation takes the time to consider the future when trying to get the most out of the present. Hoping that we can love the Bangor Mall for what it once was and learn from what it became, so that whatever comes next for these thirteen acres may outlast the desire for convenience or profit and persist on the merit of a larger purpose.

title: Supreme Court rebuffs Trump administration appeal over DEI funding cuts
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected a Trump administration appeal on DEI funding cuts to academic research even as some conservative justices raised questions about implicit bias training in a separate case.
The justices’ first decision left in place lower court rulings that the Trump administration likely ran afoul of the First Amendment when it terminated millions of dollars in grants to University of California researchers.
The cuts came after an executive order issued in January 2025 telling the government to end programs linked to DEI, which stands for diversity, equity and inclusion. The Trump administration argued that the government is not obligated to continue funding research that no longer fits its priorities.
The lawsuit, which involves only a portion of the Trump administration’s research funding cuts, will continue to play out.
No justices publicly dissented from the brief order declining to hear the case.
The Supreme Court also declined Monday to hear a challenge to California’s requirement for continuing medical education courses to include discussion of how unconscious bias can affect healthcare outcomes.
In that case, though, three conservative justices voiced an interest in the claims. Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented, saying the requirement raises questions about state regulation of private speech.
Justice Neil Gorsuch also noted briefly that he would have heard the case.

title: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the dwindling number of Pearl Harbor survivors, dies at 106
text:
BOSTON (AP) — Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the few remaining Pearl Harbor survivors, has died.
Johnson died Saturday at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts. He was 106, according to one of his daughters, Diane Johnson.
“It’s going to be a hell of a Thanksgiving,” said Diane Johnson, 72. “He’s going to be up there with all of his friends and family and my mom.”
Freeman Johnson was one of the estimated 87,000 military personnel on Oahu on Dec. 7, 1941, and was below deck working on a boiler of the USS St. Louis when the Japanese surprise attack happened. In a May 2026 interview with The Associated Press, Johnson said he didn’t hear or see the attack. He never heard his shipmates firing anti-aircraft guns at the attacking planes — shooting down a torpedo plane.
“While all the rigamarole was going on topside, I was inside a steam drum. Couldn’t see anything, absolutely nothing,” said Johnson, whose job had been known as a firefighter on the ship.
Even as the St. Louis headed into the Pacific Ocean, Johnson knew little about the attack. By the time he was topside, the St. Louis, a light cruiser, had evaded midget submarines and safely set out to sea.
“We were way out to sea, way out. You couldn’t see any land at all. All you saw was ocean,” he said. “I was just a sailor, just a swabbie, I was not an officer. They don’t tell you anything if you don’t need to know. And I didn’t need to know it. So they tell you nothing.”
The list of surviving veterans from the attack had stood at about a dozen names after the December 2025 death of Ira “Ike” Schab, who was 105.
While Johnson didn’t see the Pearl Harbor attack, which killed just over 2,400 Americans and propelled the United States into the war, he was witness to other historic moments during World War II.
He helped commission the USS Iowa and recalled the battleship’s preparations in November 1943 ahead of transporting President Franklin D. Roosevelt to the Tehran Conference with British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Josef Stalin. The ship was equipped with two elevators and a bathtub. All the ammunition and much of the oil was removed to lighten the ship as it made its way down the Potomac River to pick up Roosevelt. It was reloaded before the ship headed out to sea.
Johnson also witnessed the war’s end while aboard the Iowa. He was on the Iowa’s mast watching the surrender ceremonies about a mile away in Tokyo Bay aboard the USS Missouri on Sept. 2, 1945.
“I could see the boats coming up with the Marines escorting the Japanese onto the ship and sitting around a table,” he said. “It was all over. That was the end of the war. A bunch of us got together — the war is over. Let’s go home.”
For all the attention to Pearl Harbor, the gruff Johnson, who was known for his cackling laugh and mischievous smile, didn’t see it as one of the defining moments in his life.
Those would have been getting married after the war to his late wife and having three daughters. He worked for years in a machinist shop, then in a convenience store and, finally, delivering meals to seniors — all jobs he retired from, the last one at the age of 90.
“Pearl Harbor just happened. I can’t put it any other way,” he said.

title: Tanker’s steering failed minutes before it crashed into cruise ship, NTSB says
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A tanker ship had two minutes between a steering failure and its collision with a cruise ship on the Mississippi River, according to the National Transportation Safety Board.
The NTSB released the information Sunday in an update on Friday’s accident involving the tanker ship Atlantic Asphalt and the riverboat cruise ship American Heritage. The latter ship capsized after the crash, but everyone on board was rescued.
Investigators downloaded more than nine hours of information from the Atlantic Asphalt’s voyage data recorder, or VDR, which was recovered Saturday.
A preliminary review of that information shows a steering casualty around 12:26 p.m. that left the ship’s rudder stuck starboard, pointing the tanker directly at the east bank of the Mississippi River, the NTSB said.
NTSB Investigator in Charge Bart Barnum said the tanker was near the Crescent City Connection bridge in New Orleans at that time. He said the VDR recorded “audio sounds consistent with the following: the ship’s whistle, warnings, requests for assistance broadcast over the vessel’s marine radio, commands to deploy the vessel’s anchors and emergency ship handling orders.”
The Atlantic Asphalt passed under the bridge, veered to the right and struck the docked American Heritage, which capsized.
“At about 12:28 p.m., the Atlantic Asphalt collided with the passenger vessel, the American Heritage,” Barnum said.
Officials have said the American Heritage had 191 passengers and crew on board at the time. Everyone was rescued, including 100 passengers, crew and first responders who went into the water.
As of Sunday, six of the 32 survivors hospitalized after the accident had not been discharged. Two were in serious but stable condition, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said.
NTSB Board Member John DeLeeuw said the investigation will include what went right.
“We are also going to investigate the things that went right,” DeLeeuw said. “There were a number of reasons why there were no fatalities, so we are going to take that as part of our investigation.”
The NTSB is working to preserve evidence on the American Heritage. Divers spent Sunday on the ship searching for clues that can be salvaged and compared with the Atlantic Asphalt’s VDR data.
The NTSB said it is interviewing passengers and crew from the American Heritage on Sunday. It plans to begin interviewing the Atlantic Asphalt crew Monday.
A preliminary report is expected next month.
As of Sunday, 50 hotel rooms at the Hilton New Orleans Riverside remained occupied by passengers. City of New Orleans personnel are coordinating directly with American Cruise Lines, owner of the American Heritage, to ensure passengers and crew members can safely return home.
American Cruise Lines issued its first public statement on the incident Sunday afternoon.
“We are proud of our crew and grateful for the first responders following yesterday’s incident on the Mississippi River,” the company said in the statement. “The fast actions of Captain Leonard Stewart and our crew allowed for a rapid evacuation of the vessel after the American Heritage was struck by a large tanker while docked at the Port of New Orleans. Captain Stewart remained on the bridge as the vessel capsized, calling for aid and keeping the ship alongside the dock for as long as possible.
“We appreciate the support from Mayor Moreno and Governor Landry and are working closely with their offices. We are grateful to the US Coast Guard, the Port of New Orleans and the New Orleans Police Department, and will continue working in partnership through the investigation and salvage effort.”

title: Burlington Food Pantry volunteers help neighbors and inspire a new generation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BURLINGTON, Maine (WABI) - The Burlington Food Pantry is assisting hundreds of Mainers put food on the table, with a little help from volunteers of all ages.
“It just feels good to be able to help somebody,” said Claire Michaud, 12, a volunteer of about four years.
The pantry began in 2020 with just four people. That number has since grown to 40 volunteers, helping provide approximately 400 people with food twice a month.
“Addressing food insecurity here in northern Maine is really important to us. So we don’t ask for any income levels, we only ask if you need help with food, you’re welcome here. So everyone gets some frozen food, some dry goods, and some produce. And they drive through and pop their trunk and we fill their cars and in three to six minutes they’re on their way,” said Maureen Bean, the pantry’s executive director.
Students from Lincoln’s Mattanawcook Junior High School were among those helping out Friday, and organizers say every pair of helping hands makes a difference.
“I’m with a few of my classmates. There’s a lot of people out there that can’t get food and stuff that need it and volunteers help,” said volunteer Milo Bagley, 14. “It helps teach like younger kids that helping out with the community and helping other people is good.”
Volunteer April Theriault has been helping out at the pantry for a few months, after coming across the call for volunteers on Facebook.
“I like to give back to the community, didn’t really know how, but there it was, you know, and I came out and I did it,” Theriault said. “It’s not work, it doesn’t feel like work, it’s just, it’s fun. And you are helping people and helping a lot of good people.”
Bean said the need remains high all year long.
“There’s a lot of need. Several pantries have closed in this area. About 200 of our families never miss. We’re groceries for them. Coming into a place and asking for food is somewhat of a challenge for somebody, it’s hard to ask for help. But that’s what we’re here for,” Bean said.
The Burlington Food Pantry is looking for volunteers on Sunday, Monday and Friday mornings.
Bean adds monetary donations are accepted, too. While they do partner with organizations like Good Shepherd Food Bank, Bean said these drive-through distribution events cost about $2,000 to supply with the necessary items.

title: Isaac, a cat missing since the Brooklyn building collapse, has been reunited with his young owner
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A cat missing since last week’s deadly Brooklyn building collapse has been found alive and reunited with his young owner, New York City officials said Sunday.
Allie Taylor, director of the Mayor’s Office of Animal Welfare, said her office worked with the veterinary nonprofit Flatbush Cats to locate Isaac and reunite him with 13-year-old Zariah Coleman.
It was a bit of good news amid the tragedy of Wednesday’s collapse, which killed eight people, injured 18 others and forced the evacuation of several nearby buildings, including one next door where Zariah lives.
Zariah and her mother told The New York Times on Sunday that workers found Isaac on Sunday in a cabinet under the kitchen sink of Zariah’s apartment after hearing a soft meow. Zariah and her family hadn’t been allowed in since the collapse, which tore off the side of her building and left a hole where her bedroom wall had been.
Waiting outside, Zariah hugged the cat’s cage as workers brought him out of her apartment building. Isaac had gone four days without food or water. After his rescue, he was taken to Flatbush Cats’ veterinary clinic for a checkup.
“I had it in my heart they would find Issac,” Zariah told the Times. “I knew they would.”
Zariah tearfully spoke about her missing cat at a news conference on Friday, telling reporters: “I just really hope they come and get our cat. He’s hiding from them, and I think he’s scared.”
Mayor Zohran Mamdani heralded Isaac and Zariah’s reunion in a social media post. He thanked Taylor’s office, the city’s Buildings Department and the nonprofit for the happy outcome.
“Isaac is now receiving the veterinary care he needs,” Mamdani said. “We’re grateful to everyone who helped bring them back together.”

Authorities said the victims were among a group of individuals swimming beyond an area marked with a warning sign, cautioning against strong currents. While swimming, several swimmers were reportedly swept away by the currents, officials continued.
Related video: Teacher drowns after he rescued a girl trapped in a rip current off a South Carolina beach
The release said a nearby ferry boat assisted some of the swimmers to safety. The man and woman, who have not been identified by officials, became unresponsive and were taken to a local clinic, where they later died.
Officials said foul play is not suspected and that an autopsy will be conducted.
Police said an investigation remains ongoing.
If a swimmer becomes stuck in strong waters, such as a rip current, the American Red Cross recommends they signal to those on shore for help before swimming parallel to the shore until they are out of the current. Once free, swimmers should float or tread water before turning and swimming toward shore.

title: Patch Hall hot water outage prompts university response
text:
Between Oct. 18 and 22, residents of Patch Hall at the University of Maine experienced hot water disruptions and discolored water. Though it was mentioned in an email sent on Nov. 10 to residents that the discolored water following the hot water and steam repairs was not dangerous to shower in or consume, students were left without answers for over two weeks.
Richard Young, UMaine’s executive director of Auxiliary Enterprises, acknowledged these inconveniences via email. Young addressed the cause of the disruptions and acknowledged delays in communication between university officials and residents.
“The hot water disruption was caused by the failure of two temperature-control components in the system: the aquastat sensor and the primary thermostatic controller. The failure of this electronic control seemed to be a random occurrence,” wrote Young.
Young explained that the issue was not initially brought to the attention of higher-level university administrators.
“The communication delay occurred because the incident was not escalated to the director level, which is the procedure for emergent building issues that may impact the residents’ living environment. The first assessment and repair brought the hot water system back to temperature, but it was unable to maintain it during high use,” wrote Young.
He also addressed how communication between university officials could have better informed residents about the situation.
“Escalating the communication and briefing the Director of Housing and the Dean of Students at that point would have ensured that Residence Life staff and Housing were informed and coordinated support for residents. The residents would have known the problem, what to expect in the immediate future, and an estimate of the disruption’s duration,” he wrote.
Students were informed in the email sent to them about the outage that this will be dealt with in the future, if it were to happen again, with clearer communication, estimated repair times and faster responses. Young reiterated this point.
“We have shared the current protocol with the key administrator to review and update any information that may have changed, such as cell numbers, position changes, etc. For any future outages impacting the residents, they will receive an acknowledgment within two hours and an official update within four hours, including the cause and a timeline,” wrote Young.
Patch Hall residents were also informed of additional repairs planned during winter break.
“As a precaution, we plan to replace the system’s mixing valves during winter break. That will mean a short outage of a few hours. We will tell you the date and times at least two weeks in advance, update you on progress, and let you know where to shower if the replacement takes longer than four hours,” wrote Young.

title: Bucksport business coalition is closing
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BUCKSPORT, Maine — When the Bucksport Bay Area Chamber of Commerce dissolved in May 2020, businesswoman Teri Doty founded the Bucksport Bay Business Coalition LLC as a way to fill the hole left by the chamber’s closing.
Over time, Doty said, the group shifted its focus to organizing community events and changed from a nonprofit to a for-profit organization. After six years, Doty announced that the coalition will dissolve at the end of 2026.
The coalition’s last events will be Christmas Tree Lighting and Winter Festival on Dec. 12. In an interview, Doty said, “I’ve been doing the coalition for six years and wanted to refocus on my other business that I’ve set aside to do coalition events.”
In 2026, the coalition sponsored the summer Vendor Bender series, Splash-A-Palooza, the Bucksport 250th Freedom Festival, the revival of the Bucksport Art Festival and the Halloween Block Party.
“It was a great privilege to do events for the community and [be] fortunate enough to meet some very wonderful people along the way,” Doty said. “The vendors that participated in the events are absolutely amazing … The one event I will probably hang on to is the Bridge Street Halloween Block Party.”
The events were of her own creation except for the July Freedom 250th festival, and would have to be undertaken by other organizations to continue.
Among the businesses Doty will concentrate on is Music Insider magazine, which she has operated since 2006. According to its social media page, the magazine is “your source for inside information on what is really going on in the music industry, and knowledge to further your music career.”
A gift wrapping and bake sale fundraiser was held Saturday to raise money for the Christmas Tree Lighting and Winter Festival on Dec. 12.

title: Blame for Searsmont explosion seems misplaced
text:
This is to take real exception to the screaming Nov. 11 Page 1 headline regarding the fining of seven departments of first responders in relation to the Robbins Lumber fire and explosion in May (“State cites 7 fire departments in deadly mill explosion”).
Our first responders, employed and volunteering, upon whom each and every one of us depends 24/7/356, two of whom died at the scene? Give me a break.
Buried in the piece was a good tip as to a fundamental flaw in our government: “Mill safety conditions are regulated by the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration.”
So what about suing the feds for the damages and deaths? I’m wondering what the chiefs from our police, fire and rescue departments might think.
Bill Zierden
Scarborough

title: Aroostook trailhead project secures $150,000 tourism grant
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Houlton planners have been working together to boost the region’s outdoor economy and infrastructure — and a recent multiuse trailhead grant brings that initiative one step closer.
A $150,000 Maine Office of Tourism grant, combined with $15,000 in matching funds raised by the Rotary Club of Houlton, moves the Rotary Trailhead Project from a community vision to a much more fully planned, actionable project, said Houlton Rotary President Johnanna Johnston.
The trailhead project is part of a broader regional focus on building outdoor recreation infrastructure across southern Aroostook and neighboring Penobscot and Washington counties.
Island Falls and Patten are already tackling outdoor trails projects. And the Houlton trailhead will add an access point to northern Maine’s thousands of interconnected snowmobile and ATV trails.
From the beginning planners wanted this to be much more than a Houlton project because the ATV and snowmobile trails connect communities throughout Aroostook County, said Josh McLaughlin, Chair, Rotary Trailhead Committee.
“If we can encourage more visitors to come explore our trails, stay a little longer, and support businesses along the way, that’s a win for all of us,” McLaughlin said.
Rotary officials announced the idea of creating a trailhead in Houlton earlier this year and the club hosted a public forum for riders, residents, businesses, snowmobile clubs and regional partners in March to learn more about what was important.
“Outdoor recreation is the future of Aroostook County. Investing in a new recreational trail will expand access to the outdoors and allow our community to experience the natural beauty right in our backyards,” said Greater Houlton Chamber of Commerce Executive Director Jane Torres, who is a trail planning committee member.
The Rotary Trailhead effort focuses on enhancing the experience of ATV and snowmobile enthusiasts and other visitors who use a regional trail network extending far beyond Houlton. Its committee includes representatives of Rotary, Southern Aroostook Development Corporation, area ATV and snowmobile clubs, hotel businesses, recreational sporting goods retailers, and other community stakeholders.
The tourism grant includes: Destination planning and coordination; Site assessments and feasibility; Landscape architecture and conceptual design; Community engagement; Wayfinding and visitor experience; Economic and implementation planning; Mapping and final plan development.
An important distinction is that this grant does not fund the actual construction of the trailhead or final construction engineering. Instead, it provides the professional planning, design, and feasibility work needed to position the project for future construction funding and implementation, Johnston said.
In addition to the trailhead project, Millinocket-based The Outdoor Sports Institute selected the town to participate in a Davis Conservation Foundation funded community trail planning program that takes a broader look at our existing trails, potential connections, and future recreational opportunities.
“We were selected to receive professional trail planning assistance rather than a traditional monetary grant,” Johnston said. “It will help our committee develop a broader community trail plan.”
The OSI committee includes Johanna Johnston of Southern Aroostook Development Corporation; Chris Anderson of Starkey Farm; Tammy Goetsch of Adopt-A-Block and Military Street Baptist Church; Sara Flewelling of Aurora Mills & Farms; Crystal Lewis of Houlton Parks and Recreation; Jane Torres of the Greater Houlton Chamber of Commerce; and Kim Anderson-York of the Attraction Committee.
Crystal Lewis, Houlton director of Parks and Recreation, said that her department received grant-funded bicycles several years ago but they lack convenient nearby trails where they can readily be incorporated into programming.
“I’d love to see more accessible bike trails close to town where we could bring groups, introduce children and families to cycling, and make better use of the resources we already have,” she said. “This planning initiative could open the door to some really exciting recreational opportunities for our community.”
The Rotary Trailhead project has an 18-month grant period and the OSI planning process is just getting underway.
Members of the OSI committee will work with the sports institute to evaluate existing recreational assets, identify opportunities for improvements and connections, and establish priorities for future development, Johnston said.
“The resulting community trail plan should give us a roadmap for future projects, including identifying potential funding opportunities and partnerships to bring those ideas to fruition,” she said.
“I’m genuinely excited about the potential of both initiatives, particularly from an economic development perspective,” she said. “We already have some incredible outdoor recreational assets throughout Southern Aroostook, but I think there’s tremendous opportunity to better connect, develop, and promote them.”

title: We Do Not Care Club founder Melani Sanders opens up about sharing vulnerable moment
text:
(Aging Untold) — Digital creator Melani Sanders, founder of the “We Do Not Care Club,” is known for her humorous videos, but a more vulnerable moment she shared has resonated with many people. She opened up about what led to her pressing record and sharing it.
“I was overwhelmed with emotion,” Sanders said.
What led to the post
“I said, ‘This is a lot. This is a lot,’ and all of it just hit me at one time,” Sanders said.
She began thinking about having one son left at home and about the empty nest, she said.
Why she shared it
Sanders said she wants people to know her videos are funny and include “some real talk,” but that “there’s another side.”
“Many women are suffering, and we’re suffering silently,” she said.
Community and social media
Asked how the “We Do Not Care Club” community has made a difference, Sanders said, “Sometimes I need to lean too. Every day is not a good day, and it’s OK.”
Many people suppress themselves because of embarrassment and social media can make it seem like “everything is so perfect all the time,” she said.

title: Lindsay Clancy is set to stand trial for a second time, judge says
text:
PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — A Massachusetts judge on Monday scheduled Lindsay Clancy’s second trial in the killings of her three young children for late March, over the objections of prosecutors.
Clancy is charged with three counts of first-degree murder. Her first trial end in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the killings. Eleven jurors favored acquittal on the grounds of insanity, while one disagreed.
Prosecutors had sought a May trial date, citing scheduling conflicts, but Superior Court Judge William Sullivan set the retrial for March 29 in Plymouth Superior Court.
The decision to schedule Clancy’s second trial comes a week after Sullivan rejected a defense request to dismiss the charges. He ruled that a retrial would not violate Clancy’s constitutional protection against double jeopardy.
Attorneys are scheduled to return to court at 9 a.m. Dec. 30 to discuss trial logistics, security and media arrangements. A pretrial conference is set for Feb. 18.
Clancy’s lawyers had argued that the judge should have investigated or removed the lone juror who opposed acquittal before declaring a mistrial.
Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, has never disputed that she killed her three children at the family’s Duxbury home in January 2023. Her attorneys said she was suffering from severe mental illness at the time.
Prosecutors argued Clancy planned the killings and understood what she was doing.
