title: Questions swirl around FAA's new SMART AI system, though officials say no link to ground stop
text:
The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology.
But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration’s SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems.
Officials say no connection to ground stop
The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there’s no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system, and the top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday.
The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn’t caused by “the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”
But lawmakers and outside groups raised questions about the SMART system before Friday’s ground stop. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails.
“Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” the Oct. 13 letter said. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.”
SMART, however, is not — at least not yet — set up for AI to be in charge of flight control. Rather, it is making recommendations to humans who do so.
What is the SMART system?
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a “cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics — into one platform.” SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories.
The system’s AI-supported engine synthesizes the data systems and shows a “comprehensive visualization” of where planes are going, how much traffic the system can handle and where congestion or weather could cause problems, according to the announcement. The idea is for specialists to then use the platform to fix problems before they arise.
The FAA says that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system’s recommendations.
So SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers. That was three days before the ground stop.
According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested. The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals.
SMART is also supposed to help with weather-related issues faster.
Currently, the FAA blocks off portions of airspace affected by weather as “large, rectangular boxes,” according to the fact sheet, which doesn’t reflect how weather actually looks, with quick-moving thunderstorms and storm systems that are “often irregular in shape, with narrow gaps or corridors that aircraft could safely fly through.”
To help with this, SMART gives the FAA and airspace operators a “clearer picture of how weather will affect air traffic over time,” allowing air traffic controllers to plan around storms and use available airspace instead of unnecessarily shutting down large areas.
No other country has a working AI air traffic tool like the SMART system, according to Michael McCormick, a former FAA airspace manager and an associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority, has a system in testing and several manufacturers are prototyping similar tools.
Concerns around relying on AI
While government officials and ASI, the company behind SMART, have stressed that its AI system is designed to assist humans and not run flight control, its deployment has raised concerns about relying on artificial intelligence when human lives are at stake, given that even the most advanced models are prone to hallucinations — when models fabricate false information and present it as fact.
Mike O’Donnell, a former top FAA official who worked for the agency for 17 years and now does aviation safety consulting work, said the agency “has got to make sure that this is just a tool in the toolbox and not the actual machine that’s doing the work.”
The FAA, he said, “cannot afford to be wrong on this.”
“It’s good to use it with the proper guardrails and backstops to ensure that they’re not giving wrong information to controllers based on what (AI) has come up with,” O’Donnell said. “There’s got to be a way to verify and validate what it’s doing to make sure that it’s not the wrong information.”
He cautioned against putting too much trust in AI “until we know for sure that it’s proven itself time and time again. And that’s going to take a while.”
The AI system’s launch comes amid a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers around the country. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association has been raising concerns about this for more than a decade, telling Congress in 2015 that the shortage was at a crisis level. It said then that the FAA had missed its hiring targets for five years in a row. The union represents about 14,000 controllers, roughly 3,000 of them trainees. That said, experts say no AI system can replace the human air traffic controllers who spend years training for this highly demanding and stressful job.
In an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the SMART tool is designed for traffic managers who manage the entire U.S. airspace.
“The AI does the math, the AI does the computation,” Buckendorf told NPR, but it’s ultimately up to the human operator whether to take the system’s recommendation. “They make the decision, they are the decider, they are the judge.”
Story by Barbara Ortutay and Josh Funk.

title: Trump blames nationwide grounding of planes on old technology, Biden administration
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump bristled Monday at suggestions he’s been too focused on White House building projects, and that they might have distracted him during the nationwide grounding of all planes, even insisting, “You don’t see me on a scaffold.”
Speaking publicly for the first time about last week’s air traffic snarls caused by a router issue in the aging air traffic control system, Trump got defensive during a lengthy — sometimes testy — exchange with reporters as he left the White House for his trip to Asia,
He faulted old technology and Democrats for the incident that caused upheaval at the country’s airports — especially his predecessor, President Joe Biden. “I don’t take any responsibility” for Friday’s ground stop, Trump said, explaining his Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was in charge.
“What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” the president said. He later noted: “Incredibly, everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing.” Referring to his administration’s efforts to make improvements, he added, “the only responsibility should be, for 40 years they should have done this.”
Trump was silent on the chaos until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking Congress for more money to cover the cost of system improvements.
His blame-shifting and the congressional Democratic finger-pointing follow a familiar pattern of Trump seeking to say others were a fault during major crises — and underscore political divisions that could widen when Democrats take control of Congress in January, with scrutiny of his administration accelerating.
The problems with aging equipment at the Federal Aviation Administration date back decades, well before even the first Trump administration, and past efforts to modernize the system have come up short. The last major effort to overhaul air traffic control, called NextGen, started in 2003 and consumed more than $15 billion over the years.
Airline passengers suffered more woes Monday when United Airlines said it was experiencing a systemwide outage that was affecting departing flights. The airline resolved the issue about 1 1/2 hours after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers.
Trump says he spends ‘very little time’ on White House overhaul
On Monday, when pressed about his priorities, the president spent far more time defending his extensive efforts to mold the White House to his own, often gold and gilded, tastes than he did talking about his administration’s response to the ground stop.
“I spend very little time” on building projects Trump said, adding, “You don’t see me on a scaffold.”
He said the large granite helicopter landing pad he had built on the South Lawn had received “great reviews” and had replaced broken stone walkways and common areas. He also defended the sprawling ballroom being erected, which is larger than the rest of the White House, saying it “fits like a glove.”
“See this stone? Get your cameras on it,” he commanded of reporters on the South Lawn. “This stone was badly broken.”
Pressed further, he told a reporter, “You’re so pathetic,” then continued that he had “a responsibility to make sure the symbol of our country is in decent shape.”
The president suggested that the White House had previously had broken windows and columns that were “in horrible condition,” even though the extensive damage he described wasn’t visible before he ordered so many building projects.
Asked further about who was funding so much work, Trump responded: “This doesn’t cost money. This is peanuts.” The full extent of the costs of his many projects is unknown.
Trump also sought to justify the unusually personal role he’s taken in the parade of building projects at the White House, telling a reporter: “This is called talent. You don’t have talent.”
The Trump administration is seeking additional funding
Duffy, who made the decision Friday to ground the planes, has also pushed Congress for billions more dollars to upgrade a system he said had been neglected for decades.
Duffy said the problem began when a federal contractor was replacing a section of old copper wire with new fiber wire, causing the system to overload.
The Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds,” the agency said.
Duffy said Sunday that billions of dollars are needed to build new architecture for the network and said companies — including AT&T, Verizon and Lumen — are ready to deploy it as soon as the money is there.
Upgrading the nation’s air transportation system is an effort that Congress has dedicated significant sums to in recent years.
Under Biden, Congress approved a massive infrastructure bill that included $25 billion over five years for airport and air traffic control infrastructure improvements. Much of that money went to airport projects like new runways and taxiways and updated terminals.
After Trump returned to the White House in 2025, a Republican-led Congress approved $12.5 billion in 2025 to modernize the FAA’s air traffic system.
The Trump administration said the money would provide critical updates to outdated radar systems and traffic control centers, some dating back to the 1960s. Republicans used the same bill to allocate $170 billion for Trump’s immigration crackdown, for more border security and immigration enforcement.
___
Catalini reported from Morrisville, Pa.

title: An ounce of prevention
text:

title: Where Maine’s members of Congress stand ahead of high-stakes votes on energy permitting
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
One of the last major pieces of legislation Congress may vote on before Republicans lose their majorities in January is a bipartisan energy permitting measure that is exposing divides among Democrats and drawing opposition from Maine conservation groups.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a sweeping proposal from two Republicans and two Democrats that would shorten the timelines for clean energy and fossil fuel projects to receive approval. It would not clamp down on data centers, but rather seek to ensure they pay for their energy use.
Supporters, including President Donald Trump and clean energy and oil groups, have pushed the plan as a long-sought way to meet growing electricity demand and lower costs for consumers by speeding up projects that can currently face years of regulatory delays.
Opponents, including an array of national and Maine-based conservation organizations, have argued it would lock in fossil fuel and data center development, weaken environmental protections and make it harder for communities to challenge energy projects.
It is also running into opposition from Democrats who believe the party should wait until it takes control of both chambers of Congress in January. Democrats scored major victories in the Nov. 3 midterm election that saw voters largely reject GOP candidates and Trump’s policies, including an unpopular war in Iran and tariffs that have led to higher prices at the pump and in stores.
The Senate, which is poised to flip in January from Republicans having 53 seats to Democrats having 56 seats, voted 73-25 last week to advance the bill.
Sen. Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, and Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican who is on her way out of office after losing her reelection race against Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, supported advancing the measure, which has been amended numerous times. Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota is the lone Republican to so far vote against it.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said his caucus has the votes to pass the bill in that chamber before Democrats take charge with a massive majority in January.
That leaves the Senate largely dictating whether the legislation succeeds or not. Senators passed another procedural motion late Monday to advance the bill to a final vote that may come this week.
Trump threw a wrench into things by saying last week that he will not approve wind projects covered under the legislation “because wind turbines are a major loser.”
Trump’s comments led several senators, including King, to say they would reconsider their stances after voting to advance the legislation.
“The president made an unfortunate statement … about wind power that undermines my confidence in the good faith of the administration, so that will influence my vote as well,” King said last week.
Collins remains in support of the bill, spokesperson Phoebe Keller said. The outgoing Republican has pointed to Maine’s heavy reliance on heating oil in homes and has said she wants Maine to access shale gas that comes from Pennsylvania via a pipeline.
“But the permitting for that when you’re crossing state lines is just impossible,” Collins previously told reporters. “It would make a big difference on housing as well, and I think we need to simplify and expedite the process.”
The legislation would speed up timelines for permitting decisions. For example, the bill would require the lead agency in most cases to approve or kill a project within 45 days of a published environmental impact statement. Federal agencies would have to decide on authorizing projects within 90 days if they participated in the review or within 120 days if they did not. Currently, no deadline exists for making a final decision after an environmental review.
The legislation would also make new and existing data centers pay their share of existing costs and a reasonable estimate of the added costs they trigger when joining the grid. Data centers have drawn bipartisan skepticism and moratoriums in numerous Maine towns in recent months.
The bill’s four sponsors — Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island — unveiled several amendments this month to try to win over skeptics. They include provisions to no longer allow the Trump administration to settle with energy companies to stop offshore wind projects under development; to require federal agencies to consult with Native American tribes on projects affecting cultural sites; and to extend the window for making objections to agency reports on proposed projects, among other changes.
Rep. Jared Golden, a moderate Democrat who is wrapping up his time representing Maine’s 2nd District after not seeking a fifth term, supports the legislation and sponsored similar permitting reforms that passed the House last year, spokesperson Mario Moretto confirmed.
Rep. Chellie Pingree, a 1st District progressive, has not taken a public stance on the latest bill. However, she is part of the House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition, which released a statement last week saying it supports part of the reforms while having concerns about “environmental rollbacks” included in the proposal.
Environmental groups in Maine and other states said the amendments to the legislation are still not enough. The Maine groups focused on King, in particular, in a Monday news release calling on the four members of the delegation to oppose the bill.
Officials from Citizens’ Climate Lobby, one of the few climate groups backing the bill, also met with King’s office last week.
Maine Conservation Voters Legislative Director Sarah Woodbury said in a release that the legislation makes key changes to help “accelerate the deployment of more affordable clean energy, invest in grid reliability and address concerns about data centers.”
“But it also contains language that poses serious risks to our woods, waters and wildlife and threatens long-standing protections for sacred spaces, undermining tribal sovereignty,” Woodbury said.
Jeremy Sheaffer, the Maine state director of The Wilderness Society, a national nonprofit focused on protecting public lands, said a “clean energy future and conservation are well within our reach, but this bill is tipped too far in the direction of corporate special interests.”
“You can bet your winter woodpile this bill will do more to hurt than to help Maine’s environment,” Sheaffer said.
Editor’s note: This story was updated Tuesday morning with the results of Monday’s procedural vote in the Senate.

title: AAA forecasts another busy -- but not quite as busy -- Thanksgiving travel week
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FORT COLLINS, Colo. (AP) — Pricey plane tickets and expensive gasoline are expected to keep some Americans from traveling this Thanksgiving, but not enough to make much difference in airport security lines and highway traffic, AAA said Monday.
The auto club federation predicted that 81.5 million people would travel at least 50 miles (80 kilometers) from home between the Tuesday before Thanksgiving and the Monday after the holiday.
That’s about 121,000 fewer than traveled domestically over Thanksgiving last year, or a one-tenth of a percent decline, AAA said in its annual forecast. If proven accurate, the small drop would end three years of record-setting Thanksgiving travel that followed the COVID-19 pandemic, according to AAA’s calculations.
“After three years of record highs, the number of travelers is slightly lower partly because of higher travel costs this year. But travelers won’t notice much of a difference,” AAA Travel Vice President Stacey Barber said in a statement.
AAA prepared its forecast weeks before problems with U.S. air traffic control communications and radar feeds on Friday prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to impose a nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours and disrupted weekend flights.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford said they expected air traffic to normalize well before the start of the Thanksgiving travel rush.
AAA doesn’t think Friday’s unusually long ground stop will have a major impact on Thanksgiving travel unless it happens again, spokesperson Aixa Diaz said.
“Travelers are resilient, and from what AAA has seen in the past, it takes a lot to keep holiday travelers home,” Diaz wrote in an email Sunday.
As in past years, AAA expects the vast majority of holiday travelers to opt for car trips over flights. Meanwhile, it expects buses, trains and cruise ships will serve 4% more passengers than last year combined.
Flights got more expensive as airlines’ jet fuel costs increased
Last November, a government shutdown that led the FAA to order flight cuts at 40 of the busiest U.S. airports created extra stress for airline passengers with Thanksgiving week tickets.
Air travelers who didn’t cancel their plans were rewarded; Congress ended the longest shutdown in history, and the FAA lifted its order 10 days before Thanksgiving.
This year, fuel prices that surged during the U.S. war with Iran are a concern. The overall inflation that influenced this month’s midterm elections may also have made some Americans more cautious about venturing far afield for their Thanksgiving meals.
With U.S. airlines spending more on jet fuel, airfares were more than 22% higher in September than the same month a year earlier, according to the most recent government data. Carriers also raised fees for checked bags.
Visa’s economic research group said an analysis of September credit card transactions revealed that spending on plane tickets and related travel for trips starting between Nov. 1 and Jan. 15 were down from a year earlier for households of every income level except those earning more than $200,000.
Aviation analytics firm Cirium said Thanksgiving flight bookings were running 1.6% behind last year as of late October.
Gasoline could set a Thanksgiving Day price record
Compared to last year, round-trip domestic flights booked through AAA for the Thanksgiving period were 17% more expensive, averaging $800 per ticket.
AAA expects nearly 6 million people to fly from Nov. 24 through Nov. 30, about 12,000 fewer than last year. Three Florida cities — Orlando, Fort Lauderdale and Miami — are the top three domestic destinations for Thanksgiving flights, the auto club said.
Other organizations have come up with different projections based on the data they reviewed. Trade organization Airlines for America said it expected U.S. carriers to serve more passengers during the same seven-day period, though it did not specify if that includes international flights.
The group said airfares having risen much more modestly than jet fuel prices this year.
Gasoline prices have fallen over the past week, but motorists can expect to pay more than last year heading to and from Thanksgiving destinations, AAA’s forecast said. Regular gas averaged $3.82 a gallon on Sunday compared to $3.08 a year earlier, AAA said.
If prices hold, gasoline would be more expensive this Thanksgiving Day than any previous. AAA’s previous Thanksgiving Day record was $3.58 in 2022.
___
AP writers Lisa Leff in London and Rebecca Boone in Boise, Idaho, contributed to this story.

title: Mayor: Suspect in custody after explosive device found at Illinois plant, forcing thousands to evacuate
text:
PEORIA, Ill. (25News Now/Gray News) - Local police and federal authorities continue to investigate after an explosive device was found at an Illinois plant.
Officials said an explosive device was discovered Friday at the BioUrja Renewables plant, prompting the evacuation of thousands of people in Peoria and East Peoria within a 1-mile radius of the plant.
Numerous events were canceled and downtown businesses closed while the evacuation was in effect. The order was lifted Saturday after no other suspicious objects were found at the plant.
Peoria Mayor Rita Ali said in a statement that company leadership informed her a suspect was in custody in connection with the investigation.
Police said the FBI is the lead agency and will issue information or updates as they become available. The FBI said its policy prohibits it from disclosing whether a person is the subject of an investigation.
Earlier Monday, Peoria police said they were contacted by the FBI to respond to the plant to assist with “court-authorized procedures.” A statement from the FBI said the agency, along with the ATF, Illinois State Police, Peoria County Sheriff, East Peoria Police and Peoria Police are conducting law enforcement activity in Peoria County.

title: Robert Pattinson is the next James Bond, succeeding Daniel Craig
text:
(AP) - Pattinson. Robert Pattinson.
After years of debate and endless conjecture, Pattinson was unveiled as the next James Bond on Monday, becoming the seventh actor to play the iconic British spy and the first since Amazon MGM took over the beloved film franchise.
The naming of Pattinson comes during the longest hiatus in 007 history and ends years of rampant speculation about who would inherit the role from Daniel Craig. It comes five years after 2021’s “No Time to Die,” the first film in Bond’s 64-year history on the silver screen to conclude with the character’s death. But 007 will be reborn, yet again, in the 26th Bond film, directed by Denis Villeneuve.
Amazon MGM Studios announced Pattinson’s casting on social media with a brief snippet of the actor emerging from the shadows with a gun.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”
Late to the Bond chase
Pattinson only entered the Bond rumor mill recently after the revelation that he screen-tested for the role. Others reportedly in the mix included Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult.
But they were only the finalists in a Bond search that dated back to before Craig’s final 007 film.
While producers were long expected to go with a young, less-proven star, they instead opted for one of the best-known actors of his generation. Pattinson, 40, is also relatively old to begin as 007. The actor is currently in production on another iconic role in “The Batman Part II.”
Pattinson comes in already associated with several mega-franchises in “The Batman,” “Dune,” “Twilight” and “Harry Potter.” But since his breakthrough in “Twilight,” Pattinson has worked largely in more independent, auteur-driven films such as “Good Time” with the Safdie brothers, Robert Eggers’ “The Lighthouse” and Bong Joon Ho’s “Mickey 17.”
Earlier this year, he drew rave reviews for his villainous performance in Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” and for his portrayal of “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen in the film “Primetime.” He co-stars in Villeneuve’s upcoming “Dune: Part III” as a shape-shifting assassin.
Villeneuve said it was a tough choice, but the right one.
“We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin,” the director said in a statement.
Amazon bets big on Pattinson
The casting comes at a pivotal juncture for the franchise. In 2022, Bond’s longtime studio, MGM, was bought by Amazon for $8.5 billion. After haggling over next steps for 007, producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson relinquished creative control of Bond in 2025. The still-untitled Bond 26 is the first Bond movie since 1962’s inaugural “Dr. No” in which a Broccoli didn’t handpick the super spy.
“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond as we proudly introduce Robert Pattinson as the next 007,” said Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios.
Casting a new Bond fell instead to producers Amy Pascal — the former Sony Pictures chief and “Spider-Man” producer — and David Heyman, shepherd of “Harry Potter” and “Paddington.” Casting director Nina Gold oversaw the screen tests.
Pattinson’s first 007 film, untitled but widely referred to as “Bond 26,” was penned by Steven Knight (“Peaky Blinders,” “Locke”). No production start date has been announced, though shooting is expected to begin next year.
According to a report by Puck, Pattinson is signed to a three-movie deal as Bond. Spokespeople for Amazon MGM declined to comment on the terms of Pattinson’s contract.
A long hiatus nears an end
Before Craig even left the role, rumors and odds-making persisted nearly round-the-clock on who would follow in the footsteps of Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig. Idris Elba, for one, has spent half his career deflecting 007 conjecture.
The Bond machine has historically never slowed down. But the 26th installment will follow the longest absence ever for Bond. Given that “No Time to Die” completed principal photography in 2019 (its release was delayed due to the coronavirus pandemic), the lull is even longer.
Some fans are skeptical about the new Amazon-controlled chapter for Bond. Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, has vowed to uphold the franchise’s legacy and usher in “the next phase in the legendary 007 for audiences around the world.”
At stake is one of the most lucrative film series in Hollywood, based on Ian Fleming’s series of novels. The Bond movies have grossed more than $7 billion worldwide in ticket sales. “No Time to Die” collected $774 million in 2021. The movies also spin out endless other revenue streams, from streaming deals and video games to Aston Martins.
Although some Bond actors came to view the role as a yoke around their necks, it turned Craig into a household name. The British actor wasn’t widely known before his casting and, at the time, was derided as the first “blond Bond.”
But while Craig often struggled with the restrictions of the role, he also helped elevate the productions while remaining active outside of Bond enough to avoid becoming totally tethered to it.

title: How this shopping night boosts Presque Isle’s small businesses
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Presque Isle merchants are gearing up for their biggest holiday shopping day of the year — and it isn’t Black Friday.
Local businesses will host Main Street Mania this week on Nov. 20, the Friday before Thanksgiving.
It’s the 24th year for what has become a traditional kickoff to the holiday season. The event encourages people to shop local, which boosts small businesses’ bottom lines, but also offers a nostalgic feel that typically brings people out in droves to buy gifts, dine out and socialize.
The shared excitement is a benefit all around, said Cathy Beaulieu, owner of Wilder’s Jewelry Store, a legacy business that’s been part of Main Street for 94 years.
“It’s easy now with our phones, online shopping and working from home to lose our sense of place,” Beaulieu said. “Main Street Mania is a very social event and a time when people can share what’s happened since last year.”
As one of the merchants who originally started Main Street Mania, Beaulieu has seen trends and economic factors rise and fall, including Black Friday itself.
It was big at large chain stores. Many locals remember Walmart lines snaking around the parking lot waiting for the doors to open at midnight. But there wasn’t a lot downtown 20-some years ago, Beaulieu said. So small business owners united to draw traffic before the Black Friday furor hit.
As earlier shop-local events and online buying have grown in popularity, the historically long lines and packed stores on the day after Thanksgiving have diminished, giving way to a calmer atmosphere and a longer shopping season for many Mainers.
Caribou promotes small businesses with its own local holiday market, featuring vendors in a village-style layout. Farther south, Bangor has started Plaid Friday, its own “more laid-back” alternative, and Portland last year noted less Black Friday traffic among shoppers.
Each year brings its challenges, such as the pandemic and recent tariffs, Beaulieu said. And in this year, when many people struggle with high costs, merchants are mindful. Store owners are working to try to keep their own costs down to keep prices affordable.
But that’s the way County people have done business for generations, Beaulieu said.
“People here are not Wall Street people. They’re everyday people with normal jobs,” she said. “As a business, you keep things as reasonable as possible so you can survive and they can afford to buy.”
Main Street Mania is easily the biggest retail day of the year for outdoor sports business Bike Board and Ski, co-owners Mike Chasse and Andrew Bouchard said. Not only does it drive revenue, but it turns the store into a social happening.
“It’s one of our busiest days of the year for sales,” Bouchard said. “And we like it because it brings the community out. The store ends up being a gathering place, with people chatting with people they haven’t seen in a while.”
As far as what may be trending this year for gifts, since there hasn’t — so far — been any early snow other than a few flurries, Chasse predicted outdoor clothing and accessories would be on customers’ lists.
Mania will run from 6 to 10 p.m. Other participating businesses will include Big Cheese Pizza, Country Collectibles, Designer Refind, Governor’s Restaurant, Home Ec. Market, Hub Coffee, Ignite PI, KMH Music, Neighborhood Books, Merchants on the Corner and Morningstar Art and Framing.
Main Street Mania works because merchants unite, said Jordyn Kinney Morton, owner of Home Ec. Market, which offers products for sustainable living. Bringing everyone together in a shared campaign gives each shop a spotlight and also reminds residents of the range of businesses Presque Isle has.
“Our downtown businesses make a bigger impact when we work together,” Morton said. “Thanks to the Downtown Revitalization Committee and our donors this year, more local businesses are able to take part.”
Past years saw participating businesses chip in to cover advertising and promotion, but this year a donation from the Presque Isle Downtown Revitalization Committee paid those costs, Morton said.
Each store will offer its own special promotions, which will appear on event flyers around town and on the Main Street Mania Facebook event and website, mainstreetmania.org.
Beaulieu looks forward to seeing the downtown filled. Mania has become a constant for the area, and it happens no matter the weather, just like the mail, she said. Even more than shopping, it gives people a reason to get out and lifts spirits with nostalgia.
“It’s an extremely old-fashioned feeling to have all those customers downtown,” Beaulieu said. “It’s as if it were a general store or coffee shop. We don’t have that anymore, and I feel people miss that.”

title: Father accused of killing 3-month-old son by aggressively rocking bouncer to get him to stop crying
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) - A Hawaii man remains in custody after being charged with manslaughter in the death of his 3-month-old son.
Joshua Kaleolani Agbayani Soto Paiva, 20, appeared in court Thursday. His bail was set at $1 million, and he is expected back in court Monday.
The investigation into the death of Paiva’s 3-month-old son, John-Charles Saiki-Paiva, is ongoing.
Foul play suspected
Puna patrol officers responded to a home in the Hawaiian Paradise Park subdivision at 11:50 a.m. Oct. 25 for a report of an unresponsive male infant.
Hawai‘i Fire Department paramedics took the infant, identified by authorities as John-Charles Saiki-Paiva, to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 1:06 p.m.
The preliminary results of an autopsy indicated John-Charles died from head injuries, and foul play was suspected.
Court documents detail allegations
Court documents allege Paiva told police he was playing “Overwatch,” an online multiplayer video game, and his son wouldn’t stop crying.
He said as he prepared a bottle for John-Charles, he heard the baby “coughing and gagging with milk coming out” and “then went completely quiet,” the documents said.
After police informed Paiva of the baby’s injuries, he admitted he had been lying, according to the documents. Paiva then said that he began “aggressively rocking” the baby bouncer with enough force that John-Charles’ head and body flailed and hit the bouncer’s frame for about 15 minutes, documents said.
According to police, Paiva said he grabbed the baby’s right leg, yanked him off the bouncer and placed him on an ottoman, where he applied his own body weight — about 220 pounds — until the baby stopped crying.
“A case like this is really difficult with especially our investigators as well, everybody involved, the personnel that responded to the scene, the medical staff that worked on the infant,” said Lt. Derek Morimoto with the Hawai‘i Police Department. “So, a lot of people are affected by a case like this.”

title: Free Beer takes home this year’s Battle of the Bands crown
text:
On Friday, Nov. 13, the University of Maine’s Student Government (UMSG) organized and hosted this year’s Battle of the Bands. The face-off was held in the Collins Center for the Arts and judged by fans via an online vote. The local bands that competed were Free Beer, Free Parking, Fishscale, Gunshot Glitter and Somerset Hall.
Somerset Hall started off the evening with its covers of rock and grunge classics. The ensemble is made up of students who established the band in the namesake hall. Members include lead guitarist Ben Redfield, rhythm guitarist and backup vocalist Nate Lee, drummer Evan Cummings, bassist Declan Nicholas and their talented lead vocalist, Harlow Keener. They did a cover of “Zombie” by The Cranberries that was especially exceptional and set a good tone for the rest of the event.
Following them was the jazz-funk fusion band, Free Parking. The band is made up of Zach Sanderson on keys, Wayne Shaw playing guitar, drummer Owen Fitts, Isaac Atkinson on bass and Autumn Carmona with vocals. Free Parking entered the performance with style and control, slowly introducing each member to the song and stage. They played funky covers and originals. Atkinson’s original composition stood out in particular for its complexity and flow.
In the middle performance slot was Gunshot Glitter, and they certainly brought the energy. They performed originals and covers, including a rather unique cover of Gracie Abrams’ “I Love You, I’m Sorry,” although the band professed they had a disdain for her music. Gunshot Glitter also had a very interactive relationship with the crowd, talking in between songs. They brought an early 2000s pop-punk sound to the battle that no other band quite had. Some of the members include lead singer and guitarist Harry Burns, guitarist Thomas Runco and bassist Gabriel Chambers.
Free Beer was the penultimate performance and the band that took home the victory. Their performance of “Creep” by Radiohead got the crowd involved more than any song, leading to flashlights and hands swaying back and forth to the iconic lyrics. Other notable covers were “Mississippi Queen” and “Even Flow” by Mountain and Pearl Jam. Wyatt Horning on vocals, Otto Reid playing bass, guitarists Josh Sullivan and Jake Fogg and James Corgan on drums make up this five-pack.
Ending the night was Fishscale. The band was welcomed to the stage with quite the reception and was one of the most popular of the night. They performed multiple covers and a new original titled “The One.” Their set list was the shortest of any of the bands performing, but they left quite an impression in the little time they had. Fishscale had a softer sound than most of their competition, incredible vocals and an accordion that generated quite the uproar. Members include lead singer and guitarist Kate Barry, drummer Charlie Howe, Lily Decataldo on bass, guitarists Lara Luczak and Andrew Atwater and Riley St. Pierre playing the keyboard and accordion.
After the bands were done performing, The Maine Steiners and UMaine Renaissance each came out and performed a song, then came together for the final musical performance of the night. The final standings were Free Beer in first, Fishscale in second and Gunshot Glitter in third.

title: Defying court order, Energy Department again forces Michigan coal plant to stay open past retirement
text:
Defying court order, Energy Department again forces Michigan coal plant to stay open past retirement
The Energy Department has again extended an order forcing an aging Michigan coal-fired power plant to stay open past its scheduled retirement date, defying a court order that set aside the agency's previous actions as unlawful.
Video above: Nearly half of US children live in counties with failing air quality, report says
Energy Secretary Chris Wright issued an emergency order late Friday extending the continued operation of the 64-year-old J.H. Campbell Generating Plant near Grand Rapids, saying the plant is needed to prevent blackouts and preserve customers' access to reliable, secure electricity.
The Energy Department said it disagrees with the September decision by a three-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit and has petitioned for a rehearing in front of the entire court.
The emergency order is among a series of actions by President Donald Trump and his administration to boost the struggling U.S. coal industry, including a plan announced in June to spend nearly $700 million to support coal-fired power plants and coal exports.
The Environmental Protection Agency, meanwhile, has repealed rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. The agency under Administrator Lee Zeldin also is moving to prevent future administrations from regulating climate pollution from power plants.
Environmental groups slammed the latest emergency order on coal — the seventh such declaration for the Campbell plant since May 2025 — and said there is no evidence that the Michigan plant has ever been needed to avoid a grid emergency or has ever prevented power outages. The extension order costs families in the Midwest more than $600,000 per day to keep the old, polluting plant online, they said.
“At a time when prices are soaring and Americans are struggling to make ends meet, the Trump administration’s decision to issue yet another illegal and expensive extension is punishing,” said the Sierra Club's Jessi Eidbo.
According to a Burning Money tracker compiled by the group, the administration’s orders extending the lives of fossil fuel plants in six states have cost ratepayers more than $600 million, with over half of that total stemming from the Campbell plant in Michigan.
“Instead of saving families’ money and letting the plant retire as planned, the Trump administration keeps putting its thumb on the scale for costly coal," said Ted Kelly, director of U.S. clean energy at Environmental Defense Fund, another environmental group.
Wright and other officials have said the Campbell plant and others are needed to ensure reliable electricity, and he used emergency powers to keep them operating. Environmental groups and multiple states — including Michigan, Illinois and Minnesota — went to court to try to overturn orders keeping the plants online.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit sided with the states and the groups, saying there was no real emergency under the law. A decision is pending on whether the full Appeals Court will hear the case, which could end up at the Supreme Court.

title: We Do Not Care Club founder Melani Sanders opens up about sharing vulnerable moment
text:
(Aging Untold) — Digital creator Melani Sanders, founder of the “We Do Not Care Club,” is known for her humorous videos, but a more vulnerable moment she shared has resonated with many people. She opened up about what led to her pressing record and sharing it.
“I was overwhelmed with emotion,” Sanders said.
What led to the post
The post included the lines “Watching my mother get older. Watching my kids leave. Watching my body start to change on me. Nobody prepared me for this.”
Sanders said she has three sons: one in law school, one in undergrad and one at home. Her mother is aging and she has an elderly dog.
“I said, ‘This is a lot. This is a lot,’ and all of it just hit me at one time,” Sanders said.
She began thinking about having one son left at home and about the empty nest, she said.
“My body is changing. You know, I don’t know who I am from day to day. It just all hit me at one time, and I just said, you know what? Press record,” Sanders said.
Why she shared it
Sanders said she wants people to know her videos are funny and include “some real talk,” but that “there’s another side.”
“Many women are suffering, and we’re suffering silently,” she said.
Community and social media
Asked how the “We Do Not Care Club” community has made a difference, Sanders said, “Sometimes I need to lean too. Every day is not a good day, and it’s OK.”
Many people suppress themselves because of embarrassment and social media can make it seem like “everything is so perfect all the time,” she said.
“You got to walk a certain way, talk a certain way, look a certain way,” Sanders said. “We simply should not care so much about those things and say how you feel.”

title: Doctors said he’d never walk again. Then, he finished a marathon
text:
(Aging Untold) — A Kansas man who doctors said would never walk again was determined to show he could. Eleven years later, he finished his first marathon with support from his family.
James McGinnis, 29, completed the race in 8 hours, 10 minutes, with his father and best friend beside him. Resistance bands kept him upright during the course.
Injury during televised football game
Eleven years ago, McGinnis, then a senior at Olathe East, collapsed on the field after a hit during a televised high school football game against Olathe South.
His father, Patrick McGinnis, said he knew the injury was serious.
“When they turn him over on his back, though, I knew then it was serious,” Patrick McGinnis said.
James McGinnis suffered a traumatic brain bleed. Doctors gave him less than a 7% chance to survive. He spent weeks in the ICU.
Patrick McGinnis said he began researching brain injury recovery and the next steps.
On day five, James McGinnis signed “I love you,” which gave his parents a glimpse of hope.
Doctors called it a reflex, Patrick McGinnis said
“And I was like, no, I don’t think so. I think it’s purposeful,” he said.
From walking to running
Patrick McGinnis said doctors initially told the family that his son’s recovery would not be a sprint — “it’s a marathon” — and that James would never walk again.
It took James McGinnis nine months to walk on his own and nine years to run.
He started with a mile, then ran a 5K and a 10K. He completed a half marathon in 2024, then set his sights on a marathon.
Patrick McGinnis now runs three times a week with his son.
“I do it because every time we go out, James gets better,” he said.
Quotes at every mile
Along the marathon course, Patrick McGinnis recorded what the family calls “James-isms,” which are his son’s core beliefs. He recorded one at every mile.
The James-ism at mile 10 was: “Tell me I can’t, and I will show you I can.”
After the race, James McGinnis said doctors told him and his family the journey would be a marathon.
“Well, I did my marathon,” he said.
Rehabilitation doctor responds
Dr. Brad Steinle, James McGinnis’ rehabilitation doctor, said McGinnis’ prognosis was grim and his recovery has been remarkable. Steinle said McGinnis’ strength has made him a better physician.
“I have hundreds of patients that, while I think that we help them, they help us,” Steinle said. “I haven’t had anybody quite like James.”
Next goals
James McGinnis’ next goals are running the Boston Marathon and possibly competing in the 2028 Paralympics

title: Pakistan vows US-Iran diplomacy, urges Afghan action during ECO meeting
text:
Pakistan vows US-Iran diplomacy, urges Afghan action on terrorism at regional economic bloc meeting
Pakistan Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said his country would proceed with diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between the United States and Iran with the support of other regional countries gathered Monday at a meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organization.
The meeting of the 10-member ECO in Pakistan’s capital Islamabad was attended by foreign ministers and senior diplomats from several Asian countries, including Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The meeting is expected to focus on expanding regional cooperation, particularly in trade and commerce, through stronger transportation and trade links between members including Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan, Turkey and several former Soviet republics.
Related video: Falling gas prices aren’t proof gas companies inflated prices to hurt Trump
Dar also said improved ties with neighboring Afghanistan depended on the Afghan Taliban government’s actions to stop terrorism. There was no diplomat from Afghanistan at the meeting on Monday.
Tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan have escalated this year during repeated border clashes and Pakistani airstrikes, deepening a longstanding dispute over militant activity.
Pakistan says regional stability key to economic development
Pakistan hosted the first round of direct talks in April between the U.S. and Iran. The two sides signed an interim deal in June to end the conflict while accusing each other of prolonging the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz.
At the ECO meeting Monday, Dar said peace and stability were essential for economic development and that Pakistan remained “deeply concerned about conflict and instability” in the region.
“Their consequences extend beyond national boundaries, disrupting trade routes, energy supplies, investment, and the economic projects of our peoples,” he said. “Peace and development reinforce each other.”
Araghchi urged ECO members to strengthen cooperation and turn shared commitments into concrete action, adding that Iran had consistently upheld international law and the peaceful settlement of disputes, Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency reported.
“Over the past two years, Iran has remained committed to diplomatic engagement and peaceful solutions,” he said.
Araghchi accused the U.S. of pursuing “aggression, threats, targeted assassinations, economic coercion, and blockades,” which he described as violations of international law and the U.N. Charter. He blamed the U.S. and Israel for insecurity in the Persian Gulf and developments surrounding the Strait of Hormuz.
“This reality cannot be misrepresented,” Araghchi said.
Pakistan has consistently advocated for “the peaceful resolution of disputes through dialogue and diplomacy in accordance with international law and the United Nations Charter,” Dar said, adding that Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir remained closely engaged with regional countries and international partners to facilitate peaceful outcomes.
“Pakistan will continue these diplomatic efforts in support of dialogue, de-escalation and lasting regional stability,” Dar said.
Pakistan has repeatedly called for reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The closure of the strategic waterway has caused a sharp increase in oil prices and impacted Pakistan's ailing economy.
Pakistan seeks ‘meaningful progress’ with Afghanistan
Pakistan wants its neighbor Afghanistan to be peaceful, prosperous and stable, fully integrated into the ECO framework and at peace with itself and neighboring countries, Dar said.
“Such an outcome would serve not only the Afghan people, but also the wider region, opening important avenues for trade, transit and economic cooperation,” he said. “At the same time, meaningful progress requires the Afghan authorities to address the legitimate security concerns of the neighboring countries, particularly the threat of terrorism.”
Pakistan frequently accuses Afghanistan’s Taliban government of sheltering the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, as well as the outlawed Baloch Liberation Army, or BLA, and al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent, an affiliate of the global extremist network.
The TTP is separate but closely allied with Afghanistan’s Taliban and has been emboldened since the Taliban returned to power in 2021. Pakistan says militant violence has surged because of the Afghan government's support of TTP and other Pakistani militants, a charge Kabul denies.

title: Injured Australian lawmaker leaves hospital after alleged SUV attack
text:
Injured Australian lawmaker Helen Haines leaves hospital after alleged SUV attack
An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack thanked well-wishers around the world Monday and revealed she had been discharged from a hospital where she spent the past month.
In her first public statement since being struck by a SUV on Oct. 19, Helen Haines said she was “very pleased to confirm” she had left Melbourne’s The Alfred hospital.
Witnesses said she was repeatedly rammed by the vehicle outside her electorate office.
Related video: Officials give update two days after lawmaker struck by SUV
The 65-year-old independent lawmaker said she would remain in Melbourne for the “rehabilitation stage” of her recovery. Her staff would not disclose where her rehabilitation would take place for privacy reasons.
Haines describes hospital discharge as ‘positive’
“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage,” Haines said.
“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across (my electorate) Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing,” she added.
Haines was in critical condition hours after she was struck when she was flown to Melbourne by helicopter from her hometown of Wangaratta, 236 kilometers (147 miles) to the northeast.
Surgeons amputated both her legs within a few days.
The hospital listed her as critical until Oct. 24 when her condition was downgraded to serious but stable. She had been listed as stable since Nov. 6.
Haines' family asked well-wishers to make donations to the international charity Save the Children instead of sending flowers. The appeal has raised more than 1.4 million Australian dollars ($950,000), Save the Children Australia said Monday.
Lawmaker says she is overwhelmed by generosity
Haines was “overwhelmed by the generosity of Australians” through their donations and looked forward to working with Save the Children to use the money to “improve the lives of children,” she said.
Her shocking injuries renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers. However, public incitement against officials is growing.
Security at several lawmakers’ electorate offices has been enhanced in response to the alleged attack.
Prime minister remains in contact
Within hours of Haines being struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser Troop Carrier, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told a news conference her catastrophic injuries were not an accident.
“All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery,” Albanese said in a statement Monday in response to her hospital discharge.
“I have been in regular contact with Helen and her extraordinary family. We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation,” Albanese added.
Police have yet to disclose a motive for the alleged attack. Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old man who lived in the Wangaratta area, has been charged with offenses including intentionally causing serious injury.
Nugent has been in custody since bystanders dragged him from his SUV and rendered first-aid to Haines at the scene.
His father, Rod Nugent, released a statement a day after Haines was hospitalized describing the lawmaker as a “friend for more than 20 years” and the circumstances of her injuries “unfathomable.”

title: Trump appeals to state and federal courts to erase hush money conviction
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A federal appeals court is weighing whether it can — or should — intervene in President Donald Trump’s hush money case now that a New York State appellate court has heard arguments in his quest to erase the historic conviction.
A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday spent more than an hour questioning Trump’s lawyer and a state prosecutor about the president’s latest bid to shift the case from state court to federal court, where he could seek to have it dismissed on immunity grounds. There was no immediate decision.
The sides were in court for the second time in 11 days as Trump pursues a two-pronged legal strategy in an attempt to get the May 2024 verdict thrown out. Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film performer Stormy Daniels.
Along with his federal court fight, the Republican president is also waging a traditional appeal through New York’s state court system, which included arguments before the mid-level Appellate Division on Nov. 5. That court has yet to rule.
Regardless of the outcome, Trump will forever be associated with the case, which went to trial as he was campaigning for his return to the White House. Trump denies wrongdoing and was given no punishment. Now, with little over two years left in his presidency, he is steadfast in trying to rid himself of the dubious distinction of being the first U.S. president convicted of a crime.
Trump’s lawyer says case could go to the Supreme Court
Trump’s lawyer, Robert Giuffra Jr., urged the 2nd Circuit judges on Monday to issue an order as soon as possible — even before writing their full decision — to take control of the case and stop the Appellate Division’s deliberations.
Without federal court intervention, Trump “will likely have to wait years” for state appellate courts to rule before he can take the matter to the U.S. Supreme Court, Giuffra said in a letter previewing his argument.
But Judge John M. Walker Jr., who was appointed to the appeals court by his cousin, President George H.W. Bush, and Chief Judge Raymond J. Lohier Jr., who was appointed by President Barack Obama, weren’t so sure.
“How does that work?” Walker asked. “I mean, assuming we were to agree with you, there’s been an argument in the Appellate Division. Briefs have been filed in the Appellate Division. Will those briefs be refiled by everybody here?”
Federal law doesn’t spell out precisely how such a move would play out.
Giuffra suggested the case would first go to a federal district court judge, who would adopt the state court verdict, before going to the 2nd Circuit for arguments and a decision on dismissal on presidential immunity grounds. The briefs, he said, would remain the same — albeit with different covers.
“You’re asking us to embrace an entire procedural mechanism that I don’t see anywhere authorized by Congress,” Lohier said.
“We think it is authorized,” Giuffra said, calling a provision of the law that allows such post-verdict transfer petitions “a safety valve that’s intended to protect against exactly the gamesmanship that’s gone on here.”
A federal judge declined Trump’s transfer bid 3 times
Trump asked the 2nd Circuit to step in after a federal judge in August ruled against the president for a third time. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein, who died last month at 92, wrote in his decision that “paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity.”
Trump first sought to move the case to federal court weeks after he was indicted in March 2023. He tried again after his conviction and the Supreme Court’s July 2024 ruling that presidents and ex-presidents can’t be prosecuted for official acts and prosecutors can’t use official acts as evidence that unofficial actions were illegal.
Giuffra argued to both the state and federal appellate panels that prosecutors used the type of official acts evidence that was later barred by the Supreme Court’s immunity ruling, including testimony about his Oval Office conversations, workflow and social media posts.
Giuffra also took issue with the prosecution’s description of the hush money payment as an illegal campaign contribution under the Federal Election Campaign Act, arguing that such allegations belong in federal court, not state court.
After Trump appealed Hellerstein’s second denial, the 2nd Circuit ordered the judge to reconsider, finding that he had failed to weigh “important issues relevant” to the president’s request to move the case.
That panel, which also included Lohier, said it expressed no view on how he should rule but instructed Hellerstein to closely review evidence that Trump claimed was related to official acts and whether Trump could argue those actions were taken as part of his White House duties.
Steven Wu, chief of the appeals division at the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office, urged the 2nd Circuit panel to uphold Hellerstein’s ruling and leave the case in state court. Even if Trump were to prevail, he argued, the state appeals court would still be free to rule.

title: Zoo monitoring Fiona the hippo after she ingested object ‘tossed’ by visitor
text:
CINCINNATI (WXIX/Gray News) — Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s hippopotamus, is being closely monitored after she ingested a knit cap that a visitor “accidentally tossed” into her habitat.
How the hat entered the habitat
According to a zoo spokesperson, the hat was tossed into the air in front of Fiona’s habitat at Hippo Cove and got caught by a ceiling fan. The fan then “catapulted” the hat into the 1-foot opening above the viewing windows.
“We probably couldn’t make that happen again if we tried. It was clearly an accident,” the spokesperson said.
Fiona’s care
The zoo’s veterinary team and hippo care staff are watching Fiona around the clock to help her pass the hat safely.
“Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self,” the zoo wrote in a Facebook post.
Until then, Fiona will not make an appearance at the Hippo Cove habitat.
Zoo’s request to visitors
“Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately,” the zoo said.
Officials said they will keep people updated on Fiona’s health.

title: Doctors are raising concerns about US babies born with measles
text:
For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles.
Congenital measles happens when a pregnant woman passes the virus to her fetus in the womb. It can lead to serious complications or even be deadly for newborns.
From the start of 2025 through the end of this September, 13 congenital measles cases were reported to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention during large measles outbreaks, according to preliminary figures published in a medical journal on Monday.
“This is a brand new phenomenon,” said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy.
The condition’s emergence is driven by declining vaccination rates, which have fueled the virus’s spread so much that the Pan American Health Organization is expected to officially announce Tuesday that the U.S. has lost the measles-free status it’s had since 2000. In the past two years, according to the CDC, there have been more than 7,500 measles cases.
“We’re now seeing levels of measles that we haven’t seen in 30 years,” said Dr. Adam Ratner, a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ infectious diseases committee. “When you have measles under control,” congenital measles doesn’t happen.
The preliminary case figures were released in a public health alert published by NEJM Evidence in partnership with the center Osterholm directs. The alert also said there were 112 cases of confirmed measles during pregnancy — almost all among women who didn’t get vaccinated against measles beforehand or whose vaccination status was unknown. The alert said getting vaccinated before pregnancy and having high vaccination rates in the community “are important to prevent measles and related complications.” CDC scientists authored the alert.
Guidance on congenital measles from the pediatrics academy is already reaching doctors. And Pennsylvania’s health department published an advisory last month for healthcare providers, schools, childcare centers and others in the state, which currently has the largest measles outbreak in the nation.
A new reality allows congenital measles to emerge
People gain immunity to measles by getting the disease or the vaccine. Before the shots existed, lots of people were infected by the extremely contagious virus in childhood. Later, high vaccination rates protected everyone. But a new and historic reality — shaped both by the success of the vaccine and recent skepticism about it — has triggered congenital measles.
“What’s happening is we have so many women of childbearing age who were not vaccinated in the last 25 years, nor have they ever had exposure to measles because for the last 25 years we have beaten it back,” Osterholm said. “Now, this group is highly susceptible to measles.”
Doctors say the best way to prevent the disease is for women to get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, before pregnancy. This protects the fetus too because antibodies pass from mother to baby through the placenta. Protection can last a few months after birth.
MMR can’t be given during pregnancy. Unvaccinated women who have never had measles and are exposed while pregnant can get a solution containing antibodies within six days to reduce the risk of infection and complications.
Congenital measles can seriously harm babies
If a woman gets measles toward the end of pregnancy, there’s a good chance she will pass it along. An estimated 25% to 30% of babies born to someone who gets measles shortly before delivery may become infected, the pediatrics group says.
Babies are considered to have congenital measles if they were exposed in the uterus and doctors find evidence of measles very soon after birth. Common symptoms include fever, jaundice and a measles rash. Severe complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and a rare condition known as SSPE, a brain disorder that generally develops many years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal.
Ratner, who wrote a book about measles, said there are indications that kids with congenital measles are at higher risk for SSPE and may develop it sooner after having measles than other children. “That’s something that sadly we’re learning more about,” he said.
Doctors worry things may get worse if vaccination rates keep dropping. Outbreaks are considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate, but rates in many communities have dipped below that threshold. Nationally, the CDC said, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received required MMR shots.
This puts many vulnerable people at risk, including infants too young to be vaccinated. The first MMR dose is routinely given at 12 to 15 months old, and the earliest babies can get the shots is 6 months in outbreak areas.
“We need to get back to the point where everybody who can get vaccinated is getting vaccinated, and that’s gonna take some doing,” Ratner said. “It’s going to be a lot of work on the part of pediatricians and public health institutions and lots of others. But it’s an important thing for us to do.”
___
AP Medical Writer Mike Stobbe contributed from New York.

title: Scrutiny of FAA intensifies after communications meltdown leads to nationwide grounding
text:
The nationwide grounding of flights last week will only intensify scrutiny of the Federal Aviation Administration, which has been under a spotlight since a midair collision last year that killed dozens.
The agency has been plagued for decades by underfunding, outdated technology and staffing shortages. Yet isolated technical problems went largely unnoticed by the flying public, even as experts saw them as signs of serious trouble brewing.
The FAA says it is trying to make long-overdue upgrades by the end of President Donald Trump’s second term with $12.5 billion Congress approved last year. But experts warn that rushing the process could make things worse.
“What we’re seeing has been decades in the making,” said Mike McCormick, who used to oversee air traffic control at the agency before becoming a professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University.
Improving aviation safety has been a focus of the Trump administration since last year’s midair collision outside the nation’s capital killed 67 people. A prolonged government shutdown last year highlighted the chronic shortage of controllers, while communications disruptions that affected Newark Liberty International Airport last spring, and again in September, also raised concerns.
But overhauling the air traffic control system without causing problems is not easy. The FAA has been struggling to do that for decades, said Tom Lintner, who worked as an air traffic controller and eventually became a top official at the agency. Friday was the second time in less than four years that a technical issue grounded planes nationwide.
“Go back and look at the history of the past 40 years. The track record does not make you encouraged that the modernization will succeed,” said Lintner, who is now an aviation safety consultant.
Long overdue overhaul is underway
Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to modernize much of the key infrastructure that more than 45,000 flights a day rely on to reach their destinations safely. The funds were earmarked for replacing outdated technologies such as copper wires, floppy discs and radars built in the 1980s, but much of that money will also go toward runway upgrades and other construction projects.
Still, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has said that’s not nearly enough money to complete the work. Duffy had already been asking for $30 billion more. But on Friday evening, when the FAA lifted the ground stop after more than four hours, Duffy increased that request to $50 billion.
That request was met with skepticism by Democrats on the House Appropriations Committee. On Sunday, they asked why they should approve more money when the FAA hasn’t spent what the agency received last year. Duffy says the money is committed to various projects, but he can’t spend money for new radars and other gear until they get built, perhaps sometime next year.
Aviation safety experts wonder whether the rush to complete the modernization projects by the end of Trump’s term contributed to Friday’s problems.
Duffy said the closure of U.S. airspace was needed after a new router installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, resulted in a cascade of intermittent communications and radar signals at 17 of the 22 regional air traffic control centers. These centers direct planes cruising at high altitudes. The Government Accountability Office warned in September that was a distinct possibility if the work moved too fast.
Duffy and Trump are quick to blame the Biden administration, but the air traffic control problems date back to well before the first Trump administration. Some members of Congress question whether the current leadership at the FAA can truly deliver better results.
Rick Castaldo, who spent decades at FAA as an electrical engineer, said he doubts the agency will be able to complete the overhaul because many of the same people who failed to complete past projects are advising Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. With Democrats taking control of Congress in January, politics could make it even more difficult, he said.
“They’re going to start strangling the money,” said Castaldo, who worries that many projects will be “left half done.”
Problems happen when maintenance and repairs get delayed
In September, the primary and backup communications lines went down at a key FAA facility in Philadelphia. Similar communications outages also disrupted flights in Minneapolis and Dallas over the past year.
The last time flights were grounded nationwide was in January 2023. That episode was caused by a contractor working on a different FAA system that distributes the Notices to Airmen, or NOTAMs, that pilots consult before taking to the air to learn about any potential hazards along their routes. That upgrade had also been deferred for years beforehand.
But sometimes the problems are more mundane such as an air-conditioning failure that unexpectedly forces a key air traffic control facility to close while the decades-old building is repaired.
The FAA relies heavily on contractors to help its limited staff of technicians. But the head of the technicians’ union told Congress in 2024 that the agency’s own technicians could do more of the upgrades if enough of them were hired and given a chance. The union said Saturday it wasn’t consulted about the work that caused all the problems on Friday; Duffy said he didn’t bother because the FAA doesn’t even own the network.
A private company called L3Harris owns and maintains the system under contract with the government. Their technicians were the ones replacing old copper wires in Arkansas when the system went haywire.
A new router they installed malfunctioned and in short order overwhelmed a nationwide network of signals vital to air traffic controllers. That prompted the ground stop because the system was unreliable.
Experts work to determine exactly what went wrong
On Saturday, Duffy said he wasn’t sure whether the crew doing the work made mistakes or if the routers themselves were faulty. The investigation into what happened is just beginning.
The FAA could have scheduled this work in the middle of the night when few planes are in the air, but officials believed there was a low chance of problems because the work was being done in a remote location. After all, hundreds — perhaps thousands — of miles of copper wire have been replaced in the past couple years without any problems, said aviation safety expert John Cox.
“If they followed the same procedure using similar equipment, there’s no reason to believe this was going to occur,” said Cox, who leads the Safety Operating Systems consulting firm.
But former FAA executive Mike O’Donnell said the agency shouldn’t be deflecting blame. It has to ensure the safety of the system no matter who performs the repairs and upgrades.
“Ultimately the FAA is responsible — doesn’t matter whether you hire a contractor or it’s an FAA employee that did it,” said O’Donnell, who oversaw airport safety programs and accident investigations for much of his 17 years at FAA. “They need to take responsibility for it.”

title: Doctors said he’d never walk again. Then, he finished a marathon
text:
(Aging Untold) — A Kansas man who doctors said would never walk again was determined to show he could. Eleven years later, he finished his first marathon with support from his family.
James McGinnis, 29, completed the race in 8 hours, 10 minutes, with his father and best friend beside him. Resistance bands kept him upright during the course.
Injury during televised football game
Eleven years ago, McGinnis, then a senior at Olathe East, collapsed on the field after a hit during a televised high school football game against Olathe South.
His father, Patrick McGinnis, said he knew the injury was serious.
“When they turn him over on his back, though, I knew then it was serious,” Patrick McGinnis said.
James McGinnis suffered a traumatic brain bleed. Doctors gave him less than a 7% chance to survive. He spent weeks in the ICU.
Patrick McGinnis said he began researching brain injury recovery and the next steps.
On day five, James McGinnis signed “I love you,” which gave his parents a glimpse of hope.
Doctors called it a reflex, Patrick McGinnis said
“And I was like, no, I don’t think so. I think it’s purposeful,” he said.
From walking to running
Patrick McGinnis said doctors initially told the family that his son’s recovery would not be a sprint — “it’s a marathon” — and that James would never walk again.
It took James McGinnis nine months to walk on his own and nine years to run.
He started with a mile, then ran a 5K and a 10K. He completed a half marathon in 2024, then set his sights on a marathon.
Patrick McGinnis now runs three times a week with his son.
“I do it because every time we go out, James gets better,” he said.
Quotes at every mile
Along the marathon course, Patrick McGinnis recorded what the family calls “James-isms,” which are his son’s core beliefs. He recorded one at every mile.
The James-ism at mile 10 was: “Tell me I can’t, and I will show you I can.”
After the race, James McGinnis said doctors told him and his family the journey would be a marathon.
“Well, I did my marathon,” he said.
Rehabilitation doctor responds
Dr. Brad Steinle, James McGinnis’ rehabilitation doctor, said McGinnis’ prognosis was grim and his recovery has been remarkable. Steinle said McGinnis’ strength has made him a better physician.
“I have hundreds of patients that, while I think that we help them, they help us,” Steinle said. “I haven’t had anybody quite like James.”
Next goals
James McGinnis’ next goals are running the Boston Marathon and possibly competing in the 2028 Paralympics
