title: Does Maine law ban ‘free beer’ promotions?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Yes.
Under Maine law, licensed establishments can’t offer or serve free alcoholic beverages, including beer, or advertise promotions offering them.
The restrictions also prohibit drinking contests, awarding alcohol as prizes and offering unlimited drinks for a fixed price, except at private functions.
Discounted drinks, including happy hour specials, are allowed. Exceptions to the free alcohol ban include authorized tastings and samples. Restaurants also may include alcoholic drinks in meal packages.
The restriction appears in Maine’s 1987 liquor laws. The state’s liquor law guide permits offering free food or entertainment, but says advertising “2-for-1” drink specials is also prohibited.
Maine is among a minority of states with bans on free alcohol. As of January 2021, 14 states prohibited it at bars and restaurants, according to a 2022 federal report. Twenty-four states prohibited unlimited drink specials.
The report cites research linking discounted alcohol promotions to heavier drinking among college students.

title: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the dwindling number of Pearl Harbor survivors, dies at 106
text:
BOSTON (AP) — Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the few remaining Pearl Harbor survivors, has died.
Johnson died Saturday at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts. He was 106, according to one of his daughters, Diane Johnson.
“It’s going to be a hell of a Thanksgiving,” Diane Johnson said. “He’s going to be up there with all of his friends and family and my mom.”
Freeman Johnson was one of the estimated 87,000 military personnel on Oahu on Dec. 7, 1941, and was below deck working on a boiler of the USS St. Louis when the Japanese surprise attack happened. In a May 2026 interview with The Associated Press, Johnson said he didn’t hear or see the attack. He never heard his shipmates firing anti-aircraft guns at the attacking planes — shooting down a torpedo plane.
“While all the rigamarole was going on topside, I was inside a steam drum. Couldn’t see anything, absolutely nothing,” said Johnson, whose job had been known as a firefighter on the ship.
Even as the St. Louis headed into the Pacific Ocean, Johnson knew little about the attack. By the time he was topside, the St. Louis, a light cruiser, had evaded midget submarines and safely set out to sea.
“We were way out to sea, way out. You couldn’t see any land at all. All you saw was ocean,” he said. “I was just a sailor, just a swabbie, I was not an officer. They don’t tell you anything if you don’t need to know. And I didn’t need to know it. So they tell you nothing.”
The list of surviving veterans from the attack had stood at about a dozen names after the December 2025 death of Ira “Ike” Schab, who was 105.
While Johnson didn’t see the Pearl Harbor attack, which killed just over 2,400 Americans and propelled the United States into the war, he was witness to other historic moments during World War II.
He helped commission the USS Iowa and recalled the battleship’s preparations in November 1943 ahead of transporting President Franklin D. Roosevelt to the Tehran Conference with British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Josef Stalin. The ship was equipped with two elevators and a bathtub. All the ammunition and much of the oil was removed to lighten the ship as it made its way down the Potomac River to pick up Roosevelt. It was reloaded before the ship headed out to sea.
Johnson also witnessed the war’s end while aboard the Iowa. He was on the Iowa’s mast watching the surrender ceremonies about a mile away in Tokyo Bay aboard the USS Missouri on Sept. 2, 1945.
“I could see the boats coming up with the Marines escorting the Japanese onto the ship and sitting around a table,” he said. “It was all over. That was the end of the war. A bunch of us got together — the war is over. Let’s go home.”
For all the attention to Pearl Harbor, the gruff Johnson, who was known for his cackling laugh and mischievous smile, didn’t see it as one of the defining moments in his life.
Those would have been getting married after the war to his late wife and having three daughters. He worked for years in a machinist shop, then in a convenience store and, finally, delivering meals to seniors — all jobs he retired from, the last one at the age of 90.
“Pearl Harbor just happened. I can’t put it any other way,” he said.

title: Maine town uses mystery $55K found in woods to help families pay heating bills
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FALMOUTH, Maine (WGME) — A mysterious stash of tens of thousands of dollars found in a safe in the Maine woods several years ago will now help families pay their heating bills.
Police said $55,000 was found, but a question remains: Where did the money come from?
“We’re surmising that it was there for pickup and something else was going to get dropped off, um, but yeah, we don’t know,” Falmouth Police Chief John Kilbride said.
Falmouth police traced the cash to a bank in New Hampshire and confirmed the money was not stolen. Police said they followed protocol, contacted several law enforcement agencies and advertised that they had a large sum of unclaimed cash, but they could not crack the case.
“It was an intriguing way of getting funds. It’s, you know, this was not taxpayer money,” Falmouth Town Council Chair Bryce Hawke explained. “This was not something that was a product of any really even, um, thoughtful policy. This is just literally a find in the woods.”
Under state law, the unclaimed money had to be used for a charitable purpose.
The Falmouth Town Council voted to direct the funds to the low-income home energy assistance program, or LIHEAP.
Hawke said the decision was a no-brainer. Going into peak heating season, the council believes it could go a long way in helping Mainers in a pinch.
“Knowing how needed these funds are for heating right now, knowing how expensive fuel is for heating, and knowing that we’re going right into the winter. This was a true, a true gift for our community and one that literally fell on our lap,” Hawke said.
The money is expected to be available starting in January.

What caused the nationwide ground stop and where does the investigation stand?
FAA and DOT officials are set to brief committee members on the outdated air traffic control system after a router issue caused a nationwide ground stop Friday
What caused the nationwide ground stop and where does the investigation stand?
FAA and DOT officials are set to brief committee members on the outdated air traffic control system after a router issue caused a nationwide ground stop Friday
The Federal Aviation Administration and Department of Transportation are expected to brief congressional staff today on Capitol Hill about the outdated air traffic control system following Friday's nationwide ground stop.
According to a statement from top Democrats who serve on committees overseeing aviation, the agencies will likely explain their request for $50 billion to address the aging system, despite Congress previously approving more than $12 billion for modernization under President Donald Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill."
"The safe travel of the flying public must always be our top priority. Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again," Rep. Rick Larsen and Rep. André Carson said in part in their joint statement.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the funding already allocated is insufficient to resolve all issues with the airspace, prompting his request for an additional $30 billion.
"If we don't make these upgrades, we have a less safe system. We can't continue on technology from the '80s," Duffy said during Saturday's press conference.
Duffy explained that a router overloaded the air traffic control system during upgrades to telecommunications lines Friday, leading to the nationwide ground stop. The router is currently being examined at a lab in Florida.
"We have to unwind: Was this a technical install error or was this an issue with the router itself?" Duffy said. "When I have that information, I'll pass it along, but that investigation is just beginning right now."
For travelers this week, Duffy said he expects flights to be back at full capacity today.

title: US gives states another 6 months before they have to remove people from Medicaid for not working
text:
US gives states another 6 months before they have to remove people from Medicaid for not working
President Donald Trump’s administration told states Friday that they can wait until July before removing people from Medicaid for failing to meet a work requirement.
The requirement is scheduled to take effect nationally on Jan. 1, and states have been scrambling to put in place the staffing, training and technology to implement it by then. The administration clarified that while states still have the option to take action at the beginning of the year, they won't have to kick anyone off or deny coverage for failure to meet the requirement until July 1.
Medicaid is the joint state-federal health insurance program for lower-income people. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services told state Medicaid directors on Friday that they'll still need to determine whether many enrollees and applicants for benefits are meeting new requirements that they are working, in school or volunteering.
The move announced Friday gives state social service departments more time to make sure complicated changes are ready to run before there are consequences. CMS said that states are making progress but have implementation challenges.
“I think these extra six months are going to give states the ability to respond to the change, and there will be fewer people that lose their coverage due to administrative failures” resulting from states’ inability to prepare, Kathy Hempstead, senior policy officer for the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, told The Associated Press.
Still, she said it's not clear which states will opt to use the additional time.
Kate McEvoy, executive director of the National Association of Medicaid Directors, said state Medicaid leaders “appreciate the additional flexibility that CMS is providing."
There's political pressure over the requirement
The decision also could give some breathing room to Congress while it considers changes to the requirement. Democrats who are taking control of both chambers in January after their sweeping election victories last week have said they want to roll back the requirements.
The news comes after Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, of Oregon, and Rep. Frank Pallone Jr., of New Jersey, wrote to CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz this week, asking to delay implementing the work reporting requirements. Their letter cites, in part, a recent decision out of a Boston federal court that determined medically frail people should not be bound by the work requirement qualification rules.
“The practical reality is that this significant implementation issue may not be definitively resolved for months, creating untenable uncertainty for states that need a final resolution of this issue before going live with work reporting requirements,” the letter states. “The court ruling is an important victory for the millions of medically frail people who rely on Medicaid for their health care coverage."
Under the policy, many Medicaid beneficiaries must work or volunteer at least 80 hours a month or be in school at least half-time. The new policy applies only to people who receive Medicaid under a voluntary expansion that 40 states undertook and which was intended to get health coverage to more lower-income adults who don’t have kids at home. There are exceptions for those who are over 64, caring for kids under 14 or deemed too medically frail to work.
Critics say that most enrollees covered by the mandate are already working and that people are more likely to lose coverage because of the paperwork to prove it rather than failing to work.
The federal government is pushing states to use data from other government departments or elsewhere to verify whether beneficiaries are working as a way to reduce the burden on the beneficiaries to show proof.
Critics worry that the paperwork part will be the biggest issue
A few states have launched the work requirements early.
The first of them was Nebraska, which started in May.
Preliminary data presented to the state’s Medicaid Advisory Committee showed that more than 9 in 10 people subject to the work requirement and due to have their benefits renewed in July and August qualified.
But 533 people were denied continuing coverage. For most of them, it was over paperwork: They didn’t show that they were working or were exempt from the requirement. Of those denied, 43 lost coverage because they did not meet the new requirement.
Similarly, most of the new Medicaid applicants who were denied coverage due to work requirements from May through August did not get the coverage because they did not provide information to verify whether they were complying.
Among both groups, it’s not clear how many people didn’t provide information because they weren’t working — or how many might meet the requirements but failed to show it.
“There are likely people who are still eligible for coverage who lost it,” said Amy Behnke, the CEO of the Health Center Association of Nebraska.

title: SpaceX’s Starship caught by launch pad arms on return from orbit in a dramatic first
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) - SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.
It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch, still the goal for accelerating moon and Mars travel.
Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.
The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster’s messy miss. Cameras panned the spacecraft up and down as it hung high above the ground, supported by the arms of the launch tower.
“Can you believe it?” SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted, dragging out each word. “Look at her! Baby, she’s back!”
Calling it an “epic day,” Musk later ascended the launch tower to take up-close video with his phone. He even hugged the spacecraft. “Looks great,” he reported via X.
SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling. Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.
NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.
“It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X. “Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to (emojis of the moon and the U.S. flag).”
The world’s largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX’s Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.
Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps.
It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.
SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.
As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it wasn’t in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.
SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA’s next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.
Artemis III’s four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity’s first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

title: Rare North Atlantic right whale population drops, alarming scientists
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rare North Atlantic right whale population drops, alarming a consortium of scientists
The population of one of the world's rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years, worrying scientists who fear the animal could still be at risk of extinction.
The North Atlantic right whale now numbers 382 animals, according to a consortium of scientists that released its annual population estimate for the animals on Monday. That represents about a 2% decline from last year's estimate, which showed a recent slow but steady climb in the whales' population continuing.
The whales were decimated by centuries of commercial whaling that mostly ended in the 1930s. The enormous animals have been slow to recover, and today they are threatened by entanglement in fishing gear and collisions with ships.
Those threats, combined with a warming ocean, have conspired to hold the population down, said Heather Pettis, chair of the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. Pettis said the warming of the ocean has caused the whales' food — tiny organisms called copepods — to move, and the whales have followed them into areas of ocean not protected from ship strikes and entanglements.
“We know that this population can and will move around to find food, and if we aren't protecting them throughout their range, we may see another situation where we have this tremendous decline again,” Pettis said.
The whales' population fell about 25% from 2010 to 2020 during a time when years of poor reproduction coincided with high mortality. Recent years have been slightly more encouraging, but scientists and conservationists have warned that the whales need years of high birth counts coupled with new protections to have a chance to rebuild.
The loss in population last year underscores the need to spare the whales from entanglements and ship strikes, said Nora Ives, a marine scientist on the environmental group Oceana’s right whale campaign.
Oceana was one of several environmental groups that opposed a proposal in Congress to delay new right whale protections until 2035. The proposal, which has passed the U.S. House of Representatives, is intended to protect commercial fishing interests from regulations that members of the industry describe as burdensome.
“The latest numbers are disappointing and make the road to recovery longer for critically endangered North Atlantic right whales. This iconic whale will not escape extinction if its population cannot grow,” Ives said.
The right whales, which can weigh 150,000 pounds (68,039 kilograms), give birth off the Carolinas, Florida and Georgia in the winter and venture north to feeding grounds off New England and Canada. Large groups of the animals that sometimes include a fifth of the entire population are sometimes seen off Massachusetts in spring. Last year was one of the most successful calving seasons on record with more than 20 babies born.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has said the last nine years have also been a time of unusually high numbers of injuries and deaths for the whales. The population is down to just 73 reproductive females, which makes replenishing the stock difficult.
Right whales were hunted heavily because they tend to live fairly close to shore and floated when killed, and they yielded a high volume of oil. Some sources say they got their common name from the perception that they were the “right” whale to hunt.

title: Aging Untold: Meet founder of the ‘We Do Not Care Club’ started; Cut sodium without giving up flavor

title: Oxford Fire On Friday The 13th: Hot Wood Stove Ashes In A Plastic Container Sparked It
text:
Maine's top fire officials are reminding people that use wood stoves to pay attention to how the dispose of those ashes, or run the risk of causing a fire.
This comes on the heels of a Friday the 13th fire in the town of Oxford, where multiple agencies and departments responded to a structure fire on the East Oxford Road.
Maine Fire Marshal's investigators were able to determine the cause of the blaze and said it was improper disposal of ashes from a wood stove that created the issue.
"The fire was determined to have been caused by hot ashes from a woodstove that had been improperly discarded in a plastic container. The hot ashes ignited the combustible container, causing the fire to spread throughout the residence. The fire was classified as accidental."
Authorities warn against ever putting hot ash into a plastic container, or dumping them near a building or other combustible materials.
According to one local insurance company, MMG Insurance, improper disposal of ashes has caused dangerous issues like wildfires and house fires across the nation, not just in Maine.
"According to the National Fire Protection Association, every year in the U.S. nearly 10,000 fires are caused due to improper removal and disposal of hot ashes. Hot coals, when hidden in ashes and therefore well insulated, can stay hot for up to four days – and all they need to flare up again is oxygen."
Local public safety officials like the Maine Forest Rangers echo that, stating that responding to fires created by ashes is something are very familiar with as it's becoming a years event.
Read More: Bangor Firefighters Contain Early Morning Center Street Blaze
They suggest being mindful of what you use to store your ashes, and the location where you decide to dump them.
"Be sure to allow ashes to cool completely before disposing of them. Place ashes in a tightly covered metal container and keep it at least 10 feet away from any buildings. Never empty the ashes directly into a trash can or on the ground. Pour water on the ashes. Make sure they are cold to the touch before emptying the container."
State Fire Marshal's deemed the Oxford fire as accidental. Thankfully there was no one home in the residence at the time the fire broke out.

title: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the dwindling number of Pearl Harbor survivors, dies at 106

The list of surviving veterans from the attack had stood at about a dozen names after the December 2025 death of Ira “Ike” Schab, who was 105.
While Johnson didn’t see the Pearl Harbor attack, which killed just over 2,400 Americans and propelled the United States into the war, he was witness to other historic moments during World War II.
He helped commission the USS Iowa and recalled the battleship’s preparations in November 1943 ahead of transporting President Franklin D. Roosevelt to the Tehran Conference with British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Josef Stalin. The ship was equipped with two elevators and a bathtub. All the ammunition and much of the oil was removed to lighten the ship as it made its way down the Potomac River to pick up Roosevelt. It was reloaded before the ship headed out to sea.
Johnson also witnessed the war’s end while aboard the Iowa. He was on the Iowa’s mast watching the surrender ceremonies about a mile away in Tokyo Bay aboard the USS Missouri on Sept. 2, 1945.
“I could see the boats coming up with the Marines escorting the Japanese onto the ship and sitting around a table,” he said. “It was all over. That was the end of the war. A bunch of us got together — the war is over. Let’s go home.”
For all the attention to Pearl Harbor, the gruff Johnson, who was known for his cackling laugh and mischievous smile, didn’t see it as one of the defining moments in his life.
Those would have been getting married after the war to his late wife and having three daughters. He worked for years in a machinist shop, then in a convenience store and, finally, delivering meals to seniors — all jobs he retired from, the last one at the age of 90.
“Pearl Harbor just happened. I can’t put it any other way,” he said.

title: Customers at major banks report difficulty accessing accounts online
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Customers reported difficulty accessing the online accounts at some major banks Monday.
Bank of America, Chase, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo and Zelle were listed by users as down or experiencing issues, according to the website downdetector.com.
Chase Bank’s services are experiencing a technical bug issue, not a cyber issue, a spokesperson said Monday.
“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”
The reports follow a major outage by Microsoft that began Friday and lasted for hours which impacted services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot.
Some Chase customers received a message that said “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”

title: Author Talk with Art Dingley at the Farmington Public Library, November 18
Questions swirl around FAA's new SMART AI system, though officials say no link to ground stop
text:
The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology.
But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration’s SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems.
Officials say no connection to ground stop
The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there’s no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system, and the top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday.
The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn’t caused by “the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”
But lawmakers and outside groups raised questions about the SMART system before Friday’s ground stop. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails.
“Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” the Oct. 13 letter said. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.”
SMART, however, is not — at least not yet — set up for AI to be in charge of flight control. Rather, it is making recommendations to humans who do so.
What is the SMART system?
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a “cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics — into one platform.” SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories.
The system’s AI-supported engine synthesizes the data systems and shows a “comprehensive visualization” of where planes are going, how much traffic the system can handle and where congestion or weather could cause problems, according to the announcement. The idea is for specialists to then use the platform to fix problems before they arise.
The FAA says that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system’s recommendations.
So SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers. That was three days before the ground stop.
According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested. The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals.
SMART is also supposed to help with weather-related issues faster.
Currently, the FAA blocks off portions of airspace affected by weather as “large, rectangular boxes,” according to the fact sheet, which doesn’t reflect how weather actually looks, with quick-moving thunderstorms and storm systems that are “often irregular in shape, with narrow gaps or corridors that aircraft could safely fly through.”
To help with this, SMART gives the FAA and airspace operators a “clearer picture of how weather will affect air traffic over time,” allowing air traffic controllers to plan around storms and use available airspace instead of unnecessarily shutting down large areas.
No other country has a working AI air traffic tool like the SMART system, according to Michael McCormick, a former FAA airspace manager and an associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority, has a system in testing and several manufacturers are prototyping similar tools.
Concerns around relying on AI
While government officials and ASI, the company behind SMART, have stressed that its AI system is designed to assist humans and not run flight control, its deployment has raised concerns about relying on artificial intelligence when human lives are at stake, given that even the most advanced models are prone to hallucinations — when models fabricate false information and present it as fact.
Mike O’Donnell, a former top FAA official who worked for the agency for 17 years and now does aviation safety consulting work, said the agency “has got to make sure that this is just a tool in the toolbox and not the actual machine that’s doing the work.”
The FAA, he said, “cannot afford to be wrong on this.”
“It’s good to use it with the proper guardrails and backstops to ensure that they’re not giving wrong information to controllers based on what (AI) has come up with,” O’Donnell said. “There’s got to be a way to verify and validate what it’s doing to make sure that it’s not the wrong information.”
He cautioned against putting too much trust in AI “until we know for sure that it’s proven itself time and time again. And that’s going to take a while.”
The AI system’s launch comes amid a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers around the country. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association has been raising concerns about this for more than a decade, telling Congress in 2015 that the shortage was at a crisis level. It said then that the FAA had missed its hiring targets for five years in a row. The union represents about 14,000 controllers, roughly 3,000 of them trainees. That said, experts say no AI system can replace the human air traffic controllers who spend years training for this highly demanding and stressful job.
In an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the SMART tool is designed for traffic managers who manage the entire U.S. airspace.
“The AI does the math, the AI does the computation,” Buckendorf told NPR, but it’s ultimately up to the human operator whether to take the system’s recommendation. “They make the decision, they are the decider, they are the judge.”
Story by Barbara Ortutay and Josh Funk.

title: Emanuel Nine Memorial opens in Charleston, 11 years after Mother Emanuel AME Church shooting
text:
Emanuel Nine Memorial opens in Charleston, South Carolina, 11 years after Mother Emanuel AME Church shooting
More than 11 years after a gunman killed nine people during a Bible study at Mother Emanuel AME Church, a memorial in memory of their lives is now open to the public.
Hundreds gathered Saturday in downtown Charleston, South Carolina, for the opening of the Emanuel Nine Memorial. But while the day marked a painful chapter in Charleston's history, many of those who spoke emphasized a message of hope, forgiveness and unity.
"What happened here on June 17th, 2015, did not define Charleston," Charleston Mayor William Cogswell said. "But what came afterwards revealed a lot about who we are."
On June 17, 2015, nine people were killed when a gunman opened fire during a Bible study at the historic church in a racially motivated attack.
Survivor Polly Sheppard reflected on the night that changed her life and the importance of making sure the victims are never forgotten.
"Eleven years ago, on the darkest night of my life, a gunman looked at me and told me he was going to leave me here to tell the story," Sheppard said.
She said the memorial should serve as a reminder not only of the nine lives lost, but also of the importance of unity.
"It's time to clear out the hatred, the racism and the division and replace it with empathy, forgiveness and enduring love. Together we can change," Sheppard said.
A place to remember the Emanuel Nine
The outdoor memorial sits next to Mother Emanuel AME Church at 120 Calhoun St. in downtown Charleston.
The memorial was designed by architect Michael Arad, who also designed the National September 11 Memorial in New York City. The space features two curved marble benches and a marble fountain with the names of the nine victims carved along its edge.
A cross at the far end of the courtyard provides another space for quiet reflection and prayer.
Honoring a mother's legacy
For Chris Singleton, the memorial is a reminder that his mother's life and the lives of the other victims will not be forgotten.
Singleton's mother, Reverend Sharonda Coleman-Singleton, was among the nine people killed in the shooting.
During Saturday's ceremony, Singleton encouraged people to show love to those around them, saying that sometimes a simple gesture can make a difference for someone who is grieving.
"One of the biggest fears that I have is that people will forget my mom and how amazing she was as a human being," Singleton said.
But after seeing the memorial for the first time, he said he felt reassured that the victims' stories would live on.
"As I stood out here last night and I saw the water coming down the memorial, I saw the names across the side, I thought to myself, 'We won't forget these amazing nine souls, because we have this amazing memorial,'" Singleton said.
Visiting the Emanuel Nine Memorial
The memorial is located at 120 Calhoun Street in downtown Charleston, next to Mother Emanuel AME Church.
Current visiting hours are:
- Tuesday through Saturday: 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
- Sunday: Noon to 5 p.m.
- Monday: Closed
Hours may change based on site operations and special events.

title: Cause of death released for Gypsy Rose Blanchard's partner, Ken Urker
text:
Cause of death released for Gypsy Rose Blanchard's partner Ken Urker
The cause of death for Gypsy Rose Blanchard's former partner, Ken Urker, has been released, according to the Lafourche Parish Coroner's Office in Louisiana.
Ken Urker, who is the father of Blanchard's child, died of an accidental drug overdose, the coroner's office said.
Deputies say on Oct. 1, around 6:18 p.m., they were dispatched to a welfare concern in reference to Urker at a home in Raceland, Louisiana.
According to deputies, the welfare concern was due to Urker not answering his phone or the door to his residence.
Anita Blanchard and Dylan Blanchard also told deputies that Urker was at church with them on Wednesday, and they stated Urker made comments about being depressed and upset.
They also told deputies he was on TikTok Live around 11 p.m., driving without saying anything.
Due to his behavior and not showing up for work, they decided to check on him and contact the Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office.
Before deputies arrived, Anita Blanchard, Dylan Blanchard, and Justin Daigle were able to gain access to the home through a bedroom window that was unlocked, and they were able to see Urker lying on his bed unconscious.
Once they realized he was not answering, they entered through the window and located Urker on the bed and stated he was cold to the touch and not breathing.
When deputies arrived, they said they were able to see Urker from the living room area lying on his back in the bed.
Deputies say they located drug paraphernalia, including syringes and a spoon in the bathroom next to a brown powdery substance.
They say they also located a syringe and a handgun on the nightstand next to the bed, and Urker was cold to the touch and appeared to have been there for an extended period of time.
His face and arms were blue, and a paper towel was placed on his left arm with what appeared to be blotches of blood on the paper towel, according to deputies.

title: Takeaways from big weekend of Maine high school football
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Week 11 of Maine high school football featured state title games (eight-man), regional finals (Class A, B and D) and state semifinals (Class C) played throughout the state. Two teams lifted Gold Balls, and eight others earned the right to play for one.
There’s plenty to dissect as we put a bow on the eight-man season and move ahead to the 11-man state championships. So here are five takeaways from the penultimate week of the 2026 season as we near the finish line.
Yarmouth caps off remarkable run
Is this Yarmouth team the best in Maine eight-man football history? The Clippers certainly can make a strong argument. A 72-26 demolition of Old Town in the Large School championship game Saturday capped off an 11-0 season that has few parallels.
The Clippers finished the season with 692 points scored, an average of 62.9 per game. Both are eight-man records. The win followed a 34-point win over Spruce Mountain in the Large School South final, a result that was somehow Yarmouth’s closest game this season.
Leading the way all season for Yarmouth were senior quarterback Iggy McGrath and junior running back Stephen Connolly. McGrath passed for 2,380 yards, 38 touchdowns and no interceptions this season, while Connolly rushed for 2,089 yards and 33 scores on 130 carries.
Orono takes a different road to glory
While Yarmouth was clearly the top team in eight-man Large all year, Orono, the state Small School champ, went 3-4 in the regular season. The Red Riots’ improbable playoff run included a North title game win over Stearns and a come-from-behind 22-14 state final win over Old Orchard Beach on Saturday.
The triumph over OOB made history for Orono, which became the first eight-man team to win a state title after posting a losing record in the regular season. It’s possible the Red Riots are the only Maine team to have achieved this feat — it hasn’t happened since at least 2004.
Cony’s wide receivers put on a show
You can always count on Cony’s aerial attack to pose a threat. After losing Anderson Noyes to another injury early in the Class B North final against Fryeburg Academy, the Rams had to rely as much as ever on their passing, which was boosted by phenomenal plays by their receivers.
With 4 minutes, 7 seconds left in the first half, Landen Perry changed his route pre-snap and then dragged his foot to bring in a 17-yard touchdown pass that put Cony up 14-0. With 27 seconds left in the half, the Rams got a one-handed grab from Jacob Fifield in tight coverage to take a three-score lead to the break.
“We have stud receivers,” said Cony quarterback Drew Lindquist. “I’ve never thrown to better receivers in my life. … It’s not like I have only one receiver I can throw to — I’ve got all my guys.”
Defense rules the weekend
Speaking of Cony, the Rams’ defense was not to be outdone. Cony didn’t allow a single big play to standout Fryeburg quarterback Marcus Sutton, and the Rams limited the Raiders to 109 yards of total offense.
Cony was far from the only team to shine on defense in Class B, as Marshwood prevailed 14-8 in overtime of its B South title game with Kennebunk. Winthrop claimed a 13-3 D South championship win over Freeport, while Leavitt (26-0 over Foxcroft) and Hermon (17-10 over Greely) won defensive battles in Class C.
However, could the best defensive performance of the week have been Orono’s? Defense is no easy task in eight-man, and the Red Riots’ win over an Old Orchard team averaging 42.2 points per game was sealed when they made a late defensive stand to seal the title. The Seagulls’ 14 points were their fewest since a 26-6 loss to Telstar in 2021.
Bonny Eagle shocks the state
None of our 10 Varsity Maine prognosticators predicted Bonny Eagle to take down Thornton Academy in the Class A South title game. The undefeated Golden Trojans had outscored opponents 458-75 on the year, winning by fewer than 28 points just once. That included a 49-14 win over the Scots just three weeks ago.
Bonny Eagle, though, showed how little that mattered Saturday. The Scots avenged their only loss, beating Thornton 35-28 to claim the South title at Hill Stadium. It’s the first regional championship since 2019 for Bonny Eagle, which ended the Trojans’ streak of seven consecutive Class A title game appearances.

title: Beyoncé becomes the first artist to reach 100 Grammy nominations
text:
(CNN) - Beyoncé is making Grammy history once again.
The superstar is now the first artist to reach 100 career nominations.
Her latest nod is for Best R&B Solo Performance for her song “MORNING DEW (DONK).”
The previously unreleased track dropped in July, ahead of the 20th anniversary of her album “B’Day.”
Beyoncé has been nominated for Grammys almost every year since her group Destiny’s Child picked up two nods in 2000 for “Bills, Bills, Bills.”
She is also the most-awarded artist in Grammy history, with 35 wins.

title: Take a moment to learn about turkeys
text:
Thanksgiving Day is upon us. For many, that means family; a feast featuring such staples as roast turkey, mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, and, of course, pumpkin pie; and a bevy of football games on television. For naturalists, one item on this list is particularly intriguing: turkey.
The bird we buy from Hannaford or a local organic farm is a far cry from the Wild Turkeys freely roaming Mount Desert Island. Over hundreds of years, turkeys have been selectively bred for meat production. They have become so muscle-bound as to render them flightless, barely resembling those birds first domesticated some 2,000 years ago by the peoples of southern Mexico — the Maya, Zapotec, and later the Aztecs.
In the 1500s, Spanish conquistadors and traders took the Mesoamerican domesticated turkey back to Europe where they rapidly spread across Europe and Asia. During the colonial period in what are now the Atlantic states, settlers brought European-lineage, domesticated birds back across the pond. We have continued tinkering with the breed, resulting in the delectable Thanksgiving centerpiece.
The six subspecies of Wild Turkey are widely distributed, ranging from southern Mexico to southernmost Canada, each with well-defined geographical limits. These limits led to subspeciation.
In biology, species are groups of living organisms whose members produce fertile offspring. Subspecies are a further breakdown of species. Though different populations can look and act differently, subspecies are still genetically similar enough to interbreed and also produce fertile offspring.
The scientific name for the Wild Turkeys that were the source for today’s Thanksgiving dinner is “Meleagris gallopavo gallopavo,” genus species subspecies, with the official common name of “South Mexican” Wild Turkey (“South Mexican” in quotes delineates it as an appellation of Wild Turkey). Meanwhile, the subspecies ranging from the Midwest through New England is “Meleagris gallopavo silvestris” or “Eastern” Wild Turkey.
As is usual in the system used for scientific nomenclature, the names tell us something of the species. “Meleagris” derives from the ancient Greek for guinea fowl; “gallopavo” combines the Latin for rooster and peacock, references to the Wild Turkey’s build and showy displays. When the subspecies name repeats the species name (in this case, “gallopavo gallopavo”), it means it was the “type specimen,” that is, the first one of a species identified by science. That explains its attribution to the “South Mexican” Wild Turkey. Our local “silvestris” subspecies takes its Latin roots from “silva,” meaning forest or wood, which is precisely where you expect to find Wild Turkeys here in Maine.
To look at these two subspecies, two differences would immediately be obvious. First would be the plumage. Our local turkey’s rich sheen of iridescent bronze contrasts with the duller plumage of its southern counterpart. Second would be size.
As you head north in most species’ range, they get larger. This is true, too, of Wild Turkey. These latitudinal size differences were noted by 19th-century anatomist Carl Bergmann. He formulated the zoological principle that body size in closely-related warm-blooded animals tends to increase in colder climates.
As a related aside, when leading nature tours, people frequently tell me they saw an unkindness of ravens in Acadia National Park (“unkindness” being the collective noun for a group of ravens). Ravens are rarely found in groups larger than their immediate family of two to four. Instead, they are seeing American Crows. Maine’s crows are notably larger than those in southern states, meaning they have greater thermal mass which better enables them to maintain their body temperature during cold of winter. This is Bergmann’s Rule at work. But I digress.
Early colonial era Wild Turkeys were arguably “wilder” than they are today, having had to contend with more predators, including humans. The landscape was more intact with vast forests far more extensive than anything we see today, inhabited by an estimated 7-10 million Wild Turkeys. As our country grew, the forest cover reached the nadir of their extent by the late 1800s. By the early 1900s, that, coupled with hunting pressure, reduced the turkey population to roughly 30,000 birds. To ensure the long-term viability of this important gamebird, wildlife agencies took an active hand in managing Wild Turkey.
Thanks to trap and transfer programs, strict hunting regulations, and reforesting habitat, Wild Turkey populations have rebounded back to historic levels. Today’s turkeys are thriving, having habituated to people, backyard feeders, and traffic, and thus becoming less “wild,” has enabled them to adapt to a landscape that is increasingly fragmented and suburban.
So, let’s look at the Wild Turkeys of MDI. In the aftermath of The Great Fire of 1947, Northern Red Oak have become a major constituent of forests once dominated by conifers. Their acorns constitute a substantial part of the turkeys’ diet, along with a wide range of other seeds. When food is scarce, turkeys may dig up flower bulbs from your garden. They will even eat salamanders, snails, beetles, and insects to supplement their diet.
Beginning in March, we see the showy males, or “toms,” doing their elaborate courtship displays, puffing out their feathers, fanning their tails, strutting around like a dandy. After courting, the toms have nothing more to do with the females until next year. Come later spring, hen turkeys lay up to 14 eggs. They lay one egg per day and do not begin incubation until the entire clutch is ready. Delaying incubation (which takes about 28 days) means all of the eggs will hatch within a 24- to 48-hour window.
The newly-hatched chicks, called “poults,” are precocial, able to run around and feed almost immediately. In five to six weeks, flight feathers have developed and the young birds will now roost in trees. It is not uncommon for multiple groups of hens and poults to join together.
If young turkeys can survive their first few years without becoming another animal’s meal, they can live as long as 10 years.
Next time you see a group of Wild Turkeys, take a moment to consider both their natural history and the role they have played in our own society.

title: Cornell to examine future of Greek life after report of gang rape at a fraternity house
text:
Cornell to examine future of Greek life after report of gang rape at a fraternity house
Cornell University will launch a sweeping review of its Greek system and its future on campus after a report of a gang rape at a fraternity house in 2024, the university's president said Monday.
Related previous coverage in the video player above: 'You deserve to be safe': bipartisan campus safety bill promises help for survivors
The review will focus on the Greek system's relationship to housing and residential life, President Michael Kotlikoff said in a letter to the Cornell community. Details will be announced in the coming weeks, he said.
The announcement marks the university's latest response to outrage over its handling of a woman's report that she was drugged and sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house. The woman, identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, sued Cornell and seven men in September.
Cornell expelled or suspended several students after an internal investigation and barred the fraternity chapter from campus. The accused men have denied wrongdoing, and none has been criminally charged.
Kotlikoff has faced criticism for his handling of the case, including his acknowledgment that he never read the campus police report and did not follow up on the outcome of the investigations. He has defended the university’s disciplinary process and said administrators were prohibited from interfering in criminal investigations.
Cornell previously suspended parties at fraternities and announced additional measures to prevent sexual violence on campus.
“To prevent sexual assault, we must reshape the social environments, interactions, and physical spaces that can contribute to increased risk,” Kotlikoff wrote Monday.
He also outlined plans to expand sexual assault prevention education, create more late-night social opportunities outside residential spaces and establish an academic center dedicated to researching campus sexual violence. The university said it is exploring ways to revitalize businesses and develop public gathering places in Collegetown, a neighborhood near campus where many students live and socialize.
Jane Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said in a statement that while they welcomed action by Cornell's administrators to address sexual assault on campus, “words, task forces, and prospective reviews cannot erase years of institutional inaction.”
“Jane Doe welcomes any genuine effort that prevents another student from enduring what she suffered. However, meaningful reform requires full transparency into how past reports of sexual violence were mishandled, real consequences for those responsible, and a permanent end to a culture that prioritizes institutional reputation over student safety,” Giuffra said.
The announcement comes just over a week after Cornell’s Faculty Senate passed a vote of no confidence in the university administration’s ability to address sexual assault on campus.
In his letter Monday, Kotlikoff directly acknowledged the loss of confidence in Cornell’s administration.
“I know many in our community have lost confidence in the Cornell administration’s ability to prevent and respond to sexual violence,” he wrote. “You have raised necessary questions about what the administration is doing to keep our students safe and where we have fallen short.”
Kotlikoff pledged more regular communication about the university’s efforts, including a new public accountability dashboard tracking its progress.
Meanwhile, an independent review led by former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates is underway. Kotlikoff said its findings would guide longer-term changes to how Cornell investigates and adjudicates allegations of sexual misconduct.

title: ‘Just tragic’: 18-year-old Georgia football commit dies after sudden medical emergency
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) - A community is left heartbroken after the death of an 18-year-old Georgia football commit who suffered a sudden medical emergency.
Marcellus Young Casario, 18, was a senior and boarding student at Rabun Gap-Nacoochee School in northeast Georgia. He planned to graduate in December and enroll at the University of Georgia in January, the school said.
Casario suffered a medical emergency Friday morning and was taken to the hospital, where he died. No further details have been released.
A native of Halifax, Nova Scotia, Casario, who was known as Mar, came to Rabun Gap as a junior. The school described him as “a natural leader, a loyal friend, and a standout student-athlete.”
The 18-year-old was a defensive lineman with a passion for football. He committed to Georgia on June 15. ESPN ranked him as the nation’s No. 49 defensive end and a three-star recruit.
“He was everything a coach wants in a player,” Rabun Gap head football coach Derek White said. “Mar truly embodied our mission to ‘love one another.’ He was known for his relentless dedication, and his journey as a student-athlete was marked by hard work and a true brotherhood with his teammates.”
Georgia head coach Kirby Smart addressed Casario’s death Saturday in a postgame press conference.
“One of the toughest calls I’ve ever gotten,” Smart said. “It’s just tragic to have a loss of life at that age. Can you imagine if that’s your child? And he was such a great kid. He was always smiling, always positive and had a great future in front of him.”
Smart added that he and the team are praying for Casario’s family.
Rabun Gap says it is providing counseling and care services for its students, faculty and staff following Casario’s death.
“Mar brought light, faith, and character to everything he did, and his absence is a tremendous void in our close-knit community,” said Head of School Bob Ahrens. “Our community is mourning, and our hearts and prayers are with his family in Halifax, his teammates, and his friends as we navigate this unimaginable loss together.”

title: Bangor Mall condemned following housing redevelopment discussions
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Bangor Mall has been a longtime shopping destination for eastern Maine residents, with stores such as JCPenney, Dick’s Sporting Goods and Spencer’s remaining open despite a decline in storefronts over the years. However, the recent condemnation of the mall has left local residents and businesses facing uncertainty about its future.
In April, WABI TV5 announced that a group called Bangor Marketplace and Residences LLC was seeking to redevelop the property and space for condominiums, assisted living facilities and even some medical offices. However, an important investor pulled out of the deal in October, and any remaining plans rapidly went down the drain when the building was announced to be condemned.
According to News Center Maine, the remaining stores were just as shocked to hear the news as the public was.
Tenants like Some Theater Company, a local theater group, stated that they had not been given notice that the mall would be closed.
“…Just got posted notifications that the mall was condemned. There was no real warning,” said Logan Bard, a member of the nonprofit, in the News Center Maine article.
While the two Bangor Mall staples, JCPenney and Dick’s Sporting Goods, will remain open, other tenants are suddenly seeking quick relocation for their businesses. Luckily for Some Theater Company, they were able to find a new location in just days. But whether or not other businesses will have that much luck with relocation is up in the air.
Why the shopping center suddenly went from new future plans to condemned in the span of a few months has finally been released to the public. David Warren, Bangor City Manager, released a statement on WABI 5 in a Nov. 4 article.
“As of Monday, portions of the mall did not have properly operating heating systems. The City was compelled to shut off electric service to both corridor entrances due to a roof that continues to leak. The lack of proper illumination creates additional safety issues,” Warren said in his statement.
Some Bangor locals have expressed concern on social media platforms such as Reddit and Facebook about where the annual November craft fair will be held. According to the craft fair’s event page on Facebook, it seems that it will be held at Furniture Mattresses and More in Bangor on the weekends of Nov. 7 and Nov. 14. Though Furniture Mattresses and More is part of the Bangor Mall, it is owned separately and will remain open despite the mall being condemned.
Brooke Murphy, a fourth-year business management student at the University of Maine, weighed in on the mall being condemned.
“I did know about the Bangor Mall closing. I didn’t know the reasoning why. I just heard they were turning it into apartments, so I was pretty caught off guard when I heard it was being condemned,” said Murphy.
The mall being condemned does not automatically mean the building will be demolished. It is simply not up to standards for human habitation or use. The owners of the building and property, Namdar Realty Group, have 30 days to appeal the decision to condemn the mall, or to make the necessary repairs in order to make it safe to reopen.

title: Young bald eagle rescued in Ogunquit being treated for lead poisoning
text:
Young bald eagle rescued in Ogunquit, Maine, being treated for lead poisoning
The Center for Wildlife in Maine said a young bald eagle that was rescued in the town of Ogunquit last week faces a difficult road to recovery after being diagnosed with lead poisoning.
Ogunquit firefighters and police officers were able to safely capture the bald eagle on Wednesday, Nov. 11, after receiving several reports that the bird did not seem well. People were concerned about the eagle, which had been seen frequently around the Marginal Way, because it appeared to be spending too much time on the ground and acting strangely.
First responders then brought the bald eagle to the Center for Wildlife in Cape Neddick for evaluation and care. The Center for Wildlife said they could see the bird was exhausted and emaciated, which is not unusual for juvenile raptors this time of year, but blood draws and diagnostics showed that the eagle had high lead levels, a low packed cell volume and a parasitic infection in its upper respiratory tract. The eagle was also dehydrated and had feather lice, according to the Center for Wildlife.
"The lead levels, as well as bloodwork and state of emaciation are usually in the veterinary recommendation of euthanasia, and this eagle’s prognosis is very guarded and honestly poor," the Center for Wildlife said in a Facebook post. "At this state of emaciation, the body begins turning to consuming its own organs, and this stage of lead toxicity can be painful and cause heart and respiratory issues."
The Center for Wildlife noted, however, that the eagle was responding to its emaciation protocol, which began with fluids and rehydration and has advanced to being tube-fed liquid calories.
At this stage, the Center for Wildlife team is monitoring the eagle to see if it is processing the liquid and calories, if it is depressed and still not able to stand and if its plasma, oxygenation and liver function are improving.
"This will be a difficult road to recovery. We are focused on getting this eagle out of his body’s emaciation shutdown, treating the parasites to alleviate that stress, and getting him stable enough to endure chelation therapy for the lead," the center said.
X-rays did not show lead shot embedded in the eagle's system, nor a lead sinker, according to the Center for Wildlife. Because of this, the center believes the eagle has a high lead level because it either ate bait piles with shot or a seabird with lead shot. It is illegal to hunt over the water with lead, but the Center for Wildlife said it still admits many waterbirds with lead shot.
"This national symbol is telling us a story of poisoning our own water, fish/food, and the wildlife we revere," the center said. "We can easily stop lead from being in the environment by using lead alternatives, and spreading the word."
The Center for Wildlife runs completely on donations from individuals, local businesses and family foundations. People who are interested in supporting the center's work can visit an online donation page or send a donation to PO Box 620, Cape Neddick, ME 03902.

title: United Airlines resolves technology issue that delayed departing flights
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights Monday, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop.
Chicago-based United said in a statement that flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not affected. The airline also said there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”
United apologized on social media to customers for the inconvenience. It resolved the issue about one hour and 40 minutes after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers.
United did not immediately provide details about which of its systems were affected, but pilots told air traffic controllers that the problem was related to a system that helps them determine a plane’s final weight.
Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft’s weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying.
The information is also used to guide the autopilot system and the decisions pilots make, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.
“It is extremely important to have all of these numbers accurate and precise,” said Arroyo, who flew for United. “Pilots use that information to establish guidance and performance for their flights from takeoff to landing.”
Arroyo said he has seen problems with the weight and balance system before in his career, but the airline did the right thing by delaying flights to ensure safety.
Years ago, pilots used to do all those weight calculations manually with a pencil and paper and then radio in the numbers, but today it is all calculated electronically and then loaded into the plane’s computers.
In August 2025, United grounded planes at major U.S. airports, delaying more than 1,000 flights because of an hourslong outage of a system called Unimatic, which houses flight information that is fed to other systems including those that calculate weight and balance and track flight times.
United said in response to a message from The Associated Press that it had no further information to provide about whether the same system was affected by Monday’s outage.
A recording posted Monday on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.
The flight-tracking website FlightAware showed United with about 600 delayed flights Monday evening, though it was unclear how many were directly related to the system outage.
The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days.
On Friday, the FAA ordered every flight grounded because a newly installed router malfunctioned, overwhelming the aging air traffic control system.
And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored.

title: Family mourns 18-year-old killed in crash after driver running from police runs red light
text:
MILWAUKEE (WISN) - A Wisconsin family is mourning an 18-year-old high school senior who was killed when investigators say a driver running from police ran a red light and crashed into his car.
David Hunt, an 18-year-old senior at Milwaukee School of Languages, planned to study physical therapy at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, but his future was cut short Nov. 1.
David’s father, Paul Hunt, got a crash alert from his son’s phone that night and rushed to the scene.
“When that went off, I just knew something was not right,” Paul Hunt said. “I came across the crash scene, and I kind of knew what was up already. I mean, there was no mistaking what I saw.”
Prosecutors say 36-year-old Antwan White was speeding away from Milwaukee police after officers tried to pull him over for running a stop sign. He reached speeds of 90 mph before running a red light at an intersection and crashing into David Hunt’s car, according to a criminal complaint.
David Hunt was later pronounced dead.
“It’s been the hardest thing I’ve ever gone through, obviously. I’m hoping it’s the hardest thing I’ll ever have to go through,” said David’s older brother, Ian Hunt.
He described his brother as someone who could “make you laugh without saying a word.”
“He always lit up a room whenever he walked into it,” Ian Hunt said.
The family says they understand the need for police to apprehend people breaking the law, but they now question how much risk innocent bystanders, like David Hunt, should have to face.
“I don’t know where the line is for accepting the collateral damage versus justice for people breaking the law,” Paul Hunt said.
Even if change does come, David Hunt’s family knows it won’t bring him home.
“I wouldn’t say it’s worth the life of my brother,” Ian Hunt said. “Whatever comes out of it, we don’t get him back, and that’s the biggest thing.”
Investigators say White later told police he fled because he had drugs in his car. He faces charges including reckless homicide and is due back in court in December.

title: Grammy nominations snub Harry Styles and hip-hop, while surprises include Dolly Parton
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The 2027 Grammy Award nominees are here and there’s a lot to discuss, from Raye and Rosalía dominating the nominations to John Cale receiving his first nod at 84.
Like every year, there were a few artists who made the coveted list Monday and a few who didn’t. Snubs and surprises are in no short supply across the 100 categories that will be awarded Feb. 7.
No hip-hop in most of the general field categories
It’s a 180 from the 2026 Grammys, where, for the first time, there were three releases nominated in both the rap album and album of the year categories. This year, there isn’t a single rap release in the record, song or album of the year categories.
According to Billboard, Drake — the only rapper to score a No. 1 hit on the all-genre Hot 100 this year, with “Janice STFU” — did not submit his three 2026 albums or any of their songs for Grammy consideration. But even without his star power (or that of last year’s nominees Kendrick Lamar, Clipse and Tyler, the Creator), hip-hop seems like a huge absence.
A$AP Rocky’s first full-length album in eight years, “Don’t Be Dumb,” is also noticeably absent, as is Baby Keem’s “Ca$ino.” It seems all eyes will be on Don Toliver, the rising trap and R&B rapper-singer, who scored a best new artist nomination in addition to a rap album one.
But let the record show Drake did secure one nomination: for the newly minted best Latin song category, for his Spanish-language feature on Karol G’s “Ahí.”
Women dominate many of the major categories … and in country
For the first time, the six artists with the most nominations at the Grammys are all women.
And women make up every nominee in the album and song of the year categories, save for Grammy favorite Bruno Mars. For album of the year, Raye and Rosalía will face off against Phoebe Bridgers, Olivia Dean, Ella Langley, Olivia Rodrigo, Taylor Swift and Mars. The list of artists is nearly identical for song of the year — just swap Bridgers for Ariana Grande — and add a first-ever general field nomination for Björk, who is featured on Rosalía’s “Berghain.”
However, there were some strong contenders omitted. Those include Stella Lefty, whose ubiquitous “Boston” did not earn her a single nom, or Gracie Abrams’ “Daughter From Hell.”
But beyond the top categories, women dominate in other, interesting places: dance pop recording, R&B solo performance and in the contemporary country album category, now in its second year. Langley, Kelsea Ballerini, Carter Faith, Megan Moroney and Kacey Musgraves will go head-to-head there. And just as interesting: Only men are nominated in the traditional country category.
Leading men like Harry Styles and Noah Kahan get less love
Harry Styles’ fourth studio album, “Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally.,” did not receive a nomination. The same should be said about Ed Sheeran’s “Play.” Noah Kahan’s critically acclaimed “The Great Divide” received only one nod, in the newly created contemporary folk album category. Justin Bieber’s surprise album “Swag II” didn’t receive a nomination, either.
Newcomer Malcolm Todd was shut out as well, despite lots of love for his album “Do That Again.” It was the same for his sister, the singer-songwriter Audrey Hobert, who was seen as a leading candidate for best new artist.
Beyoncé once again makes history
She’s no stranger to raising the bar. At the 2023 Grammys, Beyoncé became the most-awarded artist in the show’s history. Then, two years later, with “Cowboy Carter,” she became the first Black artist to win country album of the year and the first Black woman to win album of the year since Lauryn Hill’s “The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill” in 1999. She’s now received her 100th career nomination, for “Morning Dew (Donk)” in the R&B solo performance category. The song was the lead single of her 20th anniversary re-release of “B’Day.”
Dolly Parton and Tim Curry receive posthumous nominations
Dolly Parton, who died earlier this year, received three nominations. She’s nominated in the country duo/group performance category twice — for “Butterfly” by Zac Brown Band featuring Parton and “Light of a Clear Blue Morning,” a Parton classic performed with Lainey Wilson, Miley Cyrus, Queen Latifah and Reba McEntire. She’s also nominated in the audiobook, narration and storytelling recording category for her work, “Star of the Show: My Life on Stage.”
In the latter category, competition is fierce: Actor Tim Curry, who also died earlier this year, is nominated for “Vagabond: A Memoir.” And Michelle Obama is nominated in the category for a third time, for “The Look.” Obama has won the award twice before.
BTS and the Asian pop performance category
And now for a little controversy: This year, the Recording Academy created five new Grammy categories, including Asian pop music performance, meant to celebrate releases across K-pop, J-pop, C-pop and beyond. Some fans were excited; others viewed the new category as a racialized barrier for Asian performers.
Not long afterward, K-pop powerhouse BTS said they would not submit their music for consideration. As a result, they did not receive any nominations this year. BTS has never won a Grammy, though they’ve been nominated for five across their career. In fact, no K-pop act had ever won a Grammy before 2026, when “Golden” from “KPop Demon Hunters” took home the trophy for best song for visual media.
After consulting experts, managers, artists and others, the Recording Academy decided to proceed with the category. Another massive K-pop group, Stray Kids, also opted not to submit, but other groups, like the Filipino boy band SB19 and girl group BINI, spoke in support of the category.
Both SB19 and BINI received nods, for their songs “Visa” and “Unang Kilig,” respectively. They’re competing with Japanese singer LiSA’s “Yes,” Japanese kawaii metal band Babymetal’s “Sunset Kiss” featuring Polyphia and two K-pop girl groups: KiiiKiii’s “404 (New Era)” and IVE’s “Bang Bang.”
Notably absent are a few K-pop groups who had huge songs this year, like aespa’s “Lemonade,” Hearts2Hearts’ “Rude!” and BigBang’s “BiiiG.”
___
For more coverage of the 2027 Grammy Awards, visit: https://apnews.com/hub/grammy-awards
