title: South Portland city network outage prompts cybersecurity investigation
text:
South Portland city network outage prompts cybersecurity investigation
South Portland City Hall is closed amid a cybersecurity investigation; officials say "bad actors" caused a network outage, with some municipal services still being impacted.
South Portland city network outage prompts cybersecurity investigation
South Portland City Hall is closed amid a cybersecurity investigation; officials say "bad actors" caused a network outage, with some municipal services still being impacted.
The city of South Portland is investigating a network disruption that has impacted municipal computer systems and services.
The city said initial information suggests the incident may involve "bad actors," and it is coordinating its response with state and federal agencies.
According to officials, the duration of the outage is currently unknown. City Hall, the Assessing Office and the South Portland Library are closed to the public Monday while staff work with the IT Department on restoring some services.
Other city buildings will remain open, although some services will be unavailable, including the city phone system, in-person credit card payments, online administrative portals, mapping services and printed materials such as receipts.
Separately, the city's Citizen Self Service online bill payment system had been experiencing intermittent outages since late the previous week. The city said that the vendor issue was not connected to the network disruption.
Due to the payment problems, the property tax deadline has been extended to Monday, Nov. 23. Residents are still allowed to leave payments in the secure drop boxes outside City Hall.
Vehicle registration renewals remain available through the state's Rapid Renewal website, according to the city. The city said it would provide further updates as its review progressed.

title: Developer acquires historic Rockland school
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — The city has formally transferred ownership of the former McLain School to the developer who plans to convert the existing building, and a new building that will be constructed in the back, into 29 apartments.
The deed transfer was signed Nov. 2 and filed Thursday in the Knox County Registry of Deeds between Rockland and DC McLain LP. DC is Developers Collaborative.
A start date on the work is expected for early 2027.
The affordable workforce housing project at the former McLain School was selected last year to receive funding from the Maine State Housing Authority.
The development will convert the historic McLain School building into 17 units, as well as a new 12-unit, 2.5-story, 4,000-square-foot residential building fronting on Summer Street. The buildings will have a mix of studio, one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments designed as multigenerational housing for families of varying sizes.
The Planning Board gave its final approval in August 2025.
The City Council voted in July 2025 to approve a 30-year tax agreement with the developer that will return half of the additional property taxes created by the project back to the developer for operational purposes. Once completed, the project is expected to begin generating more than $91,000 annually in property taxes, with half of that returned to the developer.
In August 2025, the developer estimated rents would range from $875 for a studio apartment to $1,400 for a three-bedroom unit. Income caps of households eligible for apartments would range from $35,000 to a high of $60,000, depending on the number of people in the family.
Developer Kevin Bunker said last year income now is limited to 50% to 60% of area median income but he is looking at having some units be up to 80% of area median income.
Green buffers, traffic circulation and pedestrian access were approved to improve privacy and safety. Infrastructure and stormwater plans were updated to protect adjacent properties and city systems, the city noted.
The project cost was estimated at $11 million to $12 million.
Built in 1896, the building served for nearly a century as a neighborhood elementary school. For about 25 years, the building had been used for administrative offices and for alternative education programs. The school district turned the property over to Rockland in early 2025 which, in turn, agreed to sell it to the developer for $1 with the condition that affordable housing be created.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Trump clipped Biden's payouts for stranded travelers. It may not have helped during the ground stop
text:
President Donald Trump has blamed the nationwide grounding of all planes last week on old technology, as well as on his Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden.
Trump’s administration weakened Biden-era rules to help stranded travelers — though it would not likely have helped many after Friday’s FAA-ordered ground stop. That remuneration was tied to issues with the airlines themselves. And officials have said that the disruption that marooned thousands of travelers and led to cascading flight issues that bled into the new week resulted from a router issue in the aging air traffic control system — not with the airlines.
Here’s a look at what the Biden administration proposed to help alleviate travelers’ stress, and Trump’s subsequent actions:
Biden proposed cash compensation for delayed travelers
In its closing days at the end of 2024, the Biden administration took steps toward requiring airlines to pay cash and cover lodging and meals for stranded passengers. Awards started at $200, with compensation as high as $775 proposed for delays of nine hours or more.
The rule went far beyond requirements for airlines to pay ticket refunds, putting U.S. policy more closely in line with airline consumer protections in Europe. But the mechanism also hinged on issues with the airlines, not agencies like the FAA; flight cancellations or significant delays needed to originate with a mechanical problem with the plane or an airline computer outage.
Following last week’s ground stop, airlines largely waived rebooking fees for travelers seeking another flight and offered travel credits for use on a future flight. There were not blanket reimbursements offered for hotel and meal costs, not to mention the costs incurred for renting a car or somehow finding alternate travel.
Trump scrapped the compensation plans
Last year, the Trump administration announced it was abandoning the plan, calling the reversal “consistent with Department and administration priorities.” Under Secretary Sean Duffy, DOT formally withdrew its airline passenger-rights proposal a year ago, citing Trump’s directives aimed at reducing private companies’ financial burden to comply with regulations.
Industry trade group Airlines for America, which represents carriers including United, Delta and Southwest Airlines, welcomed the move by the Trump administration. Airlines already offer some level of customer service when they cause flight cancellations or severe delays, but passengers usually have to ask for help at the airport, and airline promises don’t carry the weight of federal rules.
Biden’s flight refund policy remains in effect
Thanks to a separate measure introduced in the Biden administration, airlines do have to give cash refunds but only when certain conditions are met, like if a flight is canceled and a passenger doesn’t want to take a rebooked trip.
A passenger would also be entitled to a refund if a domestic flight were delayed more than three hours, and they opted not to continue the trip.
___
Meg Kinnard can be reached at http://x.com/MegKinnardAP

title: Nationwide Emergency Alert System test scheduled Tuesday: What to know
text:
Nationwide Emergency Alert System test scheduled Tuesday: What to know
An important national emergency test is set for Tuesday, federal officials say, and is expected to interrupt television and radio programming nationwide.
On Nov. 17 around 2:20 p.m. ET, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, in coordination with the FCC, will conduct a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System.
It’s simply a test of the national public warning system, which is required by law to happen at least once every three years.
Related video above | FEMA wants states to shoulder more disaster costs. Can they afford it?
The test will briefly interrupt programming nationwide, and will last about one minute. If there is a true emergency during that time, federal officials say a backup test date is scheduled for Dec. 3.
The Emergency Alert System, or EAS, is a national public warning system that sends emergency messages over radio and television, as well as cable and satellite services.
It’s designed to let the president address the public within minutes during a national emergency, but state and local authorities also use it to warn people about threats such as severe weather and other emergencies.
Authorized officials send alerts through the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Integrated Public Alert and Warning System, which can distribute them to broadcasters and other services.
Radio and TV stations carry the alert, often interrupting regular programming with a distinctive tone and message.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency and Federal Communications Commission coordinate the system, with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration also involved in weather alerts. Broadcasters are required to test their EAS equipment regularly to check that alerts can be received and relayed.
This year’s test will not include Wireless Emergency Alerts sent to cell phones.

title: Drexel men’s basketball uses late free throws to hold off UMaine
text:
Senior guard LaDricus Pittman sank a pair of free throws with nine seconds left, and senior forward Pagonis Panagiotis added two of his own seven seconds later as Drexel University downed UMaine men’s basketball 66-64 in Orono on Saturday.
Drexel (PA) improved to 2-2, while UMaine fell to 1-4. It was UMaine’s third straight loss. All three losses in the losing streak have come by six points or less.
Drexel used a 14-6 run late in the game to build a 62-52 lead, but the Black Bears rallied to within one using a 9-0 run led by Darius Lopes and Hudson Franz.
Pittman’s free throws made it 64-61, and the Black Bears turned the ball over, enabling Pagonis to put the game out of reach with his pair from the stripe.
Drexel put five players in double figures.
Pagonis had 14 points and also contributed seven rebounds and three steals. Graduate student guard Amaree Abram had 13 points, four rebounds, four assists and two steals. Freshman Latief Lorenzano-White had 11 points, while freshman forward David Simonovic and junior forward Clem Edomwonyin each chipped in with 10 points.
Simonovic also had six rebounds and two steals.
Freshman guard Franz had a game-high and career-high 16 points, and his four 3-pointers were also a career high. Redshirt sophomore Lopes had a career-high 15 points.
Sophomore forward Ace Flagg from Newport had 12 points and five rebounds along with two assists. Senior forward Wyatt Triestman had eight points and two rebounds.
UMaine will travel to Hamden, Connecticut, to play Quinnipiac at 7 p.m. Thursday, while Drexel will host Philadelphia rival Saint Joseph’s at 7 p.m. Friday.

title: Technical issue triggers online banking delays across major US banks
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
However, Chase said Monday that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and that it was working to bring banking services back online by the end of the day Monday.
“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system — it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for the bank.
EN ESPAÑOL | Reportan interrupción en el servicio de varios bancos del país
The disruption comes days after technology troubles affected other parts of the U.S. economy: A major Microsoft outage on Thursday impacted services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. An outage affecting the nation’s air traffic control system Friday grounded all U.S. flights for several hours and disrupted air travel across the country over the weekend.
On Monday, United Airlines said that it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights,
In the same statement, Evangelisti said that this was a Chase-only issue.
“This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” he said.
Monday’s technical issues seemed to be centered at Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, including Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services.
A spokesman for U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly impacted but that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
Zelle is the peer-to-peer payment system that major U.S. banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed. Zelle is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.
A spokesman for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational.
“An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,” the spokesman said.
Some Chase customers received a message that said, “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”

title: Lindsay Clancy is set to stand trial for a second time, judge says
text:
PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — A Massachusetts judge on Monday scheduled Lindsay Clancy’s second trial in the killings of her three young children for late March, over the objections of prosecutors.
Clancy is charged with three counts of first-degree murder. Her first trial end in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the killings. Eleven jurors favored acquittal on the grounds of insanity, while one disagreed.
Prosecutors had sought a May trial date, citing scheduling conflicts, but Superior Court Judge William Sullivan set the retrial for March 29 in Plymouth Superior Court.
The decision to schedule Clancy’s second trial comes a week after Sullivan rejected a defense request to dismiss the charges. He ruled that a retrial would not violate Clancy’s constitutional protection against double jeopardy.
Attorneys are scheduled to return to court at 9 a.m. Dec. 30 to discuss trial logistics, security and media arrangements. A pretrial conference is set for Feb. 18.
Clancy’s lawyers had argued that the judge should have investigated or removed the lone juror who opposed acquittal before declaring a mistrial.
Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, has never disputed that she killed her three children at the family’s Duxbury home in January 2023. Her attorneys said she was suffering from severe mental illness at the time.
Prosecutors argued Clancy planned the killings and understood what she was doing.

title: Maine's heating oil prices have fallen 3%
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s heating oil prices have fallen 3% over the past week.
The average price for a gallon of heating oil is now $5.84, down from last week’s average of $6.01, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
In eastern and Down East Maine, prices range from a low of $5.16 to a high of $6.10.
Despite prices falling over the past two weeks from a record high of $6.05, that statewide average is 72% higher than this time last year, when heating oil went for $3.40 a gallon.
Mainers will still have to spend an additional $671 to fill a standard 275-gallon tank.
Energy prices have been climbing globally since February when President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched a surprise war against Iran. Although Trump said that the war would last only weeks, it has dragged on for more than eight months.
That war effectively halted fuel shipments out of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s natural gas and oil passes, for much of the year. The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine also has strained global fuel supplies as both sides have traded blows on each other’s energy infrastructure, and Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have attacked Saudi energy sites and seized territory along the Red Sea coast, another key trade route.
Last month, the Trump administration released about $37 million in low-income heating assistance for Maine. An additional $1.4 million was awarded to the state’s four federally recognized tribes. The administration also is tapping the Northeast heating oil reserves for the first time since 2012 when Hurricane Sandy devastated the northeastern U.S.
About half of Maine households ( more than 300,000) rely on heating oil to stay warm during the winter, and consumption can average 2 to 7 gallons a day, depending on how cold it is outside. That means the 13.2 million gallons flowing from the Northeast stockpile would amount to approximately nine days of consumption at a rate of five gallons a day.
Gov. Janet Mills last week renewed calls for Congress to increase federal low-income heating assistance, saying the program should be bolstered with $3 billion in additional funding to offset rising energy costs that are eating away at the aid’s purchasing power.
Rising energy costs and anger over the Iran war contributed to heavy losses for Republicans in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, including the ousting of U.S. Sen. Susan Collins after three decades representing Maine in Washington.
It’s unclear whether the election results will mean any relief from high oil prices. Last week, Trump declared the war “militarily effectively over” while saying that the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Iran and ordering Vice President JD Vance to redirect his attention away from diplomacy with the Islamic Republic to a domestic anti-fraud campaign. But later in the week, Trump left open renewed military strikes if the U.S. sees signs of activity near Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, the site of a nuclear facility bombed early in the 8-month conflict.

title: Athenahealth lays off 4% of workers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Healthcare technology company Athenahealth eliminated 4% of its jobs Friday, according to the Boston Globe.
It was not clear Monday how many employees at the company’s office in Belfast, if any, had been laid off in the job cuts. As of 2019, the Belfast office had about 900 employees.
In an email to the firm’s thousands of employees, CEO Bob Segert described several reasons for the layoffs, saying the company structure was overly complex, making it difficult to hold employees accountable, The Globe reported Monday. He also cited a low number of visits to healthcare providers, and an “opportunity … to rethink the work itself” using artificial intelligence, The Globe reported.
Athenahealth was co-founded in 1997 by Jonathan Bush, who lost the GOP primary this year to be the party’s nominee for governor of Maine. The company produces scheduling and billing software for doctors, and telehealth services.
In recent months, enhanced Affordable Care Act Marketplace subsidies have expired, likely causing patients to postpone procedures, the Globe reported.
A previous round of Athenahealth layoffs took place in February 2023, when 178 positions — less than 3% of the company’s workforce at the time — were cut.
Multiple Athenahealth employees at the Belfast branch declined to comment Friday. One employee said she was not aware of any layoffs, as her department had not been affected. The Athenahealth public relations team did not reply to a request for comment.
The Maine Department of Labor said Monday that it had not been notified of the layoffs. Under the Worker Adjustment & Retraining Notification Act, employers must provide 60 days of advance notice under certain conditions:
- They are closing a facility or operating unit of 50 or more workers
- Laying off 50 to 499 workers that make up 33% of the work force at a site
- Or laying off 500 or more workers at a site

title: Gorgeous Weather This Week—Sunny Skies and Warming Temperatures
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Strong high pressure over the Ohio Valley today will gradually build toward the East Coast as the week progresses. This will provide us with a beautiful week of weather for mid-November with sunshine... dry conditions... and warming temps as we head through the week.
We’ll see partly to mostly sunny skies today (leaning toward mostly sunny for much of the state)... with the bulk of the clouds across far northern and western locales. Temperatures will be seasonable with highs topping off in the low to mid-40s this afternoon. Clear skies and light winds will lead to a colder night tonight with lows dropping to the mid-20s to around 30°.
Tuesday will feature lots of sunshine with temperatures warming a few degrees better than today. Look for highs on Tuesday to range from the mid-40s to low 50s from north to south across the state. We’ll see a few more clouds on Wednesday especially across the north as moisture slides along a stalled out front well to our north. Expect partly to mostly cloudy skies Wednesday with the bulk of the clouds across Aroostook County. Temperatures will be a bit warmer with highs mainly in the 50s. Thursday and Friday look fantastic with sunshine and highs in the 50s to around 60°.
Of course it’s always great to get a beautiful stretch of weather like we have in store for the week ahead but it certainly doesn’t help us any with regard to the ongoing drought. With much of the state under moderate to severe drought conditions... we need rain badly. That being said... the next best chance of precipitation looks to be the potential for some showers later Sunday into Monday and even that doesn’t look like much at this point. Stay tuned for updates as we get closer and enjoy the week ahead.
Rest of Today: Partly to mostly sunny. Highs between 39°-47°. Northwest wind 5-10 MPH with gusts to 15-20 MPH possible.
Tonight: Clear and cold. Lows in the mid-20s to around 30°. Light and variable wind.
Tuesday: Lots of sunshine. Highs in the mid-40s to low 50s. West/northwest wind 5-10 MPH.
Wednesday: Partly to mostly cloudy... most clouds north. Highs in the upper 40s to mid-50s.
Thursday: Partly to mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s to around 60°.
Friday: Partly to mostly sunny. Highs in the 50s to around 60°.

title: York County substance recovery center touted as a first for Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A 50,000-square-foot substance use treatment and recovery center, under construction since last year in the York County town of Alfred, is expected to wrap up in mid-December and begin accepting patients in February.
The project is the first of its kind in Maine, Rachel Stansfield, chief advancement officer with First County Foundation, told Mainebiz.
The recovery center has 58 beds for medication-assisted detox, long-term residential treatment and intensive outpatient programming under one roof, which does not exist elsewhere, Stansfield noted.
“Further, our center will accept all forms of insurance, private pay and uninsured, making access to this center low-barrier,” she added.
First County Foundation, York County government’s charitable arm, was founded in 2023 to expand funding and diversify revenue for community initiatives. The money includes $40 million allocated to the county in American Rescue Plan funds and $4.5 million from opioid settlements.
Out of the total, $28 million was allocated to two major initiatives, both in Alfred: construction of the York County Substance Use Treatment and Recovery Center and the York County First Responder Training Facility.
Responder training
The 44,000-square-foot first responder training center has been open since January.
“The building is fully operational; we began holding classes in January 2026,” said Stansfield. “It’s a very nice building and has had hundreds of students/professionals utilizing the space, trainings and classes.”
The center is designed to be a regional training hub for police, firefighters, emergency medical services and dispatchers. The center also houses an Emergency Logistics Operations Center, which plays a crucial role in disaster response coordination.
A key component is a five-story, multi-use drill tower manufactured by Draeger, an international firm with a U.S. base in Houston. The tower is made of recycled steel shipping containers and has 12 compartments where instructors can engineer a variety of scenarios to prepare students for real-world work. Components of firefighting — including ventilation, heat management, door control — can be facilitated using the tower.
Recovery center
The recovery center, next to the training center, is the foundation’s biggest focus.
“We will be hiring many positions,” she said. “This includes, but is not limited to, registered nurses, clinical drug and alcohol counselors and case managers.”
The need for the facility is pressing, Stansfield said.
“The opioid epidemic has plagued our communities, taking the lives of our neighbors, parents, sons, daughters and friends,” she noted.
In 2023, Maine law enforcement and emergency medical services responded to 9,659 overdoses throughout the state, including 606 that were fatal.
“Unfortunately, the state of Maine only has five non-hospital detox facilities and 19 residential treatment facilities to support the thousands of Mainers battling substance use disorder,” she said.
On average, those centers have the capacity to treat only 13 or 14 individuals at a time, leaving many with nowhere to go, and York County currently has no detox treatment centers.
Even with the new center, the need is likely to persist.
“Unfortunately, the need for residential treatment and recovery programs may never be met,” Stansfield said. “However, York County is taking a big step in the right direction by opening a facility that will have 58 beds, open 24/7/365, and by offering a broad reach of trauma-informed, holistic treatment options in one location.”
$44 million
The project cost for both facilities is $44 million, funded by the American Rescue Plan Act, opioid settlement funds, county reserves, charitable contributions and congressionally directed spending.
The project team includes Landry/French Construction Co. in Scarborough to manage the build, design team Lassel Architects in South Berwick and Biddeford’s Oak Point Associates, and engineering firms Sebago Technics in South Portland and JSN Associates in Portsmouth, N.H.
Both centers provide services to all 29 towns in York County as well as surrounding communities. For the responder center, it’s anticipated that some training opportunities will draw from other states.
As long as there are beds available, the recovery center will take individuals from other counties or out-of-state.

title: UN-backed talks consider possible rules on lethal autonomous weapons
text:
UN-backed talks consider possible rules on lethal autonomous weapons
Killer robots and drones come up for a reckoning this week as government envoys rev up a discussion and could decide whether to launch negotiations toward setting rules for use of the deadly machines — or not.
Pope Leo XIV, the U.N. chief and advocacy groups cast the issue as an existential debate: Whether robots can be allowed to kill and whether humans must maintain some control of and accountability for use of lethal autonomous weapon systems.
Related video: Air travel expected to recover Monday following ground stop as lawmakers debate next steps
Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones like Ukraine and the Middle East, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened.
Scary would-be scenarios, like armed drones flying amok and gunning down civilians with pinpoint precision, have peppered years of discussions about killer robots. But those talks haven't produced any international restrictions.
The United States and Russia, longtime rivals, want to limit any curbs on their abilities to develop and roll out powerful new tools for the high-tech arms race — just as AI is gaining steam and changing battle plans.
UN meeting comes after 7 countries seek negotiations
The issue comes to a head at U.N. offices in Geneva, where a 7th review conference about the awkwardly named Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons will consider whether to start talks on regulation of killer robots.
Supporters of an accord acknowledge powerful forces are in the way, but point to precedent: Governments have already struck a deal to regulate blinding lasers.
Most countries support reining them in. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ deadline this year for the launch of talks toward regulation has given the issue urgency, but some top military powers are hesitant.
Last month, seven countries— Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand, and Panama— submitted a proposal to launch negotiations of a new legally binding agreement on autonomous weapons at the conference.
The various sides have been gearing up for the diplomatic standoff.
On Friday, International Committee of the Red Cross president Mirjana Spoljaric said in a statement: “States must act to ensure the future of warfare is not handed over to machines.”
Stop Killer Robots, an advocacy group, says 130 countries support new international rules on the weapons systems.
Activists began running advertisements in the streets and subways of Berlin, London and Paris touting public support for reining in killer robots.
Russia says talks on restrictions are ‘premature’
In his first encyclical in May, the pope denounced a “culture of power” driving the AI race, especially in developing ever more sophisticated methods of remote warfare, and said it's not permissible to entrust decisions about life and death to remote AI systems.
The U.N. human rights chief, Volker Türk, called Monday for nations to “urgently” agree on binding rules on lethal autonomous weapons systems.
“The international community has critical choices to make, right now, about the future of armed conflicts and the role of human beings in decisions over the use of force," he said.
Under the convention’s rules, decisions must be made by consensus. That means that any single country can thwart an agreement, and that any such deal is likely to be based on a low common denominator. Another sticking point is how long negotiators might be given to try to agree on language.
In the run-up to this week’s conference, humanitarians and activist groups said Russia looked ready to deploy tactics to slow or even stall progress toward launching formal negotiations.
“Russia attaches great importance to the successful outcome of the conference and to reaching mutually acceptable agreements that will help strengthen the Inhumane Weapons Convention and further its universalization,” Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told reporters on Wednesday.
Moscow wants “organizational matters” to be ironed out first and see a process “free from politicization,” she said.
Most tellingly, Zakharova said: “We consider it premature to argue that the time has supposedly come to develop restrictive or prohibitive measures concerning such systems.”

title: Maine man seeks personal growth in restoration of historic racing yacht he bought for $10
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Tom Hollyday’s first time living and working on a boat through a high-stakes restoration project taught him many valuable life lessons.
After an “unconventional” childhood, he had found structure, a livelihood and a safe place to live in Maine’s schooner industry. That led him to a big undertaking restoring one boat, and the feeling of the hard work paying off is one he’ll probably chase for the rest of his life, he said.
Hollyday, now of Brooksville, is chasing that feeling with a new project: one of the country’s oldest racing yachts, the Elf, which he bought from its longtime owner for just $10.
The boat has its problems, but he’s working on plans and a search for investment to make it seaworthy. Hollyday aims to have it in the water this summer in Brooksville and eventually hopes to offer it for community sailing to pay forward what he learned working in Maine’s windjammer industry — skills that helped him adapt to adulthood and grow as a person.
“The one thing I feel I can give back is those skills,” he said. “So this becomes kind of a platform for me for not only the community to enjoy an old boat, but for me to do right by those people who’ve taught me those things, by keeping those skills alive.”
Elf was designed for racing and built around 1888, according to materials nominating it for the National Register of Historic Places, where it has been listed since 1980.
It was the start of small class racing yachts, or 30- to 35-foot yachts that people used for longer cruising trips, Hollyday said. Its original owner also used it as a kind of laboratory for splicing wire to rope, he said, a technique now commonly used in boat rigging.
An early owner sailed Elf from Massachusetts to Nova Scotia in 1893, according to an account in its National Register nomination. Offshore cruising in small yachts was “almost unknown” at the time and became a sport after that trip, he wrote.
Elf’s most recent owner, Richard Carrion, bought it in 1971 as a 19-year-old student working his way through college in Maryland, he wrote in nominating the vessel for the national register. He moved onboard and did the necessary work himself, docking near campus and bicycling to class during the semester.
In the 1980s, he started a decades-long rebuild of the vessel with a shipwright, using mostly timber from his own tree farm, finally relaunching it in 2009, according to Hollyday. Carrion kept its original deadwood keel and stem at its front.
Last year, Hollyday found Elf listed online for around $300,000 and talked him down to $10 based on problems visible in photos, bringing it from Maryland to Maine last January.
He’d been keeping his eye out for a new boat to work on after a pandemic-era project with the Hesper, which he oversaw restoration of and ran expeditions on for an employer in Portland and later as his own expedition business based in Camden.
Hollyday’s boss had originally given him the go-ahead to run a sailing program if he could find a suitable boat, but the Hesper arrived in worse shape than expected. He lived in his van next to the boat shed, pulling long days with everything he had at stake – and succeeded.
Working and living on a vessel exposes one’s weaknesses and requires facing them, he said.
“You learn about completion and like attention to detail and being focused and kind of having everything simplified for you,” he said. “…Those basic, kind of like human things, you know, the boat’s just proven to be kind of like a camp for me for that.”
He’d also never felt the accomplishment of making something objectively beautiful through the work of his hands, he said. Hesper eventually won an award for the most photogenic boat at the Eggemoggin Reach Regatta, a wooden boat race in Brooklin.
“That was kind of a feeling that I’ve always kind of wanted to chase again, because it’s really a culmination of like, oh, you can finish a task, you can complete a project, you can, you know, wake up on time and like get in and do these things, right?” Hollyday said. “Like, you’re capable of doing that, and this is the evidence…and I think that as a human being, I’m probably gonna need to chase that for the rest of my life, unfortunately.”
After Hesper sold, he came to Brooksville in 2025 to manage the Buck’s Harbor Marina in town. He wanted to find his next boat, but it had to be unique.
Now, Elf faces some fundamental problems tied in part to those remnants. The newer nails fastening the boat together are rusted out, and the rebuild appears to have made the Elf shorter than it looks in historical photographs, throwing off the lines.
That complicates plans for restoration, Hollyday said.
He’s had a 3D scan made and is working with Brooklin builders Hylan and Brown to create a work proposal.
Next steps would also depend on the interests and goals of an investor, and he couldn’t estimate a cost, he said.
A rebuild would require work from a larger yard, either creating an entirely new boat or opening up the existing one and lengthening it.
But Hollyday plans to do some basic work himself to get Elf in the water at Buck’s Harbor this summer where people can see it, making it a more marketable project. The marina already rents out unique wooden vessels through the “classic boat collective” program Hollyday founded, though he said Elf is a separate personal project.
Hollyday has seen many other wooden boat restoration projects falter, often because they don’t have access to marina services, but his project is unique because Buck’s Harbor resources essentially come with the boat, he said.
He thinks it’s possible to shore up Elf without having to create an entirely new boat from a mold of the existing one. It’s not clear how that might affect the National Register listing, but that’s less important than what the vessel itself means, he said.
It’s an ancient question, going back to the philosophical thought experiment of the Ship of Theseus: as each board on a vessel is replaced over time, when is it no longer the same vessel?
To Hollyday, the answer doesn’t really matter.
“It’s more about like how the boat invests in me and helps me stay on track as a human,” he said.

title: Hospitals are adding programs to support family caregivers
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A growing number of hospitals are offering programs designed to support family caregivers. Experts say that support can improve outcomes and reduce costly trips to the hospital.
More than 60 million Americans provide care that includes bathing, managing medications and getting sick or aging loved ones to appointments.
According to AARP, family caregivers provide more than $1 trillion worth of unpaid care each year. Nearly a quarter of them say the role makes it hard to take care of their own needs.
A family faces a terminal diagnosis
Joe and Ashleigh Quirarte were married in 2017 and promised “in sickness and in health.” Ashleigh said she did not expect that vow to be tested so soon.
“I thought maybe one day I’d take care of you, but we’d be like 80,” Ashleigh said.
In late 2024, at 38, Joe had a medical emergency.
“Randomly, with no warning whatsoever, I had a seizure at my mom’s house one night,” Joe said.
“Over the course of the next few days, we learned that he had a tumor,” Ashleigh said.
Joe was diagnosed with glioblastoma, a rare and aggressive brain cancer without a cure. Ashleigh became his primary caregiver with no medical background.
“I had no idea where to even start,” Ashleigh said. “It’s so incredibly overwhelming, and even the smaller things like caring for his wound after the surgery were still really intimidating.”
Program supports caregivers of brain tumor patients
Ashleigh said the University of California San Francisco’s neuro-oncology caregiver program helped her find strength and support.
“The caregiver program is absolutely a lifeline, and my heart breaks for people who have to go through this and don’t have that support, because it’s crucial,” she said.
Cherrie DeMayo, a UCSF nurse coordinator, said caregiver support is built into the care plan. It includes education, guidance and connection.
“That form of connection, we’ve found, has really made people be more resilient and able to kind of keep moving forward,” DeMayo said.
Ashleigh said she began attending monthly support groups.
“For the first time, was able to feel like other people understood what I was going through,” she said.
The program launched in 2014 and has supported more than 5,000 caregivers, according to the report. It is free for caregivers of UCSF brain tumor patients. Dr. Susan Chang, UCSF’s director of neuro-oncology, founded and directs it.
DeMayo said much of the support is emotional and includes anticipatory guidance.
“Figuring out kind of what to expect in the coming months. What are these symptoms that they’re experiencing?” DeMayo said.
Ashleigh said her caregiver community helped her recognize Joe’s personality changes during treatment as more than stress.
“I’ve learned so much through the caregiver program just about what to expect for possible side effects for treatment, different treatment options, sort of these like peripheral symptoms,” she said. Asked if she felt better prepared, she said, “Absolutely.”
“This is a necessary part of taking care of a patient, is taking care of the caregiver,” Chang said.
Asked if she hopes the program serves as a national model, Chang said: “Absolutely. We want this to be a priority for institutions, for medical health care systems, to recognize that these are what I call the silent heroes.”
UCSF says its program is the first of its kind in neuro-oncology.
Serving caregivers regardless of condition
In Chicago, Rush University Medical Center created a program for caregivers, no matter what condition their loved one is facing.
“Caregivers are already doing everything they can, and they’re really the default health care, long-term care system. So we owe them,” said Diane Mariani, program manager for Rush’s Caring for Caregivers.
Mariani said the model connects caregivers to counseling, support groups, respite and community resources such as Meals on Wheels. Sessions can be billed through insurance.
“We’re reducing the stress, and some of those symptoms that caregivers are having,” Mariani said.
Mariani said outcomes are improving for caregivers and for patients, including shorter hospital stays and fewer emergency room visits.
“What we see and what we hear from our caregivers is they’re just more confident and don’t feel like, ‘Oh, my gosh, this is an emergency,’” she said.
Rush created its model in 2019 to support caregivers of patients over age 60. Mariani said Rush hopes to expand it in the coming years.
Rush is sharing the model with support from grant funding. Mariani said about a dozen health systems around the country are implementing it, and she would like to see that number grow.
“Health systems are all kind of stretched, I would say. It’s kind of where we’re at in our world,” she said.
Need is outpacing help
For years, communities have relied on local organizations for caregiver assistance, including area agencies on aging, a federally funded network of more than 600 nonprofit organizations.
USAging, the national association of area agencies on aging, says the need is outpacing the help.
“The caregiver’s role is increasing. It’s also becoming more complicated because of the level of care that people need,” said Sandy Markwood, USAging’s CEO.
Markwood said the organization is collaborating with hospitals to support family caregivers. She said she would like to see this workforce become a greater national priority.
Asked what her message would be to lawmakers, Markwood said: “This is an issue that can’t be ignored anymore. We need to keep people living well, aging well at home and in the community, and they can’t do that unless we also invest in their important caregivers.”
“This is a call to action for all of us taking care of patients, where we put a priority on also taking care of the caregiver,” Chang said.
Federal legislation
In May 2026, legislators introduced a bill to better identify the needs of people caring for children and aging parents at the same time.
In 2025, Congress reintroduced a bill that would offer working family caregivers a federal tax credit of up to $5,000.
Since sharing his story with InvestigateTV+, Joe Quirarte has passed away. He died peacefully on Oct. 17, 2026, surrounded by his loved ones.

title: Endangered whale population drops again
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The North Atlantic right whale population slipped again in 2025, alarming scientists who warn that the endangered species remains locked in a fight for survival because of human-caused injuries and shifting ocean conditions.
The population dipped from an estimated 389 individuals in 2024 to 382 in 2025, according to whale researchers gathered at the annual North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium in Halifax, Nova Scotia, on Monday. The new count carries a margin of error of plus or minus 11 whales and comes against the backdrop of the most successful calving season since 2009.
“More work is needed to protect this species,” said consortium chairman Heather Pettis, senior scientist at the New England Aquarium. “The population is not yet on a clear path to recovery and is incredibly vulnerable to entanglements and vessel strikes, threats we know how to reduce.”
The population drop arrives at a critical time for Maine’s $2 billion lobster industry, which has spent years fighting federal regulations designed to protect the whale from gear entanglements. Lobstermen say their gear plays a smaller role in whale deaths than what regulators initially assumed.
Only one right whale death can be directly attributed to entanglement in Maine lobstering gear, industry officials say. Whale scientists note most whales that die from entanglement no longer have any rope attached, so knowing which fishery is to blame is impossible.
The industry’s arguments might have won over federal regulators, if not consortium scientists. Earlier this month, regulators announced initial findings from a new scientific model that indicate U.S. fisheries account for about 25% of entanglements — half the amount previously assumed.
Carl Wilson, the commissioner of the Maine Department of Marine Resources, welcomed the agency’s shift in a bulletin to lobstermen. He said the update represents a commitment to sound science that avoids relying on worst-case scenarios.
This reduction could bring estimated U.S. fishery mortality within the federal limit known as potential biological removal, which defines the maximum number of human-caused deaths a marine mammal population can sustain and still recover.
In 2019, regulators decided to attribute half of the annual whale deaths to U.S. fisheries, which exceeded that biological removal limit and prompted a wave of whale-protective fishing rules, such as the three-month closure of 967 square miles in Maine’s offshore lobstering grounds.
State research funded by federal grants has demonstrated that right whales rarely enter Maine state waters, resulting in far less overlap between local lobster gear and migrating whales than federal models projected.
In 2023, the Maine Lobstermen’s Association won a federal appeals court ruling that rejected previous government risk models as flawed. Federal lawmakers have delayed new fishery rules through 2028, and are considering extending that moratorium to 2035.
Consortium scientists warned federal regulators against rolling back any protection measures.
“Recovery for this species depends on sustained protective actions,” said Pettis, the consortium’s chair. “Actions to further delay entanglement protections and deregulate vessel strike reduction measures will stall meaningful progress that is already underway to protect the species.”
Human activities continue to harm the species, scientists say.
Researchers logged two right whale deaths in 2026, alongside eight human-caused injuries. In January, a 4-year-old male entangled in Canadian snow crab gear died off North Carolina. A 3-year-old female washed ashore dead in Virginia in February from unknown causes.
Of seven reported entanglements in 2026, three whales were observed still carrying the ropes, according to consortium data. One whale carried Massachusetts state lobster gear, while two were seen in Canadian waters with gear of unknown origin.
The right whale’s 2025 population is 20% below the species’ recent peak of 483 whales recorded in 2011. Scientists estimated that the number of breeding females held steady at 73, highlighting the ongoing difficulty of replenishing the stock.
Researchers pointed to one encouraging sign: Females gave birth to 24 calves during the 2025–26 calving season, the highest single-year total since 2009. Scientists don’t include newborn calves in the 2025 population estimate because young whales face high mortality rates.
“The whales are doing their part,” said Philip Hamilton, a senior scientist at the New England Aquarium. “But the overall lack of growth in the population is even more concerning when seen in the context of a number of proposed management setbacks in the U.S. this year.”
The consortium will compile a comprehensive annual report early in 2027, giving regulators and fishermen a clearer look at the right whale’s future before federal advisory meetings on how the new statistical model will affect Maine’s lobster fleet resume in March.

title: Trump’s handpicked party chair faces a rebellion after midterm losses test president’s grip on GOP
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A nascent rebellion is underway against President Donald Trump’s handpicked chairman at the Republican National Committee, and it’s already getting ugly.
Some members are calling for a forensic audit of spending decisions, including hair and makeup services for Trump and other officials, as well as the hiring of the daughter of Trump’s former chief of staff. Feuding Republicans are leaking emails and opposition research on rival factions. The White House is threatening to cut off fundraising assistance if the rebels don’t fall in line.
The emerging fight, which will shape the 2028 presidential nominating contest, represents a rare challenge to Trump’s dominance, even after the party’s worst midterm performance in a generation. Despite the broad losses, Republican leaders across Washington have shown little desire to move past Trump and have largely stood behind his most unpopular policies.
But inside the Republican National Committee, an organization of 168 members elected from every state who oversee the party’s national political operation, a small and growing collection of concerned Republicans are backing an attempt to depose Joe Gruters. Trump wants to keep him in charge.
The dissidents are rallying behind Kentucky’s KC Crosbie, the RNC’s second-in-command. She launched her bid just two days after the Nov. 3 election in a letter that drew the fury of both the White House and Gruters’ allies.
Crosbie remains a vocal Trump supporter who backs his “Make America Great Again” agenda, but her opponents view her gambit as a direct challenge to the president and his power.
“Our job is to elect Republicans broadly, not to support one man all the time,” said RNC member Oscar Brock of Tennessee, who is supporting Crosbie’s candidacy. He said that requires a change in leadership because “there’s so much frustration that Chairman Gruters didn’t pull his weight in this election.”
In her letter, Crosbie described the midterms as “a serious setback” and called for the RNC to provide “an honest account” of what went wrong.
Crosbie declined to be interviewed.
The leadership election will be held in January at the RNC’s winter meeting in Arizona.
Inside the rebellion against Gruters
Some would-be Crosbie supporters privately acknowledge they’re worried about a backlash from the White House, especially with Stephen Miller taking over as Trump’s chief of staff. Others believe in the committee’s tradition of having presidents pick their own party chiefs.
Gruters also has vocal backers.
Lauren LePage, an RNC member from Maine, praised Gruters’ leadership and efforts to help her father, Paul LePage, flip a congressional seat — a rare bright spot for Republicans this cycle.
“From my perspective, as chairman, he did his job,” she said, adding that Trump’s endorsement is “something that the committee should take very seriously.”
The Republicans who have lined up behind Crosbie insist a leadership change is needed to send a clear message that the party will do things differently after losses even in Republican strongholds like Texas, South Carolina and Mississippi.
Patti Lyman, an RNC member from Virginia, said it would be “catastrophic” and “insulting” to the party’s base “to keep the same leadership and pretend that we don’t need to do anything different, that we don’t need new players and a new plan.”
Sue Cienki, an RNC committee member from Rhode Island, predicted that Crosbie would have the backing of at least two members from 10 states — a total of 20 — at the committee’s January meeting. That’s the minimum required for a successful nomination.
Trump is furious with Crosbie
Trump and senior White House officials were livid about Crosbie’s Nov. 5 letter and the fact that they were given no heads-up. The president soon released a lengthy statement on his Truth Social social media platform hailing Gruters as a “MAGA Warrior” and giving him his “Complete and Total Endorsement.”
Trump is expected to play a central role in picking the party’s next presidential nominee.
The party’s future is at stake
Allies of Gruters say a leadership change now would put the RNC at a severe disadvantage heading into the next presidential cycle because a new team would need time to get up to speed. They say friction between the president and the committee’s leadership would curtail their ability to organize and raise money.
They also reject Crosbie’s call for a postelection review, which they said would do little more than consume six months rehashing the past and put all their grievances on paper.
Gruters spent much of this week holding private phone conversations with committee members. Those who participated in the calls said Gruters listened to their grievances, but said little about what he would do differently.
Spending faces scrutiny
The opposition to Gruters has focused on the RNC’s spending decisions under him. Republicans had a massive fundraising advantage and still had deep losses.
“There’s clearly a groundswell of support for a forensic audit,” said Brock, the RNC member from Tennessee.
In a letter to RNC members sent Thursday night and obtained by The Associated Press, Gruters acknowledged concerns about spending and other issues.
Gruters defended a $22,500 expenditure for hospitality space at the Presidents Cup, a golf event, saying the space was offered to major donors and “resulted in $2.5 million in renewed contributions to the RNC.”
He also addressed “a brief contract” between the RNC and Caroline Wiles, a longtime Republican consultant, who is the daughter of Susie Wiles, Trump’s former chief of staff. Gruters said she was hired by his predecessor at the committee, Michael Whatley.
“While I have no reason to doubt Caroline Wiles’s value to the RNC or Chairman Whatley’s reasons for bringing her on, this was a brief six-month engagement that ended when I was elected Chairman,” he wrote.
Gruters also defended the RNC’s decision to pay for “hair and make-up services” for senior White House officials, including Trump, Vice President JD Vance and former press secretary Karoline Leavitt.
“This was a request made of us so that the expense did not fall to taxpayers,” Gruters wrote, adding that the beneficiaries “generously gave so much of their limited time and energies to help the RNC this cycle” and “did not ask for much of us in return, so we felt this was a request we could accommodate.”

title: Grammy Awards 2027: See the list of nominees
text:

The British singer-songwriter Raye became this year’s most nominated performer, scoring 11 nods, while Spanish artist Rosalía and country star Ella Langley weren’t far behind, with nine and seven nominations, respectively.

title: 13 Maine spots for thrifters seeking vintage with variety
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Sure, shopping at secondhand or vintage stores for old clothes, furniture or dishes can be great a way to save money.
But it’s also a ton of fun, and educational. It’s like a cultural history expedition, browsing some giant flea market, multi-vendor consignment shop or antiques mall. You’re likely to find a huge variety of vintage treasures, including old Bakelite radios, colorful vintage Fiestaware or a Boy Scout uniform from 1961.
Luckily Maine has plenty of places where you can browse all kinds of secondhand stuff — including vintage and antiques — for hours and hours. Here are a few suggestions.
1713 Portland Road, Arundel. arundelantiquevillage.com
This giant two-story building has goods from more than 200 dealers in some 250 display areas, including some in locked cases. There’s lot of cool ephemera, like postcards, magazines and maps, as well as housewares, clothes, toys, tools and myriad other stuff. This spot is really a two-for-one browsing adventure, since Antiques USA is right across the street. That cavernous building, with areas divided up into hundreds of spaces for dealers, has lots of furniture and decor, plus old advertising signs, clothes, toys and dishware.
156 Main St., Biddeford. On facebook.com.
This is a curated, multi-vendor store with collectibles, antiques and vintage items. There are shoes, clothes, decor, art, lamps, and cookware, radios, figurines and art. The vendors are also collectors themselves.
19 Main St., Cornish. cornishtrading.com
In the center of picturesque Cornish village, this is a multi-dealer antique shop that’s been in business since 1988 in a classic old building on Main Street. Its eclectic and upscale selection includes early American and Continental furniture and accessories, country antiques, architectural elements, textiles, decorative furniture and objects.
382 Skowhegan Road, Fairfield. fairfieldantiquesmall.com
This massive complex has thousands of antiques and vintage pieces on five levels, brought in by more than 100 dealers. There’s antique furniture, arranged in roomlike settings, rustic bumper pool tables, taxidermy, old gas station signs, clothing, bowls and dishes and much more.
308 U.S. Route 1, Freeport. On facebook.com
There are more than 30 dealers at this antique group shop. Browsing you’ll find dishware, furniture, old ad signs, art, tools and more. You can see some of the merchandise on the venue’s Instagram account.
26 U.S. Route 1, York. hiddentreasuresmaine.com
There are 90 antique dealers at this multi-dealer shop, with inventory being updated daily. The place carries a wide variety of antiques, collectibles and vintage clothing, as well as toys, decor, pottery, trading cards and more.
855 Roosevelt Trail, North Windham. On facebook.com
This shop is crammed with vintage and retro collectibles and goodies. You are likely to find shoes, glassware, maps, jewelry, holiday decor, tote bags and purses, cookware, an old radio and more. You can also take a look at some of the inventory on the store’s TikTok account.
585 Congress St., Portland. openhouseportland.com
This multi-dealer venue is in the space where Flea-For-All was. It’s well staged, with some sections looking like a museum of mid-20th century furniture. There are often some pretty substantial pieces, like wall-sized bookcases or extra-long couches. There’s also usually a really big selection of vintage clothes. You can see some of what’s been there on the store’s Instagram account.
919 Congress St., Portland. portlandantiquesmall.com.
This space near Maine Medical Center is part of the same group that includes the Fairfield Antiques Mall and the York Antiques Mall & Gallery. It opened in March where Salvage BBQ had been located. There are booths and display cases housing the wares of more than 75 vendors, on two floors. There’s lots of furniture, wall art, collectibles, memorabilia, plus salvage and unique finds.
151 Water St. Hallowell. therusticatorsemporium.com
This multi-vendor shop is in downtown Hallowell, long known as an antiquing destination. The place offers curated antiques, decor and gifts. You can see some of their inventory on Instagram.
59 Main St., Bridgton. On facebook.com
This multi-vendor group shop in the heart of Bridgton is located in a bright yellow old house. Two floors are filled with an eclectic mix of vintage items, collectibles, handmade goods and more.
14 Maine St., Brunswick. On facebook.com
This 25,000-square-foot indoor flea market is housed in the historic Fort Andross Mill, downtown. There are more than 60 long-term vendors in 90 booth spaces, with pop-up vendors as well. Among the massive selection, you’ll find antiques, collectibles, clothing, jewelry, furniture, home décor, original artwork, books and ephemera, among other things.

title: Mainer Amy Allen could make history at the Grammys again
text:
Maine native Amy Allen could make history at the Grammys again
Allen, who grew up in Windham, has been nominated for Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical at the 69th Grammy Awards, an award she won back-to-back in 2025 and 2026.
Maine native Amy Allen could make history at the Grammys again
Allen, who grew up in Windham, has been nominated for Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical at the 69th Grammy Awards, an award she won back-to-back in 2025 and 2026.
Maine native and three-time Grammy winner Amy Allen has once again been nominated for 2027 Songwriter of the Year in the non-classical category.
Allen is the only person to win the category multiple times. This is Allen's fourth nomination in the category, and a win would make her the category's first three-time winner.
In 2025, she became the first woman to win the award, and at the 2026 Grammy Awards she became the first person to win the award twice in a row. Allen also has a Grammy win from 2023, for her work on Harry Styles' album "Harry's House," which won Album of the Year.
Allen, who is originally from Windham, announced her inclusion in the 2027 nominees during "Good Morning America" on Monday
"It's shining a light on a craft that has long been behind the scenes," Allen said. "As we've learned from the inspiring songwriters before us, it all begins with a song, and great songs begin with who else, the songwriters. Congratulations to all the nominees."
Allen is being nominated for her songwriting credits on "Cry Ugly" by FLO, "Dashboard" by Noah Kahan, "drop dead" and "expectations" by Olivia Rodrigo, "For Always" by Ed Sheeran, "Likey Likey" by Young Miko, "So Easy (To Fall In Love)" by Olivia Dean, "Stupid" by Megan Moroney, and "Virtuoso" by Ryan Beatty.
The other artists nominated for 2027 Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical include Edgar Barrera, RAYE, Joybeth Taylor, and Theron Thomas.
The 69th Annual Grammy Awards will be held Sunday, Feb. 7, 2027, in Los Angeles.

title: Beyoncé becomes the first artist to reach 100 Grammy nominations
text:
(CNN) - Beyoncé is making Grammy history once again.
The superstar is now the first artist to reach 100 career nominations.
Her latest nod is for Best R&B Solo Performance for her song “MORNING DEW (DONK).”
The previously unreleased track dropped in July, ahead of the 20th anniversary of her album “B’Day.”
Beyoncé has been nominated for Grammys almost every year since her group Destiny’s Child picked up two nods in 2000 for “Bills, Bills, Bills.”
She is also the most-awarded artist in Grammy history, with 35 wins.
The 2027 Grammy Awards are set for Feb. 7in Los Angeles.

title: UMaine needs some advice on its advising system
text:
EDITORIAL: The ins and outs of the college system can be complex. To combat this, colleges widely offer a faculty advisor to help students out with making decisions and completing certain tasks. However, the effectiveness of the advising system is at many times limited due to the lack of availability of the advisors. This can leave students, especially those who lack prior knowledge of the college system or guidance from family members, to make decisions that are not in their best interest and can cost them time and money. For these reasons, the University of Maine needs to rethink its academic advising system.
Just to be clear, we are not casting blame on the professors, or graduate and doctoral students, who are put into the advisor role. They are concerned with many things: teaching classes, trying to get research funded, trying to get published, finishing their dissertation and most importantly, keeping their jobs. The life of a college professor is one that is filled with many responsibilities and pressures. This reality has only grown since most colleges have moved toward a model that is more dependent on adjunct and assistant professors and gives fewer and fewer professors tenure. Combine that with the fact that universities are tightening their budgets nationwide, and it’s no wonder why advising isn’t on the top of most professors’ minds.
While it is unfair to place this responsibility on an already overworked faculty member, it is also unfair what most undergraduate students are getting from their advising. Advising is more than just telling you what classes you need to take. If that was the case, the Degree Progress Report would be all you need. Advising is helping you make decisions about your future, it’s getting help with the logistics and paperwork of applications, dropping a class late, handling troubles that pop up in your academic career and above all else, a human to human connection to help you through college. But in many cases, we, the students, are not even able to get a hold of our advisors, let alone establish a relationship that delivers on the things previously mentioned.
So how does this system change for the better? Our idea is that UMaine shifts the role of the advisor from professors to an actual position, which would allow the employee to have the time to connect with and assist students in their academic career. This is not something that is foreign to most colleges or even UMaine. The Honors College has a dedicated honors advisor, Sandra Caceres Tijerina, who assists honors college students both in completing their curriculum and in their future endeavors. She provides services like connecting students with people in their desired fields and brainstorming opportunities for future careers.
Different colleges in the university could implement similar positions, hiring individuals with a specialized skill set to help students in a way that is actually useful, instead of using the system we have currently.
UMaine should make the student advisor an actual position. This would provide students from all backgrounds with a much better college experience and prepare them for life after graduation.

title: What to know about measles outbreaks as the US faces losing its elimination status
text:
What to know about measles outbreaks as the US faces losing its elimination status
An international committee met last week to decide whether the United States no longer has eliminated measles.
Measles cases have surged in the U.S. over the past couple of years. In 2026, the number of cases has already reached 5,412 — the highest since 1991.
The Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission met from Nov. 10-13 to discuss both the status of measles in the U.S. and Mexico. Last year, Canada lost its elimination status for the illness.
The Get the Facts Data Team broke down what to know about measles outbreaks in the U.S.
How many measles infections have been reported in the U.S. this year?
The more than five thousand cases reported in 2026 are more than double the amount from 2025. Infections have been reported in 46 states plus Washington, D.C.
Measles was considered eliminated from the U.S. in 2000. Elimination requires a country to not have very large outbreaks and 12 months or more of uncontrolled transmission, according to KFF.
Prior to the creation of the measles vaccine in 1963, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that three to four million people were infected every year.
Where are measles outbreaks the worst?
Almost every state has reported measles infections in 2026. The most measles cases have been reported in Pennsylvania, where more than 1,500 people have been infected and seven people have died, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.
Lancaster County has seen the highest concentration of infections, with 528 as of Friday.
How have measles vaccination rates changed?
The nationwide rate of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine has declined over several years, reaching 92.4% among kindergartners in the 2025-26 school year.
The rate of vaccinations declined overall among kindergartners, with a record 4% of nonmedical exemptions documented. That's an increase from 1.9% in the 2020-21 school year.

title: Days of sunshine ahead
text:
Days of sunshine ahead
Days of sunshine ahead
Our stretch of dry and unusually mild November weather will continue through the week and into the weekend. High pressure will keep storms away from northern New England, with afternoon temperatures running well above normal. Highs could reach 60 to 65 degrees in parts of southern Maine and New Hampshire, although clear skies and light winds will allow for chilly nights.
While the mild weather may be enjoyable, the continued lack of rain will only worsen the ongoing drought across much of the region.
Looking ahead to early next week, there are signs of a possible storm system that could bring some much-needed precipitation. However, models still disagree on the timing, track, and how much rain we might receive. We'll be watching this closely over the coming days.
