title: Right whale population dipped again in 2025
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The North Atlantic right whale population dropped by about 2% in 2025, according to new estimates released Monday from the New England Aquarium and the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium.
Scientists estimate there are about 382 right whales, down slightly from the previous year’s count, which was adjusted up to account for new data.
The new estimates will be reviewed by the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium, which is holding its annual meeting in Nova Scotia this week.
Heather Pettis, a senior scientist who leads the aquarium’s right whale research program and chairs the Consortium, said the population is not yet on a clear path to recovery.
Right whales, she added, remain vulnerable to entanglement in fishing gear and vessel strikes.
“It’s the trend coupled with still seeing these really impactful injuries — human-caused injuries to the population — in the absence of sustained growth,” Pettis said.
There were no reported mortalities in 2025, but two right whales have died this year, according to the aquarium.
And so far in 2026, there have been seven documented entanglements and at least one ship strike.
Of the seven reported entanglements in 2026, three right whales were seen carrying gear. One was spotted in U.S. waters and carried lobster gear from Massachusetts, Pettis said. Two others were spotted in Canadian waters, and the origin of the gear is unknown, she added.
Pettis cautions that most entanglements and right whale mortalities are not observed in real time.
One bright spot: There were 24 calves born this year, the most since 2009. But that’s not part of the 2025 population count. The number of new calves born this year is a promising sign, Pettis said.
“It’s one thing for a calf to be born, and for that many calves to be born. It’s another thing for them to survive. That’s where the concern is,” she said. “Right whales, we know, are doing their part. They’re reproducing. We had a lot of calves this year. We had three new moms this year. That’s all great. And so now we just need to make sure that those animals survive to adulthood to then themselves contribute to the population.”
The latest estimates come at an uncertain regulatory time for the right whale population.
The Trump administration has taken steps to roll back vessel speed rules intended to protect the critically endangered species.
And a moratorium on new federal regulations for fisheries that are intended to protect right whales is in place at least until the end of 2028.
A group of federal officials, fishery managers, conservationists and other stakeholders were supposed to begin meeting in December to begin a lengthy process of writing new regulations.
But the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration recently announced that it would temporarily postpone those meetings to give officials time to review the latest right whale population data, as well as a new scientific method for apportioning right whale entanglements by country based on new gear marking data.
That method is under peer review and may indicate that the U.S. proportion of entanglements is less than previously estimated, the agency said.
That’s promising for Maine’s fisheries, Carl Wilson, commissioner of the state’s Department of Marine Resources, said last week in a message to the industry.
“This announcement is positive news for Maine’s fixed gear fisheries, including lobster, and represents the commitment by [the National Marine Fisheries Service] to a scientifically sound approach to assess risk posed by fixed gear fisheries that does not rely on ‘worst case” scenarios,'” he said.
At the same time, Congress is also considering a bill to delay the start of any new regulations. That measure, known as the Northeast Lobsterman Protection Act, would extend an existing moratorium on new federal rules for fishermen until 2035.
Maine’s lobster fishery has said that more time is needed to study where the whales are and how their presence overlaps with key fishing areas before negotiations about new regulations can begin.
Pettis, however, said she fears any additional delay will end what she described as productive conversations among scientists, fishermen, conservationists and others about ways to preserve the right whale population.
“We want these discussions to continue,” she said.
The bill cleared the U.S. House mostly along party lines earlier this year and is awaiting action in the U.S. Senate.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Hospitals are adding programs to support family caregivers
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A growing number of hospitals are offering programs designed to support family caregivers. Experts say that support can improve outcomes and reduce costly trips to the hospital.
More than 60 million Americans provide care that includes bathing, managing medications and getting sick or aging loved ones to appointments.
According to AARP, family caregivers provide more than $1 trillion worth of unpaid care each year. Nearly a quarter of them say the role makes it hard to take care of their own needs.
A family faces a terminal diagnosis
Joe and Ashleigh Quirarte were married in 2017 and promised “in sickness and in health.” Ashleigh said she did not expect that vow to be tested so soon.
“I thought maybe one day I’d take care of you, but we’d be like 80,” Ashleigh said.
In late 2024, at 38, Joe had a medical emergency.
“Randomly, with no warning whatsoever, I had a seizure at my mom’s house one night,” Joe said.
“Over the course of the next few days, we learned that he had a tumor,” Ashleigh said.
Joe was diagnosed with glioblastoma, a rare and aggressive brain cancer without a cure. Ashleigh became his primary caregiver with no medical background.
“I had no idea where to even start,” Ashleigh said. “It’s so incredibly overwhelming, and even the smaller things like caring for his wound after the surgery were still really intimidating.”
Program supports caregivers of brain tumor patients
Ashleigh said the University of California San Francisco’s neuro-oncology caregiver program helped her find strength and support.
“The caregiver program is absolutely a lifeline, and my heart breaks for people who have to go through this and don’t have that support, because it’s crucial,” she said.
Cherrie DeMayo, a UCSF nurse coordinator, said caregiver support is built into the care plan. It includes education, guidance and connection.
“That form of connection, we’ve found, has really made people be more resilient and able to kind of keep moving forward,” DeMayo said.
Ashleigh said she began attending monthly support groups.
“For the first time, was able to feel like other people understood what I was going through,” she said.
The program launched in 2014 and has supported more than 5,000 caregivers, according to the report. It is free for caregivers of UCSF brain tumor patients. Dr. Susan Chang, UCSF’s director of neuro-oncology, founded and directs it.
DeMayo said much of the support is emotional and includes anticipatory guidance.
“Figuring out kind of what to expect in the coming months. What are these symptoms that they’re experiencing?” DeMayo said.
Ashleigh said her caregiver community helped her recognize Joe’s personality changes during treatment as more than stress.
“I’ve learned so much through the caregiver program just about what to expect for possible side effects for treatment, different treatment options, sort of these like peripheral symptoms,” she said. Asked if she felt better prepared, she said, “Absolutely.”
“This is a necessary part of taking care of a patient, is taking care of the caregiver,” Chang said.
Asked if she hopes the program serves as a national model, Chang said: “Absolutely. We want this to be a priority for institutions, for medical health care systems, to recognize that these are what I call the silent heroes.”
UCSF says its program is the first of its kind in neuro-oncology.
Serving caregivers regardless of condition
In Chicago, Rush University Medical Center created a program for caregivers, no matter what condition their loved one is facing.
“Caregivers are already doing everything they can, and they’re really the default health care, long-term care system. So we owe them,” said Diane Mariani, program manager for Rush’s Caring for Caregivers.
Mariani said the model connects caregivers to counseling, support groups, respite and community resources such as Meals on Wheels. Sessions can be billed through insurance.
“We’re reducing the stress, and some of those symptoms that caregivers are having,” Mariani said.
Mariani said outcomes are improving for caregivers and for patients, including shorter hospital stays and fewer emergency room visits.
“What we see and what we hear from our caregivers is they’re just more confident and don’t feel like, ‘Oh, my gosh, this is an emergency,’” she said.
Rush created its model in 2019 to support caregivers of patients over age 60. Mariani said Rush hopes to expand it in the coming years.
Rush is sharing the model with support from grant funding. Mariani said about a dozen health systems around the country are implementing it, and she would like to see that number grow.
“Health systems are all kind of stretched, I would say. It’s kind of where we’re at in our world,” she said.
Need is outpacing help
For years, communities have relied on local organizations for caregiver assistance, including area agencies on aging, a federally funded network of more than 600 nonprofit organizations.
USAging, the national association of area agencies on aging, says the need is outpacing the help.
“The caregiver’s role is increasing. It’s also becoming more complicated because of the level of care that people need,” said Sandy Markwood, USAging’s CEO.
Markwood said the organization is collaborating with hospitals to support family caregivers. She said she would like to see this workforce become a greater national priority.
Asked what her message would be to lawmakers, Markwood said: “This is an issue that can’t be ignored anymore. We need to keep people living well, aging well at home and in the community, and they can’t do that unless we also invest in their important caregivers.”
“This is a call to action for all of us taking care of patients, where we put a priority on also taking care of the caregiver,” Chang said.
Federal legislation
In May 2026, legislators introduced a bill to better identify the needs of people caring for children and aging parents at the same time.
In 2025, Congress reintroduced a bill that would offer working family caregivers a federal tax credit of up to $5,000.
Since sharing his story with InvestigateTV+, Joe Quirarte has passed away. He died peacefully on Oct. 17, 2026, surrounded by his loved ones.

title: Long dry stretch underway, freezing cold night ahead
text:
Long dry stretch underway, freezing cold night ahead
High pressure dominates the forecast this week, keeping New England dry with a gradual warming trend expected.

title: Conservationists are trying to save Louisiana’s cypress forests, here’s why
text:
ST. FRANCISVILLE, La. (InvestigateTV) — Sandy Couvillon of Alexandria was on a road trip with some friends when they spotted a sign for the Cat Island National Wildlife Refuge.
They made a quick detour for a ride down bumpy roads and a short hike down a walking trail for a look at the star attraction in this swamp, the largest tree east of the Sierra Nevada Mountains.
“It’s amazing, it’s worth the trip,” said Couvillon as she stood in the shadow of the National Champion Bald Cypress tree, 90 feet high, 17 feet in diameter and 50 feet around.
While no one knows its precise age, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service estimates the tree is 1,500 years old.
Will DeGravelles, director of land protection for the Nature Conservancy, said the tree’s size is difficult to capture.
“It really is hard to capture on camera and film and telling people. You kind of have to be here to really feel it,” DeGravelles said. “Cypress knees that are the height of people take hundreds of years to get that way.”
Why the giant survived
The tree survived logging in part because it was hollow and ill-shaped compared to other massive cypress trees, DeGravelles said.
The tree and others nearly as large thrive in one of few places where the Mississippi River remains connected to the landscape. Regular spring floods feed them fresh water and nutrients.
“A flood plain of this size that is connected naturally to its river and has a natural hydrology is very, very rare,” DeGravelles said.
Decades of loss
There were once 25 million acres of bottomland hardwood and swamps along the river, DeGravelles said. Many fell to logging. Along the coast, scientists say saltwater intrusion, a sinking delta, and sea-level rise remain threats.
“We’ve lost perhaps 50-75 percent of our bottomland hardwood and swamp forests across Louisiana,” DeGravelles said.
Replanting efforts
Each year, volunteers working with conservation groups plant thousands of young cypress trees.
To be successful, those plantings must include a nutria guard, a piece of often recycled plastic to protect young seedlings from being gobbled up by the invasive rodents.
“If we were to plant trees without the nutria protectors, even 20 years ago or today, we would see almost 100% mortality of those trees,” said Kristi Trail, who runs the Pontchartrain Conservancy.
The conservancy has planted thousands of trees over the years, including in the Madisonville area along the Tchefuncte River and in the LaBranche Wetlands in St. Charles Parish.
“We need this storm surge buffer in these swamps to make sure those levees can do their job,” Trail said.
The Pontchartrain Conservancy says the success rate from the plantings now tops 95 percent.
MRGO closure key to success
The closure of the Mississippi River Gulf Outlet was key to the improved survival rate, Trail said.
The MRGO was built as a shortcut from the Port of New Orleans to the Gulf. During Hurricane Katrina, it funneled storm surge into St. Bernard and Orleans parishes. Scientists say the MRGO turned Lake Pontchartrain saltier and helped kill the cypress forests surrounding the lake.
“When MRGO was open, a lot of salt water was able to enter our basin, change the salinity of these soils, and a lot of these cypress trees died as a result,” Trail said.
Following Katrina, the Army Corps of Engineers installed a rock dam to close the waterway and later a surge barrier.
Scientists have been studying salinity levels to pinpoint areas that are now candidates for cypress plantings.
“We’ve been able to identify areas in the estuary like this, like the LaBranche Wetlands, that are now ready for reforestation,” said Pontchartrain Conservancy Chief Scientist Eva Hillman.
Results from earlier plantings
A planting roughly 15 years earlier on the east bank of the Mississippi River in Plaquemines Parish shows the potential. The trees now tower about 30 feet high.
The Caernarvon River diversion nearby feeds fresh water and nutrients into the area.
“Even just those few pulses of fresh water, with nutrients and sediments, increases the growth rate of the planted trees there,” Hillman said.
Conservation groups and a government program that pays farmers to convert marginal agricultural land back into forested wetlands have also contributed to restoration efforts. Some conversions last 30 years, some are permanent.
The Nature Conservancy says restoration efforts in the Mississippi River Valley recently hit 1 million acres.
“That’s a huge accomplishment and we have millions more acres to do,” DeGravelles said.
DeGravelles said Louisiana will never get back to 25 million acres of swamp, but the efforts are a start.
“We are not talking about restored forests. It will take decades for those to become fully mature forests like we’re standing in,” DeGravelles said.

'The Night The Stars Fell': The Leonid meteor shower through history
text:
'The Night The Stars Fell': The Leonid meteor shower through history
The meteor storms of the Leonids have captured attention for centuries
'The Night The Stars Fell': The Leonid meteor shower through history
The meteor storms of the Leonids have captured attention for centuries
It's time again to look to the skies.
The Leonid meteor shower peaks this week. The Leonids are an annual fall meteor shower active between Nov. 6 and 30, peaking on the evening of Nov. 17. They are one of the most prominent meteor showers of the year, considered to be some of the fastest meteors and often known to be colorful, according to NASA.
Related video above: See the moment a meteor lights up the sky above an erupting volcano
This year, we can expect to see anywhere from 3 to 15 meteors per hour. But though it won’t happen this November, the Leonids are also known to make a roaring comeback every 33 years, coinciding with the orbital period of the comet that they originate from, 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. And when Tempel-Tuttle is near enough to Earth, it can cause a meteor storm, which is when more than 1,000 meteors can be seen in just an hour.
The Leonids are hundreds of years old, and the meteor storms have been seen several times across recorded history.
According to NASA, the earliest observation of the Leonids was in 902 A.D. when Chinese astronomers and observers in what is now Egypt and Italy reported seeing the first meteor storm from the Leonids. Accounts of the storm varied, but the sentiment was the same: "Stars fell like rain."
Perhaps the most famous Leonid meteor storm in the modern era was the storm of 1833. The storm was so severe that one estimate stated that over 240,000 meteors were observed overnight. The engraving above appeared in an 1844 edition of "Bible Readings for the Home Circle," a Christian reading guide that sought to answer many questions about the world for followers of Christian thought. One such question accompanying the picture in a section titled "Sign of the Times" was: Could this shower foreshadow the second coming?
An answer quotes the physicist and astronomer Denison Olmstead, writing, "The extent of the shower of 1833 was such as to cover no inconsiderable part of the earth's surface ... This is no longer to be regarded as a terrestrial, but as a celestial, phenomenon; and shooting stars are now to be no more viewed as casual productions of the upper regions of the atmosphere, but as visitants from other worlds, or from the planetary voids." Olmstead would come to be known as the father of "meteor science" after the intense Leonid storm of 1833 spurred him to better understand the elusive phenomenon.
The shower of 1833 was also notably seen over Niagara Falls, inspiring several paintings and woodcuts.
Also in 1833, explorer and writer Josiah Gregg chronicled his time with Indigenous tribes along the Santa Fe Trail. Gregg spent time with the Cheyenne tribe, including during the Leonid meteor storm. Gregg wrote that the Cheyenne sacrificed a white bison on "The Night the Stars Fell" and wrote a peace treaty with the U.S. on its skin.
The radiant of the Leonids is the constellation Leo. The shower is visible in the eastern night sky after midnight. Also, Jupiter and Mars will be in conjunction near Leo the same night, just above Regulus, one of the brightest stars in the sky.
The latest Leonid meteor storm took place in 2002. According to NASA, comet 55P was independently discovered by both Ernst Tempel and Horace Tuttle just a year apart, in 1865 and 1866, so it was named for both of them.
Leonid meteor storms aren't always exactly 33 years apart. Certain conditions have to be met to cause a significant storm, usually involving clouds of debris that follow the comet's orbit. From 1998 to 2002, the solar conditions were so unique that they caused several storms in a row, producing around 3,000 meteors in an hour at times. Before 1998, the most recent storm was in 1966.
Unfortunately for us, the next predicted dense meteor storm is actually in 2099, though the 2033 and 2034 Leonids could show off a significant stream of anywhere from 30 to 500 meteors per hour.

title: These doctors had a history of being disciplined. Prison officials hired them anyway
text:
KANKAKEE, Ill. — (InvestigateTV)
When John Paris married his wife, Vikki, in 2008 he took the vow to see her through sickness and in health, for better or for worse. Even before saying those words, he knew what would be required – given his new bride was serving time behind bars in an Illinois prison.
“We loved each other deeply and didn’t care what anybody else thought,” he said.
Their relationship would be tested again a decade later, when Vikki – a bladder cancer survivor – had testing done that revealed potential warning signs the disease could be making a return.
A year went by before Vikki was finally seen and got the diagnosis they’d been dreading. It was bladder cancer.
But by then, it was too late – the disease had already spread to her lungs and kidneys.
Within months, Vikki was dead. Her husband claimed in a civil lawsuit that prison doctors were negligent and delayed Vikki’s care - leaving him without his best friend.
“Just basically took everything from me,” he said. “She deserved a lot better.”
But what John learned later from InvestigateTV added to his dread. Several of the physicians involved in Vikki’s case had histories of providing inadequate care, according to an InvestigateTV analysis of state medical board records.
Their disciplinary histories show sanctions for failures to diagnose, follow-up and notify patients about important medical issues.
But the issue is not isolated to Illinois. InvestigateTV spent months analyzing personnel records from state correctional agencies nationwide and searching for matches in state medical board disciplinary records. We found dozens of doctors with disciplinary histories practicing behind bars.
Those physicians, InvestigateTV’s research uncovered, had records that included medical license suspensions, restrictions that limited what procedures they could do and who they could treat, as well as medical license revocations.
In a small number of cases, InvestigateTV even found doctors whose histories showed their licenses had at one point been limited to practicing only within a correctional setting.
And these doctors - paid by tax dollars - were, with the full knowledge of state officials, hired or allowed to remain on the prison medical staff to treat men and women who can’t choose their own doctors.
“I don’t know if it’s widely known that these health care providers, some of whom have quite serious histories of misconduct, are essentially being foisted upon a captive population who has no choice,” said David Fathi, the director of the ACLU’S National Prison Project.
Andrea Armstrong, a professor of law at Loyola University New Orleans College of Law said, “if it’s your brother, if it’s your uncle, if it’s your cousin, if it’s your neighbor. You know, these are things that matter.”
Many prisons keep doctors’ names secret
Many prison officials refused to turn over names of physicians working behind bars for a variety of reasons, even though their positions are paid with tax dollars.
InvestigateTV filed public records requests with the correctional agencies in all 50 states.
Michigan estimated that it would need $800 in payment from InvestigateTV to fill the request. Nebraska wanted as much as $4,500 for the 140 hours of staff time the state claimed would be needed to respond.
Others, including Tennessee and North Carolina, delayed responding for months despite repeated attempts to follow up and gain access to records.
Eighteen other states either denied InvestigateTV’s requests, said they had no responsive records, or referred us to private contractors that provide medical care in state prisons. Idaho redacted provider names as “trade secrets” and Vermont shielded physicians from disclosure, saying the release of contracted names is exempt “due to privacy concerns”.
“We, as taxpayers and residents – we have the right to understand what the government is doing in our names and with our tax dollars. So, the failure to provide records is bewildering,” said Armstrong.
When unable to obtain information about providers through public records requests, InvestigateTV used salary databases made available online by individual state governments to track down some physicians working in state prison systems.
Ultimately, InvestigateTV was able to obtain the names of prison doctors employed in prison systems from 25 states, some dating as far back as 2020.
Doctors of ‘last resort’
After obtaining the names of prison providers, InvestigateTV used publicly searchable records from state medical boards to determine if doctors working in correctional settings had disciplinary histories.
Our team spent six months reviewing records for nearly 1,500 doctors from across the nation - finding at least 120 physicians in 17 states had at some point been disciplined by medical boards. While all had active licenses at the time of employment, some physicians had multiple actions against them, including discipline handed down after criminal convictions.
At least 30 had faced suspensions in the past.
Other physicians had practice restrictions, and some had surrendered their licenses or had them revoked – including some doctors who had been employed as Medical Directors in correctional settings.
“When somebody’s been disciplined, especially when their license has been restricted, that means that a colleague has expressed doubts about their ability to safely deliver care,” said Armstrong. “Just like in the real world, people make mistakes. They’re disciplined for those. And we as consumers of health care have an opportunity to choose our doctors. But that looks radically different behind bars because there is no choice.”
The conduct that resulted in discipline included drug and alcohol abuse, criminal convictions for drug offenses, DUI and fraud, sexual misconduct, missed diagnoses, improper prescribing, involvement in pill mills, drug diversion and inadequate care, records showed.
“What we know is that most of these systems are using doctors of, in some ways, last resort,” Armstrong said. “These are people who cannot practice anywhere else. And so, if they want to earn a living with the degree that they earned, then it only happens behind bars.”
Some doctors themselves had served time in prison. Some could see patients only with a chaperone, and some were barred from treating female patients. A few were even restricted at some point to practicing solely in prison settings.
“There should be no double standard,” Fathi said. “Doctors found unqualified to treat people in the community should not treat incarcerated patients.”
Yet that’s what happened in a South Carolina case settled in August that involved a physician with multiple license suspensions in his history in multiple states following incidents of self-prescribing, substandard care as well as a conviction for domestic violence.
Court filings in that civil lawsuit claim the doctor was working on behalf of a contractor that provides prison healthcare in several states and had been hired despite egregious conduct in his history. The suit claims negligent care led to the 2023 death of a young man who was being held in a county jail.
While the doctor died last year - before his death, records showed, his license had been limited, with the state medical board saying he “must work only at sites within the South Carolina Department of Corrections.”
The South Carolina Board of Medical Examiners told InvestigateTV the physician applied for and was offered a position in a correctional setting, which the board approved. They said he was not mandated to work in a correctional institution and was free to petition the board to remove the restriction or request approval to change employment – which did not happen before his death.
The South Carolina Department of Corrections did not respond to requests for comment.
‘Incarcerated people pay, often with their health, and sometimes with their lives’
South Carolina isn’t the only state where families say a risky hire had real consequences.
The Paris case in Illinois is another example. Vikki Paris was convicted in Illinois in 2005 in the shooting death of her first husband. Multiple records said the shooting followed years of spousal abuse. She took a plea deal and was given 20 years in state prison.
Her husband, John Paris, says she ended up with a death sentence instead, because of delays in her care.
“Your Hippocratic oath does not say heal all except those in prison. No, no. Do no harm is the main thing. And by ignoring people, that’s the exact opposite of your oath,” he said.
In 2021, Paris filed a civil lawsuit against five of the doctors involved in his wife’s care as well as Wexford, the company contracted by the Illinois Department of Corrections and paid with tax dollars to provide medical services.
Despite Vikki Paris experiencing months of severe pain and repeatedly reporting blood in her urine, the suit claims prison doctors didn’t get a second opinion, order additional testing or refer her to a urologist – delaying her diagnosis until it was too late.
Wexford declined to comment, and the Illinois Department of Corrections never responded to repeated requests from InvestigateTV. Just days before securing a settlement, the physicians involved were dropped from the suit – none provided responses to questions sent by email.
But InvestigateTV found three of the doctors named as defendants had prior disciplinary records, including action taken because of problems with patient care. One of the physicians had been reprimanded by the Illinois State Medical Board just three years before Vikki’s cancer reemerged.
Records show that disciplinary action followed settlement in a case that resulted from an “an alleged failure to timely diagnose breast cancer leading to a delay in treatment and poor prognosis” in a different patient.
That physician, InvestigateTV found, is still listed as an independent contractor in the Illinois prison system.
David Fathi said he was disturbed but not surprised by the discovery.
Second chances for problem providers
Dr. Keith Ivens, a Tennessee-based physician who oversaw prison health care for his own company and private contractors in states nationwide before retiring, said hiring for medical jobs in prisons can be challenging.
Lower paying salaries, the often-remote location of prison facilities and the complexity of the patient population are key reasons he said correctional institutions struggle to consistently hire top providers into the industry.
“If I had a university professor who wanted to work in my facility versus somebody with a fraud or sexual crime history, I want to hire the university professor,” Ivens said. “University professors are not lining up to take my jobs. I have to get medical providers into these institutions.”
Ivens admitted hiring doctors with serious discipline in their history does involve risk, but he said employers can and must monitor those with difficult histories. In his experience, he said some doctors with a dark past have performed “extraordinarily well” when given an opportunity to return to medicine through work in a correctional setting.
David Fathi with the ACLU doesn’t see it that way.
“If an airline is having trouble hiring enough pilots, they don’t get to say, well, we’ll just hire the person who lost their license for a while because they were flying while drunk. No, they have to hire someone who’s qualified, and the rule should be exactly the same when it comes to health care, which is every bit as much a matter of life and death,” he said.
‘Safe, competent care’ must be a priority
Until last month, Ivens chaired the National Commission on Correctional Health Care, a nonprofit that sets voluntary national quality standards for prison medicine. InvestigateTV sent the organization our findings.
The organization wouldn’t comment specifically but said in an emailed statement “Our mission is to improve correctional health care, not to defend inadequate practices or excuse shortcomings. Correctional facilities face significant challenges recruiting and retaining qualified health care professionals, reflecting broader workforce shortages across the country. However, staffing challenges do not justify compromising professional qualifications or standards of care. NCCHC’s position is that incarceration should never mean accepting a lower standard of health care. Ensuring that patients receive safe, competent care must always be the priority.”
The organization said its standards, which are voluntary, call for facilities to check providers’ licenses and credentials, including querying state licensing boards and a national repository of disciplinary information for any sanctions or disciplinary actions. The standards, the statement said, also prohibits clinicians from practicing under licenses that restrict their practice solely to correctional health care – in contrast to what InvestigateTV found in a few situations.
The commission emphasized there’s an important distinction between a history of professional discipline and a current license restriction, writing, “Disciplinary actions vary in severity, and restrictions may subsequently be lifted. NCCHC standards require verification of disciplinary histories but do not automatically prohibit employment based solely on past disciplinary action.”
InvestigateTV contacted correctional agencies in the 17 states that our investigation found employed physicians with a disciplinary history – either directly or through a contractor – asking about specific provider conduct and overall policies related to the employment of previously sanctioned doctors.
Only a few including Kentucky, Louisiana, North Carolina, Oregon and Washington provided full responses – with states saying the disciplinary actions identified by the investigation had been resolved and that doctors, like the people in their care, deserve a second chance.
SEE FULL STATE RESPONSES BELOW
Improving care: ‘We have a long way to go’
Experts from industry and advocacy agree that there are solutions that could improve healthcare provided behind bars.
Fathi said staffing shortages can be addressed by offering higher pay, more vacation or flexible hours. When courts have required prison systems to increase medical staffing, he said, those systems have found a way to do so.
Dr. Ivens echoed the call for higher salaries to entice more desirable candidates and pointed to telemedicine as a way to get in-demand physicians into the system without requiring them to move to rural locations.
For her part, Armstrong suggested partnering with public health agencies already experienced in providing complex care to the wider population. But she and others said the real solution is drastically reducing the number of people in incarceration so that their care can be managed effectively.
“There has to be a level at which a prison can say, “No, I can’t safely take any more people into custody because I don’t have the staff to provide the constitutionally required services,’ and that’s on the prisons to alert the public that they cannot do what they’re obligated to do because of the numbers,” Armstrong said.
Until changes happen, the loved ones of people impacted by the care provided by problematic doctors believe the incarcerated will pay the price.
“You’re costing money and lives. That’s all there is to it,” John Paris said.
Paris fought tirelessly for his wife’s release after her diagnosis, successfully securing clemency from Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker in March 2020.
Vikki Paris was home just four days before she died from cancer that her lawsuit claims could have been treated if it was caught earlier.
“She said, ‘Don’t worry about it. I’ve made my peace. I’m home with you. You kept your promise. You’re not letting me die in prison’,” he said.
RESPONSES FROM STATE CORRECTIONAL AGENCIES TO QUESTIONS FROM INVESTIGATETV
CALIFORNIA: “California Correctional Health Care Services (CCHCS) is committed to providing safe, appropriate, and professional medical care to incarcerated patients. Because personnel records and peer review information are confidential, CCHCS cannot comment on specific employees, former employees, or allegations involving individual providers.”
IDAHO: “The Idaho Department of Correction follows the terms of our contract with Centurion regarding information they designate as confidential or proprietary. When Centurion marks information as a protected trade secret under Idaho Code 74‑107(1), IDOC is required to review and redact that information before release. For additional information about Centurion’s classification of provider identities, you may contact Centurion directly."
INDIANA: “Thank you again for your inquiry. Unfortunately, since the individuals whose names you’ve requested are employees of Centurion and not the State of Indiana, we need to direct you to Centurion’s media team.”
IOWA: “Sounds like you reached out to most of the States with this request. Please reach out to our Open Records staff at docopenrecords@iowa.gov if you are wanting more information.”
KENTUCKY: “The Kentucky Department of Corrections is committed to ensuring the safety and well-being of all individuals in state custody. The Department of Corrections has several contracts in place with a variety of medical providers. Currently, the Department contracts with Wellpath, an independent medical provider, to afford those in state custody access to medical care and treatment; Diamond Pharmaceuticals has the contract for all prescription medication; Mid-America has the contract for dental care. These vendors are responsible for employing qualified medical personnel and ensuring they meet applicable licensing and professional requirements. All employees providing services through these contracted vendors are employed by the vendor and not the state. For a list of medical providers/employees, you would need to contact the vendor directly. At any time, the Department is made aware of inappropriate behavior, misconduct, or actions not aligned with departmental policy, the vendor is immediately notified, and if warranted, the Department will request the employee not be allowed further admission to the prison. Thank you.”
LOUISIANA: “The Louisiana Department of Public Safety & Corrections takes all allegations of professional misconduct seriously and recognizes its responsibility to ensure that individuals employed in medical positions are qualified to perform their duties and provide appropriate care to those in our custody.
The Department thoroughly reviews matters brought to its attention and considers relevant circumstances, professional qualifications, licensure status, and applicable employment requirements when making hiring and personnel decisions. A history of disciplinary action or criminal involvement does not necessarily constitute an automatic disqualification from employment, provided an individual meets the legal and professional requirements of the position.
As an agency that emphasizes rehabilitation, reentry, and second chances for the individuals in our custody, we believe those principles should extend beyond the walls of our correctional facilities. It would be inconsistent with our mission to advocate for second chances while categorically denying employment opportunities to qualified individuals who have taken the necessary steps to move forward from past mistakes.
Our responsibility is to evaluate individuals based on their qualifications, their ability to fulfill the essential duties of their positions, and their adherence to the professional and ethical standards expected of Department employees. We remain committed to maintaining those standards while recognizing that past mistakes do not necessarily define an individual’s ability to contribute meaningfully to our workforce."
NEVADA: “Medical contractors are reviewed before being hired. We can’t release personnel information, but we can say any disciplinary cases were closed before hire.”
NORTH CAROLINA: “The Department of Adult Correction takes seriously its responsibility to provide health care services to the incarcerated population by providing care that is consistent with standards of care that would be received in the community.
The people on the list you provided are all currently employed with the NC Department of Adult Correction. For the five you highlighted, we are aware of the past actions by the NC Medical Board.
Those physicians are fully licensed to practice medicine in North Carolina with unrestricted licenses. They have resolved their past issues—none of which involved criminal allegations or charges—to the full satisfaction of the medical board.
All NCDAC employees undergo a thorough criminal background check before employment. With all our medical professionals, we monitor all licensure actions and review in detail every two years with re-credentialing.”
OREGON: “The health and well-being of those in our care is a high priority. Too often the people coming into our prison system have complex medical conditions, high mental health needs, substance use disorders, and co-occurring disorders. It’s also an aging population with approximately 1,400 adults in custody age 60 years or older. We recognize the challenges facing correctional healthcare in Oregon, and as an agency we are dedicated to addressing them with innovation and process improvement. Patient-centered care must be central to what we do, and I am grateful for the dedication and hard work of our healthcare staff. As we move forward, I am committed to a transparent process of change in our Health Services Division to ensure we have the leadership, resources, and support needed to provide the highest standard of care.”
SOUTH CAROLINA: “The SC Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation issues medical licenses and determines whether someone is eligible to practice medicine in South Carolina. Those licenses are necessary for employment. If someone has a valid medical license in SC, they are eligible to be considered for employment. Also, SCDC believes in second chances. Every day we ask employers and community members to give inmates second chances. A previous act does not always define a person’s current reality.”
TEXAS: “The agency partners with University of Texas Medical Branch and Texas Tech to conduct medical care. Thus, these individuals would be employees of those institutions. Please reach out to them.”
VERMONT: “Our medical provider is WellPath.”
WASHINGTON: “DOC holds its medical professionals to high standards. Before being hired, they are subjected to background checks through the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) and under the Prison Rape Elimination Act (PREA). We also seek board certifications, where appropriate, and confirm that candidates have an active license.
If a current employee is accused of misconduct that violates their license, the alleged violation is reported to the Department of Health and DOC also conducts its own investigation. If the allegations are substantiated and the individual loses their license, they are terminated.
Incarcerated individuals in our care and custody deserve excellent health care. The agency has made significant strides in recent years to improve the level of care we offer. Our Health Services division has transitioned to a model centered on the patient and focused on prevention to improve outcomes. We implemented a fatality review process that examines each unexpected death in our facilities to determine if anything could have been done differently. DOC is currently implementing a much-needed electronic health records system that will replace an antiquated and inefficient paper system.”
RESPONSES FROM PRISON MEDICINE CONTRACTORS TO QUESTIONS FROM INVESTIGATETV
THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS MEDICAL BRANCH: “The University of Texas Medical Branch is committed to providing patients in the Texas Department of Criminal Justice system with safe, high-quality care. Everyone UTMB hires for Correctional Managed Care must go through TDCJ’s clearance process before they start. When we hire licensed clinicians, UTMB reviews their licensure and board history. After that, they are required to report any change in license status to UTMB. Any exception is reviewed on a case-by-case basis and approved by TDCJ. As a matter of policy, UTMB does not comment on individual personnel matters.”
Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center: “Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center is committed to providing safe, high-quality healthcare to the patients we serve, including those in the Texas Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ) system. TTUHSC maintains rigorous standards for clinical quality, patient safety and professional accountability.
Prior to employment, all physicians undergo a comprehensive credentialing process that includes verification of licensure, training, qualifications, professional history and review of any disciplinary actions or restrictions associated with their medical license. When appropriate, other specialists, including representatives from human resources, compliance and legal, may provide input on a pending application. Physicians hired to provide care through TTUHSC’s correctional healthcare programs must also complete the TDCJ’s clearance process before beginning employment.
Following employment, concerns related to patient care or professional conduct are evaluated through established peer review processes and may result in corrective action, termination, and, when appropriate, reporting to the Texas Medical Board.
As a matter of policy, TTUHSC does not comment on individual personnel matters."
WEXFORD: “Wexford Health appreciates your inquiry, but we do not have any comment or response at this time.”

title: Midcoast duo bringing affordable homes to a housing-starved part of Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing
This section of the BDN aims to help readers understand Maine’s housing crisis, the volatile real estate market and the public policy behind them. Read more Housing coverage here.
An uncle and nephew are building dozens of midcoast apartments for workers who earn too much for housing aid but too little for market rent.
Ed Libby and his nephew, Caleb Lincoln, started Lake City Holdings a few years ago to build housing for the people who work in the Rockland and Rockport area but can’t afford the rising housing costs in the region.
That middle group of renters and homebuyers has grown across Maine since the pandemic, when an influx of new residents helped push home prices up faster than local wages. This trend boxed many Mainers out of their local real estate markets.
“If you’re in an apartment and suddenly house prices are higher, now you can’t move out of your apartment,” Libby said. “So you’re staying, other people are trying to get apartments and nobody’s building apartments, so the pressure just keeps building.”
Rising construction costs make the problem worse. Developers say they often have to build high-end housing to turn a profit, or rely on government subsidies to close the gap between what it costs to build and what renters or buyers can pay.
“There’s a huge gap in the middle where the cost of construction doesn’t justify what people are able to pay, so that’s one of the reasons why we’re here,” Libby said.
So far, the pair have built two projects totaling 27 units with 59 more on the way.
The pair’s first project, the Criehaven Lofts, opened in March 2025 above the Loyal Biscuit Co. pet store on Main Street in Rockland. Funded through MaineHousing’s Rural Affordable Rental Housing Program, its nine one- and two-bedroom apartments are reserved for people earning up to 80% of the area median income.
In Rockland, that’s $55,100 a year for one person or $62,950 for a two-person household, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. Rents run $1,476 for a one-bedroom apartment up to $2,045 for a three-bedroom unit.
A market-rate one-bedroom apartment in the city averages $1,500 a month, and a three-bedroom can range from $2,300 to $2,400, according to data collected by Zillow.
The apartments filled within a day or two, Libby said.
“What we’re hearing from the municipalities and employers is that people are driving farther and farther — upwards of an hour or more — to their jobs in Rockport or Rockland,” he said. “That’s just not sustainable, so we’re hoping to let people live where they work.”
The team quickly pivoted to a former medical office on Madelyn Lane in Rockport. Using financing from MaineHousing’s Rural Affordable Rental Housing Program and support from private donors, including the Lesher Family Foundation, the company gutted the building to create 18 apartments.
The units were ready for residents by May 2026 after taking roughly a year to complete. Rent prices for the one-, two- and three-bedroom units are again capped for families earning 80% of the area median income.
But it still wasn’t enough.
Today, crews are working on Libby and Lincoln’s latest project on Cross Street in Rockport. Once complete, the site will hold two three-story buildings, each with 12 apartments.
Half of the one- and two-bedroom apartments will be reserved for those earning 80% of the area median income. The remaining 12 units will be for households “that earn slightly more than 80% AMI, but not enough to comfortably afford the area’s inflated market rate rent pricing,” Lincoln said.
Construction is expected to wrap next fall, but Libby and Lincoln are already involved in two more housing endeavors in Rockland, both of which grew out of requests from the city.
Libby and Lincoln, in partnership with Portland-based Developers Collaborative, won a city-issued request for proposal to create affordable housing in the McLain School on Lincoln Street, which most recently housed school district administrative offices.
The existing building will hold 17 apartments and a dozen more will be built on an adjacent property. Construction on the one-, two- and three-bedroom units is expected to begin early next year.
With Portland-based Developers Collaborative, they won the city’s bid to turn the McLain School on Lincoln Street, most recently school district offices, into housing. The plan calls for 17 apartments in the existing building and 12 more in a new building next door, with construction expected to start in early 2027.
Lincoln said the project will be funded mostly through low-income housing tax credits issued by MaineHousing, along with state and federal historic tax credits.
They also plan to build six single-family starter homes on Rockland Street, on a former junkyard and brownfield site the city took over for unpaid taxes. Each two-bedroom, one-bath home would be about 1,000 square feet and sell for no more than $347,000 to households earning up to 120% of the area median income.
The median sale price for a home in Knox County has grown to $475,000 in recent months, according to the Maine Association of Realtors.
Libby said the goal is to offer move-in-ready homes at a price more people can afford, instead of a fixer-upper.
“Part of the challenge in Rockland is the age and condition of the existing housing stock,” Libby said. “We felt like it would be interesting not only to bring starter homes, because no one else is doing it, but to give somebody a different option at that price point.”
Correction: An earlier version of this report misstated the number of housing units that Ed Libby and Caleb Lincoln intend to build.

title: Judge sets March retrial for Massachusetts mother accused of killing her 3 children
text:
PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — A Massachusetts judge on Monday scheduled Lindsay Clancy’s second trial in the killings of her three young children for late March, over the objections of prosecutors.
Clancy is charged with three counts of first-degree murder. Her first trial end in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the killings. Eleven jurors favored acquittal on the grounds of insanity, while one disagreed.
Prosecutors had sought a May trial date, citing scheduling conflicts, but Superior Court Judge William Sullivan set the retrial for March 29 in Plymouth Superior Court.
The decision to schedule Clancy’s second trial comes a week after Sullivan rejected a defense request to dismiss the charges. He ruled that a retrial would not violate Clancy’s constitutional protection against double jeopardy.
Attorneys are scheduled to return to court at 9 a.m. Dec. 30 to discuss trial logistics, security and media arrangements. A pretrial conference is set for Feb. 18.
Clancy’s lawyers had argued that the judge should have investigated or removed the lone juror who opposed acquittal before declaring a mistrial.
Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, has never disputed that she killed her three children at the family’s Duxbury home in January 2023. Her attorneys said she was suffering from severe mental illness at the time.
Prosecutors argued Clancy planned the killings and understood what she was doing.

title: How Old Each James Bond Actor Was When They Got the Job
text:
Robert Pattinson: Is He Too Old to Play James Bond?
Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond.
Although Pattinson’s name surfaced in the press as last-minute contender to replace Daniel Craig as Ian Fleming’s super-spy, it’s still a surprising choice. Bond actors tend to be younger, with less name recognition and fewer credits to their names. Pattinson has been a movie star for almost 20 years, and he’s already got several signature roles to his name, including Edward Cullen in The Twilight Saga and Bruce Wayne in The Batman.
No one would call Pattinson an up-and-coming actor, they way many people did when Daniel Craig landed the starring role in 2006’s Casino Royale. But does that mean he’s too old for the part? Let’s compare Pattinson at the start of his James Bond career to his 007 predecessors.
How Old Were the Other James Bond Actors When They Got the Job?
READ MORE: Robert Pattinson Is the New James Bond
Pattinson will be the seventh actor to play James Bond when he stars in the upcoming 26th Bond adventure for director Denis Villeneuve. Here’s the age of each of the six other Bond actors on the day their first James Bond movie opened in theaters:
- Sean Connery - 32 years old
- George Lazenby - 30 years old
- Roger Moore - 45 years old
- Timothy Dalton - 41 years old
- Pierce Brosnan - 42 years old
- Daniel Craig - 38 years old
The average of those six men’s ages is 38. (The James Bond of Fleming’s books is generally in his middle and late 30s.) Robert Pattinson turned 40 in May of this year. So he’s older than the average, but not much — although it should be noted that while Pattinson got the job in 2026, his first Bond movie isn’t coming out for at least two years, and probably more like three years.
How Old Were the Other Bond Actors In their Final Bond Film?
Every Bond actor except one (George Lazenby) appeared in multiple films as the character. So age here is not just a matter of now; it also affects how long a star can play James Bond, and how many films he can make before he’s handed his retirement papers.
Here is the age of each of the previous Bond stars when their final 007 film debuted (and the total number of Bond movies they made in parenthesis):
- Sean Connery - 53 years old (6 official, 1 unofficial)
- George Lazenby - 30 years old (1)
- Roger Moore - 57 years old (7)
- Timothy Dalton - 43years old (2)
- Pierce Brosnan - 49 years old (4)
- Daniel Craig - 53 years old (5)
By the time Roger Moore made his final Bond, 1985’s A View to a Kill, he was in his late 1950s and the subject of a lot of mockery about his age and his looks and the fact that he appeared old enough to be the father of his Bond girl co-stars. I don’t think Pattinson wants to be in that position.
If Amazon really ramps up production, it doesn’t seem unreasonable that Pattinson could easily make three or four James Bond movies before it’s time to pass the Walther PPK to the next not-super-young actor. Any more than that might be pushing it.
Is Robert Pattinson Too Old to Play Bond?
Short answer: No.
Long answer: He’s too old to outpace Roger Moore or Daniel Craig as guys who held the job for well over a decade, but he’s roughly the same age as guys like Timothy Dalton and Pierce Brosnan when they got the gig 40 and 30 years ago.
I suspect people complaining that Pattinson is too old to play Bond are doing so because the last guy who got the job, Daniel Craig, was hired specifically to anchor a series of movies about James Bond at the start of his career. In Casino Royale, Craig’s Bond is a comparative rookie, completing his first assignment and first kill, making some mistakes, learning how to be 007. The sequels that followed charted his maturation in the job; the final one, No Time to Die, depicted his death.
As a result, some fans might assume Pattinson’s first Bond will start over at square one all over again the same way Casino Royale did. But the history of the James Bond franchise tells you that probably will not be the case — and with the hiring of Pattinson arguably shouldn’t be the case.
Roger Moore took over as James Bond in Live and Let Die and played the part as if he’d always been the character and this was just his latest adventure. Pierce Brosnan’s debut Bond, GoldenEye, expressly treated him like a Cold War relic, one who might no longer have a place in the politically correct 1990s.
I have no idea what form Pattinson’s 007 will take, but I would be surprised if Villeneuve’s movie is in any way an origin story. That would be like remaking Casino Royale. Whatever they do, it will be something new for the character.
As for Pattinson himself: A year or two ago, he showed up as a surprise guest at the New York Film Critics Circle Awards to present a prize to Brady Corbet for The Brutalist. The moment he walked into the room, the whole energy changed. The guy has the kavorka. He looks the part, he’s an incredible actor, and he’s already proven in films like Tenet and The Batman that he’s very comfortable in large-scale action movies. If he wanted to do it, how could Amazon not cast him?

title: UMSG grants preliminary recognition to the Poetry Club
text:
The University of Maine Student Government (UMSG) met on Nov. 10 in the Bangor Room of the Memorial Union.
Club Business
General officer Monica Weiblen from the UMaine Poetry Club stood before the Senate seeking preliminary recognition. Weiblen described the purpose of the club as “a safe space for people to come together, write poetry and connect with their peers, and to inspire new forms of writing and ways to think about writing.”
The club already has 20 members and expects rapid growth as the year progresses. Planned events include an open mic night and presentations from guest speakers. The club is not requesting any funds from the Senate. After a brief discussion, the Senate approved the request for recognition.
President Koba Cone and Vice President Brooke Abbott of the International Affairs Association presented a summary of their participation in the annual University of Pennsylvania Model United Nations conference in October. Twelve students from a variety of majors and age groups attended to practice public speaking, deliver speeches and debate policies in their committees. The conference allowed participants to connect with other students and network for future opportunities.
Funding Requests
Maine Animal Club President Makayla Dingle stood before the Senate to request $1,700 for 16 students and one adviser to participate in an agricultural competition hosted by Rutgers University in New Jersey on Feb. 27, 2027. Dingle also requested $1,290 to cover lodging costs and $1,200 for van rental costs. After discussion, the Senate sent the request back to committee for revision. After revision, the request will be revisited the following week.
Upcoming Events
The Commuter and Non-Traditional Student Organization will host a work readiness seminar that includes free grilled cheese sandwiches and soup in the Wade Center on Nov. 16.
Wilde Stein will host a Trans Day of Remembrance candlelight vigil on the steps of Fogler Library at 7 p.m. on Nov. 20. Wilde Stein will also host Gay Thanksgiving on Nov. 21 from 6 to 8 p.m. in the Bangor Room of the Memorial Union.
Women’s ice hockey is seeking to break the Hockey East women’s attendance record. The team will play the University of New Hampshire on Dec. 4 at 6 p.m. It will also host a fan festival before puck drop from 3 to 5 p.m.
With no further matters to discuss, the meeting adjourned.

title: Questions swirl around FAA’s new SMART AI system, though officials say no link to ground stop
text:
(AP) - The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology.
But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration’s SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems.
Officials say no connection to ground stop
The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there’s no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system, and the top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday.
The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn’t caused by “the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”
But lawmakers and outside groups raised questions about the SMART system before Friday’s ground stop. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails.
“Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” the Oct. 13 letter said. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.”
SMART, however, is not — at least not yet — set up for AI to be in charge of flight control. Rather, it is making recommendations to humans who do so.
What is the SMART system?
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a “cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics — into one platform.” SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories.
The system’s AI-supported engine synthesizes the data systems and shows a “comprehensive visualization” of where planes are going, how much traffic the system can handle and where congestion or weather could cause problems, according to the announcement. The idea is for specialists to then use the platform to fix problems before they arise.
The FAA says that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system’s recommendations.
So SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers. That was three days before the ground stop.
According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested. The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals.
SMART is also supposed to help with weather-related issues faster.
Currently, the FAA blocks off portions of airspace affected by weather as “large, rectangular boxes,” according to the fact sheet, which doesn’t reflect how weather actually looks, with quick-moving thunderstorms and storm systems that are “often irregular in shape, with narrow gaps or corridors that aircraft could safely fly through.”
To help with this, SMART gives the FAA and airspace operators a “clearer picture of how weather will affect air traffic over time,” allowing air traffic controllers to plan around storms and use available airspace instead of unnecessarily shutting down large areas.
No other country has a working AI air traffic tool like the SMART system, according to Michael McCormick, a former FAA airspace manager and an associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority, has a system in testing and several manufacturers are prototyping similar tools.
Concerns around relying on AI
While government officials and ASI, the company behind SMART, have stressed that its AI system is designed to assist humans and not run flight control, its deployment has raised concerns about relying on artificial intelligence when human lives are at stake, given that even the most advanced models are prone to hallucinations — when models fabricate false information and present it as fact.
Mike O’Donnell, a former top FAA official who worked for the agency for 17 years and now does aviation safety consulting work, said the agency “has got to make sure that this is just a tool in the toolbox and not the actual machine that’s doing the work.”
The FAA, he said, “cannot afford to be wrong on this.”
“It’s good to use it with the proper guardrails and backstops to ensure that they’re not giving wrong information to controllers based on what (AI) has come up with,” O’Donnell said. “There’s got to be a way to verify and validate what it’s doing to make sure that it’s not the wrong information.”
He cautioned against putting too much trust in AI “until we know for sure that it’s proven itself time and time again. And that’s going to take a while.”
The AI system’s launch comes amid a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers around the country. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association has been raising concerns about this for more than a decade, telling Congress in 2015 that the shortage was at a crisis level. It said then that the FAA had missed its hiring targets for five years in a row. The union represents about 14,000 controllers, roughly 3,000 of them trainees. That said, experts say no AI system can replace the human air traffic controllers who spend years training for this highly demanding and stressful job.
In an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the SMART tool is designed for traffic managers who manage the entire U.S. airspace.
“The AI does the math, the AI does the computation,” Buckendorf told NPR, but it’s ultimately up to the human operator whether to take the system’s recommendation. “They make the decision, they are the decider, they are the judge.”

title: Isaac, a cat missing since the Brooklyn building collapse, has been reunited with his young owner
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A cat missing since last week’s deadly Brooklyn building collapse has been found alive and reunited with his young owner, New York City officials said Sunday.
Allie Taylor, director of the Mayor’s Office of Animal Welfare, said her office worked with the veterinary nonprofit Flatbush Cats to locate Isaac and reunite him with 13-year-old Zariah Coleman.
It was a bit of good news amid the tragedy of Wednesday’s collapse, which killed eight people, injured 18 others and forced the evacuation of several nearby buildings, including one next door where Zariah lives.
Zariah and her mother told The New York Times on Sunday that workers found Isaac on Sunday in a cabinet under the kitchen sink of Zariah’s apartment after hearing a soft meow. Zariah and her family hadn’t been allowed in since the collapse, which tore off the side of her building and left a hole where her bedroom wall had been.
Waiting outside, Zariah hugged the cat’s cage as workers brought him out of her apartment building. Isaac had gone four days without food or water. After his rescue, he was taken to Flatbush Cats’ veterinary clinic for a checkup.
“I had it in my heart they would find Issac,” Zariah told the Times. “I knew they would.”
Zariah tearfully spoke about her missing cat at a news conference on Friday, telling reporters: “I just really hope they come and get our cat. He’s hiding from them, and I think he’s scared.”
Mayor Zohran Mamdani heralded Isaac and Zariah’s reunion in a social media post. He thanked Taylor’s office, the city’s Buildings Department and the nonprofit for the happy outcome.
“Isaac is now receiving the veterinary care he needs,” Mamdani said. “We’re grateful to everyone who helped bring them back together.”

title: Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo is undergoing care after eating a hat that got into enclosure
text:
CINCINNATI (AP) — The Cincinnati Zoo says its beloved hippo Fiona, who became a global celebrity after her premature birth nearly a decade ago, is undergoing veterinary care after swallowing a knit hat that got into her enclosure.
Zoo veterinarians and staff are monitoring Fiona and working to help her pass the hat, the zoo said in a statement Monday.
“Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self,” the zoo said.
The cap got into Fiona’s habitat after it was tossed into the air by a visitor and caught by a ceiling fan that catapulted it through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows, said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.
Fiona was born six weeks premature in January 2017, and her fight to survive grabbed international attention.
She initially couldn’t stand on her own and weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms) at birth, 25 pounds (11.3 kilograms) less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
Fans followed her progress online, and she became so popular that books were written about her. She also inspired a line of beer, all sorts of clothing and an ice cream flavor.
One couple even got engaged in front of her exhibit, with Fiona getting into the picture while underwater in the background.

title: Robert Pattinson Is the Next James Bond
text:
Robert Pattinson Is the New James Bond
In a twist worthy of a world-class spy thriller the man to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond won’t be an up-and-coming actor or a total unknown. It won’t be any of the names that were bandied about for years as potential 007 candidates since Craig hung up his Walther PPK after 2021’s No Time to Die.
It will be Batman.
Okay, technically it will be the guy who plays Batman, Robert Pattinson. He isn’t just a former Dark Knight star, though. Pattinson is the guy at the center of the current Batman franchise. (He’s finishing The Batman: Part II for Warner Bros. right now.) But after that, he’ll ditch the mask and cape for a tuxedo.
(If you’re a fan of Pattinson’s The Batman, I would not take this as an encouraging sign for the odds of a The Batman: Part III.)
Amazon announced the news of Pattinson’s casting with a simple photo on social media. The caption reads: “Robert Pattinson is James Bond.”
READ MORE: Fans Upset After Amazon Makes a Change to the James Bond Posters
They also released a brief teaser video as well.
The news of Pattinson’s casting comes a little under a month after word leaked that the “final screen tests” for the role were underway. Initially, the names mentioned as finalists included One Night Only’s Callum Turner and Slow Horses star Jack Lowden.
Then about ten days ago came word that there were additional screen test being done with bigger name actors, including Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult — who has his own ongoing DC Comics role as the Lex Luthor in James Gunn’s Superman series.
Pattinson’s first Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, from a screenplay written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight. Villeneuve and Pattinson just worked together on Dune: Part Three, which opens in theaters next month. Their Bond will be the 26th official entry in the James Bond movie franchise that began with 1962’s Dr. No.
Pattinson becomes the seventh actor to play James Bond in the series, following Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, and Daniel Craig.
Pattinson’s The Batman: Part II is currently scheduled to open in theaters on February 18, 2028.

title: Tanker’s steering failed minutes before it crashed into cruise ship, NTSB says
text:
NEW ORLEANS (WVUE/Gray News) - A tanker ship had two minutes between a steering failure and its collision with a cruise ship on the Mississippi River, according to the National Transportation Safety Board.
The NTSB released the information Sunday in an update on Friday’s accident involving the tanker ship Atlantic Asphalt and the riverboat cruise ship American Heritage. The latter ship capsized after the crash, but everyone on board was rescued.
Investigators downloaded more than nine hours of information from the Atlantic Asphalt’s voyage data recorder, or VDR, which was recovered Saturday.
A preliminary review of that information shows a steering casualty around 12:26 p.m. that left the ship’s rudder stuck starboard, pointing the tanker directly at the east bank of the Mississippi River, the NTSB said.
NTSB Investigator in Charge Bart Barnum said the tanker was near the Crescent City Connection bridge in New Orleans at that time. He said the VDR recorded “audio sounds consistent with the following: the ship’s whistle, warnings, requests for assistance broadcast over the vessel’s marine radio, commands to deploy the vessel’s anchors and emergency ship handling orders.”
The Atlantic Asphalt passed under the bridge, veered to the right and struck the docked American Heritage, which capsized.
“At about 12:28 p.m., the Atlantic Asphalt collided with the passenger vessel, the American Heritage,” Barnum said.
Officials have said the American Heritage had 191 passengers and crew on board at the time. Everyone was rescued, including 100 passengers, crew and first responders who went into the water.
As of Sunday, six of the 32 survivors hospitalized after the accident had not been discharged. Two were in serious but stable condition, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said.
NTSB Board Member John DeLeeuw said the investigation will include what went right.
“We are also going to investigate the things that went right,” DeLeeuw said. “There were a number of reasons why there were no fatalities, so we are going to take that as part of our investigation.”
The NTSB is working to preserve evidence on the American Heritage. Divers spent Sunday on the ship searching for clues that can be salvaged and compared with the Atlantic Asphalt’s VDR data.
The NTSB said it is interviewing passengers and crew from the American Heritage on Sunday. It plans to begin interviewing the Atlantic Asphalt crew Monday.
A preliminary report is expected next month.
As of Sunday, 50 hotel rooms at the Hilton New Orleans Riverside remained occupied by passengers. City of New Orleans personnel are coordinating directly with American Cruise Lines, owner of the American Heritage, to ensure passengers and crew members can safely return home.
American Cruise Lines issued its first public statement on the incident Sunday afternoon.
“We are proud of our crew and grateful for the first responders following yesterday’s incident on the Mississippi River,” the company said in the statement. “The fast actions of Captain Leonard Stewart and our crew allowed for a rapid evacuation of the vessel after the American Heritage was struck by a large tanker while docked at the Port of New Orleans. Captain Stewart remained on the bridge as the vessel capsized, calling for aid and keeping the ship alongside the dock for as long as possible.
“We appreciate the support from Mayor Moreno and Governor Landry and are working closely with their offices. We are grateful to the US Coast Guard, the Port of New Orleans and the New Orleans Police Department, and will continue working in partnership through the investigation and salvage effort.”
