title: Cruise lines and their passengers spent $35M in Maine last year
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
More than 3,000 visitors at eight ports in Maine were surveyed regarding their experiences onshore, their likelihood to return to the state and the economic impact of their spending while cruising here in 2025.
Cruise visitors and cruise lines, including crews, spent $35 million statewide. That provided $28 million to Maine’s gross domestic product, $3 million in tax revenue and supported 450 jobs.
Most surveyed said Maine’s ports were welcoming and service at restaurants was very good.
Nearly 60% recommend Maine for its shore experiences and 40% said they would return. Each visitor spent about $80 during a port visit with 68% staying overnight before a cruise began, with an average expense of $140 per night. The average cruise visitor tends to be 60 or older and lives in the Northeast or Southeast.
When Portland visitors are segregated from all other visitors:
Cruise passengers and cruise lines spent a combined $22 million in the Portland area, out of the $35 million in cruise-related spending statewide.
That spending increased Portland’s GDP by $17.5 million, out of $28 million statewide.
Cruise-related economic activity also supported 300 full-time equivalent jobs in the Portland area, out of 450 statewide and generated $1.8 million in state tax revenue, out of $3 million statewide.
A Portland-based watchdog group said a survey of cruise visitors to Maine fails to paint a clear picture of the real impacts of the industry on the state.
Portland Cruise Control said the data highlighted by the state office of tourism and industry supporters doesn’t include effects on public health, infrastructure and the environment.
It also questioned disembarkation rates provided by the Cruise Line International Association, which Portland Cruise Control called a biased source.
The survey was prepared by Digital Research Inc. for Visit Portland.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: L.L.Bean, Press Herald Toy Fund once again ‘turning the Bootmobile into Santa’s sleigh’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A giant boot, packed to the brim with toys, will be rolling through Maine this week.
L.L.Bean and one of its famous Bootmobiles have teamed up with the Portland Press Herald Toy Fund once again this year to deliver toys to children in Lincoln and Knox counties.
One of the outfitter’s iconic vehicles, holiday lights strung along its laces, arrived at the newspaper’s office in South Portland on Monday to pick up this year’s cargo.
“There are a lot of kids in Maine that need toys, and we’re happy to help out delivering them,” said Tucker Van Dusen, an experiential marketing specialist at L.L.Bean, who will be delivering nearly 47 bags full of toys, with each carrying gifts for two to three children, to locations in Damariscotta, Waldoboro and Camden for distribution. “We’re turning the Bootmobile into Santa’s sleigh.”
In the past, longtime volunteers like Craig Kinney, who is also a Press Herald Toy Fund board member, have made the deliveries to beneficiaries who live too far from the Press Herald’s office to pick them up themselves. The partnership with L.L.Bean last year was a success, and they hope it lasts for years to come.
“This is a perfect fit for us,” Kinney said. “It’s worked out really well.”
The more than 130 children benefiting from the Bootmobile delivery are only a fraction of the roughly 4,000 children set to receive gifts this year. With the application period still open for families, organizers say they wouldn’t be surprised to serve close to 5,000 children this year.
Volunteers also noted on Monday that the demand has consistently risen in recent years, with beneficiaries citing the heightened cost of living — from electricity and heating oil to rent and groceries. At this time last year, about 3,600 children were signed up.
“I have three kids and with the rising costs of heat and rent this year we are having a hard time making it,” a mother from Androscoggin County said when applying for the Toy Fund this year. “I am worried about not being able to give my children a Christmas.”
“We’ve been doing our best to manage our household expenses and provide for our children, but this year has been particularly difficult financially,” said two parents from the Midcoast. “With most of our income going toward essential expenses like housing, groceries, utilities and transportation, there is very little left over for Christmas gifts.”
HOW TO HELP:
To make a donation online, go to pressherald.com/toy-fund.
Checks made out to the Portland Press Herald Toy Fund may be mailed to 295 Gannett Drive, South Portland, ME 04106.
Names of donors are published in the Press Herald unless a donor wishes to remain anonymous.

title: A new cafe on Mill Street: The launch of Sip Lab
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In general, it seems that small towns in Maine rarely introduce new attractions or businesses to their downtown areas. For students at the University of Maine, Orono’s downtown has familiar staples like Pat’s Pizza, but there haven’t been many recent additions. Next to Pat’s, a business has finally taken over the vacant space, bringing fresh flavors to the greater Orono community. Sip Lab, founded by owner Joyce Lin, hopes to revitalize the space and introduce a variety of tea and coffee drinks to the community.
The idea for Sip Lab stems from their interest in “creating innovative drinks.” Moreover, Lin broke down the name: “Sip represents enjoying a drink, while Lab represents exploring flavors and developing new ideas.”
Though Sip Lab shares the area with many other cafes, its menu sets it apart by offering a variety of drinks, including Chinese-inspired teas. Lin said the name choice originates from a desire to “create fresh and exciting drinks for our customers.”
While the new flavors are exciting for students, Orono may seem like an unexpected location for the business, especially compared to the more culturally diverse communities of southern Maine. However, Lin said she chose Orono because it is such a “vibrant, energetic community.”
Being close to campus, Lin also had the goal of creating a place where “people could stop in when they need a little pick-me-up or get together with a few good friends.” Sip Lab’s space on Mill Street has a large amount of seating, allowing for parties of all sizes. Though Lin’s mission for the cafe is to create community, she also said that her goal is to “bring more creative drinks to the community and give people something new to look forward to” when they visit.
Lin said that their classic boba milk tea is the current bestseller, but with their grand opening last week, more customers have had the opportunity to try their extensive menu. Their flavors aren’t the only thing that’s bringing something new to Orono; their ordering system is entirely digital, with a large screen that shows customers pictures of menu items greeting them upon entry.
Lin wants Sip Lab to be a “welcoming part of everyday life.” With options for morning pick-me-ups as well as nightcaps, Lin plans to use the venue and patrons as a way to “keep bringing fresh ideas to [their] menu.”
Given their extensive menu, Lin labeled her favorite drink category as the green tea drinks, “especially those made with jasmine green tea.” This is because the “tea’s natural fragrances come from [Lin’s] hometown” in China. UMaine often fosters a culture that people fondly remember as their home, and Sip Lab offers Lin an avenue to add her home and culture to that picture.
Overall, Lin is “excited to grow with the Orono community,” with their sign adding a new face to the food and beverage businesses that line Mill Street. While the street holds many businesses essential to the culture of UMaine and the surrounding Orono community, Sip Lab is hoping to join these ranks and introduce a new cuisine to students and residents alike.

title: Letter: Social Security would save a lot of money by paying less to rich Americans
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
While most Social Security payments are needed, and even considered sacrosanct, many go to well-off recipients who don’t really need them. The Social Security Administration disbursed $1.6 trillion in 2025. The wealthiest 20% received more than a third of those benefits.
Social Security payments are adjusted regularly to reflect cost-of-living increases. These adjustments can be reduced for the wealthiest recipients, as can their basic payments.
These recipients would not be happy, but they could not claim that their lifestyles were impaired because their payments are a small fraction of their annual earnings.
If the cost-of-living adjustments were maintained for recipients earning up to, say, $200,000 annually, but reduced along with their basic payments for those more well-off, total payments could be substantially reduced. These annual reductions could be made greater over time until their value exceeded the amount paid out to the top 20%, or even an amount in excess of $1 trillion.
These annual Social Security savings to the federal government could be used to pay down the national debt, or for any purpose that Congress felt to be appropriate.
Raymond Tillman
Westbrook

title: ‘Just tragic’: 18-year-old Georgia football commit dies after sudden medical emergency
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) - A community is left heartbroken after the death of an 18-year-old Georgia football commit who suffered a sudden medical emergency.
Marcellus Young Casario, 18, was a senior and boarding student at Rabun Gap-Nacoochee School in northeast Georgia. He planned to graduate in December and enroll at the University of Georgia in January, the school said.
Casario suffered a medical emergency Friday morning and was taken to the hospital, where he died. No further details have been released.
A native of Halifax, Nova Scotia, Casario, who was known as Mar, came to Rabun Gap as a junior. The school described him as “a natural leader, a loyal friend, and a standout student-athlete.”
The 18-year-old was a defensive lineman with a passion for football. He committed to Georgia on June 15. ESPN ranked him as the nation’s No. 49 defensive end and a three-star recruit.
“He was everything a coach wants in a player,” Rabun Gap head football coach Derek White said. “Mar truly embodied our mission to ‘love one another.’ He was known for his relentless dedication, and his journey as a student-athlete was marked by hard work and a true brotherhood with his teammates.”
Georgia head coach Kirby Smart addressed Casario’s death Saturday in a postgame press conference.
“One of the toughest calls I’ve ever gotten,” Smart said. “It’s just tragic to have a loss of life at that age. Can you imagine if that’s your child? And he was such a great kid. He was always smiling, always positive and had a great future in front of him.”
Smart added that he and the team are praying for Casario’s family.
Rabun Gap says it is providing counseling and care services for its students, faculty and staff following Casario’s death.
“Mar brought light, faith, and character to everything he did, and his absence is a tremendous void in our close-knit community,” said Head of School Bob Ahrens. “Our community is mourning, and our hearts and prayers are with his family in Halifax, his teammates, and his friends as we navigate this unimaginable loss together.”

title: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the dwindling number of Pearl Harbor survivors, dies at 106
text:
Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the dwindling number of Pearl Harbor survivors, dies at 106
Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the few remaining Pearl Harbor survivors, has died.
Johnson died Saturday at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts. He was 106, according to one of his daughters, Diane Johnson.
“It’s going to be a hell of a Thanksgiving,” Diane Johnson said. “He’s going to be up there with all of his friends and family and my mom.”
Freeman Johnson was one of the estimated 87,000 military personnel on Oahu on Dec. 7, 1941, and was below deck working on a boiler of the USS St. Louis when the Japanese surprise attack happened. In a May 2026 interview with The Associated Press, Johnson said he didn’t hear or see the attack. He never heard his shipmates firing anti-aircraft guns at the attacking planes — shooting down a torpedo plane.
“While all the rigamarole was going on topside, I was inside a steam drum. Couldn’t see anything, absolutely nothing,” said Johnson, whose job had been known as a firefighter on the ship.
Even as the St. Louis headed into the Pacific Ocean, Johnson knew little about the attack. By the time he was topside, the St. Louis, a light cruiser, had evaded midget submarines and safely set out to sea.
“We were way out to sea, way out. You couldn’t see any land at all. All you saw was ocean,” he said. “I was just a sailor, just a swabbie, I was not an officer. They don’t tell you anything if you don’t need to know. And I didn’t need to know it. So they tell you nothing.”
The list of surviving veterans from the attack had stood at about a dozen names after the December 2025 death of Ira “Ike” Schab, who was 105.
While Johnson didn’t see the Pearl Harbor attack, which killed just over 2,400 Americans and propelled the United States into the war, he was witness to other historic moments during World War II.
He helped commission the USS Iowa and recalled the battleship’s preparations in November 1943 ahead of transporting President Franklin D. Roosevelt to the Tehran Conference with British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Josef Stalin. The ship was equipped with two elevators and a bathtub. All the ammunition and much of the oil was removed to lighten the ship as it made its way down the Potomac River to pick up Roosevelt. It was reloaded before the ship headed out to sea.
Johnson also witnessed the war’s end while aboard the Iowa. He was on the Iowa’s mast watching the surrender ceremonies about a mile away in Tokyo Bay aboard the USS Missouri on Sept. 2, 1945.
“I could see the boats coming up with the Marines escorting the Japanese onto the ship and sitting around a table,” he said. “It was all over. That was the end of the war. A bunch of us got together — the war is over. Let’s go home.”
For all the attention to Pearl Harbor, the gruff Johnson, who was known for his cackling laugh and mischievous smile, didn’t see it as one of the defining moments in his life.
Those would have been getting married after the war to his late wife and having three daughters. He worked for years in a machinist shop, then in a convenience store and, finally, delivering meals to seniors — all jobs he retired from, the last one at the age of 90.
“Pearl Harbor just happened. I can’t put it any other way,” he said.

title: Maine should honor Sen. Muskie’s environmental legacy
text:
Colin Phillips, MD, FACC, is immediate past governor of the Maine chapter of the American College of Cardiology.
All who enjoy clean air owe a debt of gratitude to Maine Sen. Edmund Muskie. Starting in the 1960s, Sen. Muskie set in motion the Clean Air Act, reducing air pollution while simultaneously driving innovation and economic growth.
Today, particulate pollution levels are rising again in part due to efforts that undo Muskie’s legacy. Through executive orders, Supreme Court decisions and direct deregulation by the Environmental Protection Agency, the federal government is attacking protections to safeguard public health. This includes weakening emission standards and controls on air pollution and limiting the accountability that companies that pollute have to neighboring communities and public health at large.
As particulate pollution is the second leading risk factor for death worldwide, the cost of deregulation is measured both in economic terms due to lost productivity and increased healthcare spending and personal terms through premature death. As an interventional cardiologist, I am personally concerned with how the particulate pollution we breathe increases the risk of a heart attack.
Two specific Congressional Review Acts, both of which have passed the U.S. House of Representatives and are introduced in the U.S. Senate as S.J.Res.209 and S.J.Res.210, further these deregulatory efforts and attacks on public health.
The premise of these resolutions is that the federal government can undo the work done at the state level to limit air pollution. While focused on a set of EPA waivers utilized by California ports, if passed, this would further disincentivize companies to transition away from fossil fuel pollution and take responsibility for the pollution they introduce in neighboring communities. In Portland, this has real impact as the city works to mitigate cruise boat air pollution.
While Maine hasn’t adopted the standards that Congress is considering cancelling, allowing other states legislative authority to implement these programs drives investment and innovation in technologies that Maine ports and companies can benefit from.
When California ports advance technologies such as high-efficiency engines to “cold ironing” equipment that allow boats to plug into electricity and turn off their engines while docked, we all benefit. These are real life examples of reducing pollution at massive ports for Portland to follow. When California’s ports mandate less pollution, companies worldwide innovate to improve the air quality in surrounding communities.
Our leaders must focus on reduced dependence on fossil fuels and true energy independence through renewable sources. This transition not only results in cleaner air for all, but also less economic pressure on Maine families as demonstrated by skyrocketing fuel prices in the wake of global conflict disrupting oil markets. Renewable energy generated and stored locally means economic resilience in addition to clean air.
Change is possible when we have a playbook to follow. Imagine a summer scene where cruise ships are docked in Portland without billowing particulate pollution into the Old Port or dissolving and blowing it into Casco Bay.
The results of the midterm elections will usher in new leadership nationwide and serves as a rejection of the country’s current trajectory and a repudiation of leadership seemingly intent on making life worse for all but a few. This presents an opportunity to reaffirm previous commitments to public health through achievable and commonsense environmental standards and rules.
Sen. Collins and Sen. King both tout their independence and efforts to improve the material conditions for people working and living in Maine. In the waning weeks of the 119th Congress, voting “No” on both S.J.Res.209 and S.J.Res.210 follows Sen. Muskie’s legacy to do just that.

title: A new SNAP proposal could cut benefits for millions. Here's what to know
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new SNAP proposal could cut benefits for millions. Here's what to know
A new federal proposal could make it harder for some families to qualify for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that 6.3 million people nationwide could lose SNAP benefits by the 2029 fiscal year if the proposal is finalized.
This story was originally published on MySA, a Hearst publication.
Currently, states can use certain Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) benefits to help households qualify for SNAP, even if their income is above the program's usual limit. However, the proposal, announced Nov. 10, would end that option for noncash services such as child care assistance and job training.
The change could also affect school meals. USDA estimates 1.8 million children would lose automatic eligibility for free meals through SNAP, but says 97% would still qualify for free or reduced-price meals based on household income.
The agency hasn't estimated how many could be affected, as the proposal isn't in effect. Public comments are due Dec. 10 and can be found on the proposal's tabs. USDA expects the rule to reach its full effects in 2029 if finalized.
Trump's team put forth a similar plan 7 years ago
The first Trump administration proposed to clamp down on such tactics in 2019. But that proposal was withdrawn by President Joe Biden's administration in 2021.
"Simply put, we did not want to remove millions of people from the program, particularly working poor or children," said Stacy Dean, a former USDA official under Biden who is now executive director of the Global Food Institute at George Washington University.
The latest proposal is more sweeping and could prevent states from basing SNAP eligibility on TANF-funded benefits such as job-related counseling or one-time vouchers for vehicle repairs so that people can get to work, said David Super, a law professor at Georgetown University who has studied the food aid program.
"The administration here is basically proposing to eliminate the flexibility that Congress gave the states to serve working poor people," Super said.
SNAP is also connected to other programs for low-income people
Being in a household that receives SNAP benefits also makes school children eligible for free meals. The Agriculture Department says that nearly 1.8 million children would lose eligibility with their family losing SNAP — but that 97% of them would still qualify for free or reduced-price school meals through another process.
But the government says some of the children would not get the lunches, even if they are eligible, if their families don't apply.
The proposal comes at a time when the number of people receiving the aid has fallen sharply — and on the heels of sweeping election gains for Democrats across the country.
"The public indicated they want their elected officials to focus on making life affordable," the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning policy research institute, said in an analysis of the proposal. "Yet the Trump Administration is doubling down on making it harder for people to feed their families."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Characters of the County: Soren Barker Helps Students Grow
text:
Soren Barker compares his ability to balance everything in his life to the way a bee flies.
“The physics goes against their ability to fly,” Barker said. “I think the same thing is true of life and art … Physically, it doesn’t make sense but we’re making it happen.”
Many aspects of Barker’s life focus on storytelling and connection. He spends his time directing a show at the Lincoln Theater in Damariscotta, teaching middle school social studies at Boothbay Region Elementary School, serving in his church, and spending time with friends on a longstanding Dungeons and Dragons campaign.
Growing up on the Boothbay peninsula, Barker said he always wanted to move away. It took him until he grew older to want to come back.
“What we have is remarkable,” Barker said. “The trust that we have in each other and the true sense of community is something that is missing in other parts of the world and is still alive and well here.”
In his teens, Barker joined the Boothbay Region YMCA Y-Arts program and began participating in community theater. That same year, he devoted himself to his faith in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Damariscotta.
Barker continued pursuing his love of theater at Brigham Young University in Rexburg, Idaho. There he met the woman who would become his wife, Emily Sue Barker, in a theater makeup class. A year into college, he left to complete his church mission sharing the Gospel and providing service to others in Anaheim, Calif.
After returning to college, Barker soon left again with Emily Sue Barker for Nanjing, China to teach English. While there, Soren Barker learned more about how people are the same despite many things being different in other countries, he said.
The lesson Barker learned is something he said he tries to teach in his social studies lessons.
“You need to know that people on the other side of the planet are people too,” Barker said. “And yes, they have different contexts in history and cultural values. If we can understand that we’ll be able to work together and if we can’t understand that then we’re doomed to fail.”
It was both the humanities courses he took at university and his experience teaching abroad that Barker said convinced him to pursue teaching full-time.
“I really enjoy sharing and explaining and being a part of the educational journey and being one of those guides along that road and journey of life,” Barker said.
When he returned from China, Baker graduated from Brigham Young University campus in Provo, Utah in 2018 with a bachelor’s degree in theater education and minors in humanities and history education. Barker saw a job posting at Boothbay Region Elementary School and immediately applied.
Barker said growing up in Boothbay gives him a unique perspective when teaching because he knows many of the tricks his seventh and eighth grade students try to pull to get out of doing work.
“I see myself in many of my students and it gives me hope for them that middle school is just a chapter, it’s a stop along the journey of life,” Barker said. “We’re all a little bit nutty at this time of our lives.”
Barker teaches social studies, a field he views as all-encompassing. He incorporates everything from history and civics to math and language arts to provide his students with a fuller picture of why people made the decisions they did in the past.
“If we don’t learn from the past and we don’t understand why certain choices were made for good or ill, then we won’t know what choice we need to make now,” Barker said.
One of his goals is getting students out of the classroom and into the community, especially through service, Barker said. This year, students raised money for the Maine Cancer Foundation at the Boothbay Region Elementary School Cancer Walk Fundraiser on Oct. 30.
“As the human brain goes through the middle school years of those early teenage times, thinking outside of yourself and being empathetic and looking towards others, it’s very hard,” Barker said.
Community theater has continued to hold a place in Barker’s life. He is currently directing “The Inn at Little Bethlehem” for Lincoln County Community Theater, a role he finds similar to his job teaching. In the same way he helps students refine research projects or essays, he helps actors reach the best performance they can give, sometimes not in the way he foresaw.
Part of how Barker helps students and actors fulfill their potential is by having high expectations, which cause people to rise to meet them.
“Then you have so many kids who are like, ‘I never knew I could make something like that,’ or actors who are like, I never knew this is what could happen,” Barker said.
Involvement in theater plays into Barker’s community service, as it creates moments where the audience is listening as one, he said.
“It’s a sacred act to create life on stage, to provide a window of time where people can come together in a dedicated space to examine what it is that makes us human,” Barker said.
Similarly to how he teaches history, Barker also said he views storytelling in theater as ways to inform how people comprehend the world.
“That’s why I do theater, because how do we understand who we are,” Barker said. “It’s through ‘Seussical,’ it’s through Shakespeare.”
Barker is also involved with his church as the elders quorum president, handling ministry and service project coordination. He said his belief system has played a large role in his life by drawing his family together and helping him look outward.
“It’s a belief system that helps shape how I look at the world and look at other people as being brothers and sisters and children of god but also with the intrinsic desire to serve others,” Barker said.
On top of his busy schedule, Barker also balances taking care of his two sons, Jack Barker, age 4, and Luke Barker, age 8.
In his spare time, Barker enjoys playing Dungeons and Dragons with his friends, an extension of his love of storytelling. His group is two years into a campaign centered on fairy tales.
“We’ve had some of the most profound depths of despair where we are sobbing at the death of a character or we are just crying at the joy of love or cheering in success and raining justice down on the wicked or whatever it may be, it’s another one of those cathartic things in society,” Barker said.
In the future, Barker said he hopes to continue directing shows for the community and encouraging actors and students to find their best way to showcase their talents.
“Everybody has greatness in them,” Barker said. “It just takes a little bit of dusting and polishing and celebrating to make that greatness grow.”

title: More people are using ‘buy now, pay later’ for basic expenses
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PHOENIX, Az. (InvestigateTV) — For big ticket purchases, people would often use a “buy now, pay later” method to help break up the cost.
According to a recent LendingTree survey, 25% of buy now, pay later users have used the microloans to buy groceries. The services, which include platforms like Klarna and Affirm, are often used to split up larger purchases like flights or appliances.
Cody Bortle, a teacher who started in 2023, said covering bills has become more difficult.
“Everything has just gotten way too expensive,” Bortle said.
Bortle said car payments, groceries and rent have all increased. His rent recently jumped $150 per month.
“I never imagined I’d be in my professional career as a teacher, just paycheck to paycheck,” he said.
He maxed out $15,000 worth of credit cards and now covers some expenses with buy now, pay later microloans, including a trip home to visit his grandparents.
“I can afford $70 a month, but I can’t afford a $400 plane ticket right now, so let me pay $100 right now, and I’ll pay 70 for the next few months,” Bortle said.
Late payments increasing
More people are making late payments on buy now, pay later services. According to LendingTree, 41% of people who use BNPL options have made at least one late payment in the past year, up from 34% the previous year.
“The fact that they’re so attractive and so easy to get is what also makes them so dangerous,” said Miguel Velasco, the senior director of counseling at Money Management International (MMI), a nonprofit that helps people get out of debt.
The buy now, pay later industry touts its products as more consumer-friendly and more available than other lending options, like credit cards and payday loans.
“When [consumers] start buying essentials with buy now pay later, that’s the moment to stop,” Velasco said. “We really need to stop and understand what the financial situation is.”
If you don’t make your payments on time, these companies could freeze your account and possibly turn you over to a collection agency.
Around 90% of people who have asked to have a late fee waived actually had success either getting it reduced or removed, according to LendingTree.
Creating a budget
Velasco said it starts with a budget. He recommends writing down all money coming in and all money going out, then making changes.
“Those are hard conversations to have because you’re telling people they need to stop their spending habits. You’re telling people they need to go get a second job. You’re telling people they need to maybe incorporate some roommates or find a way of making money work,” Velasco said.
Bortle connected with MMI for help to get out of debt. He’s on track to pay off his credit cards by 2030. Along the way, he’s sharing lessons about money with his students.
“I’m very transparent with my kids,” Bortle said. “You have to be really smart with your money now, especially if you have jobs in your high school years. Start saving that because you will need it.”

title: Cooper Flagg’s love of PB&J makes young fans feel seen
text:
Leo Harrington is a Cooper Flagg superfan. The 11-year-old from Arlington, Massachusetts, attended the basketball camp at the University of Maine run by Flagg and his brothers, Hunter and Ace. He and his mother, Kelly Harrington, were among the first in line when the Portland Sea Dogs held a Cooper Flagg bobblehead giveaway in August.
Now Leo knows that he and Flagg share more than a love of basketball and goofy sports collectibles. The two are connoisseurs of peanut butter and jelly sandwiches.
Flagg’s fondness for the basic lunch staple was revealed when he was spotted eating a peanut butter and jelly sandwich on the bench Nov. 6 during the Dallas Mavericks’ win over the Utah Jazz. A few days later, Flagg was scarfing down a PB&J during a win over the Brooklyn Nets.
Flagg, one of the NBA’s brightest young stars, didn’t make PB&J hip or chic, he made a connection with fans who already felt close to him due to his humble Maine roots. When Leo Harrington saw his favorite player taking big bites of a sandwich on the bench during a game, he felt seen.
“So I’m not the only one who likes peanut butter and jelly,” he said on the TD Garden concourse Sunday before the Mavericks took on the Boston Celtics.
The relationship between NBA players and peanut butter and jelly sandwiches goes back a few years, to when Kevin Garnett popularized them as an easy pregame snack while with the Celtics. A PB&J provides between 350 and 450 calories. A player can burn more than 1,000 calories in an NBA game. In this regard, Flagg is not a trendsetter.
Flagg, however, is a 19-year old kid playing a physical game against grown men. He won’t celebrate his 20th birthday until late December. Since he’s been in the public eye so long, it’s easy to forget he’s just a few years older than the kids wearing his jersey.
As such, the 6-foot-10, 205-pound Flagg needs to get bigger and stronger. A mid-game sandwich is a means to that end.
Asked about the sandwiches last week, Flagg said they’re a part of the Mavericks’ plan to help him through the grind of an NBA season. The game in Boston was the second night of back-to-back games for Dallas, following a Saturday game in Cleveland, and was the Mavs’ third in four days, all on the road.
Flagg also noted he prefers smooth peanut butter over chunky, and grape jelly. Think of the sponsorship deals that could evolve.
“The only thing smoother than Cooper Flagg’s moves on the court is the Skippy in his sandwich.”
Or this: Our commercial fades in to Flagg struggling on the court. He’s tired and lethargic. Dallas coach Dusty May puts in a sub and Flagg comes to the bench. A trainer hands him a sandwich, and a closeup reveals a generous helping of Smuckers grape jelly acting as a buttress between a layer of peanut butter and two slices of basic white bread. Flagg eagerly inhales the sandwich, then returns to the court and dominates. As he’s about to celebrate a dunk with his teammates, a ref discretely points to the glob of jelly across the 32 on the front of his jersey.
Madison Avenue, you’re welcome.
Flagg wasn’t spotted on the bench eating a sandwich Sunday. It probably wouldn’t have helped: The Celtics led by 33 points after one quarter and cruised to a 131-94 victory. Flagg scored 17 points.
Colton Everett, 15, of Bangor, said he’d never seen an NBA player casually eat a sandwich on the bench. Logan Boone, 13, of Pittsfield said he thinks a peanut butter and jelly sandwich can only be good for Flagg.
An NBA player’s life is nothing that could be considered normal. By enjoying something as basic as a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, Flagg found a touch of normal with which his fans in Maine and around the world can very much relate. He collects basketball cards, like us. He eats peanut butter and jelly, like us.
Flagg said he occasionally might have a peanut butter and banana sandwich with honey. Otherwise it’s the basic classic so many of us carried in a lunch box to school. There are ways of churching up a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, of course. Artisan bread, peanut butter made with rare heirloom peanuts grown in climate-controlled soil, and jelly made from grapes raised by monks who took a vow of silence.
No thanks. We gave the hipsters avocado toast. We’re keeping PB&J simple, and acknowledging it’s now a bond between everyday Mainers and their basketball icon.

title: Sacopee Valley students team up to spread birthday cheer
text:
Sacopee Valley students team up to spread birthday cheer
At Sacopee Valley Middle School, academics are, of course, a critical part of the school day, but the staff prioritizes service, too. Each trimester, the eighth grade team works together on a project. This term, they're making birthday kits to donate to local food pantries.
"Your birthday is only once a year, and it's always-- you want it to be special," said Lyricc Merrill, one of the many students involved. The kits contain decorations, a handmade card, and ingredients for a cake — including one can of Sprite.
Eighth grader Leo Hernandez explained the soda is used as a substitute for oil and eggs. He said, "It's just an activator, so it works the same way."
Each class volunteered to collect different items before coming together to assemble the kits. All of the pieces were put in a disposable cake pan and sealed with colorful ribbon, which the students learned to curl.
Spreading birthday cheer was their goal throughout the project. Special education teacher Lindsey Bridges said, "If you're struggling to get the basics, you're probably not going to be able to afford a birthday party for your kid."
Annabelle Rich, another eighth grader, hopes these kits help parents get those basics and something special for their child. "If a kid really wanted something for their birthday, the parent could spend more money on that and be able to not have to spend as much on all the supplies," she said.
Rich added that she likes helping other people and making a positive impact. Merrill agrees. She said, "It always feels good once you do it, and you know, they might go and spread that kindness more, and eventually it might circle back around to you."
Next trimester, the eighth grade teachers are planning to make blankets with their classes. The final project of the year is still undecided, and, after that, the students will move on to high school.
"Part of being a teacher is getting kids together and caring about each other and teaching them how to care about each other," Bridges said. "I was happy to be a part of something where they could do that."
Hernandez, Rich, and Merrill hope to inspire others to care about their community too. "You're more powerful than you think you are," Hernandez said. "You can truly make an impact."
Merrill suggests acts of service can be small. She said, "Even if you can't donate stuff or if you can't buy somebody something, just little acts of kindness — a simple hello, a polite tone, or a smile — can go a long way, make somebody's day."

title: Cooper Flagg scores 17 points in Boston homecoming; Celtics crush Mavericks
text:
Cooper Flagg scores 17 points in Boston homecoming; Celtics crush Mavericks
The Dallas Mavericks lost to the Boston Celtics by 37 points at TD Garden Sunday night, where Maine fans turned out to watch Cooper Flagg’s return to New England.
Flagg scored 17 points and went scoreless in the first quarter for just the third time in his career.
Flagg had scored 43 points less than a week earlier during the Maverick's 125-122 win against the Indiana Pacers.
The Celtics would outscore the Mavericks 41 to 9 in the 1st quarter, making it the largest lead in Celtics' history. Jayson Tatum led all scorers with 32 points on 11-18 shooting in 30 minutes. The final score was 131 to 94.
After Sunday's loss, Flagg said that he had been battling an illness but wanted to play in front of fans who had come to see him.
“I try to play every game,” Flagg said. “Obviously, being back home and a lot of people showing up to watch it means a bit more.”
The Mavericks return to Texas and are scheduled to play the Golden State Warriors on Wednesday night.

title: Pastor, wife hit and killed by car walking to grandson’s wedding reception
text:
TYLER, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) — A Texas church is mourning the death of its founding pastor and his wife, who were struck and killed by a car Saturday while walking to their grandson’s wedding reception.
Caleb Hawley, lead pastor of LifeSource Community Church, confirmed the deaths of senior teaching pastor John Offutt and his wife, Carla Offutt, during a livestream of Sunday’s service.
“For those of you who don’t know, pastor John and his beautiful wife, Carla, were struck by a car last night walking across the road to their grandson’s reception after the wedding and were hit by a car and killed instantly,” Hawley said, fighting back tears from the pulpit.
Crash details
According to the Texas Department of Public Safety, the incident occurred around 6:15 p.m. Saturday.
Crash investigators said a vehicle traveling westbound on Farm-to-Market Road 515 struck the couple, who were pronounced dead at the scene.
The driver, identified as Ruth Rohrbach, 46, of Winnsboro, was taken to CHRISTUS Winnsboro for treatment, according to the Texas Department of Public Safety.
No charges have been filed against Rohrbach.
Executive pastor Sean Graver said John Offutt had officiated his grandson’s wedding and was walking with his wife to a reception at the Coke Schoolhouse in Como when a vehicle struck them as they crossed the highway.
Church leaders speak after deaths
Hawley said John Offutt was his father-in-law, mentor and friend. The two had worked together to lead LifeSource for nearly 12 years, he said.
“John and I have planned together, dreamed together, led this church together, and I honestly thought I had a lot more years, more conversations, more opportunities to learn from his depth of wisdom, more time to grow together,” Hawley said.
Hawley said the loss had changed the family’s world and urged those grieving not to hide their emotions.
“It’s OK not to be OK,” he said. “We don’t have to pretend this morning. We don’t have to hold back tears. We don’t have to have the right words.”
A church representative said details about arrangements would be shared as they become available.

title: Injured Searsmont EMS Chief shares thank you letter ahead of Wednesday’s homecoming
text:

A welcome home celebration is planned for Searsmont EMS Chief Sarah Tompkins Wednesday afternoon.
We’re told Tompkins will not be speaking to the media on Wednesday, but Monday, she did put out a letter saying in part.
“I have worked in EMS for eight years, but for the last 6 months I have been the one being cared for after my worst day.
I spent close to five months in the hospital and seven weeks in rehab. I still have wounds and scars, but I am also filled with so much hope for all of us.
Thank you to the EMTs, paramedics, firefighters, and life flight crews that saved my life, to the CNAs, nurses, doctors and therapists who cared for me and took the time to learn who I am as a person," said Tompkins in a letter.
An escort will start in Augusta Wednesday, ending with a Welcome Home Gathering at the Searsmont Fire Station.
At last check, the town says Tompkin’s arrival time will be around 2:15 p.m.

title: InvestigateTV+: The support for caregivers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Tens of millions of Americans are caring for sick or aging loved ones and most of it is unpaid. InvestigateTV+ takes an in-depth look at how some hospitals are stepping up to support them and inspires a conversation about the people behind the patient.
Then, centuries-old giants thrive in southern swamps, and we explore how communities are fighting to protect them and the natural defense they provide.
Plus, a surrendered pup gets a front row seat to adventure that’s bringing joy to people across the country.
Caregiver support
A growing number of hospitals are offering programs designed to support family caregivers. Experts say that support can improve outcomes and reduce costly trips to the hospital.
More than 60 million Americans provide care that includes bathing, managing medications and getting sick or aging loved ones to appointments.
Saving cypress forests
Each year, volunteers working with conservation groups plant thousands of young cypress trees.
To be successful, those plantings must include a nutria guard, a piece of often recycled plastic to protect young seedlings from being gobbled up by the invasive rodents.
The conservancy has planted thousands of trees over the years, including in the Madisonville area along the Tchefuncte River and in the LaBranche Wetlands in St. Charles Parish.
‘Buy now, pay later’
For big ticket purchases, people would often use a “buy now, pay later” method to help break up the cost.
But as budgets tighten, more people are turning to buy now, pay later options to cover basic expenses, including groceries.
Her motorcycle & her dog
Paige Parlato kicks her motorcycle alive, and her Doberman mix, Han, is ready to ride.
“He’s very laidback, he really likes to be where I’m at, but he really can have some energy if he wants to,” Parlato said.
Parlato and Han cruise weekly through her town, turning heads everywhere they go.

title: Route 196 in Topsham reopened after closing due to ‘suspicious package’
text:
Part of Route 196 in Topsham is back open after closing Monday because of a “suspicious package” on the side of the road.
The town had informed commuters on social media around noon Monday that the stretch of road near Harpswell Auto Sales and the Lisbon town line was closed.
The road was reopened around 1:30 p.m.
In an update later Monday, Topsham police said officers went to the scene after receiving a report of a package that looked like an explosive device. It was wrapped in Styrofoam and duct tape with wires protruding from it.
Local police contacted the state police bomb unit and shut down the road. Maine State Police X-rayed the package and deemed it safe.
With the road reopened, buses from School Administrative District 75 are operating on their normal schedules and routes, the district posted on Facebook.
Topsham police encouraged anyone with information about the package to contact Officer Jose Gomez at (207) 725-4337 or [email protected].

title: Jackson Lab working with Maine oncologists on cancer biomarker testing
text:
BAR HARBOR, Maine (WABI) - Scientists at The Jackson Lab are working with oncologists around Maine on biomarker testing used to diagnose and treat cancer.
Lindsey Kelley, a board-certified genetic counselor for Jackson Lab, said biomarker testing can be a key component of diagnosing and treating cancer.
What biomarkers are
“Biomarkers in general are a test result that gives us an idea about someone’s health or a disease they might have. Biomarkers that people might be familiar with are things like blood pressure monitoring or cholesterol testing,” Kelley said.
Cancer is caused when the DNA in cells changes. Biomarkers can focus on a particular part of the body. HER2 is a biomarker for breast cancer, and EGFR is a biomarker for lung cancer.
Biomarkers can be tested through bloodwork or tissue samples.
Biomarker testing differs from genetic testing because it focuses solely on tumor cells, as opposed to inherited cells that could increase the risk for cancer.
How testing is used
“We actually do a testing of the tumor itself, or the tumor DNA in the bloodstream, and we use that information to give us a better idea about what might have caused that cancer, how it’s growing, how we expect it to progress and then how we might be able to treat it best,” Kelley said.
Kelley said biomarkers also can be used to monitor patients.
“We could monitor biomarkers to see if any of them are starting to look like there might be a presence of cancer. We can use biomarkers as another way to monitor response to treatment. In addition to that, patients who have finished their treatment, are being monitored to just ensure there’s no recurrence of that cancer,” she said.
Availability in Maine
Cancer biomarker testing is available in Maine. How readily a patient can get it depends on the cancer, the provider and insurance coverage.
Jackson Lab developed the Maine Cancer Genomics Initiative, which offers free support to oncologists throughout the state.
“Some oncologists will reach out to us when they have a result that they’re really struggling to understand. We have other oncologists that do send almost every test report to us, just for a second opinion. So that any cancer patient in Maine is really receiving the same type of cutting edge care no matter where they live,” Kelley said.
Legislation on insurance coverage
Last year, a bill to require health insurance coverage for biomarker testing was introduced in the Maine Legislature. It passed in the House but did not pass the Senate before lawmakers adjourned for the session.

title: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond: Here's how stacks up against the past 007 actors
text:
How Robert Pattinson stacks up against the past James Bonds
At 40, with several blockbuster franchises already under his belt, Robert Pattinson becomes one of the most accomplished actors to play James Bond.
Related video above: A first look at Pattinson as James Bond
Amazon MGM Studios, the new stewards of the iconic spy, announced the pick Monday. The move ends years of rampant speculation over who would inherit the mantle from Daniel Craig — who was once seen as an unconventional pick, but one who helped elevate the franchise to new heights.
Six actors have played Bond over the course of 25 official films — David Niven in 1967's “Casino Royale” spoof doesn't quite count here. Here's an overview of their careers before and as 007. Ages are as of their first Bond film's release.
Sean Connery
Age at Bond debut: 32
Times playing Bond: Seven
Known for, before Bond: Not much. He had acted onstage and in a spate of films, but his first leading role, in “On the Fiddle,” came just a year before his real breakthrough in “Dr. No”
Bond films: “Dr. No,” “From Russia With Love,” “Goldfinger,” “Thunderball,” “You Only Live Twice,” “Diamonds Are Forever” and (see below) “Never Say Never Again”
Sean Connery, the first to portray Ian Fleming's creation onscreen (drawing some skepticism from the author), is also the only one whose time in the role was not continuous. The Scottish actor's time as Bond technically spanned 21 years, from 1962 to 1983. He left after 1967's “You Only Live Twice,” returned after George Lazenby's one-off movie, left, and returned again during Roger Moore's run.
1983’s “Never Say Never Again,” which was released the same year as a Moore film, wasn’t made by the usual Bond producers, Eon Productions, and isn’t counted as an official film, despite Connery’s presence.
George Lazenby
Age at Bond debut: 30
Times playing Bond: One
Known for, before Bond: Nothing! James Bond was his very first film role, though he had some experience modeling and acting in commercials
Bond films: “On Her Majesty's Secret Service”
George Lazenby holds the distinction of being the only Bond hailing from outside the U.K. and Ireland; he was Australian. He declined the opportunity to reprise the role, citing in part on-set treatment and onerous contractual terms.
Roger Moore
Age at Bond debut: 45
Times playing Bond: Seven
Known for, before Bond: Mainly television, including the long-running thriller series “The Saint”
Bond films: “Live and Let Die,” “The Man With the Golden Gun,” “The Spy Who Loved Me,” “Moonraker,” “For Your Eyes Only,” “Octopussy” and “A View to Kill”
Roger Moore was the oldest Bond, debuting at 45 and hanging up his dinner jacket in 1985 at 57. “I was only about 400 years too old for the part,” the Englishman once said about his last jaunt as Bond. After a cameo as Bond on a 1960s sketch show, he was known for a lighter take on the character.
Timothy Dalton
Age at Bond debut: 41
Times playing Bond: Two
Known for, before Bond: Stage roles and period dramas, including the films “Wuthering Heights” and “Mary, Queen of Scots” and the “Jane Eyre” series
Bond films: “The Living Daylights” and “Licence to Kill”
Timothy Dalton was actually approached for Bond in his mid-20s, but felt he was too young for the part. The British actor ultimately took the role in 1987's “The Living Daylights.” A dispute between producers and MGM scuttled the third film in his contract, and he declined to return once it was settled.
Pierce Brosnan
Age at Bond debut: 42
Times playing Bond: Four
Known for, before Bond: The television series “Remington Steele” and the new boyfriend in “Mrs. Doubtfire”
Bond films: “GoldenEye,” “Tomorrow Never Dies,” “The World Is Not Enough” and “Die Another Day”
Pierce Brosnan was also rumored for, and even offered, Bond before he became 007 in 1995's “GoldenEye.” The Irish actor's late wife, Cassandra Harris, had even had a part in “For Your Eyes Only.” Timothy Dalton's decision not to return for a third movie opened the door for Brosnan. His last Bond film was 2002's “Die Another Day” — it seemed he might have a fifth outing, but in 2004 he told the Toronto Sun that producers had decided to go in another direction.
Daniel Craig
Age at Bond debut: 38
Times playing Bond: Five
Known for, before Bond: Mostly stage and supporting roles onscreen, including in “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider” and “Layer Cake”
Bond films: “Casino Royale,” “Quantum of Solace,” “Skyfall,” “Spectre” and “No Time to Die”
Daniel Craig's casting perhaps engendered the most controversy — blond and under 6 feet, the English actor broke the mold of previous Bonds. Craig told The Associated Press that even he felt “incredibly flattered and deeply confused” by his selection. 2006's “Casino Royale” served as Bond's origin story and reboot, and Craig's gritty portrayal earned widespread critical acclaim. Craig made it clear he was done with the role after five films and — spoiler alert — his Bond dies despite the title of 2021's “No Time to Die.” “If we kill Bond, we can begin again,” he told The Times.
Robert Pattinson
Age cast: 40
Times playing Bond: Amazon MGM declined to comment on the terms of his deal, but Puck reported it would be for three films.
Known for, before Bond: Several franchises — including “Harry Potter,” “Twilight” and “Batman” — but also a slew of auteur-driven indie movies, from David Cronenberg's “Cosmopolis” to Lynne Ramsay's “Die My Love”
Bond films: Denis Villeneuve's still-untitled “Bond 26,” for sure

title: Two children found dead by firefighters responding to a house fire
text:
BELOIT, Wis. (WMTV/Gray News) - Two children died after a fire broke out at a Wisconsin home early Sunday morning, city officials said.
Firefighters found two children dead inside the home, and an adult was taken to a hospital. The children’s names and ages have not been released.
The Rock County Medical Examiner’s Office is assisting in the investigation.
Interim Beloit Fire Chief Todd Farley spoke about the tragedy, saying, “There were attempts by the mother to save the two children that were on the second floor with her. The fire just grew very rapidly, and the mom was not able to do that.”
Officials added that the mother of the children escaped the fire through a second-story window and was injured in the fall.
Though there were no working smoke detectors in the home at the time of the fire, fire officials said it’s unclear whether smoke alarms would have made a difference because of how quickly the fire spread.
Neighbor Javier Perez said he found it hard to put the incident into words.
“The kids are gone,” Perez said. “So we, the neighbors, don’t know what to do; we don’t know what to say.”
The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

title: Man charged after allegedly sending peanut butter-covered mail to woman with severe allergy
text:
PLANTATION, Fla. (Gray News) — A Florida man is facing criminal charges after allegedly sending mail smeared with peanut butter to a person who has a life-threatening allergy to peanuts.
Victim reported card
The Plantation Police Department said a victim called officers Aug. 14, 2025, after receiving a peanut butter-covered greeting card in the mail.
The woman has a severe peanut allergy and tried to remove the peanut butter from her hands right after realizing it was on the card, the police department said. She still reacted and experienced hives, itching and tingling in her arms.
Detectives identify sender
Detectives determined that Joseph Gerard Cancellare Jr., 68, of Plantation, sent the envelope.
According to police, Cancellare and the victim knew each other personally, and he was aware of her severe allergy. Investigators did not provide a motive.
Arrest and charges
Cancellare was arrested Nov. 13, 2026, and taken to the Broward County Jail on charges of aggravated battery and culpable negligence.
“This case reminds us that actions intended to harm others can have serious, potentially life-threatening consequences,” Plantation police said.

title: Grammy nominations snub Harry Styles and hip-hop, while surprises include Dolly Parton
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The 2027 Grammy Award nominees are here and there’s a lot to discuss, from Raye and Rosalía dominating the nominations to John Cale receiving his first nod at 84.
Like every year, there were a few artists who made the coveted list Monday and a few who didn’t. Snubs and surprises are in no short supply across the 100 categories that will be awarded Feb. 7.
No hip-hop in most of the general field categories
It’s a 180 from the 2026 Grammys, where, for the first time, there were three releases nominated in both the rap album and album of the year categories. This year, there isn’t a single rap release in the record, song or album of the year categories.
According to Billboard, Drake — the only rapper to score a No. 1 hit on the all-genre Hot 100 this year, with “Janice STFU” — did not submit his three 2026 albums or any of their songs for Grammy consideration. But even without his star power (or that of last year’s nominees Kendrick Lamar, Clipse and Tyler, the Creator), hip-hop seems like a huge absence.
A$AP Rocky’s first full-length album in eight years, “Don’t Be Dumb,” is also noticeably absent, as is Baby Keem’s “Ca$ino.” It seems all eyes will be on Don Toliver, the rising trap and R&B rapper-singer, who scored a best new artist nomination in addition to a rap album one.
But let the record show Drake did secure one nomination: for the newly minted best Latin song category, for his Spanish-language feature on Karol G’s “Ahí.”
Women dominate many of the major categories … and in country
For the first time, the six artists with the most nominations at the Grammys are all women.
And women make up every nominee in the album and song of the year categories, save for Grammy favorite Bruno Mars. For album of the year, Raye and Rosalía will face off against Phoebe Bridgers, Olivia Dean, Ella Langley, Olivia Rodrigo, Taylor Swift and Mars. The list of artists is nearly identical for song of the year — just swap Bridgers for Ariana Grande — and add a first-ever general field nomination for Björk, who is featured on Rosalía’s “Berghain.”
However, there were some strong contenders omitted. Those include Stella Lefty, whose ubiquitous “Boston” did not earn her a single nom, or Gracie Abrams’ “Daughter From Hell.”
But beyond the top categories, women dominate in other, interesting places: dance pop recording, R&B solo performance and in the contemporary country album category, now in its second year. Langley, Kelsea Ballerini, Carter Faith, Megan Moroney and Kacey Musgraves will go head-to-head there. And just as interesting: Only men are nominated in the traditional country category.
Leading men like Harry Styles and Noah Kahan get less love
Harry Styles’ fourth studio album, “Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally.,” did not receive a nomination. The same should be said about Ed Sheeran’s “Play.” Noah Kahan’s critically acclaimed “The Great Divide” received only one nod, in the newly created contemporary folk album category. Justin Bieber’s surprise album “Swag II” didn’t receive a nomination, either.
Newcomer Malcolm Todd was shut out as well, despite lots of love for his album “Do That Again.” It was the same for his sister, the singer-songwriter Audrey Hobert, who was seen as a leading candidate for best new artist.
Beyoncé once again makes history
She’s no stranger to raising the bar. At the 2023 Grammys, Beyoncé became the most-awarded artist in the show’s history. Then, two years later, with “Cowboy Carter,” she became the first Black artist to win country album of the year and the first Black woman to win album of the year since Lauryn Hill’s “The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill” in 1999. She’s now received her 100th career nomination, for “Morning Dew (Donk)” in the R&B solo performance category. The song was the lead single of her 20th anniversary re-release of “B’Day.”
Dolly Parton and Tim Curry receive posthumous nominations
Dolly Parton, who died earlier this year, received three nominations. She’s nominated in the country duo/group performance category twice — for “Butterfly” by Zac Brown Band featuring Parton and “Light of a Clear Blue Morning,” a Parton classic performed with Lainey Wilson, Miley Cyrus, Queen Latifah and Reba McEntire. She’s also nominated in the audiobook, narration and storytelling recording category for her work, “Star of the Show: My Life on Stage.”
In the latter category, competition is fierce: Actor Tim Curry, who also died earlier this year, is nominated for “Vagabond: A Memoir.” And Michelle Obama is nominated in the category for a third time, for “The Look.” Obama has won the award twice before.
BTS and the Asian pop performance category
And now for a little controversy: This year, the Recording Academy created five new Grammy categories, including Asian pop music performance, meant to celebrate releases across K-pop, J-pop, C-pop and beyond. Some fans were excited; others viewed the new category as a racialized barrier for Asian performers.
Not long afterward, K-pop powerhouse BTS said they would not submit their music for consideration. As a result, they did not receive any nominations this year. BTS has never won a Grammy, though they’ve been nominated for five across their career. In fact, no K-pop act had ever won a Grammy before 2026, when “Golden” from “KPop Demon Hunters” took home the trophy for best song for visual media.
After consulting experts, managers, artists and others, the Recording Academy decided to proceed with the category. Another massive K-pop group, Stray Kids, also opted not to submit, but other groups, like the Filipino boy band SB19 and girl group BINI, spoke in support of the category.
Both SB19 and BINI received nods, for their songs “Visa” and “Unang Kilig,” respectively. They’re competing with Japanese singer LiSA’s “Yes,” Japanese kawaii metal band Babymetal’s “Sunset Kiss” featuring Polyphia and two K-pop girl groups: KiiiKiii’s “404 (New Era)” and IVE’s “Bang Bang.”
Notably absent are a few K-pop groups who had huge songs this year, like aespa’s “Lemonade,” Hearts2Hearts’ “Rude!” and BigBang’s “BiiiG.”

The three-year grant will support reading programs and expand literacy opportunities for Portland Public Schools students
Portland Public Schools will receive $500,000 over three years to support early literacy programs through a collaboration with several local organizations.
The Foundation for Portland Public Schools was awarded the funding through the Nellie Mae Education Foundation. Portland was one of 30 sites across New England to receive the funding as part of the foundations New England District-Community Consortium.
The initiative looks to improve student outcomes and well-being by bringing school districts together with nonprofit organizations and community partners.
The Foundation for Portland Public Schools will work in partnership with the Boys & Girls Club of Southern Maine, United Way of Southern Maine, Portland Public Library and I'm Your Neighbor Books.
"This grant will directly support the achievement pillar of our Strategic Plan," Portland Public Schools Superintendent Ryan Scallon said. "It will leverage community partners to collaborate with our schools and provide research-based reading interventions for students. It is a win for our students, a win for our partners, and a win for the community."
Portland Public Schools is Maine's largest school district serving more than 6,200 students. According to the district, approximately one-third of students come from homes where languages other than English are spoken.

title: Frozen Takes the Stage at Houlton High
text:
HOULTON, Maine (WAGM) - If you’re looking for a bit more theatre fun this weekend, Houlton High School is putting on Disney’s Frozen. Cast members at Houlton High School are putting their all into rehearsals as they get closer to the opening night. 52 students along with several staff members have been working for weeks putting together their production of Frozen. We spoke with a couple of the cast members about how rehearsals are going.
Presley Goodwin, one cast member who’s playing Elsa in the production said: “Yesterday we had our all-day rehearsal and it went really good. So, we’re hoping that the actual show goes as good.”
Isabella White, another cast member who’s playing Anna added: “They definitely have been coming together more as we get closer to the show, but I think it’s really nice to see it all come together as we get closer.”
“Yeah, and we have a lot of newer kids this year. So, it’s been fun getting to see them grow and kind of helping them get used to how everything works,” continued Presley.
This year the school chose Frozen for their production. Isabella and Presley said they had a big part in helping choose this year’s play since as seniors it’s their last year to perform. “We’ve wanted to do this since our like, freshman year. We really wanted to be Anna and Elsa because we’re really good friends,” said Isabella.
“So, we kind of pushed our directors to pick this one for a couple of years,” added Presley.
“We’re also like really sad because it is one last one, but a few tears have already been shed but we’re really excited,” added Isabella.
Isabella and Presley say they’re hoping the community turns out for their last performance. “It’s a really good one for kids but I think it’s just gonna be a lot of fun to watch. We have a lot of cool things that you’re gonna get to see and I think it’ll be worth it,” continued Presley.
The play will be put on in the Houlton High School auditorium on Nov. 20th and Nov. 21st at 7 p.m., and Nov. 22nd at 2 p.m. To purchase tickets locals can email music@rsu29.org or call 538-3129. Tickets are $10 for adults and $8 for kids, students, and seniors. For these two friends, the play is a chance to bring a longtime dream to life before their final curtain call.

title: Hannah Pingree wants a public healthcare option for Maine. Is it possible?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree pushed for a government-run healthcare option for Mainers in her campaign, a reform that could change the state’s health insurance landscape.
Pingree will begin her term with expanded Democratic majorities in the state House and Senate, making it easier to get her agenda through the Legislature. She also comes in with a mandate to bring down costs in Maine. These two factors could provide the ingredients for a public option, the change Pingree is pushing for.
But how a public option would work in Maine is not clear, as Pingree hasn’t yet formulated a specific plan.
The goal, Pingree said in an interview, is to improve access for the uninsured or those who face cost-prohibitive insurance premiums. Medicaid cutbacks and the elimination of certain Affordable Care Act subsidies are making it harder to maintain health insurance for thousands of Maine residents.
“There is just a lot of frustration on people’s ability to access the healthcare insurance system and afford healthcare,” Pingree said. “I want to help ensure people who are being left out have a more affordable option, a state-backed plan.”
Pingree said her family was one of the thousands in Maine that saw its premiums skyrocket after Congress failed to extend the Biden-era tax credits for ACA plans in 2025. She said her family’s ACA premiums jumped from about $700 per month in 2025 to over $2,000 monthly this year.
Four states currently offer public option plans: Washington, Colorado, Nevada and Minnesota.
Pingree said she aims to convene a working group shortly after she takes office in January to design a proposal.
The state has negotiating leverage with insurance companies and healthcare providers, Pingree said, arguing that public option plans would be affordable when paired with potential reforms to streamline insurance administrative overhead. She envisions a plan where the state has “skin in the game” — a reference to the state using tax dollars to help reduce the cost of the plans.
Jeff Austin, president of the Maine Hospital Association, said Pingree’s proposal is “intriguing” and that he welcomes efforts to stabilize health insurance markets.
“We know how much this was a centerpiece to Gov.-elect Pingree’s campaign,” Austin said. “Hospitals are willing to be at the table to see if it’s a viable option to help Maine people.”
Dan Demeritt, executive director of the Maine Association of Health Plans, which represents the health insurance industry at the State House, said he’s “eager to be part of the conversation.”
Demeritt said the states that currently have a public option are “falling short on affordability objectives while increasing regulatory complexity.”
But Christine Monahan, a professor with the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University, said the public options in the three states that have had them for a few years — Colorado, Washington and Nevada — have improved insurance markets in those states.
“These programs are generally helpful at making slow, incremental progress at containing cost increases, and making coverage more affordable,” Monahan said.
Monahan said if a state were to pair public options with attempts to replace some of the subsidies lost from the expired ACA credits, or were to offer plans that mimic Medicaid for people who lost their Medicaid coverage, that could make the plans attractive to purchase.
Democrats in Congress are touting new efforts to extend the expired subsidies — called the Enhanced Premium Tax Credits — and eliminate the Medicaid cuts, but they face an uncertain future with President Donald Trump in the White House.
