title: UMaine women’s basketball falls short to Oregon in fourth quarter
text:
ORONO, Maine — The Black Bears faced the University of Oregon in Orono on Friday, Nov. 13, at 7 p.m., falling just short with a score of 79-72 for their first loss of the season. This was Maine’s first time playing Oregon and its first Big Ten opponent since playing Purdue University in December 2024.
The cross-country matchup had a bittersweet story behind it. Kelly Graves, the Ducks’ head coach, plans to retire after this season and wants to coach a game in every state before he does. The matchup on Friday crossed Maine off his bucket list.
Maine took control of the game in the first quarter, ending it ahead 19-11. The Black Bears came out with strong energy and quickly established themselves on the court. Second-year guard Lala Woods came out hot with eight points, with six coming from 3-pointers. Third-year guard Maddie Fitzpatrick helped with five points and two rebounds, while second-year guard Olivia Alvarez and second-year forward Bailey Breen both contributed three points each.
The scoring stayed even for Oregon in the first, with first-year guard Brooklynn Haywood leading the scoring at five points. Third-year forward Ehis Etute and third-year guards Katie Fiso and Avary Cain each had two points. The Ducks struggled to keep pace with Maine’s early momentum but continued to fight to stay within reach.
At the half, the Black Bears still had the lead at 33-27. Maine continued to hold onto its advantage despite Oregon’s efforts to close the gap. Woods got up to 12 points, three rebounds and two assists. Fitzpatrick added five points and two rebounds to her tally, and Alvarez added two points. Second-year guard Abby Price got on the board with a 3-pointer to close out the scoring.
Fiso got things moving for Oregon in the second, racking up 12 points, three rebounds and two assists by the end of the half. The Ducks began to create more offensive opportunities as they worked to narrow Maine’s lead. Etute had six points and three rebounds, and Haywood had seven points, two rebounds and two assists.
Oregon began to close the gap by the end of the third quarter, with the score being 57-54. The game was becoming increasingly competitive as the Ducks put pressure on Maine’s lead. Woods continued to stay hot with a total of 18 points, five 3-pointers, four rebounds and two assists. Fitzpatrick got up to 16 points and seven rebounds to lead the team. Fourth-year forward Kaliyah Sain and fourth-year forward Lizzy Gruber both got on the board for the Black Bears, with Sain sinking a 3-pointer and Gruber adding two points as well as leading the team with six assists.
Oregon continued to rely on Fiso, who had 22 points by the end of the third. Her strong performance helped keep the Ducks within striking distance heading into the final quarter. Etute and Haywood both had 11 points. Third-year forward Hilary Fuller and fourth-year guard Ari Long both got their first points of the night, with both shooting a 3-pointer.
In the fourth quarter, Maine began to lose control of the game and fell behind Oregon’s unstoppable offense. The game ended in a heartbreaking loss, with the Black Bears falling 79-72. Woods finished with 21 points to lead the team, five rebounds and four assists. Fitzpatrick was right behind her with 19 points and led the team in rebounds at nine. Breen, Alvarez and Price contributed nine points each, and Gruber led the team with six assists.
The Ducks found their rhythm at the right time, putting pressure on the Black Bears and taking control of the momentum. Their star player was undoubtedly Fiso, who put up a whopping 32 points and led the team in assists with six. Haywood also had an incredible night with 24 points, and Etute stayed at 11 points but led the team with six rebounds.
The Black Bears are back home Thursday, Nov. 19, at 6 p.m. to face Virginia Commonwealth University.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Nickolas Elton King, 36, of Warren, passed away on Nov. 10, 2026. Nickolas was born in Rockport on June 28, 1990 to Paul D. King and Deborah (Peckham) King.
Nick grew up in Union, where he attended Union Elementary School and Medomak Valley High School. He had a deep love for everything about the ocean, especially fishing. It was by the water that Nick was happiest. The ocean was a special place for him, and it is fitting that it will be where his family will eventually lay him to rest.
Nick had an outgoing, friendly personality and a heart that was always willing to help others. He would do anything he could for anyone, never hesitating to lend a hand, no matter what was needed. His kindness, warm spirit, and willingness to be there for others touched the lives of many. He was deeply loved by his family and close friends, as well as so many others whose lives he crossed along the way.
Nick shared a particularly close bond with his parents, Paul and Deborah, and his siblings, twin sister Abby and brother Eric. He will forever hold a special place in their hearts, and the love they shared will remain with them always.
He was predeceased by his paternal grandparents, George and Gertrude King; his maternal grandparents, Edward and Dorothy Peckham; his uncles, Martin King, George King III, and Lloyd Moore; his aunts, Shirley Wyllie and Jeanne King; and his cousins, Tammy McAlister, Autumn Roy, and Sandy Peckham.
Nick is survived by his parents, Paul King, of Warren, and Deborah King, of Camden; his twin sister, Abby Blackman and her husband, Cliff, of Plymouth, Mass.; his brother, Eric King and his companion, Raina, of Wiscasset; his uncles, Eugene King, of Warren, and David Wyllie; his aunts, Rose Gay and her husband, Skip, of Appleton, Doreen Moore, of Warren, Sally Peckham, of Baileyville, Melinda Peckham, of Thorndike, and Dottie King; close friends, Dustin Day, Savannah Wotton, and Ralph and Charlene Boyington; and close cousin, Ben Clark; along with several nieces, nephews, and cousins.
From Nick’s mother:
“The stars are not wanted now: put out everyone;
Pack up the moon and dismantle the sun;
Pour away the ocean and sweep up the wood;
For nothing now can ever come to any good.”
And from his aunt Rose:
“Your life was a blessing, your memory a treasure.
You are loved beyond words and missed beyond measure.
Rest now, free from every storm.
At peace at last, held forever in our hearts.”
Per Nick’s wishes, there will be no services. His family will honor his wishes and, at a later date, scatter his ashes out to sea, returning him to the place he loved so dearly.
Nick will be forever loved, deeply missed, and never forgotten.
Arrangements are under the care and direction of Hall Funeral Home of Waldoboro. To extend a condolence or share a story with the King family, please visit Nick’s book of memories at hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: Huge waves pummel the California coast, forcing the closure of iconic piers
text:
Huge waves pummel the California coast, forcing the closure of iconic piers
The California coast was pummeled again on Sunday by huge waves that inundated beaches, flooded local streets and forced the closure of iconic piers.
The National Weather Service office for the Bay Area warned that surf up to 35 feet (10.6 meters) was possible, along with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.
Related video above: Capitola Wharf reportedly damaged by large waves
“Stay out of the water, stay off rocks and jetties, and never turn your back on the ocean!” the weather service said on social media.
On Saturday, waves above 50 feet were recorded in San Mateo County, just south of San Francisco.
Surfers weren't deterred, taking advantage of giant waves at the famous Mavericks Beach near Half Moon Bay.
Farther south, the Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Office issued an evacuation warning near the coastal town of Capitola that took the brunt of the powerful surf.
In Southern California, several piers, including ones in Ventura, Manhattan Beach, Huntington Beach and San Diego's Pacific Beach, were closed during the weekend as they were slammed by waves.
At La Jolla Cove near San Diego, famous for its lounging sea lions, water overflowed the beach and crashed up a staircase leading to the sand.
Video shared with sister station KSBW shows waves crashing into the Capitola Wharf and damaging the railing. The video was taken around 12:30 p.m. on Saturday, around high tide, when 25-35 foot waves were expected to hit the Central Coast.
The Capitola Wharf suffered severe destruction during massive winter storms and high surf in January 2023, which buckled and detached the wooden walkway and washed away a middle section of the pier. The wharf reopened in September 2024, following a $10.6 million reconstruction project
Conditions were calming by Sunday afternoon, but large waves were expected all week, forecasters warned.
The ongoing super El Niño has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.

title: Legally blind hitting coach has trained young athletes for 40 years
text:
OMAHA, Neb. (Aging Untold) — Mark Wetzel has spent 40 years coaching the swings of young athletes while legally blind.
In a neighborhood outside Omaha, Wetzel’s lessons begin at the driveway, where he has a sign that says, “The smooth, straight path seldom leads anywhere.”
Coaching with limited vision
Then they continue inside a barn, where Wetzel has coached local children and minor league pros.
He said he has macular degeneration of the retina.
“I’m legally blind,” Wetzel said.
He had to stop playing baseball in his youth.
He spent decades learning to think of the game differently.
Wetzel has some peripheral vision. He said he can see a player’s profile against a wall and any movement, including excess energy, tightness or weight shift.
“I can see that profile against that wall. I can see any kind of movement, the slightest bit of movement – excess energy or tightness or weight shift,” Wetzel said.
He described the vision loss as “almost a blessing.”
Overcoming what life throws at us
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist and host of “Aging Untold,” said Wetzel’s coaching goes beyond the batting cage.
“You can get into your own head when you’re limited, and you can allow that to tell you you’re less,” Cradduck said. “We’re never less. We’re always exceptionally more than what people see us. We just have to see it ourselves first, and then we have to let everybody else see it in us. And he did. He went in there just with an exceptional amount of who he was, and he’s gifting that over to others.”
Cradduck also said watching others overcome adversity affects those around them.
“When other people watch us overcome adversity and when other people watch us overcome what life throws at us, we’re strengthening them whether we realize it or not. We’re giving them that that inherent ability to tap into that side of themselves when adversity hits them,” Cradduck said.

Part of Route 196 in Topsham was closed for approximately 90 minutes after a suspicious package was found on the side of the road, according to police.
Topsham Police Chief Marc Hagan said that at 11:45 a.m. Monday, officers responded to the area of Route 196 near the Lisbon town line after someone reported finding a package that looked like an explosive device leaning up against a utility pole.
The Topsham Police Department shared a photo of the suspicious package, which appeared to be wrapped in Styrofoam and duct tape and had wires protruding from it.
Topsham police then called the Maine State Police Bomb Squad to respond to the scene and shut down the road out of concern for the safety of drivers. Route 196 was closed near Harpswell Auto Sales, which is located at 1159 Lewiston Road.
Hagan said members of the State Police Bomb Squad arrived at the scene about 45 minutes later, X-rayed the package and deemed it to be safe.
Route 196 was reopened to traffic at 1:20 p.m., according to Hagan.

text:
WATCH: Tens of millions of red crabs swarm across roads and bridges in Australia
Tens of millions of red crabs have started their annual migration on Australia's Christmas Island.
The crabs migrate from the forests to the seas when major wet-season rainfall starts, according to Parks Australia, which oversees and monitors the migration.
Months prior to the migration, Parks Australia prepares the island for the annual event by clearing underpasses, building crab bridges and installing kilometers of roadside barriers as well as specific migration-related road signs.
Red crabs migrate each year to breed on the coast.
According to Parks Australia, the mass movement is synchronized with the lunar cycle, with the crabs aiming to spawn before dawn on a receding high tide during the moon’s last quarter.

title: Fort Kent Girls Make It Four Straight in Northern Maine
text:
The Fall Five and Five No. 5: Fort Kent Girls Make It Four Straight
Winning once is hard.
Doing it again is harder.
Getting back to the same championship game four years in a row starts to say something about a program.
That’s where we begin the season-ending Five and Five countdown.
At No. 5, the Fort Kent girls soccer team once again found itself exactly where it has spent a lot of November lately: playing for Northern Maine and then playing for a Gold Ball.
Another Fall Near the Top
Fort Kent came into the season with plenty of expectations, and the Lady Warriors never really went away.
They worked their way through the regular season and entered the Class C North championship at 14-1-2, setting up another meeting with Orono.
By that point, Fort Kent had already beaten the Red Riots twice during the regular season.
Doing it a third time, with a Northern Maine championship on the line, was another matter.
The Lady Warriors didn't leave much doubt.
Senior Reese Doucette opened the scoring on a penalty kick in the first half. Freshman Hayden Plourde doubled the lead about 12 minutes later, and Doucette added another before halftime.
Fort Kent's defense took care of the rest.
The Warriors shut out Orono 3-0 and walked away with another Class C North championship.
Four Years, Four Northern Maine Championships
That's the number that really stands out.
Four.
Four consecutive regional championships.
Four consecutive trips to the Class C state championship game.
And five state-final appearances over the last seven seasons.
High school sports aren't supposed to make that kind of consistency easy.
Players graduate. Roles change. Younger athletes are asked to step into bigger spots. Every new season brings another group of teams trying to knock you off.
Fort Kent has continued to find a way through all of it.
This year's group had experienced seniors like Doucette and Avery Werntgen, younger players such as Plourde and Laney Caron stepping into important roles, and another defense that proved difficult to break down when the games mattered most.
The names might change from one season to the next.
The results haven't changed very much.
One More Trip to the State Final
The regional championship earned Fort Kent another matchup with Maranacook, the same program that defeated the Warriors in the 2025 state championship.
Maranacook struck early in Lewiston and eventually won 2-0, ending Fort Kent's season at 14-2-2. Evelyn Stevenson scored both goals for the Black Bears.
It wasn't the ending Fort Kent wanted. But a state-final loss shouldn't erase what it took to get there.
The Warriors finished as Northern Maine champions and state runners-up for another year, continuing a run that has made them one of the most consistent soccer programs in this part of the state.
And that's why they belong in this countdown.
More Than One Great Season
When I started putting together the five stories that defined this fall, I didn't want this list to simply become five championship-game results.
The whole season had to matter.
Fort Kent's story is about what happens when excellence stops being a one-year accomplishment and becomes an expectation. Another group of players leaving its own mark on a run that started before some of them ever stepped onto the varsity field.
That's not easy to do.
And it earns the Fort Kent Lady Warriors the No. 5 spot in my five stories that defined the fall of 2026.
Tomorrow, the countdown continues with No. 4.

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Dale A. Best, 67, of Bristol, unexpectedly passed away on the afternoon of Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026 at home. Born on March 23, 1959 in Poughkeepsie, N.Y., he was the youngest son of William and Doris (Disbrow) Best.
He grew up in Poughkeepsie and when his parents bought a summer home in New Harbor, he would spend the month of August there as they refurbished the house. Dale graduated from Arlington High School, Lagrange, N.Y. and BOCES Small Engine Repair program in 1977. Later that year, he graduated from the American Motorcycle Institute in Daytona Beach, Fla. as a certified motorcycle mechanic.
Dale worked various jobs through the years, including sheetrock installer, tree service, and small engine technician for Montgomery Wards. In December 1987, he began his 32-year career with the New York State Department of Corrections at Fishkill Correctional Facility in Beacon, N.Y. as a small engine vocational instructor. There he shared his vast knowledge of small engines with his students and guided them with his leadership and views that hard work and perseverance always lead to a better future.
Dale also obtained his New York State teaching certificate by attending college part time and working full time at the prison.
Riding motorcycles, listening to classic rock music, hunting, and fishing were just some of the many things that Dale loved. He bought his first motorcycle at the age of 12 with money he earned shoveling snow, raking leaves, and mowing lawns. He was passionate not only about riding but enjoyed restoring older motorcycles. His pride and joy was a 1946 Indian Chief with a sidecar that he fully restored and earned the distinction of Best Motorcycle in Show at numerous car/motorcycle shows both in New York and in Maine, including at the Olde Bristol Days Williams-Fossett Vintage Car Show.
On Sept. 14, 1991 he married his wife, Nancy (DuPilka). Dale and Nancy grew up in the same neighborhood, and Nancy’s brother, George, and Dale were friends for many years. In 1984, Dale and Nancy reconnected and began dating, buying their first house in Poughkeepsie in 1988. They celebrated 35 years of marriage this year but knew each other for over 50 years. They bought their Bristol home in 2016 and, after retiring in 2018, Dale and Nancy moved here to enjoy the Midcoast.
Dale was a hardworking man who could fix just about anything. He would go out of his way to help others and loved his family and friends. Over the years he remained in contact with friends and coworkers, and he will be missed by many.
Dale and Nancy shared a love of dogs, and they fostered and adopted shelter and rescue pups for many years. Current pup Birdie misses her “poppy” very much!
Besides his parents, Dale was predeceased by his brother, Bill; and his brother-in-law, Frank.
Dale is survived by his wife, Nancy; his two sisters, Doris Hummel (husband Ron) and Nancy Bauer; nephews, Darren (wife Alexa, children Meranda and Stefan) and Dan; nieces, Sharon (husband Dave, children Rachel and Luke) and Yvonne; and many friends, both in New York and Maine.
Burial will be at the family plot in Poughkeepsie, N.Y.
A sincere thank-you to Bristol Fire & Rescue, Central Lincoln County Ambulance Service, Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, and Strong-Hancock Funeral Home for their response time, professionalism, and compassion when it was needed the most.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home, 612 Main St., Damariscotta, ME 04543. Condolences and messages for his family may be expressed by visiting stronghancock.com.

title: You can cut sodium without giving up flavor
text:
(Aging Untold) — For many older adults, watching sodium is part of managing blood pressure, heart health and other medical conditions.
If you think that means giving up favorite foods and flavors, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said it does not.
‘Smarter ways to make things healthier’
Rogers said people do not have to give up the foods and flavors they enjoy.
“Absolutely not,” Rogers said. “We just find smarter ways to make things healthier.”
Other spices can bring out the natural flavor of food.
“Other spices will bring out the natural flavor, because many times we’re hiding it,” Rogers said. “Many times we’re hiding it. We don’t even taste what that real food tastes like.”
She said people with high blood pressure or kidney issues may not want a lot of sodium.
“The sodium is going to make you absorb water and hold on to it,” Rogers said.
High insulin can also make the body hold on to sodium and water, she added.
“You just have to learn how to blend the spices and things like that to make your food taste actually just as well, or better,” Rogers said.
Cooking and seasoning at home
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said her husband follows a low-sodium diet. She cooks vegetables, such as carrots, for a long time to bring out their flavor, though not until they are mushy.
“I also toast and warm spices like cumin and paprika, and that brings out the flavor also,” O’Rourke said. “The less we season the food, the more you can taste the actual food.”
She said she reads labels because bread, pastries, processed foods and canned foods can contain a lot of sodium. When her husband started the diet, she looked up how much he should have.
“It’s 2,300 mg, which is a teaspoon,” O’Rourke said. “So it’s very, very little.”
Reading labels and finding hidden sodium
Rogers said some people make their own seasonings, such as garlic powder instead of salt. She also brought up the recommended daily allowance on food labels.
“If you see 5% or less, that’s a really low sodium,” Rogers said. “You start seeing 20% or higher, that’s pretty high in content.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said the biggest source of sodium is not the salt shaker.
“The most dangerous salt shaker there is isn’t even the one that’s on the table or the one that you use,” she said. “It’s what’s already in the food that you’re eating.”
The body still needs sodium
Cradduck said the body needs sodium.
“That’s what makes our nerves work. It’s what makes our muscles contract. It maintains blood pressure, normal fluid balances,” Cradduck said.
She said low sodium can be an issue in older adults, especially for people who take a diuretic or have heart failure or kidney disease.
“One is nutritional, one is metabolic, and you need to find the balance,” Cradduck said.
Sea salt, sports drinks and potassium substitutes
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said people hear that sea salt, Himalayan salt and pink salt are good for them. She said some fitness trainers recommend a certain amount of salt each day, while a low-sodium diet calls for less. She named lunch meat, fast food, canned goods and energy drinks as sources of sodium.
“I think it’s going to be individualized,” Rogers said. “You have to look at who’s getting what and who needs what.”
She said replacing sodium with potassium may not be a good idea, depending on a person’s medical conditions.
Butter and nutritional yeast
When using butter as a seasoning, check whether it is salted or unsalted, Cradduck said.
“Don’t think, ‘Oh, I’m going to get rid of the salt and I’m just going to season with butter,’ and then you use butter that’s full of salt,” Cradduck said.
Rogers also mentioned nutritional yeast, which can give a cheesy flavor.
“There’s a lot of different things that you can use that really enhance the flavors and actually taste better,” she said.
Key takeaways
- Sodium can hide in packaged foods and raise blood pressure
- Swap salt for flavor. Zest, herb blends and nutritional yeast can bring out the natural flavor of food
- Check labels to protect your heart without losing flavor

title: Acadia Community Theater returns for 'It’s a Wonderful Life'
text:
SOMESVILLE — Join Acadia Community theater for a classic American tale, capturing the holiday spirit through the life of George Bailey (Beau Goss), a hardworking, bright young man who has put aside his lofty ambitions to carry on his father’s legacy and keep the family business going alongside his blundering Uncle Billy (David Gartner) and with the unwavering support of his wife Mary (Zoe Wade). As he despairs after a misfortune, he meets his guardian angel, Clarabelle (Haley Skinner), who shows George how his life has touched everyone in his community and that “no man is a failure who has friends.”
This strong ensemble cast is directed by Mark Carignan, who chose this year’s show thoughtfully. “It is a great time to reflect on just what ‘It’s a Wonderful Life’ meant,” Carignan said in a press release. “When production began, Frank Capra had to convince Jimmy Stewart, a bomber pilot and hero struggling with the aftermath of war, to join a production so full of hope and American values. Both men found the movie a healing experience, and we hope our production will remind people how much we love our community and the country we live in. Come enjoy the magic of live theater, laugh, cry, and rediscover why ‘It’s a Wonderful Life’ is part of so many families’ holiday traditions.”
Kate Young assisted Mark in directing this show. The show’s technical team is helmed by Mori Sproule and Beverley Guay. “It’s A Wonderful Life” was adapted for the stage by James W. Rodgers from Frank Capra’s 1947 film. “It’s a Wonderful Life” is based on the story “The Greatest Gift” by Philip Van Doren Stern.
Shows are the first weekend of December, one weekend only, at the Acadia Repertory Theater in Somesville, 1154 Main Street: Friday, Dec. 4 at 7 p.m.; Saturday, Dec. 5 at 7 p.m.; Sunday, Dec. 6 at 2 p.m.
Tickets are $18 for regular admission and $15 for students, seniors and military. Tickets are available in advance at act.ludus.com and at the door. Advance tickets are recommended. Parking is limited. Overflow parking is available at the Somesville Union Meeting House and Somesville Museum and Gardens lots for all shows.

title: Now the Democrats must get to work
text:
The crucial question for the Democratic leadership: do they understand they didn’t earn the midterms? It was the work of voters who stood up to President Trump and declared “Enough.”
Almost every demographic — excepting MAGA hatemongers — shifted leftward to declare “Enough,” some in shocking numbers. The Republican oligarchs and super PACs couldn’t buy the election. But the Democrats couldn’t buy an election such as this, either.
Yes, the leadership made some savvy decisions in recruiting candidates. But they made some idiotic decisions as well. Sen. Chuck Schumer reportedly spent months recruiting Gov. Janet Mills. She finally acceded. But it was clear Mills wasn’t into it. She ran a lackluster campaign, and folded when it was clear she was going to lose the primary.
Meanwhile, Rep. Haley Stevens was aggressively pushed in the Michigan primary with the hope she’d bury a smart, well-spoken, compassionate Muslim candidate in Abdul El-Sayed. When Stevens lost, she jumped to support the Republican candidate against El-Sayed in the general election.
The Democrats do not own those who elected them in this election. It is crucial they understand this. As in no other election in my lifetime, they serve at the pleasure of the voters. They should not just pay lip service to what voters want, but act on it. And the people must press to ensure they do.
The real test of the Democrats has only just begun.
Frank Smith
South Portland

title: South Portland offices closed Monday after suspected cyberattack
text:
South Portland municipal offices were closed for a second straight day Tuesday after operationg were limited by a network disruption that the city said was possibly caused by a cyberattack.
The city’s computer and phone systems, as well as some online administrative portals and mapping services, will be unavailable until the outage is resolved. City officials don’t know how long the network will be down.
“A complete evaluation of the issue is underway, but initial information suggests activity by bad actors,” the city said in a news release Sunday night.
City officials say multiple state and federal agencies are coordinating efforts to recover the computer systems. In an update Monday night, the city said it also has engaged an independent forensic examiner to help evaluate the situation.
City staff have been working to resolve the issue since it was first discovered around 11:30 p.m. Saturday, according to the update, and a preliminary assessment indicates “the majority of city data is unaffected by this cyberattack.”
“Our IT team, staff leaders and external partners are working tirelessly to conduct an exhaustive examination and resume all city services as soon as it is possible to safely do so,” Mike Dery, the city’s IT director, said in a written statement. “It’s all hands on deck.”
South Portland City Hall, the assessing department and the library were closed Monday and Tuesday as officials work on a plan to bring services back online. Some services, such as vehicle registration renewal, can be completed online.
In-person credit card payments and receipts at some city facilities also may be affected. South Portland’s online billing system, Citizen Self Service, has been experiencing unrelated outages since late last week, according to the release.
Because of these issues, the property tax due date has been postponed until Nov. 23.
The city noted Monday that police, fire and EMS services have not been impacted.
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this story.

title: Rollover crash in Oklahoma that caused sparks caught on camera
text:
Rollover crash in Oklahoma that caused sparks caught on camera
Dashcam video captured the moments a multi-vehicle crash caused sparks and a pickup truck to roll over Monday morning on an Oklahoma interstate.
Shortly before 8 a.m., an SUV and a pickup truck were traveling east on Interstate 40 near Oklahoma City Boulevard, near downtown Oklahoma City, when they were involved in a crash.  
A viewer of sister station KOCO, who wished to remain anonymous, shared dash camera video of the incident. In the video, you can see the person driving the pickup truck trying to change lanes even though another vehicle appeared to be in their blind spot.
The person driving the SUV moved onto the shoulder and braked, but then sped up and collided with the pickup truck, which was fully in the far-left lane. The two vehicles continued side-by-side in the lane for a few seconds before the person driving the pickup truck lost control and crashed head-on into a concrete barrier wall, causing sparks.
The pickup truck then rolled over onto its passenger side before coming to a rest while on the shoulder and in part of the far-left lane.
See that video in the player at the top
KOCO's Sky 5 flew over the scene after the crash, showing a significant traffic backup that has since been cleared. The pickup truck was still on its side, and the white SUV was at the scene when Sky 5 was over the area.
Oklahoma Highway Patrol officials told KOCO that the trooper does not believe this was a road rage situation and that there was any intent behind it. No arrests were made, and both people involved stayed at the scene and complied with troopers during the investigation.

title: The deer hunt doesn’t end when you take your shot
text:
So many things go into a successful deer hunt, and often the first few seconds and minutes after a shot are just as important as the days and hours preparing for it.
You’re amped up, as you should be. If it weren’t exciting, we wouldn’t do it. Proper preparation led to this moment, and you need to compose yourself and be able to answer several questions accurately.
Where was the deer standing when you shot? Look for landmarks like a stump, a specific tree, or a clump of grass. The answer gives you an important starting point in your search for the deer. If you’re bowhunting, find the arrow, as it can tell you a lot. Is it covered in blood, or something else? Even with a rifle shot, you have a place to begin your search. Maybe there is hair on the ground. What color is it? You might find scuff marks where the deer jumped. Even if you’re confident in the shot, always start the search at the point of impact, which is challenging if you don’t know where that is.
How did the deer react to the shot? Deer react differently depending on where they’re hit with an arrow or bullet. The so-called “mule kick” often indicates a heart shot, but not always. A stumbling deer could indicate a limb hit. A hunched posture and slow walk might be a paunch hit. All these can help, but regardless of how the deer reacted, you should always assume you hit it. Many times, a deer will show no indication of a hit and bound off as they would when startled by the sound of gunfire or bow shot. That doesn’t mean you missed … trust me.
Which way did it go and where did you last see or hear it? Answering these questions gives you a general direction to go for your search. At the very least, you can eliminate 50% of possibilities, to start. More often than not, but not always, a deer will depart in one general direction, but they may turn, and if you see or hear that, it can steer you in a different direction.
Now you’re on the track, and if the signs are obvious, you can continue to follow them, slowly and quietly. If you lose sight of blood, things can get more complicated. Stop and recall the answers to the above questions.
Sometimes, the best course of action is to call in a tracking dog. It requires swallowing your pride, but the people who provide this service are practiced, professional and very good at what they do. If that is your intent, staying in the woods, disturbing the area and spreading more scent will only make their job harder. Your first interaction with them will likely be a phone call, and they’re going to ask you the same questions.
If you choose to stay on the track, consider enlisting help. The more eyes, the better, up to a point. Three seems to be the ideal number, with one to follow blood, one to look ahead, and one searching off to the sides. In any case, never get ahead of the lead tracker. If it comes down to dry tracking, every broken stick or turned over piece of moss could be a clue.
Whether alone or with help, you owe it to the game you hunt and yourself to make every effort and exhaust all possibilities to recover it. Positive results most often come from being able to answer the important questions.
Bob Humphrey is a freelance writer and Registered Maine Guide who lives in Pownal. He can be reached at: [email protected]

title: Cat missing since the Brooklyn building collapse has been reunited with his owner
text:
Cat missing since the Brooklyn building collapse has been reunited with his owner
A cat missing since last week's deadly Brooklyn building collapse has been found alive and reunited with his young owner, New York City officials said Sunday.
Related video above: Ring camera shows NYFD bringing woman to safety after building collapse in Brooklyn
Allie Taylor, director of the Mayor's Office of Animal Welfare, said her office worked with the veterinary nonprofit Flatbush Cats to locate Isaac and reunite him with 13-year-old Zariah Coleman.
It was a bit of good news amid the tragedy of Wednesday's collapse, which killed eight people, injured 18 others and forced the evacuation of several nearby buildings, including one next door where Zariah lives.
Zariah and her mother told The New York Times on Sunday that workers found Isaac on Sunday in a cabinet under the kitchen sink of Zariah's apartment after hearing a soft meow. Zariah and her family hadn't been allowed in since the collapse, which tore off the side of her building and left a hole where her bedroom wall had been.
Waiting outside, Zariah hugged the cat's cage as workers brought him out of her apartment building. Isaac had gone four days without food or water. After his rescue, he was taken to Flatbush Cats' veterinary clinic for a checkup.
"I had it in my heart they would find Isaac," Zariah told the Times. "I knew they would."
Zariah tearfully spoke about her missing cat at a news conference on Friday, telling reporters: "I just really hope they come and get our cat. He's hiding from them, and I think he's scared."
Mayor Zohran Mamdani heralded Isaac and Zariah's reunion in a social media post. He thanked Taylor's office, the city's Buildings Department, and the nonprofit for the happy outcome.
"Isaac is now receiving the veterinary care he needs," Mamdani said. "We're grateful to everyone who helped bring them back together."

title: York’s landmark honey locust tree gets a reprieve from the axe
text:
A tall honey locust tree in York village will likely be saved after residents’ monthslong fight to preserve it.
The 70-year-old tree — which has become a landmark for residents — was slated to be cut down by contractors working on the long-awaited York Village revitalization project. The traffic island it sits on is getting a facelift, which wouldn’t be possible with the tree still there, officials say.
On Monday morning, a day before the tree’s scheduled removal, residents secured their own contractor to excavate the honey locust for relocation, said Dean Lessard, director of engineering for York.
Voters approved the revitalization project 10 years ago, but several people said they don’t remember the tree’s removal being a condition of the plan. Since work began in late September, a couple hundred residents have signed a petition to save the tree, and another resident filed a request for a temporary restraining order against the town.
On Nov. 2, Justice James Martemucci granted a brief injunction awaiting oral arguments, which required the town’s crews to avoid the tree. He later denied the temporary restraining order, partially because the project is tied up in state and federal funds.
In a last attempt to save the tree, resident Susan Gillis said she started looking into relocating the tree without the town’s help. When she and a few others brought the idea to Lessard, he initially gave residents a deadline of Nov. 17 to find a contractor and have the tree removed.
Gillis said she met with four tree services across New England in hopes of getting one to agree to excavate the honey locust. Only one — Massachusetts-based Dale Tree Movers and Tree Farm — said it could be done in that timeline.
Lessard said he met with Dale Tree crews Monday morning to work out a plan and decided to push the deadline back by two days. It’ll take two days for crews to secure the right machinery and prepare the tree for its move.
By Wednesday, it’ll have a new home next to Town Hall.
Select Board members have said the town wasn’t in a position to spend the estimated $50,000 to $80,000 it would take to relocate the tree. Gillis said Monday that funding is the last remaining piece of the puzzle for residents.
Neighbors have raised about $4,500 through GoFundMe for the tree since Thursday, and Gillis said she’s been going door-to-door securing pledges. She’s hopeful enough residents will pitch in to pay Dale Tree for its work. Gillis hasn’t been given a firm funding deadline, but said she’s trying to gather the full amount as soon as possible.
“It gives people a chance to do something where they might have felt before, totally lost,” Gillis said, recalling the long battle to save the tree. “It’s an empowerment thing.”
Lessard said the tree is mostly at the end of its life, and there’s no guarantee that it’ll survive the move.
“They could move it and it could die next year,” Lessard said. “I’ve been working with this group to try to make it happen for them, and if we can, it’s a win-win for both.”

title: United Airlines resolves technology issue that delayed departing flights
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights Monday, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop.
Chicago-based United said in a statement that flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not affected. The airline also said there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”
United apologized on social media to customers for the inconvenience. It resolved the issue about one hour and 40 minutes after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers.
United did not immediately provide details about which of its systems were affected, but pilots told air traffic controllers that the problem was related to a system that helps them determine a plane’s final weight.
Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft’s weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying.
The information is also used to guide the autopilot system and the decisions pilots make, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.
“It is extremely important to have all of these numbers accurate and precise,” said Arroyo, who flew for United. “Pilots use that information to establish guidance and performance for their flights from takeoff to landing.”
Arroyo said he has seen problems with the weight and balance system before in his career, but the airline did the right thing by delaying flights to ensure safety.
Years ago, pilots used to do all those weight calculations manually with a pencil and paper and then radio in the numbers, but today it is all calculated electronically and then loaded into the plane’s computers.
In August 2025, United grounded planes at major U.S. airports, delaying more than 1,000 flights because of an hourslong outage of a system called Unimatic, which houses flight information that is fed to other systems including those that calculate weight and balance and track flight times.
United said in response to a message from The Associated Press that it had no further information to provide about whether the same system was affected by Monday’s outage.
A recording posted Monday on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.
The flight-tracking website FlightAware showed United with about 600 delayed flights Monday evening, though it was unclear how many were directly related to the system outage.
The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days.
Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem.
On Friday, the FAA ordered every flight grounded because a newly installed router malfunctioned, overwhelming the aging air traffic control system.
And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored.

title: How to give back to your community this holiday season
text:
As the holidays approach, if you’re feeling inspired to give back or volunteer, you’re not alone. Volunteerism surges during the holidays, and with dropping temperatures and lots of festivities at the end of the year, there are plenty of seasonal ways to give back.
Readers shared on social media how they like to give back to their community during the holidays — although many pointed out that people need help and kindness all year. Here are some of the organizations and programs looking for volunteers and donations this season.
This is not a comprehensive list, so if any are missing, let us know and we’ll continue to highlight them through the holiday season.
And beyond organized efforts to give back to your community, consider individual efforts at paying it forward, like paying off someone’s fuel or water bill, covering a stranger’s groceries at checkout, raking leaves and shoveling snow for neighbors or inviting them in for a meal.
HOLIDAY GIVING TREES
Businesses and organizations across the state are setting up giving trees — some are virtual, some are actual trees — where people can donate gifts to children and families for the holidays.
In Scarborough, you can find a giving tree at the Morrison Center, and in Westbrook, the lobby of the Public Safety building on Main Street will have a tree with gifts for the elderly, children and families.
Christmas Elves for Maine Teens is helping 13- to 19-year-olds celebrate Christmas with a gift from their wishlist. People can sponsor a teen by shopping from their wish list, contributing gift cards and everyday essentials or helping collect and deliver gifts.
Adoptive & Foster Families of Maine, Inc. & The Kinship Program is also helping people sponsor a child during the holidays. Their highest need is gifts for teens, from gift cards to trendy items like game headsets and self-care products. They also invite people to start a GoFundMe page and direct the funds to them so they can purchase children’s gifts. Social Goose Bar in Brunswick is partnering with them and has a giving tree in the lobby decorated with paper ornaments that have a list of gifts a child has requested.
Westbrook Santa Cause helps people “adopt” one of 150 children so they can receive gifts during the holidays. Donations will be accepted until Dec. 11 at the Westbrook Community Center, or people can donate through Venmo.
THANKSGIVING MEALS
Woodford Family Services in Westbrook has received donations to provide 250 Thanksgiving meals to families, but they are still trying to raise more money. Donating $35 will feed a family of four.
On the Saturday before Thanksgiving (Nov. 21), volunteers in Lewiston and Portland help The Root Cellar deliver over 100 laundry baskets with turkey dinners to neighbors in need. You can donate ingredients to help families celebrate Thanksgiving.
The same day, Westbrook Families Feeding Families will host a mobile food pantry to give out Thanksgiving meals at three locations in Westbrook.
The South Portland Food Cupboard is collaborating with the Equality Community Center in Portland for a Thanksgiving food drive supporting LGBTQ+ community members experiencing food insecurity. People can donate pantry staples, a grocery store gift card or gather donations at work and with friends. You can drop off donations from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on weekdays at the ECC at 15 Casco St. in Portland until Friday.
OTHER WAYS TO GIVE
The Press Herald Toy Fund has been giving gifts to thousands of children every year since 1949. Children from infants to age 16 in every community in York, Cumberland, Sagadahoc, Lincoln, Androscoggin and Knox counties have received gifts supplied through donations. You can volunteer, donate online at pressherald.com/press-herald-toy-fund-donate, and send or drop off donations at 295 Gannett Drive in South Portland.
Project GRACE in Scarborough has a Keep Our Neighbors Warm fuel fund and Neighbors Helping Neighbors fund.
Until the end of November, Maine Needs and Preble Street are partnering to collect kits to send to teens and adults during the holidays. People can make kits or donate items for kits — like lotion and journals for the wellness kits and bluetooth speakers and headphones for the music and tech kits — at 2385 Congress St. in Portland on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

title: Susan Collins’ last days in Senate should focus on Maine’s needs, not a party-line budget bill
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Dennis Keschl served four terms in the Maine House of Representatives, including on the Legislature’s Appropriations Committee. He is a former town manager for Belgrade and a U.S. Army veteran, who served in the Vietnam War, Desert Shield and Desert Storm.
Thank you, Sen. Susan Collins, for nearly 30 years of service. On Nov. 3, Maine voters chose a new senator, and Collins conceded before the race was even called. “It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate,” she said, and she pledged to help with the transition.
She ran this race on her own. The White House stayed out of Maine this fall, and Collins campaigned on her own record. Asked at the first debate on Oct. 6 about her relationship with the president, she said simply, “I’m not exactly his favorite senator.”
Her record is one Mainers can see for themselves. She chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, a role that has allowed her to bring $1.5 billion in federal money back to the state in recent years. In June she cast her 10,000th consecutive vote, a Senate record. When the tariff fight with Canada threatened Maine mills and road crews, she worked to exempt pulp, concrete and road salt. “Leadership matters in Washington,” she said at that same debate.
That leadership faces one more test. Congress returned Nov. 9 for a lame-duck session of about six weeks, and some Republicans want to spend it on a third party-line reconciliation bill before Democrats take control in January. Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio predicted in October that a loss would make the lame duck “the ‘Last Supper.’” The House budget framework, passed July 22, includes Iran war funding, farm aid and money to induce states to adopt the SAVE America Act.
Reconciliation is a shortcut. It lets the Senate pass a bill with 50 votes instead of the usual 60. It was built for budget math, not for bundling a year of unfinished priorities, from war funding to federal election rules, into one bill. Regular order is slower and more deliberate on purpose. Using the shortcut to rush through an agenda weeks after voters handed Congress to the other party would turn this month’s election result on its head.
Collins has drawn this line before. She has said plainly, “I oppose eliminating the legislative filibuster.” Last year, she voted against the final passage of the administration’s reconciliation bill and against clawing back more than $9 billion that Congress had already approved. Senate Majority Leader John Thune can lose only three Republican votes on a party-line package, and Collins holds one of them until Jan. 3.
The needs of Mainers are on the same calendar. Government funding runs out Dec. 11, and the annual defense bill is still unfinished. As Appropriations chair, Collins is the senator best positioned to pass full-year spending bills in regular order, with amendments and recorded votes, rather than folding them into a rushed package written for a different purpose.
I believe Sen. Collins owes her final weeks in office to the voters of Maine and to no one in Washington. She did not need Washington’s help this fall, and she owes Washington no December favor. She should spend the lame duck the way she spent her career, on Maine’s terms. That means no to a December reconciliation bill and yes to finishing the appropriations work only she can lead.

title: Rare North Atlantic right whale population drops, alarming scientists
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — The population of one of the world’s rarest whales has fallen after trending upward in recent years, worrying scientists who fear the animal could still be at risk of extinction.
The North Atlantic right whale now numbers 382 animals, according to a consortium of scientists that released its annual population estimate for the animals on Monday. That represents about a 2% decline from last year’s estimate, which showed a recent slow but steady climb in the whales’ population continuing.
The whales were decimated by centuries of commercial whaling that mostly ended in the 1930s. The enormous animals have been slow to recover, and today they are threatened by entanglement in fishing gear and collisions with ships.
Those threats, combined with a warming ocean, have conspired to hold the population down, said Heather Pettis, chair of the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. Pettis said the warming of the ocean has caused the whales’ food — tiny organisms called copepods — to move, and the whales have followed them into areas of ocean not protected from ship strikes and entanglements.
“We know that this population can and will move around to find food and if we aren’t protecting them throughout their range, we may see another situation where we have this tremendous decline again,” Pettis said.
The whales’ population fell about 25% from 2010 to 2020 during a time when years of poor reproduction coincided with high mortality. Recent years have been slightly more encouraging, but scientists and conservationists have warned that the whales need years of high birth counts coupled with new protections to have a chance to rebuild.
The loss in population last year underscores the need to spare the whales from entanglements and ship strikes, said Nora Ives, a marine scientist on the environmental group Oceana’s right whale campaign.
Oceana was one of several environmental groups that opposed a proposal in Congress to delay new right whale protections until 2035. The proposal, which has passed the U.S. House of Representatives, is intended to protect commercial fishing interests from regulations that members of the industry describe as burdensome.
“The latest numbers are disappointing and make the road to recovery longer for critically endangered North Atlantic right whales. This iconic whale will not escape extinction if its population cannot grow,” Ives said.
The right whales, which can weigh 150,000 pounds (68,039 kilograms), give birth off the Carolinas, Florida and Georgia in the winter and venture north to feeding grounds off New England and Canada. Large groups of the animals that sometimes include a fifth of the entire population are sometimes seen off Massachusetts in spring. Last year was one of the most successful calving seasons on record with more than 20 babies born.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has said the last nine years have also been a time of unusually high numbers of injuries and deaths for the whales. The population is down to just 73 reproductive females, which makes replenishing the stock difficult.
They were hunted heavily because they tend to live fairly close to shore and floated when killed, and they yielded a high volume of oil. Some sources say they got their common name from the perception that they were the “right” whale to hunt.

title: Westbrook City Council censures councilor for comments about city administration
text:
WESTBROOK — The Westbrook City Council voted 4-2 Monday night to censure Councilor Anna Turcotte for comments she made during a council meeting last month when she called the city administration’s actions “disgusting” and “corrupt.”
The Oct. 19 meeting during which Turcotte made those comments involved changing the code of ordinances to replace the Recreation and Conservation Commission with the Recreation and Sustainability Committee.
“I’ve been elected to this seat four times by an overwhelming majority of the vote facing many strong opponents. My constituents trust me, appreciate my service and my direct style. In my public statements I did not insult anyone, I asked hard questions, and I offered my honest opinion,” Turcotte wrote in a statement about the censure that she shared on social media and at Monday’s meeting. “I have been elected by the residents of my ward to ask hard questions and to give my honest opinion and that’s what I have done. And that’s what I’ll continue to do as an American.”
She said she didn’t aim her comments at the council or any of its members, and she believes the criticism against her is coming from outside the council.
The censure resolve was added to the agenda at the request of City Council President Jennifer Munro on behalf of the majority of the council. It claims Turcotte breached the Rules of Order by attacking the motivations of the city administration rather than addressing the issue before the council.
On Monday, a few members of the public spoke against the censure, praising Turcotte for raising her concerns and sharing an opposing viewpoint during the October meeting.
Turcotte and Councilor Victor Chau voted against the censure, although Chau shared his support for the city administration.
“Our employees are the jewels of the city,” he said. “Please leave the city employees alone and thank them for the hard work they do.”
THE OCT. 19 MEETING
Over the past few weeks, the city has been conducting a review of ordinance language for all its boards, commissions and committees to ensure consistency and accuracy.
The language about what was at the time the Recreation and Conservation Commission created legal conflicts with the authorities and duties of the council and the mayor as outlined in the city’s charter. This created confusion about the chain of command and who has decision-making authority, City Administrator Angela Holmes said during a Committee of the Whole meeting last month.
The Committee of the Whole discussed changes to the Recreation and Conservation Commission, including changing it from a commission — which is tasked with policy development and has some level of autonomy and decision-making authority — to a committee, which has an advisory role.
The citizenship requirement to participate in the committee was also removed.
Two weeks later, when the City Council voted to approve these changes on Oct. 19, Turcotte expressed her concerns that the amendments were taking away the agency and power of residents on the committee.
“This is probably the most disgusting thing I’ve seen on the council in the 11 years I’ve been on the council, and I think it’s underhanded,” Turcotte said during the meeting. “I think it’s shady; I think it is incredibly disrespectful to the constituents — many of them are mine — who care about what happens in the city.”
She said the process to amend the boards, committees and commissions was “incredibly corrupt.”
“I’m surprised that you have us here,” Turcotte said to the city administration, referring to the council. “Might as well just run the city without us.”
While Turcotte was speaking, Munro called for a point of order.

title: More people are using ‘buy now, pay later’ for basic expenses
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PHOENIX, Az. (InvestigateTV) — For big ticket purchases, people would often use a “buy now, pay later” method to help break up the cost.
But as budgets tighten, more people are turning to buy now, pay later options to cover basic expenses, including groceries.
According to a recent LendingTree survey, 25% of buy now, pay later users have used the microloans to buy groceries. The services, which include platforms like Klarna and Affirm, are often used to split up larger purchases like flights or appliances.
Cody Bortle, a teacher who started in 2023, said covering bills has become more difficult.
“Everything has just gotten way too expensive,” Bortle said.
Bortle said car payments, groceries and rent have all increased. His rent recently jumped $150 per month.
“I never imagined I’d be in my professional career as a teacher, just paycheck to paycheck,” he said.
He maxed out $15,000 worth of credit cards and now covers some expenses with buy now, pay later microloans, including a trip home to visit his grandparents.
“I can afford $70 a month, but I can’t afford a $400 plane ticket right now, so let me pay $100 right now, and I’ll pay 70 for the next few months,” Bortle said.
Late payments increasing
More people are making late payments on buy now, pay later services. According to LendingTree, 41% of people who use BNPL options have made at least one late payment in the past year, up from 34% the previous year.
“The fact that they’re so attractive and so easy to get is what also makes them so dangerous,” said Miguel Velasco, the senior director of counseling at Money Management International (MMI), a nonprofit that helps people get out of debt.
The buy now, pay later industry touts its products as more consumer-friendly and more available than other lending options, like credit cards and payday loans.
“When [consumers] start buying essentials with buy now pay later, that’s the moment to stop,” Velasco said. “We really need to stop and understand what the financial situation is.”
If you don’t make your payments on time, these companies could freeze your account and possibly turn you over to a collection agency.
Around 90% of people who have asked to have a late fee waived actually had success either getting it reduced or removed, according to LendingTree.
Creating a budget
Velasco said it starts with a budget. He recommends writing down all money coming in and all money going out, then making changes.
“Those are hard conversations to have because you’re telling people they need to stop their spending habits. You’re telling people they need to go get a second job. You’re telling people they need to maybe incorporate some roommates or find a way of making money work,” Velasco said.
Bortle connected with MMI for help to get out of debt. He’s on track to pay off his credit cards by 2030. Along the way, he’s sharing lessons about money with his students.
“I’m very transparent with my kids,” Bortle said. “You have to be really smart with your money now, especially if you have jobs in your high school years. Start saving that because you will need it.”

title: Police surveilled Maine worker 2 years before Medicaid fraud case
text:
Police were investigating a South Portland personal care agency worker at least two years before federal prosecutors accused him and others of accepting Medicaid funds for services they didn’t provide, according to newly unsealed court records.
Community Home Health Care LLC, its owner and five employees were charged with healthcare fraud conspiracy and indicted by a grand jury last month. They pleaded not guilty on Oct. 27 and were released on bail conditions.
Their trial will be held in Portland, according to U.S. District Judge John Woodcock, and is tentatively scheduled for December.
The allegations focus on services dating to 2020 that Community Home Health Care claimed to have provided to one client.
In an application for a search warrant filed this year, an FBI agent said that investigators began surveilling Adel Al Rashid, a personal support specialist at the organization, in April 2024.
Investigators surveilled Al Rashid using a pole camera that was installed outside his Augusta home that month, agent Craig Mehrmann wrote, and another camera that investigators placed outside the home of Al Rashid’s client in 2025.
Mehrmann was the lead FBI healthcare fraud investigator in Maine from July 2023 until September 2025, according to the affidavit.
Footage from three different weeks showed that Al Rashid was seldom at the client’s home during times when the state was billed for his services, Mehrmann wrote. When Al Rashid did visit, Mehrmann said, his stays were briefer than reported. Sometimes, agents saw other people going in and out of the client’s house when Al Rashid was supposed to be there.
Mehrmann had filed his request for a search warrant on March 27 because he wanted access to Al Rashid’s phone, which he said could have emails and text messages related to Al Rashid’s work, and that Al Rashid had also used an app on his phone to document services for billing.
A magistrate signed and issued a search warrant for Al Rashid’s phone the same day and it was returned in April, according to court records. The case remained sealed until Friday.
Al Rashid’s phone was was already in state police custody at the time, for a different case. Augusta police took it in November 2025 while searching his home, Mehrmann wrote, following a report about child sexual abuse materials that had originated from Al Rashid’s Snapchat account.
Al Rashid told police he believed he was hacked, according to court records, and that he did not recall receiving the child sexual abuse material.
A defense attorney for Al Rashid declined to comment on the case Friday.
Al Rashid was charged in Kennebec County Superior Court in June on multiple Class C counts of possessing sexually explicit content of a child younger than 12. He is scheduled to be arraigned in January and was released on bail in August, according to state court records.
Mehrmann’s affidavit mentions several other employees who were indicted with Al Rashid in the Medicaid case in October.
It mentions Noora Abd, the owner of Community Home Health Care, but only to the extent that she owned the company. Her attorneys said in a statement Friday that Mehrmann’s affidavit is not evidence, but “a one-sided document written by law enforcement.”
“Noora Abd is innocent and is presumed innocent under the law,” her attorney, Kristine Hanly, wrote in an email. “We look forward to trying the case in a courtroom, where the government will have to prove its case against her with actual evidence, beyond a reasonable doubt. Until then, we ask the public not to judge Noora Abd based on allegations made about someone else.”
Mehrmann also mentioned Abd’s husband, Faysal Kalayaf Manahe, who worked for her at Community Home Health Care and also oversaw his own personal care agency, Decent Care Services LLC, in Augusta. DHHS suspended Medicaid payments to both companies and three others in June.
Mehrmann said two other people were living with the client in Augusta and they appeared to be receiving personal care services from Manahe’s business, and that the federal government was still investigating whether any fraud had occurred there.
Manahe’s attorney, Thomas Marjerison, declined to comment.
Manahe was acquitted in 2023 after he and others were accused of violating the Sherman Antitrust Act during the COVID-19 pandemic by allegedly agreeing to pay their workers the same rates and not hire them away from each other, eliminating the competition for employees. Marjerison said at the time that prosecutors had brought no evidence to support their claims, and that the government’s case rested entirely on a technicality.

title: For a stronger Maine, we must invest in the next generation
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Denham Ward, MD, Ph.D., of Bowdoinham is president-treasurer of the Abbagadassett Foundation. Kristen Farnham, JD, of Falmouth is vice president of legal affairs and advancement at Spurwink.
If we want Maine to thrive, we need to invest in its young people. This investment can take many different forms, but one key way is creating opportunities that help college and high school students prepare for their future careers by having real-world experience.
Internships enable students to explore different careers and build skills they will carry into the workforce. At its best, an internship can provide educational and training opportunities; meaningful, practical and well-paid work; skill development; and mentoring. Internships also allow students to test the waters, ask questions and find out what they like and — perhaps at least as important — don’t like in an actual work environment.
In the nonprofit space, it can be challenging to fund meaningful internships. That’s where partnerships come into play — connecting people, ideas and funding to build innovative solutions. Spurwink connected with the Abbagadassett Foundation in 2024, together reimagining what a nonprofit internship can look like.
The Next Gen Nonprofit Internship Program offers paid internships that introduce low-income, first-generation and nontraditional college students to nonprofit careers while strengthening Maine’s workforce pipeline.
At a time when organizations across the state face critical shortages of qualified nonprofit and mental health professionals, Spurwink and Abbagadassett have invested in creating meaningful pathways for students to enter and stay in the field.
Through partnerships with colleges and universities, structured supervision, real-world experience and professional mentorship, the Next Gen Internship Program helps participants build the skills and confidence necessary to pursue careers serving Maine communities in diverse operational areas such as human resources, IT, finance, advancement and continuous quality improvement.
In a unique cohort model, students work within their department three days a week, and on a fourth day they gather together for peer learning and exposure to Spurwink’s leaders. Beyond their specific departments, they learn about nonprofit management and operations.
By providing a competitive hourly wage, the program removes a key barrier, as more than 90% of interns report they could not have accepted the position without pay. When we invest in the next generation of behavioral health professionals, we not only support Spurwink’s own workforce needs but also contribute to the long-term sustainability of Maine’s health and human services sector.
To date, Spurwink has hosted 34 Next Gen Interns through five cohorts. The program has already proven itself as a valuable workforce pipeline: six former interns have returned to Spurwink as employees. Other alumni are pursuing careers at different nonprofits across our state. And the word is spreading. Since its inception, the Next Gen Program has received a total of 487 applications, with the most recent cohort of eight interns selected from among 151 applications.
Jamyah, a Lewiston native, was a computer information systems major at the University of Maine at Augusta. During her summer 2025 internship with the IT Department, she was tasked with projects and responsibilities that built many new skill sets. After graduation, she was offered a full-time position at Spurwink. She is now a valued colleague, helping to run the IT help desk and impressing colleagues with her technical skills and responsiveness.
The Next Gen program also meets the goals of the Abbagadassett Foundation, a family foundation that strives to increase educational and scientific opportunities for people and communities in need. Their experience has shown that expanded research and training opportunities for high school and college students provide an important means to further their knowledge and experience in their chosen field of study while enhancing an organization’s overall impact and effectiveness in its field of service.
We make great progress when cross-sector partners come together. With programs like Next Gen, we can keep talented young people in Maine and offer them the opportunity to build a life and future around meaningful work. It’s good for them, and good for Maine.

title: Nationwide Emergency Alert System test to take place Tuesday. Here’s what will happen
text:
(Gray News) - A nationwide Emergency Alert System test is scheduled for Tuesday.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Federal Communications Commission will conduct the test at 2:20 p.m. Eastern time Tuesday.
At that time, all radio and television broadcasters will play a test message for one minute.
The message will read, “This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. This is only a test. No action is required by the public.”
If an actual emergency or significant weather event happens Tuesday, FEMA and the FCC said they might postpone the test to Dec. 3.
FEMA said it is “required by law to conduct a nationwide test of the public alert and warning system at least once every three years.” The last test was done Oct. 4, 2023.

title: FAA, NTSB investigating deadly plane crash in the Town of Sweden
text:
SWEDEN, Maine (WABI) - The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) are investigating a plane crash that happened in Sweden Monday afternoon.
An FAA spokesperson tells WABI that the crash happened around 3:45 p.m.
According to the FAA, the pilot was the only person on board the small aircraft.
Portland media partners WMTW report a male pilot was killed in the crash.
The model of the plane, which the FAA says is a Cessna 182, is a four-seat, single-engine light utility airplane.
The NTSB says two investigators are expected to arrive at the accident site on Tuesday. After the wreckage is documented, it will be recovered and moved to a secure facility for further examination.
The FAA is expected to release a preliminary incident report Tuesday. You can find the latest accident reports here.
This year has seen several high-profile plane crashes in Maine, including the private jet crash in Bangor that killed 6 people, the crash involving a Maine Warden Service plane in Avon that killed pilot Joshua Tibbetts, and the crash in Bristol that killed a New Hampshire man in August.

title: Mayor: Suspect in custody after explosive device found at Illinois plant, forcing thousands to evacuate
text:
PEORIA, Ill. (25News Now/Gray News) - Local police and federal authorities continue to investigate after an explosive device was found at an Illinois plant.
Officials said an explosive device was discovered Friday at the BioUrja Renewables plant, prompting the evacuation of thousands of people in Peoria and East Peoria within a 1-mile radius of the plant.
Numerous events were canceled and downtown businesses closed while the evacuation was in effect. The order was lifted Saturday after no other suspicious objects were found at the plant.
Peoria Mayor Rita Ali said in a statement that company leadership informed her a suspect was in custody in connection with the investigation.
Police said the FBI is the lead agency and will issue information or updates as they become available. The FBI said its policy prohibits it from disclosing whether a person is the subject of an investigation.
Earlier Monday, Peoria police said they were contacted by the FBI to respond to the plant to assist with “court-authorized procedures.” A statement from the FBI said the agency, along with the ATF, Illinois State Police, Peoria County Sheriff, East Peoria Police and Peoria Police are conducting law enforcement activity in Peoria County.
