title: Gorham foursome among Maine athletes signing with D-I, D-II schools
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
GORHAM — As a child, Hunter Finck dreamed of playing college baseball on the national stage. Shortly after he started playing at Gorham High, he realized he could do it.
On Monday, he made it official. Finck signed his commitment letter to the University of Alabama, becoming the latest Maine baseball player to head to the highest levels of college baseball.
“I’ve dreamt of this since I was just a little kid playing tee ball,” said Finck, wearing a black Alabama sweatshirt and a smile visible from across the room. “Just playing at the highest level, and this is one of the highest levels — SEC baseball is, like, the best baseball you could possibly get in college. So this is a great step.”
Finck is part of a group of four Gorham athletes going on to compete in NCAA Division I athletics. Antoine Dube and Jack Cyr signed moments after Finck to compete in track and field at the University of Maine. Liana Edwards, the two-time defending Gatorade Player of the Year in volleyball, signed Friday to play at Rhode Island.
College signing day has taken on a different dimension since the NCAA discontinued the longstanding letter of intent program in 2024. Letters of intent, which were legally binding commitments that scholarship athletes made to play for a school for one year, were replaced by forms in which athletes agree to their financial aid parameters, and which are not as legally rigid.
Essentially the signed offers work as contracts. The upshot, though, is largely the same as it always was: By signing, athletes make official where they’ll be playing next, since they cannot be recruited further by other schools.
Finck, the Varsity Maine and Gatorade Player of the Year who went 6-0 with a 0.38 ERA, batted .569 last year and has reached 95 miles per hour with his fastball. He said picking Alabama was an easy decision.
“It felt like home when I visited there,” said Finck, who was recruited as a pitcher. “The coaches, all the people, just the spot. Once I got on the plane I was like, ‘This is where I want to go.'”
Finck is the latest Maine player to crack the SEC since 2020. Gorham’s Wyatt Nadeau, Thornton Academy’s Cody Bowker, Bonny Eagle’s Jacob Humphrey and South Portland’s Hunter Owen played at Vanderbilt.
“I’m super excited for that challenge,” Finck said. “I’ve just got to keep pushing myself and putting myself in tough situations, and then I’ll be fine for when I get to Alabama.”
On Friday, Edwards, who led Gorham to a fourth straight Class A volleyball title this fall, officially made Rhode Island her destination. She initially thought the team didn’t have a need for a setter, but upon further communication picked it over other suitors including Bryant and the University of New Hampshire.
“ I’m so excited to be able to compete at the highest level and be around people who have the same goals as me, and have the same motivation,” she said. “ They’re always trying to build a relationship with me rather than just being a player on their team. I think that was really important to me.”
Biddeford also had multiple athletes sign Division I offers. Cordelia Kane will play field hockey at Merrimack College, and Jordyn Crump will play basketball at Colgate.
Kane, a defensive center midfielder, said she wondered how much interest she would get after four knee surgeries during her high school career.
“ There’s been a lot of hard work and setbacks to get me here, so I’m really grateful for this opportunity,” she said. “I love to play. It’s probably my favorite thing to do. … (It’s good) to know that I’m gonna keep playing and it didn’t end with the end of this season.”
Crump’s signing ended a recruiting push that saw her receive scholarship offers before her freshman year.
“Meeting the Colgate family and the coaches was definitely a big high for me,” she said. “It was almost a home-away-from-home feeling. … I just really liked the atmosphere and the community they had.”
Other Maine athletes who have signed with or will play for Division I schools include Addison DeRoche (Florida State, softball), Sydney Brunelle (Bucknell, lacrosse) and Macey Weisberg (Stonehill, track) from Cheverus; Reese Bryant (Maine, softball) and Taytum Lauziere (Presbyterian, soccer) from Bonny Eagle; Georgia Moon (Brown, cross country) from Falmouth; Karen Higgins (UNH, cross country) from Lincoln Academy; and Stella Stewart (Holy Cross, lacrosse) and Evelyn Stevenson (UMaine, track) from Maranacook.
Athletes heading to play at Division II schools include Ava Martin (Assumption, field hockey), Colton Jewett (Southern New Hampshire, baseball) and Anthony Salvaggio (SNHU, lacrosse) from Cheverus; Leah Storey (Franklin Pierce, softball) from Bonny Eagle; Rosa Perlut (St. Michael’s, lacrosse) and Madison Howes (St. Anselm, lacrosse) from Scarborough; and Grady Hreben (Assumption, baseball) from Maranacook.

title: SpaceX’s Starship caught by launch pad arms on return from orbit in a dramatic first
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) - SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.
It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch, still the goal for accelerating moon and Mars travel.
Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.
The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster’s messy miss. Cameras panned the spacecraft up and down as it hung high above the ground, supported by the arms of the launch tower.
“Can you believe it?” SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted, dragging out each word. “Look at her! Baby, she’s back!”
Calling it an “epic day,” Musk later ascended the launch tower to take up-close video with his phone. He even hugged the spacecraft. “Looks great,” he reported via X.
SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling. Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.
NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.
“It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X. “Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to (emojis of the moon and the U.S. flag).”
The world’s largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX’s Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.
Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps.
It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.
SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.
As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it wasn’t in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.
SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA’s next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.
Artemis III’s four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity’s first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

title: Northern Light Health lost $48M last year, documents show
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Northern Light Health lost about $48 million in its latest fiscal year, more than triple the year before, but says it’s still on track to recover from its financial crisis.
The jump is largely because Northern Light received a one-time, $52 million payment from the Federal Emergency Management Agency for outstanding COVID-19 pandemic claims the previous year, Chief Financial Officer James Rohrbaugh said. Excluding that payment, the system’s results improved over the previous two years, he said. That includes 2024, when the state’s second-largest hospital system lost $156 million.
The system has already shed more than 1,400 full-time-equivalent staff since 2024, according to pre-audit financial documents reviewed by the Bangor Daily News, and plans to regionalize services and shift toward outpatient care. Whether that’s enough will shape what care is left in rural Maine as federal Medicaid cuts and other headwinds hit hospitals in the coming years.
Operating losses grew from about $15 million to about $48 million in fiscal year 2026, the documents show. Total revenue dipped slightly by about $5 million, hovering around $2.4 billion.
The system performed better than budgeted for the year and “is on track to achieve its three-year plan for sustainability,” Rohrbaugh said.
That plan aims to build up outpatient services, which are generally cheaper than inpatient care provided during overnight hospital stays. The system is also trying to make care more flexible for patients, Northern Light’s president told the BDN earlier this month.
Contract labor costs fell by $25 million this year, while inflated equipment, utility and insurance costs added $13 million in expenses, Rohrbaugh said.
“Reimbursement does not keep pace with cost increases and that requires us to drive continual improvement across such areas as revenue cycle, supply chain, information technology, and pharmacy,” he said.
The results show the system is still under financial pressure, according to Pankaj Agrrawal, a finance professor at the University of Maine’s Maine Business School.
“They have cut down staffing, but still the expenses are rising,” he said.
Still, the rise in operating expenses over last year “should be taken with a grain of salt” because inflation ran about 3% over the past year, Agrrawal said.
The pre-audit financials were posted to the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board’s online database earlier this month. They may change slightly when the final audit is released in December, according to Rohrbaugh.

title: Grammy nominations snub Harry Styles and hip-hop, while surprises include Dolly Parton
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The 2027 Grammy Award nominees are here and there’s a lot to discuss, from Raye and Rosalía dominating the nominations to John Cale receiving his first nod at 84.
Like every year, there were a few artists who made the coveted list Monday and a few who didn’t. Snubs and surprises are in no short supply across the 100 categories that will be awarded Feb. 7.
No hip-hop in most of the general field categories
It’s a 180 from the 2026 Grammys, where, for the first time, there were three releases nominated in both the rap album and album of the year categories. This year, there isn’t a single rap release in the record, song or album of the year categories.
According to Billboard, Drake — the only rapper to score a No. 1 hit on the all-genre Hot 100 this year, with “Janice STFU” — did not submit his three 2026 albums or any of their songs for Grammy consideration. But even without his star power (or that of last year’s nominees Kendrick Lamar, Clipse and Tyler, the Creator), hip-hop seems like a huge absence.
A$AP Rocky’s first full-length album in eight years, “Don’t Be Dumb,” is also noticeably absent, as is Baby Keem’s “Ca$ino.” It seems all eyes will be on Don Toliver, the rising trap and R&B rapper-singer, who scored a best new artist nomination in addition to a rap album one.
But let the record show Drake did secure one nomination: for the newly minted best Latin song category, for his Spanish-language feature on Karol G’s “Ahí.”
Women dominate many of the major categories … and in country
For the first time, the six artists with the most nominations at the Grammys are all women.
And women make up every nominee in the album and song of the year categories, save for Grammy favorite Bruno Mars. For album of the year, Raye and Rosalía will face off against Phoebe Bridgers, Olivia Dean, Ella Langley, Olivia Rodrigo, Taylor Swift and Mars. The list of artists is nearly identical for song of the year — just swap Bridgers for Ariana Grande — and add a first-ever general field nomination for Björk, who is featured on Rosalía’s “Berghain.”
However, there were some strong contenders omitted. Those include Stella Lefty, whose ubiquitous “Boston” did not earn her a single nom, or Gracie Abrams’ “Daughter From Hell.”
But beyond the top categories, women dominate in other, interesting places: dance pop recording, R&B solo performance and in the contemporary country album category, now in its second year. Langley, Kelsea Ballerini, Carter Faith, Megan Moroney and Kacey Musgraves will go head-to-head there. And just as interesting: Only men are nominated in the traditional country category.
Leading men like Harry Styles and Noah Kahan get less love
Harry Styles’ fourth studio album, “Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally.,” did not receive a nomination. The same should be said about Ed Sheeran’s “Play.” Noah Kahan’s critically acclaimed “The Great Divide” received only one nod, in the newly created contemporary folk album category. Justin Bieber’s surprise album “Swag II” didn’t receive a nomination, either.
Newcomer Malcolm Todd was shut out as well, despite lots of love for his album “Do That Again.” It was the same for his sister, the singer-songwriter Audrey Hobert, who was seen as a leading candidate for best new artist.
Beyoncé once again makes history
She’s no stranger to raising the bar. At the 2023 Grammys, Beyoncé became the most-awarded artist in the show’s history. Then, two years later, with “Cowboy Carter,” she became the first Black artist to win country album of the year and the first Black woman to win album of the year since Lauryn Hill’s “The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill” in 1999. She’s now received her 100th career nomination, for “Morning Dew (Donk)” in the R&B solo performance category. The song was the lead single of her 20th anniversary re-release of “B’Day.”
Dolly Parton and Tim Curry receive posthumous nominations
Dolly Parton, who died earlier this year, received three nominations. She’s nominated in the country duo/group performance category twice — for “Butterfly” by Zac Brown Band featuring Parton and “Light of a Clear Blue Morning,” a Parton classic performed with Lainey Wilson, Miley Cyrus, Queen Latifah and Reba McEntire. She’s also nominated in the audiobook, narration and storytelling recording category for her work, “Star of the Show: My Life on Stage.”
In the latter category, competition is fierce: Actor Tim Curry, who also died earlier this year, is nominated for “Vagabond: A Memoir.” And Michelle Obama is nominated in the category for a third time, for “The Look.” Obama has won the award twice before.
BTS and the Asian pop performance category
And now for a little controversy: This year, the Recording Academy created five new Grammy categories, including Asian pop music performance, meant to celebrate releases across K-pop, J-pop, C-pop and beyond. Some fans were excited; others viewed the new category as a racialized barrier for Asian performers.
Not long afterward, K-pop powerhouse BTS said they would not submit their music for consideration. As a result, they did not receive any nominations this year. BTS has never won a Grammy, though they’ve been nominated for five across their career. In fact, no K-pop act had ever won a Grammy before 2026, when “Golden” from “KPop Demon Hunters” took home the trophy for best song for visual media.
After consulting experts, managers, artists and others, the Recording Academy decided to proceed with the category. Another massive K-pop group, Stray Kids, also opted not to submit, but other groups, like the Filipino boy band SB19 and girl group BINI, spoke in support of the category.
Both SB19 and BINI received nods, for their songs “Visa” and “Unang Kilig,” respectively. They’re competing with Japanese singer LiSA’s “Yes,” Japanese kawaii metal band Babymetal’s “Sunset Kiss” featuring Polyphia and two K-pop girl groups: KiiiKiii’s “404 (New Era)” and IVE’s “Bang Bang.”
Notably absent are a few K-pop groups who had huge songs this year, like aespa’s “Lemonade,” Hearts2Hearts’ “Rude!” and BigBang’s “BiiiG.”

title: Looking back week of Nov. 19
text:
Bar Harbor
Area schoolchildren, businesses and church volunteers joined forces this month to bring a Thanksgiving feast to 105 area families and to stock the Bar Harbor Food Pantry with a surplus of dry and canned goods. The charitable effort was organized by the outreach board of the Bar Harbor Congregational Church. “Every year I ask, and every year the kids enthusiastically say yes,” said Mount Desert Elementary teacher Kate St. Denis, who has been taking her classes to help with the food drive for seven or eight years. “It’s a good model. The kids learn more about the world and the people in it, and they’re helping their neighbors.” Kindergarten through eighth-grade students from the Conners-Emerson School in Bar Harbor spent a week collecting donations, as they have for each of the past five years. Each grade was assigned a different type of food, from stuffing to cranberry sauce. Hannaford’s supermarket, Bar Harbor Bank, and the Mount Desert Island Rotary Club also collected food throughout the month.

title: Winslow singer-songwriter Bella Ann releases holiday record Nov. 27
text:
WINSLOW, Maine (WABI) - Isabella Loubier, known by her stage name, Bella Ann, would get in trouble for humming in class as a child in Winslow. Now, she is now signed with Slumbo Labs, an artist development company that is a partner of RCA Records.
Winslow High School student Isabella Loubier, who performs as Bella Ann, will release a Christmas EP titled “Hope for the Holidays” on Nov. 27. She recently spent five days in Los Angeles working with producers.
Loubier is a three-sport varsity athlete at Winslow High School and a songwriter. She said she is happy with the impact her music has made in her community.
“Little girls that come to my shows with, like, Bella Ann hoodies, and, like, and they’re singing along. It already matters to people,” Loubier said. “So, even if this is as far as it goes, what a beautiful thing that I have accomplished, you know?”
She cited artists from Olivia Rodrigo to Bob Dylan as inspirations.
Studio sessions in Los Angeles
In Los Angeles, Loubier worked with producers for five days. She said she has a catalog of original music.
“I have a lot of original music. The problem isn’t that I don’t have any music,” Loubier said. “It’s, like, here’s five songs. Which one do you want to produce today?”
Her mother, Meg, attended the studio sessions. Loubier said her mother has been her biggest influence.
“She really, I think, found her voice and her independence and her way to communicate,” Meg Loubier said.
Holiday EP recorded in Maine
Loubier also continues to make music in Maine. She worked with Hallowell producer Bob Colwell well on her Christmas EP, which features three covers and one original song.
“He really just has, like, brought what is in my head to life,” Loubier said.
“Hope for the Holidays” comes out Nov. 27. Bella Ann’s music is available on streaming platforms. More information is available at BellaAnnMusic.com.

title: Portland councilors to consider cruise ship scrubber discharge ban
text:
Portland councilors approve ban on cruise ship scrubber discharge
Portland city councilors voted unanimously Monday night to stop future cruise ships from using 'scrubbers' and dumping the potentially toxic wash water while docked at two city-owned marine terminals.
Portland councilors approve ban on cruise ship scrubber discharge
Portland city councilors voted unanimously Monday night to stop future cruise ships from using 'scrubbers' and dumping the potentially toxic wash water while docked at two city-owned marine terminals.
Portland city councilors unanimously voted to approve a proposal Monday night to stop future cruise ships from using 'scrubbers' or dumping the scrubber wash water while docked at two city-owned marine terminals.
The resolution, sponsored by Councilors Regina Phillips and Pious Ali, asks the city manager to amend Portland's rules and ban the practice at Portland Ocean Terminal and the Ocean Gateway Terminal. Once implemented it will make Portland the first port in the state to take such an action. The resolution cites concerns about preventable chemical and particulate contamination in Casco Bay and its marine ecosystem.
"Scrubbers" is the colloquial term for the open- or closed-loop system that cleans pollutants from a ship's exhaust. Open-loop systems use seawater in that process and discharge the untreated or minimally treated wash water back into the ocean.
Cruise Lines International Association, a global trade group, has defended the use of scrubbers, arguing that they are a vital technology in the industry and have been approved by international regulators. The group argues that when in open-loop mode, scrubbers have "minimal impact on water and sediment quality."
However, environmental advocates have raised concerns about the potentially toxic impacts of the wash water on marine life. A 2024 study outside of Maine waters found that scrubber discharge concentrations as low as .0001% can have toxic effects on sea urchin egg fertilization and affect multiple species' larval development.
According to Friends of Casco Bay, open-loop systems do indeed reduce sulfur emissions in the air but create water pollution.
"Scientific studies from other harbors have found that exposure to these types of chemicals can harm aquatic life," writes Friends of Casco Bay on its website. "While we know of no studies from Portland Harbor that document the effects of scrubber washwater discharges on water quality, we know that these chemicals have harmful effects and seek to keep them out of the harbor."
The environmental group Portland Cruise Control also supported a ban. The group says the proposed restrictions would require ships to use cleaner distillate fuel while docked and would not impact the number of port calls, passengers or revenue paid to Portland.
"I feel very much so that they assumed that the cruise industry would go to a cleaner distillate fuel that would then they would comply and they would have the sulfur content that was necessary," said Portland Cruise Control co-founder JoAnn Locktov. "But that's not what happened. What they did instead is they wanted to keep using a very cheap, very dirty, fuel called heavy fuel oil."
According to Portland's Department of Parks, Recreation and Facilities, which oversees the Ocean Gateway Terminal, all of the cruise ships currently coming into the city already abide by these proposed rules.
The director of the department, Ethan Hipple, said the ships either use marine gas oil or a closed loop scrubber system.
"We see this as not having a large impact on actual cruise ship operations, but a good thing to do," said Hipple.
According to the schedule for 2027, at least 69 cruise ships are expected to visit Portland between April and November.
Portland's ban follows a policy adopted earlier this year that offers cruise lines a discounted passenger rate when they use low-sulfur fuels while at berth. The city said the discount was intended to reduce reliance on heavy fuel oil and the exhaust cleaning systems used with it.

title: Woodstove ashes burn Maine home

title: Technical issue triggers online banking delays across major US banks
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle on Monday after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
However, Chase said Monday that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and that it was working to bring banking services back online by the end of the day Monday.
“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system — it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for the bank.
EN ESPAÑOL | Reportan interrupción en el servicio de varios bancos del país
The disruption comes days after technology troubles affected other parts of the U.S. economy: A major Microsoft outage on Thursday impacted services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. An outage affecting the nation’s air traffic control system Friday grounded all U.S. flights for several hours and disrupted air travel across the country over the weekend.
On Monday, United Airlines said that it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights,
In the same statement, Evangelisti said that this was a Chase-only issue.
“This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” he said.
Monday’s technical issues seemed to be centered at Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, including Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services.
A spokesman for U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly impacted but that “clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.”
Zelle is the peer-to-peer payment system that major U.S. banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed. Zelle is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.
A spokesman for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational.
“An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,” the spokesman said.
Some Chase customers received a message that said, “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”

title: Father accused of killing 3-month-old son by aggressively rocking bouncer to get him to stop crying
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) - A Hawaii man remains in custody after being charged with manslaughter in the death of his 3-month-old son.
Joshua Kaleolani Agbayani Soto Paiva, 20, appeared in court Thursday. His bail was set at $1 million, and he is expected back in court Monday.
The investigation into the death of Paiva’s 3-month-old son, John-Charles Saiki-Paiva, is ongoing.
Foul play suspected
Puna patrol officers responded to a home in the Hawaiian Paradise Park subdivision at 11:50 a.m. Oct. 25 for a report of an unresponsive male infant.
Hawai‘i Fire Department paramedics took the infant, identified by authorities as John-Charles Saiki-Paiva, to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 1:06 p.m.
The preliminary results of an autopsy indicated John-Charles died from head injuries, and foul play was suspected.
Court documents detail allegations
Court documents allege Paiva told police he was playing “Overwatch,” an online multiplayer video game, and his son wouldn’t stop crying.
He said as he prepared a bottle for John-Charles, he heard the baby “coughing and gagging with milk coming out” and “then went completely quiet,” the documents said.
After police informed Paiva of the baby’s injuries, he admitted he had been lying, according to the documents. Paiva then said that he began “aggressively rocking” the baby bouncer with enough force that John-Charles’ head and body flailed and hit the bouncer’s frame for about 15 minutes, documents said.
According to police, Paiva said he grabbed the baby’s right leg, yanked him off the bouncer and placed him on an ottoman, where he applied his own body weight — about 220 pounds — until the baby stopped crying.
“A case like this is really difficult with especially our investigators as well, everybody involved, the personnel that responded to the scene, the medical staff that worked on the infant,” said Lt. Derek Morimoto with the Hawai‘i Police Department. “So, a lot of people are affected by a case like this.”

title: How to talk with older family members about driving
text:
(Aging Untold) — Families can start conversations with older loved ones about driving before it becomes a problem, according to Amy O’Rourke, an Aging Untold expert.
For many older adults, driving means independence. As people age, their health changes, and families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving.
Starting the conversation
O’Rourke suggests asking a loved one questions before driving becomes a problem.
“Do you mind if I bring this up, Dad?” O’Rourke said.
How would you feel if I brought up the car? I’m not telling you, I’m not talking about that, but I want to be prepared for when I think you might need some evaluation. I don’t want to be blindsided and I don’t want to be talking to you in a crisis,” she said.
“Start before it’s a problem and just start lobbing some questions and make it part of a routine check-in,” O’Rourke said.
Red flags to watch for
Experts say these are some of the red flags families can watch for:
- Delayed responses
- Getting lost or disoriented easily
- Increased close calls
- Difficulty seeing pedestrians, objects or other vehicles
- Dents or scrapes on the car or on surrounding objects where the person drives and parks at home
Where to find help
Families also can talk with a doctor about any health issues or medications that can affect driving.
The state DMV can provide information on driver evaluations and restrictions. Local agencies on aging can help families find transportation options.

title: Mixed reception for Maine’s paid-leave law: A win for employees, a challenge for employers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LD1964 was signed into law in July 2023. Employees could begin applying in March 2026 for paid time off starting May 1.
Most employees can take up to 12 weeks off — at up to 90% of their wages — for life events including the arrival of a child, their own or a family member’s serious health condition, managing a family member’s impending military deployment, or to stay safe or assist a family member after abuse or violence.
Eligible employees must have earned at least six times the state average weekly wage, which is $1,249, over a base period.
The legislature allocated a one-time appropriation of $25 million, but the program is now funded primarily by payroll taxes.
Starting in January 2025, employers with at least 15 employees have had to contribute 1% of wages to fund the program, half of which can be deducted from paychecks.
Employers with fewer than 15 staffers are required to pay into the program 0.5% of total wages, and they can garner the full amount from workers’ paychecks.
The application and approval process is being administered by Aflac insurance company.
Companies can choose to use the new state insurance program, to which they’ve paid in, or elect to use an approved private insurer.
Employees may take leave for more than one qualifying event annually, but the total cannot exceed 12 weeks per year.

title: Oxford Fire On Friday The 13th: Hot Wood Stove Ashes In A Plastic Container Sparked It
text:
Maine's top fire officials are reminding people that use wood stoves to pay attention to how the dispose of those ashes, or run the risk of causing a fire.
This comes on the heels of a Friday the 13th fire in the town of Oxford, where multiple agencies and departments responded to a structure fire on the East Oxford Road.
Maine Fire Marshal's investigators were able to determine the cause of the blaze and said it was improper disposal of ashes from a wood stove that created the issue.
"The fire was determined to have been caused by hot ashes from a woodstove that had been improperly discarded in a plastic container. The hot ashes ignited the combustible container, causing the fire to spread throughout the residence. The fire was classified as accidental."
Authorities warn against ever putting hot ash into a plastic container, or dumping them near a building or other combustible materials.
According to one local insurance company, MMG Insurance, improper disposal of ashes has caused dangerous issues like wildfires and house fires across the nation, not just in Maine.
"According to the National Fire Protection Association, every year in the U.S. nearly 10,000 fires are caused due to improper removal and disposal of hot ashes. Hot coals, when hidden in ashes and therefore well insulated, can stay hot for up to four days – and all they need to flare up again is oxygen."
Local public safety officials like the Maine Forest Rangers echo that, stating that responding to fires created by ashes is something are very familiar with as it's becoming a years event.
Read More: Bangor Firefighters Contain Early Morning Center Street Blaze
They suggest being mindful of what you use to store your ashes, and the location where you decide to dump them.
"Be sure to allow ashes to cool completely before disposing of them. Place ashes in a tightly covered metal container and keep it at least 10 feet away from any buildings. Never empty the ashes directly into a trash can or on the ground. Pour water on the ashes. Make sure they are cold to the touch before emptying the container."
State Fire Marshal's deemed the Oxford fire as accidental. Thankfully there was no one home in the residence at the time the fire broke out.

title: WATCH: Student with Down syndrome gets unforgettable sendoff from high school
text:
WATCH: Student with Down syndrome gets unforgettable sendoff from high school
Brady Brandon celebrated his last day at Bow High School in New Hampshire on Friday, surrounded by classmates and teachers cheering him on as he walked the halls one final time.
Brady has Down syndrome. He graduated in 2023, but because of his disability, he was able to continue attending school until he turned 22.
"It was probably one of the best moments of my life," Brady's mom, Leah Lucier-Pike, said. "I tried my hardest not to cry, but probably the proudest moment I've ever felt in my life. Just watching him. Not only just complete public school successfully, but just the friendships and the commitment from the community."
"I was super proud!" Brady said.
Lucier-Pike said the faculty, staff and community members at Bow High School made all the difference throughout her son's academic journey.
"When we can come together as a community and celebrate and recognize and acknowledge a student that's worked really, really hard. We are just fortunate to be Falcons," she said.
Now, Lucier-Pike said the focus is on establishing Brady's next chapter in adulthood.
"That's something I'm really working toward, you know, opening the eyes of what is next for people like Brady," she said.
Brady works at Market Basket and played unified sports during his time in high school. He said he's going to miss physical education class and his coach the most.
The plan is for Brady to continue working at Market Basket while his family continues to find strong support and opportunities for him as he enters adulthood.
Lucier-Pike said Brady has grown so much.
"I never would have imagined Brady being this successful when he was two, or three, or four," she said. "It's worth it. It's worth it."

title: Russia: Air defenses intercept over 1,300 Ukrainian drones in massive aerial attack
text:
Russia: Air defenses intercept over 1,300 Ukrainian drones in massive aerial attack
Russian air defenses intercepted 1,336 drones launched by Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry said Monday, in what appeared to be Kyiv’s biggest aerial attack since Moscow’s all-out invasion of its neighbor nearly five years ago.
Ukraine has scaled up its long-range aerial assaults on Russia, as well as illegally annexed Crimea, the Black and the Azov seas, with more than 1,000 drones used in some attacks in recent months.
Related video: Talks between U.S., Russia, and Ukraine continue with no breakthrough
Russia, meanwhile, has battered Ukrainian civilian areas with relentless attacks that seek to make daily life impossible and break morale, especially through strikes on the power grid.
The strikes on Russia serve an important purpose for Ukraine. They have targeted Russian oil refineries, which are an economic mainstay for Moscow
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed late Sunday that Ukrainian attacks have disabled more than 55% of Russia’s oil refining capacity. Russian officials didn’t comment on that claim, and independent verification wasn’t possible.
Ukrainian officials are keen, too, to make Russians feel the war at home, while mid-range strikes are disrupting Russia’s front-line supply routes and hampering Moscow’s efforts to get momentum on the battlefield, analysts say.
Kyiv says newly imposed speed limits on the U.S.-made Starshield system, which is SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service, have weakened Ukraine's air defenses. Ukrainian forces say they are trying to hit Russian weapons production plants and sites Russia uses to launch drone and missile attacks.
Kyiv also wants to show its supporters that it is still in the fight, as Moscow tries to depict its victory in Ukraine as inevitable and U.S.-mediated talks make no impact on the war.
There was no clear picture of the extent of damage caused by Ukrainian strikes in Russia. Moscow-based and local officials rarely provide details.

title: EMS chief who was injured in Searsmont explosion shares thank-you letter ahead of her homecoming
text:
Searsmont EMS Chief Sarah Tompkins, who was injured in mill explosion, shares thank-you letter ahead of her homecoming
Tompkins, who spent nearly five months in the hospital and seven weeks in rehab, will return to Searsmont on Wednesday, Nov. 18.
Searsmont EMS Chief Sarah Tompkins, who was injured in mill explosion, shares thank-you letter ahead of her homecoming
Tompkins, who spent nearly five months in the hospital and seven weeks in rehab, will return to Searsmont on Wednesday, Nov. 18.
The town of Searsmont's emergency medical services chief is thanking everyone who helped her over the past six months while she recovered from injuries she suffered in the May 15 fire and explosion at Robbins Lumber.
Sarah Tompkins wrote a thank-you letter that was shared by town officials Monday morning, more than 48 hours before she is set to return home.
"As a paramedic, I am used to being the one responding to other people’s worst day. First responders are pros at caring for the patient and their family during a crisis. I have worked in EMS for eight years, but for the last six months, I have been the one being cared for after my worst day. Thank you," Tompkins said in her letter. "To the EMTs, paramedics, firefighters, and LifeFlight crews that saved my life, to the CNAs, nurses, doctors and therapists who cared for me and took the time to learn who I am as a person, thank you. You took the time to console me as I cried and celebrate my successes. You made me feel like a person, not just a diagnosis."
In the letter, Tompkins said she was hospitalized at Maine Medical Center in Portland for four and a half months and has been at Spaulding Rehabilitation Hospital in Boston for the past seven weeks.
"I couldn’t see, I couldn’t walk, and everything was bandaged. As I grew stronger, my family told me more," Tompkins said. "I was surprised to learn the accident had made national news. It was painful to hear of how many were injured and how many loved ones we lost. I was surprised that hundreds of people took the time to send me supportive words and gifts."
Tompkins is also the deputy EMS chief for the town of Stockton Springs and runs Fine Line Farm in Searsmont with her partner, Hubert McCabe.
"Thank you to everyone who fed Hubert and the farm crew. Thank you to those who opened their homes to my family in Portland and again in Boston. To everyone who lent a hand on the farm, who raised and donated money, who wrote me the hundreds of cards and letters, thank you," Tompkins said. "The cards and letters, the meals, texts, phone messages, the stories of everyone who helped put up firewood to keep us warm this winter, and everyone who helped with windows, stairs, and house modifications, the stories were all told to me and each card was read to me. To all of you who have kept me in your thoughts for six months, thank you."
The Searsmont Fire Department has planned an escort for Tompkins, which is scheduled to leave the Augusta Civic Center between 1:00 and 1:15 p.m. Wednesday. The escort is for emergency vehicles only, while community members, friends and supporters are encouraged to gather safely along Route 3 and at Cox Machine to cheer on Tompkins, who is set to arrive at the Searsmont Fire and Rescue Station at about 2:15 p.m. After the escort, the fire department will be hosting a gathering at the station.
"After fighting to survive, after all the pain of surgeries and the bandage changes, after hearing the exhaustion and grief in my loved ones' voices, the re-learning how to do tasks that were once routine, and then slowly get stronger to heal, I am finally coming home," Tompkins said in her letter. "I spent close to five months in the hospital and seven weeks in rehab. I still have wounds and scars, but I am also filled with so much hope for all of us. People are good and kind."
"I can only hope that when everyone has to go through their worst day, when they have to call for help, they are treated with the same level of love and care that I have been. Yes, I am a fighter, but I didn’t fight alone," Tompkins added. "Thank you."
The May 15 fire and explosion at the Robbins Lumber mill in Searsmont caused the deaths of three people: Morrill Firefighter Andrew Cross, Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury and Robbins Lumber co-owner Alden Robbins. Tompkins and the following nine people were injured in the explosion:
- Searsmont Fire Chief James Ames
- Lincolnville Firefighter Aaron Heald
- Appleton Fire Chief Clifton Marriner
- Belmont Firefighter Katie Paige
- Robbins Lumber co-owner James A. Robbins, Alden's brother
- Searsmont EMS volunteer Lily Robbins, Alden's daughter
- Montville Firefighter Jacob Spaulding
- Lincolnville Firefighter John Ward
- Waldo Firefighter Thomas Wolf, who is also a Robbins Lumber employee
More information about the celebration for Sarah Tompkins
Searsmont officials said that cameras are welcome outside the Fire and Rescue Station, but they also asked that no photos or videos be taken inside the building.
Anyone who wishes to bring food, desserts or snacks to share at the homecoming celebration is more than welcome.
People who have questions about the homecoming or emergency vehicle escort are being asked to call Amy Drinkwater at 207-332-2309.

title: Kennebec County settles ‘Naked and Afraid’ contestant’s lawsuit for $175K
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine — Kennebec County’s publicly funded insurer paid out $175,000 to settle a federal lawsuit brought by a former emergency management staffer who accused her boss of accessing her nude photos from her participation in a reality television show and alleged other officials then retaliated against her.
The Maine County Commissioners Association Self-Funded Risk Management Pool issued the payments Sept. 29, according to records obtained Wednesday through a Freedom of Access Act request.
The agreement indicates it was reached during a judicial settlement conference in August. Lawyers officially closed out the case in U.S. District Court in Bangor on Oct. 16, court records show.
Danielle Beauchemin, who was a specialist and education coordinator in the county’s emergency management agency, received $20,000 representing lost wages and $84,595 for other alleged damages, including emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life and injury to reputation.
Her attorneys, from the Topsham law firm Johnson, Webbert & Beard, received the other $70,405 for legal services.
Beauchemin’s attorneys, Braden Beard, Kassandra Fotiadis and Ryan Schmitz, declined to comment on the settlement Thursday.
Reached via email, Peter Marchesi, one of the attorneys who represented the county and several officials named as defendants, pointed to language in the agreement that says it was reached without the admission of liability.
When the lawsuit was filed, Marchesi called Beauchemin’s complaint “an exercise in creative, sensationalist writing” that “bears little relation to the true facts surrounding the events at issue.” Marchesi, of the Waterville law firm Wheeler & Arey, added at the time that the county had made “herculean efforts” to accommodate Beauchemin’s requests and demands.
John Wall, of the Portland law firm Monaghan Leahy, who represented former Emergency Management Director Arthur True, did not respond to an emailed request to discuss the case.
The agreement contains provisions for confidentiality and prohibits the parties from making disparaging comments.
It allows only for its contents to be disclosed under certain circumstances, such as in response to court orders or subpoenas, Freedom of Access Act requests and inquiries from attorneys, accountants, therapists or law enforcement authorities. It further requires Beauchemin and county officials, if asked about the agreement, to state only that she left her employment with Kennebec County on mutual, agreeable terms.
The Augusta-based risk pool, which made the payment, provides liability coverage for Maine’s county governments. Counties, which raise most of their funds through property taxation, pay into the pool.
The risk pool billed Kennebec County approximately $294,000 this year, with about $178,000 designated for coverage of jail operations, an invoice provided by County Administrator Scott Ferguson shows.
In addition to the settlement payment in the case, the risk pool has paid out $23,098 in legal fees and other defense-related expenses, according to Malcolm Ulmer, its director of operations.
Beauchemin of Falmouth sued the county in federal court in December. The lawsuit also named Ferguson, True, Finance Director Cynthia Ferguson and Human Resources Director Christine Brawn as defendants.
In the 40-page complaint, her lawyers outlined a series of events that began when Beauchemin discovered True, her supervisor, had allegedly accessed her personal Google Photos account through her office computer. She made the discovery in April 2023, about four months after the county hired her.
True viewed and downloaded dozens of nude photos and videos of her, Beauchemin alleged, adding that he later admitted doing so to law enforcement authorities.
The uncensored, explicit files, which the complaint notes Beauchemin never accessed through her work computer and were linked to the Google account through an old personal cellphone, came from her filming of the TV show “Naked and Afraid.”
The reality series — in which participants are tasked with surviving in the wilderness for lengthy periods of time without clothing and with minimal resources — airs on the Discovery Channel. Explicit portions of footage included in episodes are blurred out.
County human resources staff appeared to minimize the issue when Beauchemin went to speak with them, and Beauchemin reported what happened to Augusta police, the complaint said.
True resigned the next day, the lawsuit said.
According to the complaint, an administrative investigation conducted by the Kennebec County Sheriff’s Office found that camera footage from around Beauchemin’s office during the alleged use of Google Photos account had been deleted, two spy cameras had been delivered to her office building the week prior, and tools and a flashlight were stored in the ceiling above her office.
In the following weeks, the lawsuit alleged, county officials retaliated and created a hostile work environment by rescinding an accommodation for Beauchemin to bring to work her service dog for mental health disabilities, belittling her, changing her job duties and blaming her for contractor payment issues, among other things.
The county at one point commissioned an internal investigation led by a Drummond Woodsum attorney, but the lawsuit said Beauchemin never learned what came of it.
Beauchemin eventually took unpaid medical leave, and the county terminated her while she was on leave, when the commissioners voted to reallocate federal COVID-19 pandemic recovery funds, the complaint said. At the time of the filing, Beauchemin claimed what happened had long-term effects on her mental, emotional and physical well-being.
True, meanwhile, faces criminal charges of invasion of computer privacy and stalking. He has pleaded not guilty.
At the request of his criminal defense attorney, Darrick X. Banda, of the Augusta law firm Bourget & Banda, a judge in March ordered the case transferred out of Kennebec County.
Maeghan Maloney, district attorney of Kennebec and Somerset counties, said at the time the case was going to be overseen by the Office of the Maine Attorney General instead of her office.
Office spokesperson Danna Hayes, however, said Thursday that a prosecutor in the office of Natasha Irving, district attorney for Knox, Lincoln, Sagadahoc and Waldo counties, was handling the case.
A Lincoln County court clerk confirmed the case remained pending there. It is on the list for docket call in January.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Jake Freudberg can be reached at jfreudberg@centralmaine.com.

title: 5 Rockland apartment buildings are going to foreclosure auction
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — A foreclosure auction is scheduled for Dec. 8 for five apartment buildings throughout Rockland that contain 19 apartments.
Keenan Auction Co. will conduct the auction for 52 Pleasant St., 38 Purchase St., 43 Broad St., 115 North Main St. and 117 North Main St. The auction will be held at the Dry Dock Restaurant at 1 Commercial St. in Rockland.
The properties are owned by a series of limited liability companies with common owners, Craig Call and Stephanie Ann Goodridge. The limited liability companies are Good Call 38 LLC, Good Call 43 LLC, Good Call 52 LLC and Good Call Development LLC, which owns the two apartment buildings on North Main Street. The city has the properties assessed for a combined total of about $1.9 million.
The 38 Purchase St. property is a duplex assessed at $261,900. Good Call purchased it in January 2022 for $175,000.
The 43 Broad St. property is four units assessed at $369,100, which the company purchased in January 2022 for $310,000.
The 52 Pleasant St. property is four units assessed at $431,400, purchased in March 2021 for $340,000.
The 117 North Main property is three units assessed at $407,200, which was purchased in May 2020 for $200,000.
And the 115 North Main property is six units assessed at $388,800, bought in May 2020 for $260,000.
Stef Keenan of Keenan Auction said: “The lender has not scheduled any evictions of the tenants. The lender is selling the properties subject to parties in possession. After the auction, the new owners will need to create new tenancy relationships with the existing parties that are occupying the properties.”

title: Paul LePage hires Gorham native and former Susan Collins aide as chief of staff
text:
Insiders saw this first. 
This story was broken in Maine Politics Insider, the BDN’s daily premium newsletter for the most ardent political news followers. If you are a new BDN subscriber, you can sign up here. Current subscribers can contact our customer service team to upgrade.
U.S. Rep.-elect Paul LePage, a Republican from the 2nd District, has hired a Gorham native who has worked for members of Congress in both chambers as his chief of staff.
Tim O’Neill has been legislative director for U.S. Rep. Tom McClintock, R-California, since May 2025. He will run the Washington and Maine offices for the 78-year-old former governor, who takes office in January as the only New England Republican in Congress.
O’Neill started on Capitol Hill in 2019 as a staff assistant for U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, whom Democrat Troy Jackson ousted in this month’s election. He later worked for former Reps. Louie Gohmert of Texas and Debbie Lesko of Arizona and for a Senate committee led by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Kentucky, according to LegiStorm, which tracks congressional staff.
LePage has tended to keep his top aides. He had only two chiefs of staff in eight years as governor. John McGough held the job from 2011 until January 2018, when he left for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Deputy Holly Lusk took over for the last year.
O’Neill’s first job will be hiring staff. A House office can have up to 18 permanent aides, paid from an allowance that averages just over $1.9 million a year. LePage’s predecessor, U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, had about 15 regular aides as of June 30, with roughly half of them in Maine.

title: Lawmakers unveil bipartisan bill to give NICU parents more time off from work
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — U.S. parents with newborns in intensive care would be entitled to up to 12 more weeks of unpaid leave under a new bill unveiled Monday by a group of bipartisan lawmakers, who described an agonizing gap faced by many families.
The bill, introduced by Rep. Brittany Pettersen, a Colorado Democrat, aims to address a long-overlooked plight facing many parents with newborns in neonatal intensive care, who often exhaust much of their parental leave before their baby comes home from the hospital. Many mothers and fathers end up working through their newborns’ NICU stays to save their time off.
The proposed legislation would amend the 1993 Family and Medical Leave Act to offer up to 12 weeks of dedicated NICU leave to eligible workers, on top of 12 weeks of parental leave already available.
The campaign for NICU leave has gained momentum since Colorado and Illinois became the first states to implement such policies earlier this year. On Tuesday, Walmart will begin offering a maximum of 12 extra weeks of NICU leave to its full-time employees, joining a handful of other companies with similar policies, including Morgan Stanley, Pinterest and organic baby formula company Bobbie.
The U.S. has no federal law mandating paid family leave but FMLA entitles eligible parents — those who have worked at least 12 months for a private employer with 50 or more employees — to job-protected unpaid leave to care for a newborn.
While Republicans have generally opposed a federal mandate for paid leave, Pettersen said she is optimistic that the amendment to the FMLA will garner bipartisan support.
“This isn’t about party, it’s about life experiences,” Pettersen said in an interview with The Associated Press. “Where we want to go is paid family and medical leave, and we will continue to fight for it. This is a step forward building off the current policy that has bipartisan support.”
Her co-sponsors were Republicans, Rep. Mike Lawler of New York and Rep. Ryan Mackenzie of Pennsylvania, and a Democrat, Rep. Morgan McGarvey of Kentucky. Mackenzie and McGarvey have both advocated for other policies benefiting NICU babies and shared their own stories as fathers with newborns in intensive care.
“For parents with a newborn in the NICU, the last thing they should have to worry about is whether they’ll have enough time off work to be there for their child,” Mackenzie said in a statement.
Lawler added in a statement that “every working parent deserves the chance to be there for their child, especially when that child is facing a serious medical challenge.”
The bill, known as the “Stand By NICU Babies and Families Act,” could face a long road. It must be reintroduced after the new Congress is seated in January, and Pettersen will have to search for new Republican sponsors. Lawler and Mackenzie both lost their reelection bids in the midterm elections that gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress.
Pettersen said she introduced the bill pro forma to put a stake in the ground as her newly empowered party readies its priorities for the next Congress.
The NICU leave bills passed in Colorado and Illinois illustrate the partisan divide over paid leave mandates. Colorado’s paid leave passed mostly along party lines, while a shorter, unpaid leave adopted in Illinois had overwhelming bipartisan support.
In both states, however, the policies were championed by legislators with their own experiences as NICU parents.
“This issue of leave for NICU parents seems to be something that people intuitively get, including people on the right and left and people in between,” said Inimai Chettiar, president of A Better Balance, a nonprofit that is advocating for state and federal NICU leave policies.
Nearly one out of 10 babies born in the U.S. are admitted to a NICU, according to the most recent figures from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Advocates say parental presence in the NICU is important because skin-to-skin contact helps improve health outcomes, while time off is critical for mothers of premature babies who are at higher risk of postpartum depression.
A Better Balance said most parents wouldn’t need the full 12 weeks of extra leave since the majority of NICU stays are much shorter, but the longer cap will help families facing more critical health situations.
McGarvey, the Kentucky congressman, said his now teenage twins spent 99 days in intensive care after they were born 14 weeks early.
“When your baby’s in the NICU, all you can focus on is getting them home,” McGarvey said in a statement.

title: Melani Sanders shares why she started the We Do Not Care Club, opens up about vulnerable video
text:
(Aging Untold) — Melani Sanders, creator of the We Do Not Care Club, met with Aging Untold for a two-part interview. She shared why she started the popular club.
She also shared what led her to open up and post a vulnerable video that has resonated with many, many people.
Sanders is a social media sensation now, but there was a time when the creator of the popular “We Do Not Care Club” wasn’t one to be in front of the camera.
That changed one day when she decided that she had reached capacity. She was already tired and still had so much to do. Instead, she recorded a video from her car in the parking lot of her local Whole Foods.
In it, she announced a new club — the WDNC, the We Do Not Care Club — and asked if anyone wanted to join her.
After posting it to all of her social platforms, she learned that people did!
Now millions have watched Sanders’ videos that address perimenopause, menopause and life after menopause.
She described the community as “that sisterhood that we need.”
Her book, “The Official We Do Not Care Club Handbook,” is a New York Times bestseller, and Sanders has gone on a nine-city, sold-out tour.
“And I did everything scared,” she said.
How the club started
In an interview with Aging Untold’s aging well coach Katherine Ambrose and board-certified physician Dr. Rhea Rogers, Sanders said she had gone to Whole Foods for ashwagandha.
In the parking lot after that shopping trip, she looked in the mirror and thought of all the things she had to do, including laundry, cooking dinner and taking a book to the library.
“And then I just said, you know what? No, you don’t,” Sanders said. “I am at capacity. I’m tired. My body is tired.”
Sanders said she’d had a hysterectomy some months before and thinks her body went into shock.
“But at that moment, in that car, I was just tired,” Sanders said. “I had had it with myself. I had it with my family, with my friends. I just had it and I was over it.”
So she hit record to see if anyone wanted to join her.
In the 20 minutes between posting that video to all of her platforms and arriving home, Sanders was gaining hundreds of thousands of followers, she said.
Response from followers
Sanders said she was “a little confused” by the response. She has been a creator for years and has had viral content before, but, “this was just something different.”
Within a few weeks, millions of people were following Sanders.
She said she became scared and for a while and turned off her computer.
Then, she decided to read the comments.
“One of the main things that women were saying was, ‘me too, me too,’ and ‘thank you for speaking up, thank you for using your voice,’” Sanders said. “All of this is just with Melani just being Melani.”
That was enough in that moment, Sanders said, and over the past year she is “slowly coming to grips with I’m enough.”
Menopause and perimenopause experience
What has surprised Sanders most about the menopause or perimenopause experience is that nobody was talking about it, she said.
Sanders said she had a great surgeon for her hysterectomy but was not told anything about perimenopause or menopause. She had to figure it out on her own.
Community and announcements
A big part of the We Do Not Care Club is Sanders’ funny “special announcements.”
She said members send ideas for them in the comments.
“‘Everyone, we’re all putting the world on notice of what we ‘simply just do not care much about anymore,’” Sanders said.
Sanders said the support from the “We Do Not Care Club” gives her courage.
Part 2 of Melani Sanders’ interview with Aging Untold
Sanders opens up about sharing vulnerable moment
The digital creator is known for her humorous videos, but a more vulnerable moment she shared resonated with many people who follow her.
She opened up about what led to her pressing record.
“I was overwhelmed with emotion,” Sanders said.
Why she shared it
The post included the lines “Watching my mother get older. Watching my kids leave. Watching my body start to change on me. Nobody prepared me for this.”
Sanders said she has three sons: one in law school, one in undergrad and one at home. Her mother is aging and she has an elderly dog.
Her mind turned to thinking about having one son left at home and the empty nest that is coming, along with other changes.
“My body is changing. You know, I don’t know who I am from day to day. It just all hit me at one time, and I just said, you know what? Press record,” Sanders said.
The other side of Melani Sanders
While Sanders said she wants people to know her videos are funny and include “some real talk,” she also wants them to know that “there’s another side.”
“Many women are suffering, and we’re suffering silently,” she said.
“Sometimes I need to lean too”
Asked how that community has made a difference, Sanders said, “Sometimes I need to lean too. Every day is not a good day, and it’s OK.”
She said many people suppress themselves because of embarrassment.
And social media can make it seem like “everything is so perfect all the time.”
“You got to walk a certain way, talk a certain way, look a certain way,” Sanders said. “We simply should not care so much about those things and say how you feel.”

title: Dozens rally in Augusta, urge Sen. Angus King to back Van Hollen for Senate majority leader
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) -Dozens of people rallied near Sen. Angus King’s Augusta office Monday, calling on him to support Sen. Chris Van Hollen for Senate majority leader.
King’s position
King has said he supports current Democratic leader Chuck Schumer. King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, has credited Schumer with helping the party win a Senate majority in the midterm elections.
Rallygoers’ message
Rallygoers said Democrats’ election wins show voters want a change in direction.
Organizer Stacy Leafsong said Van Hollen would better reflect voters’ concerns. She also criticized the influence of lobbyists and campaign funding under Schumer’s leadership.
“It’s that tone deafness for the voice of the people, people didn’t vote for more of the same ... it’s time for new blood, new energy and new ideas in the Democratic Party,” Leafsong said.
Organizers planned to deliver a petition to King’s office.
A member of King’s team confirmed to us that a form was received.

title: Letter: The hard work has just begun for Bangor’s election winners
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
There’s something special about the morning after an election. The votes are counted, the speeches are over, and somewhere in Bangor, there’s still a yard sign leaning against somebody’s mailbox.
But here’s something I’ve learned over the years. Elections tell us who gets the job. They don’t tell us what someone will do with it.
In 2008, I had the privilege of working on Barack Obama’s presidential campaign. I’ve helped win elections and had the honor of serving the people of Bangor on their city council.
And one thing I’ve learned is that winning an election and making a difference aren’t quite the same thing. To Bangor’s newly elected councilors, congratulations. I’m rooting for you. When you succeed, Bangor succeeds.
To everyone who put their name on the ballot, thank you. It takes something to step forward, knock on doors, and ask your neighbors for their trust. That’s worth recognizing.
Serving on the city council taught me a thing or two. Leadership takes conviction, a little humility, and the good sense to know when to stand your ground and when to find common ground.
I’m proud to have served Bangor. And I still believe our best days are ahead of us. Because moving Bangor forward isn’t just about who wins on Tuesday. It’s about who keeps showing up on Wednesday.
Charlie Longo
Bangor

title: Holy Spuds! Maine Ranks Among America's Top Potato Producers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Holy Spuds! Maine Ranks Among America’s Top Potato Producers
Let's play a little word association, shall we? I'll say a word, and you tell me the first thing that comes to mind. Ready? Here we go.
"Maine."
Let me guess. You immediately thought of lobster, didn't you? Or perhaps seafood in general. And who could blame you? Sure, Maine is famous for its rocky coastline, towering forests, and spectacular natural beauty. But when it comes to what truly defines the Pine Tree State, nothing quite compares to our favorite crustacean.
However, there’s another product that deserves more attention on a grand scale. It’s one that fills the farmland in the north. It’s a versatile crop that is among the most popular in the world. Yes, I’m talking about the potato.
Maine continues to be one of the top potato-producing states in the country. Whether it's the popular russet, a special hybrid developed for the Frito-Lay company, or one of the many other varieties, Maine is proud to be one of the country's true leaders in the market.
How Many Potatoes Does Maine Produce Annually?
But just how big a potato producer is Maine? Well, according to World Population Review, Maine was the eighth-highest potato-producing state last year. Hey, that's not too bad at all.
World Population Review used data from the Department of Agriculture to determine its rankings. Maine produced 17.4 million cwt (hundredweight, a unit of weight equal to 100 pounds, commonly used to measure agricultural products) in 2025. That's a heck of a lot of spuds, folks. This total put Maine just behind Michigan (20.7 million) and ahead of Minnesota (16.7 million).
The majority of Maine's potato farms can be found up north in Aroostook County, where the climate is just right. According to Visit Aroostook, Maine was even the highest-producing potato state in the nation at one point. Of course, that was back in the 1940s, and times have changed just slightly.
Visit Aroostook also points out that the most popular uses for Maine's potato crop are french fry processing, potato chips (hello, Frito-Lay), seed potatoes, and home consumption. I'd say Maine potatoes are quite versatile.
What State is Number 1 in Potato Production?
Producing nearly 18 million cwt a year certainly seems like a ton of spuds. However, it's nothing compared to what Idaho, the country's top potato producer, is pumping out. The Gem State produced a whopping 138 million cwt last year. It was the only state in America to surpass the 100 million mark. I guess that's why they call it the Potato State.
READ MORE: This Portland Taco Joint Was Just Named the Best in Maine
But Maine is still holding its own when it comes to spuds, and it's great to see. So don't forget to keep supporting Maine's potato growers. The backbone of our agricultural community deserves it.

title: Family mourns 18-year-old killed in crash after driver running from police runs red light
text:
MILWAUKEE (WISN) - A Wisconsin family is mourning an 18-year-old high school senior who was killed when investigators say a driver running from police ran a red light and crashed into his car.
David Hunt, an 18-year-old senior at Milwaukee School of Languages, planned to study physical therapy at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, but his future was cut short Nov. 1.
David’s father, Paul Hunt, got a crash alert from his son’s phone that night and rushed to the scene.
“When that went off, I just knew something was not right,” Paul Hunt said. “I came across the crash scene, and I kind of knew what was up already. I mean, there was no mistaking what I saw.”
Prosecutors say 36-year-old Antwan White was speeding away from Milwaukee police after officers tried to pull him over for running a stop sign. He reached speeds of 90 mph before running a red light at an intersection and crashing into David Hunt’s car, according to a criminal complaint.
David Hunt was later pronounced dead.
“It’s been the hardest thing I’ve ever gone through, obviously. I’m hoping it’s the hardest thing I’ll ever have to go through,” said David’s older brother, Ian Hunt.
He described his brother as someone who could “make you laugh without saying a word.”
“He always lit up a room whenever he walked into it,” Ian Hunt said.
The family says they understand the need for police to apprehend people breaking the law, but they now question how much risk innocent bystanders, like David Hunt, should have to face.
“I don’t know where the line is for accepting the collateral damage versus justice for people breaking the law,” Paul Hunt said.
Even if change does come, David Hunt’s family knows it won’t bring him home.
“I wouldn’t say it’s worth the life of my brother,” Ian Hunt said. “Whatever comes out of it, we don’t get him back, and that’s the biggest thing.”
Investigators say White later told police he fled because he had drugs in his car. He faces charges including reckless homicide and is due back in court in December.

title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.
Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”
Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”
Video: How are President Trump's tariff policies affecting businesses?
“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”
The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.
Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”
Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.
The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.
Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.
Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.
