Sunny Monday and a warm stretch begins
While high temps are unseasonably warm, the mornings still will be chilly
Sunny Monday and a warm stretch begins
While high temps are unseasonably warm, the mornings still will be chilly
We are heading into an extended stretch of quiet weather, with dry conditions and warmer temperatures expected to dominate the forecast through the week. As an area of low pressure moves away today, high pressure will build in, setting the stage for a noticeable change in the weather pattern.
Temperatures will begin climbing Tuesday, with readings trending above average through the end of the week. Some communities could reach the low 60s Wednesday through Friday. Despite the warmer afternoons, clear and dry conditions will allow temperatures to drop off at night, resulting in a cool start to each day.
The bigger concern is the lack of rainfall. Long range models show little opportunity for meaningful precipitation over at least the next seven days. That means Maine's ongoing drought will continue to worsen as rainfall deficits grow. While the upcoming stretch of sunshine and mild afternoons will be welcome for outdoor plans, the persistent lack of moisture is becoming an increasing concern.

title: Tanya Jean Wilbur (1975-2026)
Johnny Depp film ‘Ebenezer’ gets actor first No. 1 opening in 8 years
text:
(AP) - Johnny Depp is back at the top of the box office with his first studio movie in eight years, and since fallout from a contentious libel trial against ex-wife Amber Heard left his future in Hollywood in jeopardy.
But six years after he was asked to leave the “Fantastic Beasts” franchise, and three years after Depp said that he had “no further need for Hollywood,” “Ebenezer,” a Paramount Pictures release, opened in first place with about $19 million in ticket sales, according to studio estimates on Sunday. Paramount released it in 3,535 theaters.
While it might be a far cry from the heights of the “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchise, which twice opened over $100 million, or even the $62 million opening of “Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald” in 2018, it is a solid start for the film, which cost a reported $38 million to produce. Internationally, it made $23 million from 63 markets, adding up to a $42 million global debut.
Outside of his franchise fare, Depp more often had openings in the $20 million range (as with “Black Mass” and “Public Enemies”).
The audience for “Ebenezer” was about 52% female and 81% over the age of 25, according to PostTrak exit polls. About 65% of ticket buyers said they would “definitely” recommend the film to friends. Less than half, or 47%, of the “kid” demographic (ages 12 and under) said they would tell their friends they “must see it right away.”
The Charles Dickens-inspired tale is rated PG-13 and directed by Ti West, who is best known for the horror franchise X. Critics were not as warm as audiences about the film. It’s currently sitting at 52% on Rotten Tomatoes. Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin and Daisy Ridley also star.
The question still remains as to whether this marks a major comeback for Depp, but time might tell. In exit polls, 51% of moviegoers cited Depp as their reason for attending the film. Depp’s next film, a revenge thriller called “Day Drinker,” is set for a March release from Lionsgate.
“The personal lives of stars generally don’t impact the box office. It really comes down to the movie,” said Paul Dergarabedian, the head of marketplace trends for Rentrak. “The key now will be its long-term playability.”
Sony’s “Ghost Soldier” and Amazon MGM Studios’ “How to Rob a Bank” also opened this weekend to less fanfare. “Ghost Soldier,” an action film starring Jim Caviezel, debuted in sixth place with $5.2 million from 2,558 theaters. “How to Rob a Bank” landed in seventh place with just under $5.2 million from 2,810 theaters. Internationally, it made $5.1 million. The film from “The Fall Guy” director David Leitch had a reported net production budget of $40 million. Starring Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz and Pete Davidson, “How to Rob a Bank” did not receive good reviews.
“The Cat in the Hat” landed in second place in its second weekend in theaters with $11.4 million, followed by “Godzilla Minus Zero” in third place with $8.3 million (down a whopping 73% from its opening). Fourth place went to “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” also in its second weekend, with $5.5 million. And the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” rounded out the top five with just under $5.5 million, bringing its domestic total to $89 million.
“The ‘You Can See Everything’ phenomenon continues,” Dergarabedian said. “It has become the ‘have you seen’ movie of the moment.”
“Wild Horse Nine” also added 1,075 theaters in its second weekend, where it earned $4.6 million. Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid” had one of the best limited expansions of the year with $756,060 on 27 screens. And James Gray’s acclaimed crime thriller “Paper Tiger” opened in six locations in New York and Los Angeles to $215,009 before it expands nationwide next week.
Overall it was a slower weekend than last with around $86 million in total ticket sales from North American theaters. Business should pick up next weekend, however, with the release of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”
Top 10 movies by domestic box office
With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak:
1. “Ebenezer,” $19 million.
2. “The Cat in the Hat,” $11.4 million.
3. “Godzilla Minus Zero,” $8.3 million.
4. “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” $5.5 million.
5. “You Can See Everything,” $5.5 million.
6. “Ghost Soldier,” $5.2 million.
7. “How to Rob a Bank,” $5.2 million.
8. “Wild Horse Nine,” $4.6 million.
9. “Wildwood,” $4.5 million.
10. “Clayface,” $3.7 million.

title: Capitol advice for Sen.-elect Troy Jackson
text:
Out in the woods, a lumberjack knows what needs to be done. It’s easy to see the results of one’s work.
The work on Capitol Hill isn’t so straightforward. Troy Jackson may soon find himself longing for a chainsaw and a fresh stand of timber.
Years ago, during the Reagan administration, I spent months working for a member of Congress as he successfully sought to move up the ladder to claim a U.S. Senate seat for the state of South Dakota.
Initially, my job was to answer letters from constituents, a hefty share of which consisted of crazy screeds, chock full of confusion. One awful week, I simply entered one address after another into a database from credit union members who sent in pre-written postcards pleading for my boss to support their position on a long-forgotten bill.
If I wasn’t the low man on the Capitol Hill organizational chart at the time, I feel sorry for whoever was.
Jackson, who muscled aside five-term Sen. Susan Collins on Election Day, doesn’t have to start at the bottom, fortunately. He begins with easy access to the senators-only elevators and the opportunity to slurp the famous bean soup in the Senate dining room.
He’ll have lots of people telling him what to do, of course, from which freshly vacated office to occupy to how to handle the sudden need to find a place to live in Washington. Maybe former Rep. Bruce Poliquin can fill Jackson in on how to install a pull-down bed like the one he had in his old congressional digs.
Jackson’s going to have to make many decisions in a short time about things he knows next to nothing about. Before this month, I’m pretty sure I spent more time on Capitol Hill than he ever did — and even figuring out how to get from one place to another inside the buildings takes awhile.
The most important thing Maine’s newly elected senator has to determine is who to hire. If he gets people around him with whom he feels comfortable and who know what’s going on, Jackson will do just fine.
I hope Jackson takes the time to learn from Maine’s other senator, Angus King, and from Sen. Collins. Collins is no doubt feeling hurt and potentially angry about losing her seat, but I am sure she will put Maine first in providing Jackson good advice on both practical and political matters. Jackson just needs to be sure to ask her for that help.
It also wouldn’t hurt for him to reach out to many other Mainers who have extensive experience on Capitol Hill, from former lawmakers to longtime staffers. Jackson doesn’t need to do what they say, but he should hear them out before he makes any consequential decisions.
One thing that Sen. King has done, which I think is cool and worth copying in some way, is that he hosts what he calls his “Capitol Coffee” for an hour on Wednesday mornings when the Senate is in session. It offers Mainers a chance to talk to their senator in his office (and sample “coffee from various Maine roasters” as well as blueberry bread with Maine blueberries).
My own time handling constituent concerns resulted in only one pointer to offer Jackson: When lobbyists are handing out free samples on National Ice Cream Day, don’t hesitate.

title: Melani Sanders shares why she started the We Do Not Care Club, opens up about vulnerable video
text:
(Aging Untold) — Melani Sanders, creator of the We Do Not Care Club, met with Aging Untold for a two-part interview. She shared why she started the popular club.
She also shared what led her to open up and post a vulnerable video that has resonated with many, many people.
Sanders is a social media sensation now, but there was a time when the creator of the popular “We Do Not Care Club” wasn’t one to be in front of the camera.
That changed one day when she decided that she had reached capacity. She was already tired and still had so much to do. Instead, she recorded a video from her car in the parking lot of her local Whole Foods.
In it, she announced a new club — the WDNC, the We Do Not Care Club — and asked if anyone wanted to join her.
After posting it to all of her social platforms, she learned that people did!
Now millions have watched Sanders’ videos that address perimenopause, menopause and life after menopause.
She described the community as “that sisterhood that we need.”
Her book, “The Official We Do Not Care Club Handbook,” is a New York Times bestseller, and Sanders has gone on a nine-city, sold-out tour.
“And I did everything scared,” she said.
How the club started
In an interview with Aging Untold’s aging well coach Katherine Ambrose and board-certified physician Dr. Rhea Rogers, Sanders said she had gone to Whole Foods for ashwagandha.
In the parking lot after that shopping trip, she looked in the mirror and thought of all the things she had to do, including laundry, cooking dinner and taking a book to the library.
“And then I just said, you know what? No, you don’t,” Sanders said. “I am at capacity. I’m tired. My body is tired.”
Sanders said she’d had a hysterectomy some months before and thinks her body went into shock.
“But at that moment, in that car, I was just tired,” Sanders said. “I had had it with myself. I had it with my family, with my friends. I just had it and I was over it.”
So she hit record to see if anyone wanted to join her.
In the 20 minutes between posting that video to all of her platforms and arriving home, Sanders was gaining hundreds of thousands of followers, she said.
Response from followers
Sanders said she was “a little confused” by the response. She has been a creator for years and has had viral content before, but, “this was just something different.”
Within a few weeks, millions of people were following Sanders.
She said she became scared and for a while and turned off her computer.
Then, she decided to read the comments.
“One of the main things that women were saying was, ‘me too, me too,’ and ‘thank you for speaking up, thank you for using your voice,’” Sanders said. “All of this is just with Melani just being Melani.”
That was enough in that moment, Sanders said, and over the past year she is “slowly coming to grips with I’m enough.”
Menopause and perimenopause experience
What has surprised Sanders most about the menopause or perimenopause experience is that nobody was talking about it, she said.
Sanders said she had a great surgeon for her hysterectomy but was not told anything about perimenopause or menopause. She had to figure it out on her own.
Community and announcements
A big part of the We Do Not Care Club is Sanders’ funny “special announcements.”
She said members send ideas for them in the comments.
“‘Everyone, we’re all putting the world on notice of what we ‘simply just do not care much about anymore,’” Sanders said.
Sanders said the support from the “We Do Not Care Club” gives her courage.
Part 2 of Melani Sanders’ interview with Aging Untold
Sanders opens up about sharing vulnerable moment
The digital creator is known for her humorous videos, but a more vulnerable moment she shared resonated with many people who follow her.
She opened up about what led to her pressing record.
“I was overwhelmed with emotion,” Sanders said.
Why she shared it
The post included the lines “Watching my mother get older. Watching my kids leave. Watching my body start to change on me. Nobody prepared me for this.”
Sanders said she has three sons: one in law school, one in undergrad and one at home. Her mother is aging and she has an elderly dog.
Her mind turned to thinking about having one son left at home and the empty nest that is coming, along with other changes.
“My body is changing. You know, I don’t know who I am from day to day. It just all hit me at one time, and I just said, you know what? Press record,” Sanders said.
The other side of Melani Sanders
While Sanders said she wants people to know her videos are funny and include “some real talk,” she also wants them to know that “there’s another side.”
“Many women are suffering, and we’re suffering silently,” she said.
“Sometimes I need to lean too”
Asked how that community has made a difference, Sanders said, “Sometimes I need to lean too. Every day is not a good day, and it’s OK.”
She said many people suppress themselves because of embarrassment.
And social media can make it seem like “everything is so perfect all the time.”
“You got to walk a certain way, talk a certain way, look a certain way,” Sanders said. “We simply should not care so much about those things and say how you feel.”

title: Robert Pattinson is the next James Bond, succeeding Daniel Craig
text:
(AP) - Pattinson. Robert Pattinson.
After years of debate and endless conjecture, Pattinson was unveiled as the next James Bond on Monday, becoming the seventh actor to play the iconic British spy and the first since Amazon MGM took over the beloved film franchise.
The naming of Pattinson comes during the longest hiatus in 007 history and ends years of rampant speculation about who would inherit the role from Daniel Craig. It comes five years after 2021’s “No Time to Die,” the first film in Bond’s 64-year history on the silver screen to conclude with the character’s death. But 007 will be reborn, yet again, in the 26th Bond film, directed by Denis Villeneuve.
Amazon MGM Studios announced Pattinson’s casting on social media with a brief snippet of the actor emerging from the shadows with a gun.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”
Late to the Bond chase
Pattinson only entered the Bond rumor mill recently after the revelation that he screen-tested for the role. Others reportedly in the mix included Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult.
But they were only the finalists in a Bond search that dated back to before Craig’s final 007 film.
While producers were long expected to go with a young, less-proven star, they instead opted for one of the best-known actors of his generation. Pattinson, 40, is also relatively old to begin as 007. The actor is currently in production on another iconic role in “The Batman Part II.”
Pattinson comes in already associated with several mega-franchises in “The Batman,” “Dune,” “Twilight” and “Harry Potter.” But since his breakthrough in “Twilight,” Pattinson has worked largely in more independent, auteur-driven films such as “Good Time” with the Safdie brothers, Robert Eggers’ “The Lighthouse” and Bong Joon Ho’s “Mickey 17.”
Earlier this year, he drew rave reviews for his villainous performance in Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” and for his portrayal of “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen in the film “Primetime.” He co-stars in Villeneuve’s upcoming “Dune: Part III” as a shape-shifting assassin.
Villeneuve said it was a tough choice, but the right one.
“We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin,” the director said in a statement.
Amazon bets big on Pattinson
The casting comes at a pivotal juncture for the franchise. In 2022, Bond’s longtime studio, MGM, was bought by Amazon for $8.5 billion. After haggling over next steps for 007, producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson relinquished creative control of Bond in 2025. The still-untitled Bond 26 is the first Bond movie since 1962’s inaugural “Dr. No” in which a Broccoli didn’t handpick the super spy.
“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond as we proudly introduce Robert Pattinson as the next 007,” said Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios.
Casting a new Bond fell instead to producers Amy Pascal — the former Sony Pictures chief and “Spider-Man” producer — and David Heyman, shepherd of “Harry Potter” and “Paddington.” Casting director Nina Gold oversaw the screen tests.
Pattinson’s first 007 film, untitled but widely referred to as “Bond 26,” was penned by Steven Knight (“Peaky Blinders,” “Locke”). No production start date has been announced, though shooting is expected to begin next year.
According to a report by Puck, Pattinson is signed to a three-movie deal as Bond. Spokespeople for Amazon MGM declined to comment on the terms of Pattinson’s contract.
A long hiatus nears an end
Before Craig even left the role, rumors and odds-making persisted nearly round-the-clock on who would follow in the footsteps of Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig. Idris Elba, for one, has spent half his career deflecting 007 conjecture.
The Bond machine has historically never slowed down. But the 26th installment will follow the longest absence ever for Bond. Given that “No Time to Die” completed principal photography in 2019 (its release was delayed due to the coronavirus pandemic), the lull is even longer.
Some fans are skeptical about the new Amazon-controlled chapter for Bond. Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, has vowed to uphold the franchise’s legacy and usher in “the next phase in the legendary 007 for audiences around the world.”
At stake is one of the most lucrative film series in Hollywood, based on Ian Fleming’s series of novels. The Bond movies have grossed more than $7 billion worldwide in ticket sales. “No Time to Die” collected $774 million in 2021. The movies also spin out endless other revenue streams, from streaming deals and video games to Aston Martins.
Although some Bond actors came to view the role as a yoke around their necks, it turned Craig into a household name. The British actor wasn’t widely known before his casting and, at the time, was derided as the first “blond Bond.”
But while Craig often struggled with the restrictions of the role, he also helped elevate the productions while remaining active outside of Bond enough to avoid becoming totally tethered to it.

title: Fort Fairfield fire ruled an accident
text:
FORT FAIRFIELD, Maine (WABI) - A fire in Fort Fairfield Friday morning has been ruled accidental by the Fire Marshal’s Office.
Investigators say they determined the fire was caused by an overheated electrical circuit in the ceiling of the second-floor apartment.
When firefighters got to Brown Street, they say found fire in the second-floor apartment.
Officials say the fire caused significant damage to that apartment, while a first-floor apartment sustained water damage.
No one was hurt, but two adults were displaced.
The American Red Cross is helping those affected.

title: Live chickens hurled at convenience store clerk in Massachusetts, police say
text:
Live chickens hurled at convenience store clerk in Massachusetts, police say
Police are investigating after live chickens were thrown at a convenience store clerk in Hadley, Massachusetts, on Monday.
Police were called just before 2 a.m. to a Cumberland Farms convenience store after the clerk reported having several live chickens thrown at him.
In surveillance video of the incident, one person carried the chickens into the store in a tote before hurling them at the clerk, police said. Another person appeared to record the prank.
"I walk in to these two cops chasing down these chickens. One finally got the last one. They got them in these crate boxes," customer Nick Lambert said. "I've never seen anything like it."
Police said the chickens are unharmed and are being cared for at an animal rescue.
"At this time, we suspect the chickens were taken from somewhere local and are trying to identify the owners of the chickens so they can be returned home," police said.
The suspects could face animal cruelty charges and additional charges if the birds were stolen.

title: Maine fans travel to watch Newport’s Cooper Flagg face Boston Celtics at TD Garden
text:
BOSTON, Mass. (WABI) - Maine basketball fans flocked to TD Garden to see Cooper Flagg and the Dallas Mavericks take on the Celtics on Sunday night.
“We’ve been planning this for the past couple months. We’ve got 56 people down here on the bus today to support Maine. A lot of people wanted to sign up in the first 24 hours. We sold out of all the tickets we had,” said Joshua Matts, Flagg Trading Co. bus trip event organizer.
“It’s good, always being back in New England. It’s always a really warm welcome and a ton of support, so it’s always a pleasure to be able to play in the New England region and see all the love and support,” said Flagg.
They spoke about what it means for Flagg to remember his Maine roots.
“I think it’s good. You’ve got to stick with your roots, stick where you came from, stick with family too,” said Kaden Genthner, Friendship native.
“It makes me want to play basketball so much more. It’s amazing how he’s only 19,” said Owen Libby, Skowhegan native.
“It’s been unbelievable to watch all the way up through. He’s what got me back into sports. Watching him play up in high school and all the way up through has been crazy. He sets a great example (with) the work ethic, all the time that he puts in, (and) all the work that he does. He’s not out there throwing a fit on the court. He’s out there putting in the work and doing what he’s supposed to do,” said Tyler Flagg, Cooper’s cousin.
The Mavericks suffered at 131-94 loss to the Celtics.
Boston led 42-9 after the first quarter, which set a team record for its biggest lead after the first 12 minutes.
“The level (the Celtics were) competing at is something that we need to look at, look in the mirror, decide if we’re competing at that same level, and if we want it as bad as they did. I don’t think we did from the start of the game,” said Flagg.
Next up, Flagg and the Mavericks host the Golden State Warriors on Wednesday at 8 p.m.
“You have to learn how to flip the page, learn from the bad, and stay positive through everything. We’ve got to go out and perform at a lot higher level,” said Flagg.
The Celtics host the Orlando Magic on Monday at 7 p.m.

title: Safety a treetop priority
text:
A Massachusetts outdoor writer, Joe Judd, who writes a monthly column for the Northwoods Sporting Journal, reported in November that a seasoned Bay State hunter, who is a friend, was seriously injured after falling from his tree stand. According to Judd, the hunter was stepping from his climbing ladder onto his stand platform when he slipped and fell backward to the ground. Sadly, the hunter sustained life-altering injuries and is paralyzed from the “breastbone down.” Judd says that there were two other similar tree stand accidents this hunting season in his state. They all involved serious injury.
The statistics are sobering. Without question, tree stands, which are a highly effective way to hunt deer and get your scent off the ground, pose a potential peril to all hunters, more so than firearms. From 2005 to 2007 in this country there were 41 deaths resulting from tree stand injuries. That same period there were 19,000 serious injuries to hunters using tree stands.

title: Aircraft reported down in town of Sweden, emergency crews responding
text:
SWEDEN — A Cessna airplane crashed Monday afternoon in the area of Smarts Hill Road and early reports were that the pilot was killed.
Witnesses reported the debris field was scattered across the area after the plane went down at about 3:45 p.m.
By 4:30 p.m., the road was closed as emergency crews responded to the scene. The first emergency crews who arrived at the scene said the pilot was dead.
One area woman wrote on Facebook that she had seen the plane catch the light and disappear, at an angle, behind trees as she was driving up Route 5 from Lovell.
“The plane was very reflective,” wrote Sarah Strange, of Lovell. “It appeared silver until it caught the pink sunset sky; it had round-tipped straight wings. It was moving diagonally down from east to west — we viewed it from almost due north so it was traveling left to right.”
Strange initially thought it to be a remote control plane. Then she heard from her brother-in-law that a plane had crashed behind his house.
The site of the plane crash is near the Sweden-Lovell town line.
The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed later Monday night that the plane was a Cessna 182 and that only the pilot had been on board.
The Cessna 182 is described as a four-seat, single-engine light utility airplane.
Emergency crews at the scene reported the craft as heavily damaged. They remained at the scene early Monday night and the FAA and National Transportation Safety Board had been advised.
The area around the crash site is expected to be closed through Monday night as the NTSB begins its investigation.
Officials from that agency said later Monday night that two investigators are expected to arrive at the accident site Tuesday. After the wreckage is documented, an NTSB official said, it will be recovered and moved to a secure facility for further examination.
By Monday night, the name of the pilot was not available. It was not known where the plane was coming from or where it was being flown.
Sweden is a small town in western Oxford County and borders Lovell and Fryeburg.

Falmouth student published in American medical journal
text:
Falmouth 17-year-old published in American medical journal
Hanna Ajemian studied research about preeclampsia during pregnancy and how it relates to chronic hypertension later in a woman's life. The research was published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology.
Falmouth 17-year-old published in American medical journal
Hanna Ajemian studied research about preeclampsia during pregnancy and how it relates to chronic hypertension later in a woman's life. The research was published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology.
At just 17 years old, a Falmouth High School student has been published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology.
"I've always been interested in science from a very young age. I wanted to actually be an ornithologist. I wanted to study birds. And I just really, really loved science. And I thought the world and how it worked was so interesting," Hanna Ajemian said.
She knew she wanted to work in science, but it wasn't until she was a little bit older when her family experienced a cancer diagnosis did she know she wanted to study medicine. Now, she has a specific interest within medicine.
"One of the biggest gaps in health care right now is in women's health. And as a young woman, I felt really called to that," she said.
Ajemian is a senior at Falmouth High School and she has already done two women's health internships. One at a women's tech startup in Ethiopia and another at the University of Pennsylvania.
That's where she did research that has now been published in the American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology where she went back and looked at data that was already published by experts at the University of Pennsylvania.
"[It] pretty much determined to establish a baseline that preeclampsia, which is high blood pressure during pregnancy, is a risk factor for the development of chronic hypertension. Later in a woman's life," Ajemian explained.
She found that with each pregnancy a woman's risk for chronic hypertension later on increased by 35%.
She also found that the severity of the hypertension was not as important a factor as many people once thought.
She said she's proud of the fact that 80% of the women whose data she studied were women of color, a group that is not often studied.
Ajemian said women's health research is something she plans to do long term.
"This is something that I'm really interested in," she said. "We need people to go into it in the future, and if we don't, that's not good for me and the people that I love. And I want to be someone that can help the people that I love in the future."
Ajemian wants to be an OBG-YN while continuing to do research when she's older.

title: Bipartisan bill aims to give 12 more weeks of unpaid leave to parents with NICU babies
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bipartisan bill aims to give 12 more weeks of unpaid leave to parents with NICU babies
U.S. parents with newborns in intensive care would be entitled up to 12 more weeks of unpaid leave under a new bill unveiled Monday by a bipartisan group of lawmakers, who described an agonizing gap faced by many families.
Related video above: 'SkinCubator' helps parents hold their NICU babies safely
The bill, introduced by Rep. Brittany Pettersen, a Colorado Democrat, aims to address a long-overlooked plight facing many parents with newborns in neonatal intensive care, who often exhaust much of their parental leave before their baby comes home from the hospital. Many mothers and fathers end up working through their newborns' NICU stays to save their time off.
The proposed legislation would amend the 1993 Family and Medical Leave Act to offer up to 12 weeks of dedicated NICU leave to eligible workers, on top of 12 weeks of parental leave already available.
The campaign for NICU leave has gained momentum since Colorado and Illinois became the first states to implement such policies earlier this year. On Tuesday, Walmart will begin offering a maximum of 12 extra weeks of NICU leave to its full-time employees, joining a handful of other companies with similar policies, including Morgan Stanley, Pinterest and organic baby formula company Bobbie.
The U.S. has no federal law mandating paid family leave, but FMLA entitles eligible parents — those who have worked at least 12 months for a private employer with 50 or more employees — to job-protected unpaid leave to care for a newborn.
While Republicans have generally opposed a federal mandate for paid leave, Pettersen said she is optimistic that the amendment to the FMLA will garner bipartisan support.
“This isn't about party, it's about life experiences,” Pettersen said in an interview with The Associated Press. “Where we want to go is paid family and medical leave, and we will continue to fight for it. This is a step forward building off the current policy that has bipartisan support."
Her co-sponsors were Republicans, Rep. Mike Lawler of New York and Rep. Ryan Mackenzie of Pennsylvania, and a Democrat, Rep. Morgan McGarvey of Kentucky. Mackenzie and McGarvey have both advocated for other policies benefiting NICU babies and shared their own stories as fathers with newborns in intensive care.
“For parents with a newborn in the NICU, the last thing they should have to worry about is whether they’ll have enough time off work to be there for their child," Mackenzie said in a statement.
Lawler added in a statement that “every working parent deserves the chance to be there for their child, especially when that child is facing a serious medical challenge."
The bill, known as the "Stand By NICU Babies and Families Act," could face a long road. It must be reintroduced after the new Congress is seated in January, and Pettersen will have to search for new Republican sponsors. Lawler and Mackenzie both lost their reelection bids in the midterm elections that gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress.
Pettersen said she introduced the bill pro forma to put a stake in the ground as her newly empowered party readies its priorities for the next Congress.
The NICU leave bills passed in Colorado and Illinois illustrate the partisan divide over paid leave mandates. Colorado’s paid leave passed mostly along party lines, while a shorter, unpaid leave adopted in Illinois had overwhelming bipartisan support.
In both states, however, the policies were championed by legislators with their own experiences as NICU parents.
“This issue of leave for NICU parents seems to be something that people intuitively get, including people on the right and left and people in between,” said Inimai Chettiar, president of A Better Balance, a nonprofit that is advocating for state and federal NICU leave policies.
Nearly one out of 10 babies born in the U.S. is admitted to a NICU, according to the most recent figures from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Advocates say parental presence in the NICU is important because skin-to-skin contact helps improve health outcomes, while time off is critical for mothers of premature babies who are at higher risk of postpartum depression.
A Better Balance said most parents wouldn't need the full 12 weeks of extra leave since the majority of NICU stays are much shorter, but the longer cap will help families facing more critical health situations.
McGarvey, the Kentucky congressman, said his now teenage twins spent 99 days in intensive care after they were born 14 weeks early.
“When your baby’s in the NICU, all you can focus on is getting them home,” McGarvey said in a statement.

title: InvestigateTV+: The support for caregivers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Tens of millions of Americans are caring for sick or aging loved ones and most of it is unpaid. InvestigateTV+ takes an in-depth look at how some hospitals are stepping up to support them and inspires a conversation about the people behind the patient.
Then, centuries-old giants thrive in southern swamps, and we explore how communities are fighting to protect them and the natural defense they provide.
Plus, a surrendered pup gets a front row seat to adventure that’s bringing joy to people across the country.
Caregiver support
A growing number of hospitals are offering programs designed to support family caregivers. Experts say that support can improve outcomes and reduce costly trips to the hospital.
Saving cypress forests
Each year, volunteers working with conservation groups plant thousands of young cypress trees.
To be successful, those plantings must include a nutria guard, a piece of often recycled plastic to protect young seedlings from being gobbled up by the invasive rodents.
The conservancy has planted thousands of trees over the years, including in the Madisonville area along the Tchefuncte River and in the LaBranche Wetlands in St. Charles Parish.
‘Buy now, pay later’
For big ticket purchases, people would often use a “buy now, pay later” method to help break up the cost.
But as budgets tighten, more people are turning to buy now, pay later options to cover basic expenses, including groceries.
Her motorcycle & her dog
Paige Parlato kicks her motorcycle alive, and her Doberman mix, Han, is ready to ride.
“He’s very laidback, he really likes to be where I’m at, but he really can have some energy if he wants to,” Parlato said.
Parlato and Han cruise weekly through her town, turning heads everywhere they go.

title: 'Batman' and 'Odyssey' star cast to be seventh James Bond
text:

Robert Pattinson to become the next James Bond
Meet the new 007.
Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond, ending months of speculation about which young actor Amazon MGM would hand the keys to the Aston Martin.
In a statement shared by Variety, the "The Batman" and "The Odyssey" actor said he is honored to play the role, saying, "To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."
He continued, saying, "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime." 
According to E! News, several men have vied for the role, with Daniel Craig last pouring himself a glass of Macallan in 2021's "No Time to Die."
"No Time to Die" was also the last film in the series released before longtime producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli sold creative control of the franchise to Amazon MGM for $20 million.
Pattinson, 40, is almost unquestionably 2026's most in-demand movie star and has the box office record to show for it, Variety said. His recent role with Zendaya in "The Drama" acquired $134 million worldwide from a budget of $28 million.

title: Portland City Council advances plan for overhauling Franklin Street
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — The City Council on Monday formally endorsed a plan for redesigning heavily traveled Franklin Street that was at least two decades in the making. It will be at least another few years before any shovels are in the ground.
Despite concern for the loss of the mature oak trees that line the grassy median of the road between Marginal Way and Commercial Street, there was overwhelming support for the redesign among officials and the public.
The final concept calls for significant reductions in road and lane widths, restoring connections to several neighborhood streets, adding separated bicycle lanes and improving pedestrian crossings, Kevin Kraft, the city’s planning director, said during a presentation to the council.
Kraft pointed to two recent pedestrian fatalities on the stretch, and said the plan would add raised crosswalks and intersections and create tighter turning aprons to slow cars. The crossing at Marginal Way, considered by advocates to be among the city’s most dangerous, would be reduced to 70 feet from 101 feet.
The redesign would also create roughly 3.5 acres of new land for future development, or up to about 720 new housing units, according to city staff.
City residents and groups like the Franklin Reclamation Authority and Urbanist Coalition of Portland have long pushed for a redesign of the roadway to revive a neighborhood that was lost during urban renewal in the mid-20th century.
Wendy Cherubini, who has long advocated for the change, said it’s the best design she’s seen out of the many iterations over the years. While “not perfect,” she said it strikes a balance between competing interests.
Another commenter, who said they were in their 30s when discussions began and is now in their 60s, called the plan “a tremendous achievement.”
“We didn’t get everything we wanted, but there’s a lot to like,” he said.
City staff held several public sessions with the public in order to glean feedback, which included a session at the Portland Public Library in September.
Kraft said Monday that the city saw roughly 560 comments on its webpage dedicated to the effort.
Among the most debated elements of the plan have been the addition of parking between Congress and Commercial streets, and the proposed orientation of the road, which would necessitate cutting down mature trees.
Avery Yale Kamila, co-founder of local environmental group Portland Protectors, said while she supports several facets of the plan, she takes issue with clear-cutting the oak trees and she urged councilors to vote it down or modify it. She said the Bayside neighborhood already has the smallest amount of tree canopy in Portland, and that new trees planted during the project will take 20 to 50 years to reach the same benefits as ones there now.
“We will spend millions to make our downtown hotter,” she said.
Kraft said the plan calls for 230 new street trees and that the city is committed to preserving existing canopy on the outside of the road.
Councilor Sarah Michniewicz requested that the city research whether certain trees on the median could be relocated. A city staff member said that “with enough money and resources” it’s possible to relocate trees.
The design would retain two travel lanes in each direction between Marginal Way and Congress Street but reduce to one lane in each direction between Congress and Commercial streets to add on-street parking.
While some argued against the inclusion of parking, Kraft said on-street parking is a known traffic calming measure, and staff have estimated the added metered parking could bring in $260,000 in revenue. He said parking also could be used for food trucks, bike corrals, or space for outdoor dining.
The plan would create separated bike lanes and wide sidewalks on a stretch that currently has neither.
Lily Sage, a teacher at Portland schools, said she recently brought a group of seventh graders on a field trip and had to cross Franklin Street. Unfortunately, she said, she had to give the students a serious talk regarding the unsafe traffic conditions there.
“You can sense it is not your space. It was made for cars,” she said.
The plan will now advance to design and engineering, with the initial design phase already funded through a $2 million federal grant, and $500,000 in local contributions split between the city and the Maine Department of Transportation.
Kraft has said ballpark estimates for eventual construction costs are in the $30 million to $40 million range, and that once the preliminary design phase is complete, the city will seek funding for implementation.
He said in between those stages, the city may explore demonstration or pilot projects to test certain elements.

title: Customers at major US banks report difficulty with some online services
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Online banking delays for major banks triggered by technical issue at JPMorgan Chase
Thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks Monday, after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
Video above: What may have caused the Microsoft outage?
However, Chase said Monday that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and that they were working to bring banking services back online.
“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system — it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for the bank.
In the same statement, Evangelisti said that this was a Chase-only issue.
“This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” he said.
Monday's technical issues seem to be centered at Chase customers and customers at other banks trying to transact with Chase. Those banks, including Bank of America and Citigroup, were not having issues with their banking services.
A U.S. Bank spokesperson told Hearst Television that "U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted" but that "clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays."
A spokesperson for Zelle said the issues some customers were facing were because of financial institutions, not the digital payment network itself.
"Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds," the spokesperson said via email to Hearst Television. "An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers."
Zelle is the peer-to-peer payment system that major U.S. banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed. Zelle is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.
The reports follow a major outage by Microsoft that began Thursday and lasted for hours which impacted services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. This was followed by an outage with the FAA, which grounded all U.S. flights for several hours this weekend.

title: Trump’s Asia trip: Deals in Manila & Shenzhen, nuclear summit with Xi & Putin, maybe Kim meeting
text:
Trump’s Asia trip: Deals in Manila & Shenzhen, nuclear summit with Xi & Putin, maybe Kim meeting
President Donald Trump was preparing to depart for Asia on Monday, turning his focus to economic deals and historic three-way nuclear talks with Russia and China as his administration adjusts to a new political reality in Washington. He said he may meet with Kim Jong Un while in China as the U.S. looks to reengage North Korea on its nuclear program.
Trump said he plans to talk about Russia’s war in Ukraine during the highly anticipated meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin in China.
“We’ll talk about, my favorite subject, Ukraine. Ukraine’s losing Ukraine,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday morning before departing for his visit to Asia. “Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers in the month. So we’ll be talking about that.”
Trump suggested he’ll talk with the leaders about the war even after Trump administration officials on Friday told reporters that Trump would discuss nuclear disarmament and the Iran war with his Chinese and Russian counterparts but steer clear of Russia’s war with Ukraine.
Trump’s departure comes after the often-omnipresent president had remained largely out of public sight for the past several days, even as a nationwide ground stop snarled air traffic and his Republican administration faced tough questions on its handling of the situation.
His trip to Asia, which begins in Manila then continues to the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, gives Trump the opportunity to change the narrative from his domestic woes, including the air travel problems and fallout from the November midterm election where his party lost both chambers of Congress.
The controversy over tech powerhouse and chipmaker Nvidia is also certain to hang over Trump’s visit to China, despite efforts by administration officials to downplay the president’s close ties to Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent.
Beijing has said it was not involved. Trump had no plans to raise the issue with Xi when the two leaders meet, said U.S. officials who briefed reporters anonymously about the president’s Asia trip under ground rules set by the White House.
Huang accompanied Trump on Air Force One during the president’s last trip to China in May, and he has been a sporadic presence around Trump at the White House while speaking to him frequently. Trump has argued that America needs to preserve its leadership on artificial intelligence, and warned of dire consequences if China wins that competition.
Scrutiny of the Trump administration’s actions as they relate to Nvidia has been growing, including on the Commerce Department’s delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to a company led by the alleged Chinese spy with whom Huang had the affair.
Asked about the matter in an interview that aired Sunday with Fox News Channel anchor Larry Kudlow, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he will “leave the internal workings of the Commerce Department to the Commerce Department.
“I think what’s more important here, Larry, is to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the U.S. export restrictions ... and at what level?” Bessent said.
He added: “I think we’re going to see answers.”
“Jensen Huang is an incredible innovator, but that does not abrogate their duties of compliance,” Bessent said.
Regarding North Korea, Trump met with Kim on three occasions during his first term but has not been able to get him to meaningfully engage since his return to the White House. Trump has sought to set the groundwork for further talks with Kim. In August, he ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea.
Among the travelers on the Asia trip with Trump will be Elon Musk, the head of SpaceX and Tesla, who is shaping up to be a top investigative target of the incoming Democratic majority in Congress.
In the Philippines, Trump will meet with Southeast Asian leaders who look to the United States for help countering Beijing’s aggression in the region. He plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand while in Manila, the White House said.
Then he heads to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit — and at the end of the trip, the first-ever three-way talks with China's Xi and Putin to discuss nuclear stockpiles.
Trump and U.S. officials have indicated that the meeting with Putin and Xi will focus on nuclear weapons and that topics of discussion would not include Russia's war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year. Still, the president has recently played up chances for a settlement to the conflict.
The three-way meeting will also put in the spotlight the ongoing U.S. war with Iran, a country which has often allied with China and Russia. The war has been widely blamed for the Republican Party’s steep losses in the midterms, and while Trump has tried to play down the chances he will order a resumption of major strikes against Iran, he also has said he does not see the need for talks.
China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Monday that the trilateral talks would be of “groundbreaking significance” and that China aimed to have in-depth exchanges about safeguarding world peace and promoting stability.
“Under the current circumstances, the three countries shoulder an important responsibility to work together in addressing global challenges,” she said in a regular briefing in Beijing.

title: Electrical fire burns Aroostook apartment building
text:
An electrical fire burned a Fort Fairfield apartment building Friday morning.
The fire broke out about 8:50 a.m. at the Brown Street two-unit apartment building, according to Maj. Aaron Turcotte, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
When they arrived, firefighters found flames in the second-floor apartment. Crews kept the fire from spreading throughout the building, Turcotte said Monday morning.
The fire caused significant damage to the second-floor apartment, while the first-floor unit, which was not occupied, sustained water damage.
Two people were displaced. No one was injured.
Investigators determined that an overheated electrical circuit in the second-floor ceiling sparked the blaze.

title: After the blue wave, what comes next?
text:
Shortly after the midterms, President Trump said he’d be willing to work with Democrats. The King of Chaos reversed himself a few days later. No surprise.
Then he appointed Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff. Talk about tone deaf.
Miller is the guy who has been having armed and masked ICE agents pick up people off the streets or in schools and shopping malls and deport them. The agents have focused like a laser on people of color as targets. Miller is so irrational on the matter of immigration that some of his own family members have spoken out against him.
Time out. How did a narcissistic conman so lacking in empathy and character get elected president in 2016 and then reelected in 2024? Perhaps we should have heeded the warnings of two sage political observers way back in 2016.
Remember when JD Vance referred to Trump as “America’s Hitler” and “opioid for the masses?” Or when South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham issued a stark warning. “If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed and we will deserve it.”
The challenges facing the Democrats in the next Congress remind me of the jokester who said, “I feel like a mosquito in a nudist camp. I know what to do, but I don’t know where to begin.”
Incidentally, GOP House members matched Trump’s complete tone deafness about the election results when they chose the bombastic flame thrower Jim Jordan to be the House minority leader.
He’s the guy who was in constant communication with Trump during the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection on the Capitol.
And he’s never brought up a single piece of legislation.
Stephen Miller and Jim Jordan notwithstanding, Congressional Democrats should work on the issues they campaigned on: affordability and accountability. In the process, they should strive for bipartisan cooperation, working on issues about which most Americans agree: end the Iran War; end the tariffs; raise the national minimum wage; restore the cuts that were made to Medicaid; end stock trading by members of Congress; work on immigration reform; ensure voting rights.
They should also strive to establish term limits for members of Congress. (Note: 79% of Democrats, 85% of independents and 85% of Republicans believe there should be term limits, according to a poll conducted in 2025 by McLaughlin & Associates for U.S. Term Limits.)
As important, they should make accountable the people in Trump’s administration who have ignored the Constitution and/or used Trump’s shameless power grabs for their personal gain.
Keep in mind that dealing with corruption was a high priority among American voters. And please don’t argue that they can’t work on both fronts — affordability and accountability. If all members of Congress can spend the bulk of their time gallivanting around the country and campaigning, they can surely take on both challenges.
A final word: The midterm election ended with an exclamation point when Mississippi voters elected its first Black senator since Reconstruction. That result confirmed that most Americans reject the racism and sexism so apparent among Trump and his cult. Trump supporters who claim “I’m for Trump’s policies but I’m not sexist or racist” might do some soul-searching.
In next week’s column I’ll give some thoughts on changing the system for electing a president. Most Americans would probably agree that the current system isn’t working.
David Treadwell, a Brunswick writer, welcomes commentary and suggestions for future “Just a Little Old” columns at [email protected].

title: 'Nothing short of miraculous': Owl survives after being hit by tractor-trailer
text:
'Nothing short of miraculous': Owl survives after being hit by tractor-trailer going 65 miles per hour
"We were stunned" — that's what one wildlife center said after an owl became stuck to the tractor-trailer that hit it in Pennsylvania.
The Raven Ridge Wildlife Center said an owl got stuck in a tractor-trailer's air dam after being struck by the large vehicle in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, Sunday evening.
"We couldn’t picture how that was possible until John (at Old Dominion Freight Line, Inc.) and the driver sent us photos after she returned to the trucking terminal. Seeing those photos, we were stunned that the owl had survived such an impact," the wildlife center said in a post on Facebook, showing the photos sent to them.
Related video: Watch Australia's red crabs migrate
The owl was freed by freight line staff but was unable to fly on its own, prompting them to call the wildlife center for further assistance.
"It was late, but our team waited, worried about the owl’s injuries," the center said. "When the owl arrived, its feathers were a mess, but there were no broken wings or legs, no open wounds—just damage to its left eye."
The following day, Raven Ridge Wildlife officials called the company for more details, saying the driver knew exactly when she had hit the owl but did not realize it had become stuck.
"The owl was stuck headfirst in the fiberglass air dam for 70 miles at 65 miles per hour. It’s truly the luckiest owl we’ve ever seen. We took it to our vet for a full eye exam. Even the vet was amazed there wasn’t more trauma, though there was blood and swelling in the left eye," the center continued in the post.
"This whole story is just astounding," the post continued.
The great horned owl is now being monitored. Officials said they plan to drive the owl back 70 miles to release it safely once it is cleared for release.

title: Portland orgs get $500K for student reading programs
text:
A coalition of Portland organizations will receive $500,000 to help elementary students improve their reading skills even when they’re not in the classroom.
A grant from the Nellie Mae Education Foundation, given to 30 coalitions across New England, will provide funding to improve out-of-school literacy programs by bringing together several local organizations — like the school district, library system and Boys & Girls Club — with the common goal of helping students get better at reading.
There are growing concerns about early literacy in Maine, stoked by a 2024 national assessment on which the state’s fourth graders performed among the worst in the country. The latest state test found 66% of students are at or exceed state expectations for reading, a small improvement over the prior year.
As the grant recipient, the Foundation for Portland Public Schools will be responsible for distributing the funding among partners, which also include United Way of Southern Maine and I’m Your Neighbor Books, a nonprofit that shares children’s literature about the immigrant experience.
Andrea Weisman Summers, the foundation’s director, said the group has not yet earmarked all of the money, which will be distributed over three years. But she said the grant will be used to increase literacy activities outside of school time and to coordinate the efforts of the different local organizations in teaching reading.
For example, the staff who lead read-alongs at the library or tutor students in reading after school at the Boys & Girls Club will all be able to get the same professional training, allowing them to better align their work with the district’s literacy programs.
Some of the money will go toward hiring new staff, including a full-time literacy teacher at the Boys & Girls Club and a literacy educator who will travel with the library’s Bookmobile. There are also plans to host increased family literacy events and to send the Bookmobile to underserved areas, like the public housing community Sagamore Village.
Weisman Summers said the grant will pay for the purchase of a “common book” — one text that will be provided to every student in Pre-K through second grade across Portland and that will serve as a jumping off point for discussions and group activities.
The book, which has not yet been selected, will also come with an audio version translated into the six most common non-English languages spoken in Portland, so that parents who aren’t fluent in English can play a role in their child’s literacy.
“The most exciting part is having a real project for these partners to work on together,” Weisman Summers said.
Portland fourth graders performed slightly better than the state average in reading on the latest assessment, with nearly 67% of students reading at or above expectations. The district has the second-largest multilingual population in the state, with more than a third of students coming from a home where a language other than English is spoken.
Details about which other New England sites received grant funding from the Nellie Mae Education Foundation were not available Monday.

title: Going secondhand shopping? Here are some tips from a veteran thrifter
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I think I inherited my passion for thrifting from my grandmother Nana Mary. She volunteered at a thrift shop in my hometown in Massachusetts and I often got Christmas gifts from there. Plus, I’m cheap and on a budget.
Most of all, I adore all things vintage. By the way – and I apologize if this makes you feel horribly old – vintage means it’s at least 25 years old. To be considered antique, it needs to be at least 100 years old.
Here are some tips from someone who’s been hitting thrift shops, church charity shops and flea markets for more than four decades, on how to maximize your search.
DRESS FOR SUCCESS
Secondhand shopping is not the time to wear complicated footwear with a multitude of buckles and laces. Opt for slip-on shoes or something easy to take on and off. The same goes for the rest of your outfit. Overalls and fancy dresses or suits are not the way to go. Avoid wearing anything that takes more than seven seconds to remove in a dressing room. If it’s not too cold out and you’ve scored an ace parking spot, I suggest leaving your coat in your car.
SIZE ONLY PARTIALLY MATTERS
If you’re the type to buy something off the rack and take a gamble on whether it fits, consider a few things: Be aware of the return policy. Some stores have a “no returns” policy and you don’t want to be stuck with something you love that doesn’t fit. Vintage clothing sizes run smaller than today’s more generous sizing. Try stuff on when a dressing room is available. If something is too small or too big, don’t buy it unless you’re confident it can be altered.
UPON CLOSE INSPECTION
Check any electronic items and go over all clothing closely for stains, rips or missing buttons. Should you discover a flaw in a clothing item, consider whether you can repair it, clean it or live with the flaw.
DO YOUR HOMEWORK
For some items, I will look at completed listings on eBay to check the price at which it sold. Asking price means absolutely nothing.
If you see the same or a similar item that has sold for $26 and the shop is asking $80, you may want to pass, but keep in mind other considerations. You don’t pay shipping if you buy in person and you’re supporting the local economy. You also don’t know what the seller paid for it and what cleaning and repairs they made. If you look up the price of something online while at the store, don’t be obnoxious and blatant about it, because some sellers get a bit prickly about this.
WHEN TO BARGAIN
For me, there’s a hierarchy to asking for a better price. At a yard sale, it’s pretty much expected. The same goes for both outdoor and indoor multi-dealer flea markets when the booths are individually manned by the sellers. But if you think the price is fair, consider just paying it.
At a church charity shop or a thrift shop, though, do not do this. In some cases, the person at the register doesn’t have the authority to offer a discount and several shops are part of a larger non-profit. The same rule applies at vintage/antique shops. There may be a rare occasion that you want something badly that’s a little bit out of your price range. I won’t tell you to never try asking for a better price. But if you do so, be considerate and polite, rather than abruptly offering a lesser price.

title: United Airlines forced to delay departing flights after 1.5-hour-long system outage
text:
United Airlines forced to delay departing flights after 1.5-hour-long system outage
A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights Monday, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop.
Related video above | How the Trump administration is trying to prevent future travel disruptions after ground stop?
Chicago-based United said in a statement that flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not affected. The airline also said there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”
United apologized on social media to customers for the inconvenience. It resolved the issue about one hour and 40 minutes after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers.
United did not immediately provide details about which of its systems were affected, but pilots told air traffic controllers that the problem was related to a system that helps them determine a plane's final weight.
Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft's weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying.
The information is also used to guide the autopilot system and the decisions pilots make, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.
“It is extremely important to have all of these numbers accurate and precise,” said Arroyo, who flew for United. “Pilots use that information to establish guidance and performance for their flights from takeoff to landing.”
Arroyo said he has seen problems with the weight and balance system before in his career, but the airline did the right thing by delaying flights to ensure safety.
Years ago, pilots used to do all those weight calculations manually with a pencil and paper and then radio in the numbers, but today it is all calculated electronically and then loaded into the plane’s computers.
In August 2025, United grounded planes at major U.S. airports, delaying more than 1,000 flights because of an hourslong outage of a system called Unimatic, which houses flight information that is fed to other systems including those that calculate weight and balance and track flight times.
United said in response to a message from The Associated Press that it had no further information to provide about whether the same system was affected by Monday’s outage.
A recording posted Monday on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.
The flight-tracking website FlightAware showed United with about 600 delayed flights Monday evening, though it was unclear how many were directly related to the system outage.
The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days.
Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem.
On Friday, the FAA ordered every flight grounded because a newly installed router malfunctioned, overwhelming the aging air traffic control system.
And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored.

title: York Ambulance may need more money, despite $350K approved by voters
text:
An independent EMS service says it might need more money from York even after voters approved a $350,000 ballot question designed to fill a deep funding gap.
York Ambulance Association officials told the Select Board at a meeting Nov. 9 — less than a week after 85% of voters approved a $350,000 allocation — that it needs at least $130,000 more to keep operating. Without it, the company could run out of money by the end of the year, said Matt McTighe, the newly hired treasurer for York Ambulance.
The new projection comes after months of negotiations between town and EMS officials over transparency and budget concerns. The town was already set to provide $150,000 to the service for the last year of the contract but was met in July with a request for $180,000 more.
By August, the request had grown to $350,000, with ambulance officials citing rising insurance and service costs. The total $500,000 bailout was supposed to be enough to sustain the service through the final months of a three-year contract with the town ending in June 2027.
Ambulance service officials provided Select Board members with a cash-flow chart at the beginning of the Nov. 9 meeting, including estimates on the monthly installments from the town. Member Robert Palmer noted that the eight-month total was $480,000.
“So, that’s a problem,” Palmer said. “The voters thought it was going to be $350,000, and that’s not gonna be enough.”
McTighe said the EMS board is pursuing other revenue streams like private fundraising and charging for services that are normally free under its existing policy, including charging for routine lift assistance or responding to car crashes.
The EMS board is already working to finalize that policy change, McTighe said, which could take effect at the beginning of next year. The amendment would bring in another $10,000 to $15,000 in monthly revenue, depending on call volume.
“I guess the concern I have is throwing good money after bad,” Palmer told McTighe and Chief of Operations Josh Allen. “It’s just changed so dramatically.”
The town has been exploring the future of its EMS service amid the funding discussions, which may include contracting with another company or transitioning to an in-house operation. Palmer said he’s unwilling to commit another $130,000 to York Ambulance, and would rather direct that money to another solution.
In September, town officials created a handful of conditions for funding the ambulance service, such as creating a treasurer position and a plan for resolving a Small Business Association loan that’s in default. McTighe told the board on Nov. 9 that EMS officials are working out the details of the SBA plan, but it hasn’t been finalized. The service expects Medicare payments it applies to the loan — which are being withheld by the federal government — to resume by the end of December.
The Select Board voted unanimously to distribute $80,335 for the first of four biweekly installments until Dec. 23. Officials are set to discuss the issue further, including a possible revaluation of payments, in December.
