title: Base closure commission offers model for addressing our national debt
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
William A. Lee III is an attorney, former chair of the Maine Ethics Commission and retired adjunct professor in government and administrative science at Colby College.
When the national debt crossed $40 trillion this summer, it hit the news cycles with politicians and pundits decrying the massive debt and demanding action. Then, as usual, nothing was done and people moved on to the next crisis.
We will have a new Congress in January with the Democrats in control. They will likely pass ethics reform governing appointed and elected government officials, including the president, to prevent corruption. Perhaps enough Republicans will join to override the expected presidential veto. This does not come with a financial cost.
Congress will also likely pass legislation reversing the cuts to Medicaid and SNAP benefits and the termination of health insurance subsidies through the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare). If these actions are not vetoed by President Donald Trump, they will add large sums to the national debt. There are also some calling for Medicare for All. While it may be a laudable goal, it could annually add trillions to the national debt.
With the exception of the national debt being paid off in 1835 under Andrew Jackson, we have always operated with national debt. At the end of the Revolutionary War, it was $75 million. At the beginning of Ronald Regan’s presidency, the national debt was just under $1 trillion. During his terms, there were major income tax cuts without corresponding spending cuts. By the end of his presidency, the national debt had tripled to almost $3 trillion.
Both parties are to blame for our ballooning national debt. There were huge increases during the Joe Biden term and Trump’s first term. The national debt is expected to increase by another $2 trillion during 2026.
This year, we will spend $1.2 trillion in interest on the national debt, which is almost $300 billion more than the entire defense budget. This is money for which we receive no services in return.
We finance the debt through the massive sale of bonds, treasury bills and securities. The interest rate on them is rising to make them attractive to investors. These rising interest rates in turn produce increasing borrowing costs for the consumer and higher mortgage interest rates.
If investors lose faith in the government’s ability to pay its debt, it could trigger a financial panic with disastrous economic results. As the national debt increases, this risk increases.
Congress does not appear able to address this financial crisis. In the highly partisan Congress, we seemingly have some members who could not agree on the time of day if they were looking at the same clock. They are hardly going to be able to agree on the necessary modifications to the tax code to increase revenues and spending reductions to restore fiscal sanity.
Congress has been faced with the need to solve a problem before but without the ability to act. In the 1980s, the Department of Defense needed to close some military installations and reorganize others to become more efficient and save money. Members of Congress were unable to agree on what actions to take due to the political fall-out from closing or reducing military installations in their home states.
To be able to take the necessary action, Congress created the Base Realignment and Closure Commission (BRAC). It was a bipartisan commission with independent experts to advise it. When the commission delivered its recommendations, Congress was given 45 days to either accept them or reject them, with no modifications. If Congress did nothing, the recommendations were deemed adopted by Congress. This gave members of Congress political cover if a military base was closed in their state. In the five recommendations from BRAC between 1988 and 2005, they all became effective by the inaction of Congress.
Sen. Angus King is a cosponsor of the Fiscal Commission Act (FCA), which would produce recommendations to modify the tax code to increase revenues and reduce expenditures to produce a manageable national debt. The structure of the FCA is similar to BRAC. It has several cosponsors but is yet to be fully considered by Congress.
With a new Congress starting in January, now is a good time to ask your representatives to have the FCA adopted by Congress. The national debt is a ticking time bomb, and our long-term fiscal health depends on disarming it.

title: Cyber-attack halts city business in South Portland
text:
South Portland residents react to cyberattack that impacted Maine city's operations
A suspected cyberattack shut down city operations in South Portland on Monday.
City Hall and other South Portland offices were closed as officials scrambled to securely get the computer systems up and running again.
A city spokesperson said, "It's all hands on deck."
Officials blamed the suspected IT outage on "bad actors." There is no word on the identity of the bad actors.
One after another, residents came to City Hall and found the front and back doors locked with a note explaining the network disruption.
"Cyberattacks? Well, it's not good. It's not good. It's going to continue, I'm sure," said Janet Kane, a South Portland resident.
The South Portland Library and the Assessor's Office were also closed Monday.
City staff have called in state and federal agencies to assess the situation and try and figure out who is behind the incident.
"There are a lot of people who have the ability to ruin the day for millions of people without doing an awful lot," said South Portland resident Glenn Perry.
The phone system was down, so people who tried to call City Hall could not get through.
Residents were being told credit card payments at some city facilities may not work.
Officials said the duration of this outage is not known at this time.
"DHS, Homeland Security and the FBI are very well aware of it and they're going to be staying on top of it all," said Bruce Hirdler, a South Portland resident.
South Portland's network disruption comes just days after last week's Microsoft outage and a nationwide ground stop of all airlines, the latter of which officials said was triggered by a technical network overload.
Some South Portland residents said they are losing faith in these systems that are supposed to be "secure."
"That's just what it is, craziness, and we don't know the real reason for it. I mean, who knows? We're being told something, but we don't know," said South Portland resident Donna Snow.
City tax bills were due Nov. 16, but because of the outage, the property tax payment due date has been pushed to next Monday, Nov. 23.

title: Fort Kent Girls Make It Four Straight in Northern Maine
text:
The Fall Five and Five No. 5: Fort Kent Girls Make It Four Straight
Winning once is hard.
Doing it again is harder.
Getting back to the same championship game four years in a row starts to say something about a program.
That’s where we begin the season-ending Five and Five countdown.
At No. 5, the Fort Kent girls soccer team once again found itself exactly where it has spent a lot of November lately: playing for Northern Maine and then playing for a Gold Ball.
Another Fall Near the Top
Fort Kent came into the season with plenty of expectations, and the Lady Warriors never really went away.
They worked their way through the regular season and entered the Class C North championship at 14-1-2, setting up another meeting with Orono.
By that point, Fort Kent had already beaten the Red Riots twice during the regular season.
Doing it a third time, with a Northern Maine championship on the line, was another matter.
The Lady Warriors didn't leave much doubt.
Senior Reese Doucette opened the scoring on a penalty kick in the first half. Freshman Hayden Plourde doubled the lead about 12 minutes later, and Doucette added another before halftime.
Fort Kent's defense took care of the rest.
The Warriors shut out Orono 3-0 and walked away with another Class C North championship.
Four Years, Four Northern Maine Championships
That's the number that really stands out.
Four.
Four consecutive regional championships.
Four consecutive trips to the Class C state championship game.
And five state-final appearances over the last seven seasons.
High school sports aren't supposed to make that kind of consistency easy.
Players graduate. Roles change. Younger athletes are asked to step into bigger spots. Every new season brings another group of teams trying to knock you off.
Fort Kent has continued to find a way through all of it.
This year's group had experienced seniors like Doucette and Avery Werntgen, younger players such as Plourde and Laney Caron stepping into important roles, and another defense that proved difficult to break down when the games mattered most.
The names might change from one season to the next.
The results haven't changed very much.
One More Trip to the State Final
The regional championship earned Fort Kent another matchup with Maranacook, the same program that defeated the Warriors in the 2025 state championship.
Maranacook struck early in Lewiston and eventually won 2-0, ending Fort Kent's season at 14-2-2. Evelyn Stevenson scored both goals for the Black Bears.
It wasn't the ending Fort Kent wanted. But a state-final loss shouldn't erase what it took to get there.
The Warriors finished as Northern Maine champions and state runners-up for another year, continuing a run that has made them one of the most consistent soccer programs in this part of the state.
And that's why they belong in this countdown.
More Than One Great Season
When I started putting together the five stories that defined this fall, I didn't want this list to simply become five championship-game results.
The whole season had to matter.
Fort Kent's story is about what happens when excellence stops being a one-year accomplishment and becomes an expectation. Another group of players leaving its own mark on a run that started before some of them ever stepped onto the varsity field.
That's not easy to do.
And it earns the Fort Kent Lady Warriors the No. 5 spot in my five stories that defined the fall of 2026.
Tomorrow, the countdown continues with No. 4.

title: County Athletes Represent Northern Maine as Fall Soccer Meets Winter Basketball
text:
Fall Meets Winter: County Athletes Represent Northern Maine at Soccer and Basketball All-Star Events
The fall sports season is barely in the rearview mirror, and Aroostook County athletes are already making their presence felt as winter sports get underway.
It was a busy weekend for local athletes, with the Maine Soccer Coaches Senior Bowl taking place at Thomas College in Waterville and Basketball Maine hosting its All-Star Showcase Weekend in Portland.
The events brought together athletes from across the state, giving them an opportunity to compete alongside some of Maine's top players and represent their schools on a bigger stage.
Seventeen County basketball players were among those selected for the showcase, representing nine schools. Madawaska's Quinn Pelletier delivered one of the weekend's highlights, scoring 20 points and earning Game MVP honors.
North Boys Pick Up Soccer Senior Bowl Victory
The Maine Soccer Coaches Senior Bowl brought together senior standouts from across the state Sunday at Thomas College.
In the Class C/D/S boys matchup, the North defeated the South 4-2.
The South came away with victories in the remaining regional all-star games, including the Class A/B boys, Class A/B girls and Class C/D/S girls contests.
For those selected, the event offered one final opportunity to compete following the conclusion of the fall soccer season.
The games came just over a week after five St. John Valley teams competed for state championships, including Wisdom's girls, who captured the program's first state soccer title.
Basketball Maine Showcase Features 17 County Athletes
Basketball Maine's All-Star Showcase Weekend, held November 14-15 in Portland, brought together players from across the state for North versus South competition.
Aroostook County had representatives in five basketball divisions, along with a selection to the ninth-grade girls showcase.
Here's how the County was represented.
Class B Boys: Two Presque Isle Wildcats Selected
Presque Isle's Bodey McPherson and Cruze Casavant earned selections to the Class B North boys roster.
The Wildcats joined players from Erskine Academy, Ellsworth, Mount Desert Island, John Bapst, Gardiner, Cony and Belfast.
For both players, the showcase offered an opportunity to compete alongside athletes they would ordinarily face during the high school basketball season.
Class B Girls: North Defeats South
The Class B North girls earned a 72-51 victory over the South.
No County athletes have been identified on the Class B girls roster in the information available for this report.
Class C Boys: Fort Kent Sends Two Representatives
Fort Kent's Aden Jeffers and Jaden Jeffers were selected to the Class C North boys roster.
The Warriors were joined by players from Calais, Foxcroft Academy, Mattanawcook, George Stevens Academy, Washington Academy, Orono and MCI.
The South came away with an 86-79 victory in one of the weekend's closer matchups.
Class C Girls: Caribou's Lilly Bell Represents the North
Caribou's Lilly Bell, Peyton West, Quinn Corrigan, Anna Griffeth and Houlton's Ava Ezell were among the athletes selected for the Class C North girls team.
The South defeated the North 82-59 in the showcase matchup.
Their selections added two other County schools to the weekend's list of basketball representatives as the Vikings and the Shires prepare for the upcoming winter season.
Class D/S Boys: Quinn Pelletier Earns Game MVP Honors
Madawaska's Quinn Pelletier turned in one of the weekend's standout performances, scoring 20 points and earning Game MVP honors in the Class D/S boys contest.
Pelletier helped lead the North to a convincing 98-53 victory over the South.
Two other County athletes joined him on the North roster.
Mason Pelletier of Easton and Cyran Ciarleglio of Hodgdon were also selected to represent Northern Maine.
The North's 45-point victory was the largest winning margin among the five showcase results provided.
Class D/S Girls: Wisdom, Katahdin, and Central Aroostook Represented
Four County athletes were selected to the Class D/S North girls squad.
Madisyn Cyr and Peyton Roy of Wisdom, along with Polly Cullen of Katahdin and Lilly Burtt of Central Aroostook, represented Northern Maine in the matchup.
The South earned a 60-51 victory.
For Cyr, the showcase came just over a week after helping Wisdom's girls soccer team capture the program's first state championship.
The selections gave all four athletes an opportunity to compete against players from across Maine ahead of the winter season.
Ninth-Grade Girls: Caribou's Anna Griffith Selected
Caribou also had a representative among the younger athletes participating in the showcase weekend.
Anna Griffith was selected to the ninth-grade North girls roster, joining players from Gardiner, Skowhegan, Mount Blue, Oceanside, Kents Hill and Hermon.
Her selection gave Caribou two athletes recognized across the weekend's showcase rosters.

One Season Ends, Another Begins
For County sports fans, the weekend marked the first real transition between fall and winter athletics.
The soccer Senior Bowl gave graduating players one more opportunity to compete, while Basketball Maine's showcase offered an early look at athletes preparing for the upcoming winter season.
And with practices getting underway across Aroostook County, it won't be long before the attention turns to basketball courts, wrestling mats and indoor tracks.
Congratulations to all the County athletes selected to represent their schools and Northern Maine over the weekend.
The fall season may be wrapping up, but another busy winter of County sports is just around the corner.

title: Recount upholds Democratic win in dramatic flip of Maine Senate seat
text:
A recount in Maine Senate District 18 has affirmed Democrat Elizabeth Bosworth as the winner by 53 votes.
The 10,413-10,360 tally, announced by the Maine Secretary of State’s Office on Monday, added three votes to Bosworth’s total over Republican former state Rep. John Andrews.
But despite the small overall margin, the win for Bosworth was one of the bigger flips of a Maine Senate seat this year.
Two years earlier, Republican Rick Bennett won the western Maine district by 29 points. Bennett has since become an independent and ran unsuccessfully for governor this year.
District 18 voted for President Donald Trump by about 9 points in 2024.
Bosworth may have benefitted from an influx of money this year. Her race ranked seventh in the state for outside spending among Maine’s 35 Senate districts, according to campaign finance data compiled by the Bangor Daily News, and Democratic-aligned groups accounted for nearly all of that.
The win was one of a number of gains for Democrats who expanded their majorities in both chambers of the Maine Legislature in the historic national “blue wave” that saw Democratic former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson unseat five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
Maine Senate District 18 spans parts of Androscoggin, Cumberland and Oxford counties and includes Bridgton, Brownfield, Denmark, Fryeburg, Harrison, Hebron, Mechanic Falls, Minot, Norway, Otisfield, Oxford, Paris, Sweden and Waterford.
BDN writer Daniel O’Connor contributed reporting.

title: Legally blind hitting coach has trained young athletes for 40 years
text:
OMAHA, Neb. (Aging Untold) — Mark Wetzel has spent 40 years coaching the swings of young athletes while legally blind.
In a neighborhood outside Omaha, Wetzel’s lessons begin at the driveway, where he has a sign that says, “The smooth, straight path seldom leads anywhere.”
Coaching with limited vision
Then they continue inside a barn, where Wetzel has coached local children and minor league pros.
He said he has macular degeneration of the retina.
“I’m legally blind,” Wetzel said.
He had to stop playing baseball in his youth.
He spent decades learning to think of the game differently.
Wetzel has some peripheral vision. He said he can see a player’s profile against a wall and any movement, including excess energy, tightness or weight shift.
“I can see that profile against that wall. I can see any kind of movement, the slightest bit of movement – excess energy or tightness or weight shift,” Wetzel said.
He described the vision loss as “almost a blessing.”
Overcoming what life throws at us
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist and host of “Aging Untold,” said Wetzel’s coaching goes beyond the batting cage.
“You can get into your own head when you’re limited, and you can allow that to tell you you’re less,” Cradduck said. “We’re never less. We’re always exceptionally more than what people see us. We just have to see it ourselves first, and then we have to let everybody else see it in us. And he did. He went in there just with an exceptional amount of who he was, and he’s gifting that over to others.”
Cradduck also said watching others overcome adversity affects those around them.
“When other people watch us overcome adversity and when other people watch us overcome what life throws at us, we’re strengthening them whether we realize it or not. We’re giving them that that inherent ability to tap into that side of themselves when adversity hits them,” Cradduck said.

title: Lawmakers unveil bipartisan bill to give NICU parents more time off from work
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — U.S. parents with newborns in intensive care would be entitled to up to 12 more weeks of unpaid leave under a new bill unveiled Monday by a group of bipartisan lawmakers, who described an agonizing gap faced by many families.
The bill, introduced by Rep. Brittany Pettersen, a Colorado Democrat, aims to address a long-overlooked plight facing many parents with newborns in neonatal intensive care, who often exhaust much of their parental leave before their baby comes home from the hospital. Many mothers and fathers end up working through their newborns’ NICU stays to save their time off.
The proposed legislation would amend the 1993 Family and Medical Leave Act to offer up to 12 weeks of dedicated NICU leave to eligible workers, on top of 12 weeks of parental leave already available.
The campaign for NICU leave has gained momentum since Colorado and Illinois became the first states to implement such policies earlier this year. On Tuesday, Walmart will begin offering a maximum of 12 extra weeks of NICU leave to its full-time employees, joining a handful of other companies with similar policies, including Morgan Stanley, Pinterest and organic baby formula company Bobbie.
The U.S. has no federal law mandating paid family leave but FMLA entitles eligible parents — those who have worked at least 12 months for a private employer with 50 or more employees — to job-protected unpaid leave to care for a newborn.
While Republicans have generally opposed a federal mandate for paid leave, Pettersen said she is optimistic that the amendment to the FMLA will garner bipartisan support.
“This isn’t about party, it’s about life experiences,” Pettersen said in an interview with The Associated Press. “Where we want to go is paid family and medical leave, and we will continue to fight for it. This is a step forward building off the current policy that has bipartisan support.”
Her co-sponsors were Republicans, Rep. Mike Lawler of New York and Rep. Ryan Mackenzie of Pennsylvania, and a Democrat, Rep. Morgan McGarvey of Kentucky. Mackenzie and McGarvey have both advocated for other policies benefiting NICU babies and shared their own stories as fathers with newborns in intensive care.
“For parents with a newborn in the NICU, the last thing they should have to worry about is whether they’ll have enough time off work to be there for their child,” Mackenzie said in a statement.
Lawler added in a statement that “every working parent deserves the chance to be there for their child, especially when that child is facing a serious medical challenge.”
The bill, known as the “Stand By NICU Babies and Families Act,” could face a long road. It must be reintroduced after the new Congress is seated in January, and Pettersen will have to search for new Republican sponsors. Lawler and Mackenzie both lost their reelection bids in the midterm elections that gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress.
Pettersen said she introduced the bill pro forma to put a stake in the ground as her newly empowered party readies its priorities for the next Congress.
The NICU leave bills passed in Colorado and Illinois illustrate the partisan divide over paid leave mandates. Colorado’s paid leave passed mostly along party lines, while a shorter, unpaid leave adopted in Illinois had overwhelming bipartisan support.
In both states, however, the policies were championed by legislators with their own experiences as NICU parents.
“This issue of leave for NICU parents seems to be something that people intuitively get, including people on the right and left and people in between,” said Inimai Chettiar, president of A Better Balance, a nonprofit that is advocating for state and federal NICU leave policies.
Nearly one out of 10 babies born in the U.S. are admitted to a NICU, according to the most recent figures from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Advocates say parental presence in the NICU is important because skin-to-skin contact helps improve health outcomes, while time off is critical for mothers of premature babies who are at higher risk of postpartum depression.
A Better Balance said most parents wouldn’t need the full 12 weeks of extra leave since the majority of NICU stays are much shorter, but the longer cap will help families facing more critical health situations.
McGarvey, the Kentucky congressman, said his now teenage twins spent 99 days in intensive care after they were born 14 weeks early.
“When your baby’s in the NICU, all you can focus on is getting them home,” McGarvey said in a statement.

title: Council unanimously passes resolution to ban cruise ship ‘scrubber’ discharge
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Portland City Council on Monday unanimously passed a resolution that asks the city manager to amend the city’s cruise ship regulations to ban the use of exhaust gas cleaning systems, or “scrubbers,” and the discharge of scrubber wash water while berthed at city-owned piers.
Once implemented, Portland will become the first port in Maine to ban their use, but several other major cities, including Seattle, have similar bans in place.
Open-loop scrubbers use seawater to wash exhaust gases, after which the untreated or minimally treated wash water is discharged into surrounding waters. Local organization Portland Cruise Control and environmental advocates have pushed for a ban for years, pointing to evidence that scrubber wash discharge contains acidic pollutants that are harmful to marine wildlife and the ocean.
The resolution states there are viable alternatives to open-loop scrubbers, including the use of marine gas oil, a low-sulfur fuel, as well as closed-loop or hybrid scrubbers that retain wash water in holding tanks.
Several members of the public, as well as officials, called the ban a “no-brainer” given the importance of marine health to Portland, and due to other bans that have not kept cruise ships from arriving in ports.
Ethan Hipple, director of parks, recreation and facilities, said cruise ship operators were asked to fill out a survey, which found that all ships coming into Portland were either using marine gas oil or closed-loop scrubber systems.
There was some debate among councilors and staff over enforcement and whether staff has the resources to keep tabs on what cruise ships are using.
However, the resolution adds language to the city’s tariff structure for regulating cruise ships that states that the city “may, at its option, obtain from the vessel captain, owners or representatives operational records and vessel log documentation to verify compliance with this provision.”
City Attorney Michael Goldman said a federal law known as the Vessel Incidental Discharge Act directed the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to establish national discharge standards for vessels, which included stricter discharge limits for scrubber wash water that were expected to be fully implemented this year. He said those rules, once implemented, will preempt state and local laws, with the U.S. Coast Guard charged with enforcement.
“Today, it’s a verbal assurance that no one has documented publicly. Once it’s in the tariff, it’s a binding rule the city can verify, and it covers every future ship and every future fuel-price swing,” said JoAnn Locktov, co-founder of Portland Cruise Control.
Earlier Tuesday, the city highlighted a report that found that cruise visitors and cruise lines generated $22 million in spending in the Portland area during the 2025 cruise season.
The report, prepared by Digital Research Incorporated for VisitPortland, surveyed 1,565 passengers and crew members across 42 cruise ship arrivals at Portland pier locations between April 17 and Nov. 5, 2025.
In a city news release, Calvin Klopp, president of Portland Pilots Inc., said that in 2026, cruise ship arrivals declined nearly 19% compared with the previous two years. He said a decline in one sector of maritime commerce “affects the port by raising service costs for other industries.”

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Roy W. Penniman, 74, of New Harbor, passed away peacefully on Nov. 14, 2026 following a long and hard-fought battle with health complications that began in March.
Born in Boothbay to Maurice and Grace, Roy lived in New Harbor from the very beginning of his life. It was the community he called home and where he formed lasting friendships throughout his life.
Roy was a hardworking man who took pride in a job well done. Early in life, he worked as a lobsterman, learned carpentry through hands-on experience, and maintained an exceptionally long newspaper delivery route. He proudly served in the U.S. Army during the Vietnam War era, remaining stateside to help train fellow soldiers. He later owned and operated seafood processing and wholesale facilities, building a career in an industry he knew well. Even after leaving the seafood business, Roy continued putting his carpentry skills to use, always enjoying the satisfaction of working with his hands.
Roy enjoyed good company and was never short on conversation. Whether catching up with an old friend or meeting someone new, he was always happy to share a story, a laugh, or a little friendly banter.
Besides his parents, Roy was predeceased by his loving wife, Joyce Penniman, the mother of their two children, Mackenzie and Troy.
He is survived by his daughter, Mackenzie and her husband, Stewart; as well as his son, Troy and his longtime partner, Alyssa. A proud father and grandfather, Roy especially enjoyed spending time with his grandchildren, the sons of Mackenzie and Stewart, sharing stories, making them laugh, and watching them grow.
A lifelong sports enthusiast, Roy loved the New York Yankees, Boston Celtics, and New England Patriots. He was particularly proud of his 50-year softball career as a pitcher and enjoyed bowling twice a week. He also appreciated a good card game, a little friendly competition, and the occasional trip to a local casino.
Roy enjoyed classic rock, especially Led Zeppelin, along with Westerns, mysteries, sports documentaries, and a good bowl of ice cream.
At home, Roy shared his life with his partner, Linda, and his beloved animals. He adored his cats, Mikey and Cooper, and shared a special bond with his dog, Harmony. Their daily “town tours” were a favorite routine, riding around together and taking in the familiar sights of the community he called home.
Roy will be remembered for his love of family, his easy conversation, and his appreciation for life’s simple pleasures. His presence, humor, and the memories he leaves behind will be missed by those who knew and loved him.
A service for Roy will be held at 11 a.m. on Sunday, Nov. 29, 2026 at the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home in Damariscotta, where a reception will follow the service.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home, 612 Main St., Damariscotta, ME 04543. Condolences and messages for his family may be expressed by visiting stronghancock.com.

title: Trump backs campaign to reinstate Nvidia CEO despite allegations he had an affair with a Chinese spy
text:
Trump backs campaign to reinstate Nvidia CEO despite allegations he had an affair with a Chinese spy
President Donald Trump on Monday backed a long-shot bid to get Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, an extraordinary endorsement from a U.S. president given that his own intelligence agencies have reportedly determined Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy.
Trump suggested the ex-CEO of Nvidia could return, saying Huang "learned a big lesson" and he "would certainly not mind" if he was reinstated.
There's a "big group of people that would like him to return," Trump added.
The comments came as a "Stand with Jensen" petition set up last week gathered momentum, gaining signatures from current and former Nvidia staff, investors and other Silicon Valley supporters, including SpaceX boss Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, CEO of video game maker Epic Games.
The petition calls on the board to bring back Huang while an independent investigation proceeds or there's "compelling evidence" that his departure is in the company's best interests.
"I'm signing it too," Musk posted on X, while Sweeney wrote, "Save Jensen!"
It's unclear whether Trump's endorsement will make a difference
It's unclear whether the big name endorsement will make a difference in light of Huang's damaged reputation, China's emerging chip threat and a pending congressional investigation into Nvidia's troubles.
"After this global scandal, the old Jensen with the black leather jacket and rock star persona is gone for good," wrote financial analyst Dan Ives of research firm Yorkville Ives.
As for the petition itself, corporate governance expert Charles Elson said it showed how out of touch many in Silicon Valley are with the American public given the national security threat and that Huang violated the company's own ethics rules.
"A few in Silicon Valley adhere to the genius theory — 'No matter what the genius does is forgivable. Geniuses have their own rules of the road,'" said Elson, founding director of the John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware. "That's a terrible way to run a business, a way to run a country."
Huang resigned last week from Nvidia, apparently ousted by the board after revelations that he had extramarital affairs, both with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of being an intelligence asset for Beijing and with a senior executive who reported to him. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO while the board searches for a replacement.
The push for reinstatement has opened a split at the highest levels of the Trump administration, which has shown little tolerance for dissent.
Trump's endorsement of Huang's potential return comes after his own treasury secretary called for a "dramatic shakeup" in Nvidia's leadership on Fox News over the weekend.
Questions mount about Trump's role in the scandal
Meanwhile, questions about Trump's role in the alleged spy scandal are mounting after a New York Times report that he was told last year, then again earlier this year, that Huang was having an affair with a woman that U.S. intelligence had determined was a Beijing spy — but did nothing about it.
On Monday, Trump downplayed the scandal. "Nobody's proven that she's a spy. She may not be a spy," the president said.
Trump suggested that more investigation was needed. But he added that "any woman coming to the country — that's a beautiful woman that comes from China — they say she's a spy."
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the petition.
The Financial Times reported Huang's ambitions for a comeback over the weekend, citing multiple anonymous sources. The newspaper said he has been discussing the possibility with confidants, as his allies assembled a "war room" of Silicon Valley allies to lobby for his return.
"We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process," the petition's organizers said in an open letter. "We do not have access to the Board's private deliberations. We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy."
The identities of the signatories could not be independently verified, and the website said that their "affiliations are self-reported and not verified."
Some people posted on their personal accounts that they supported the effort.
The petition urged institutional investors who back Huang to dial into the company's next quarterly earnings call, scheduled for 5 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, to give "a voice to the supporters."
The leadership scandal has thrown the wider artificial intelligence industry into turmoil because Nvidia is a key player in the AI boom, and its chips are vital for cloud computing and data centers that underpin the technology.
Huang was a driving force in building the company into a tech giant since co-founding it more than three decades ago, thanks to his technical knowledge, as well as his flair for publicity, underscored by his signature leather-jacket look.

title: Bar Harbor deserves better
text:
To the Editor:
I moved to Bar Harbor with my husband in May 2018. I designed and draped costumes for over 300 productions, specializing in historic costumes, working at Equity theatres, such as Actors Theatre of Louisville. Upon my retirement, I chose to focus my time and talents on volunteer work at the Bar Harbor Historical Society. I believe that in preserving garments of the past, we can better understand the lives and times of those who wore them.

title: Woman and her dog killed after being hit by car, police say
text:

The crash happened near 7th Street and Indian School Road around 6:30 p.m., according to police.

title: MaineDOT commissioner to retire later this month
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Maine Department of Transportation Commissioner Dale Doughty is retiring later this month.
Gov. Mills’ office announced the retirement Monday afternoon.
Doughty first joined the MaineDOT in 1996. He left the department to serve in other public service roles at the state and municipal levels over the past three decades, including the Office of Environment and the Bureau of Planning, as well as the City of Lewiston. He returned to the DOT as deputy commissioner in 2023.
Doughty became acting commissioner following Bruce Van Note’s retirement in 2025.
“Dale’s focus has always been creating safer, more reliable infrastructure for the next generation through his effective, pragmatic leadership,” Governor Janet Mills said. I’m grateful for Dale’s decades of service to Maine’s communities and for his leadership in my Administration. I wish him the best in retirement.”
Doughty’s last day is Nov. 28. An interim commissioner has not been named.
“As I prepare to retire, I take the greatest pride in the people of this department and their commitment to Maine,” Doughty said in a statement.

title: Trump attributes nationwide grounding of planes to old technology, Biden administration
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Monday laid the blame for the nationwide grounding of all planes last week on old technology as well as his Democratic predecessor Joe Biden.
“What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” Trump said Monday outside the White House ahead of his trip to Asia.
He added: “The Biden administration hooked up a lot of copper into glass and copper.”
Trump’s comments came after a rare nationwide grounding of airplanes Friday because of a router issue in the aging air traffic control system. The Republican president hadn’t spoken publicly or commented on the flight grounding until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking for more money to cover the cost of system improvements.
Trump’s blame-shifting and congressional Democratic finger-pointing underscore political divisions that could widen when Democrats take control of Congress in January, with scrutiny of his administration accelerating.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who made the decision Friday to ground the planes, also pushed Congress for billions more dollars to upgrade a system he said had been neglected for decades.
Duffy said the problem began when a federal contractor was replacing a section of old copper wire with new fiber wire, causing the system to overload.
The Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds,” the agency said.
Duffy said on Sunday that billions of dollars are needed to build new architecture for the network and said companies — including AT&T, Verizon and Lumen — are ready to deploy it as soon as the money is there.
Upgrading the nation’s air transportation system is an effort that Congress has dedicated significant sums to in recent years.
Under Trump’s immediate predecessor, President Joe Biden, Congress approved a massive infrastructure bill that included $25 billion over five years for airport and air traffic control infrastructure improvements. Much of that money went to airport projects like new runways and taxiways and updated terminals.
Under Trump, a Republican-led Congress approved $12.5 billion in 2025 to modernize the FAA’s air traffic system.
The Trump administration said the money would provide critical updates to outdated radar systems and traffic control centers, some dating back to the 1960s. Republicans used the same bill to allocate $170 billion for Trump’s immigration crackdown, for more border security and immigration enforcement.
___
Catalini reported from Morrisville, Pa.

title: What to know about the online banking delays affecting major US banks
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused problems throughout the financial system Monday, resulting in thousands of customers reporting difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle.
Here’s what we know.
What’s behind the outage?
JPMorgan Chase, the largest U.S. bank by total assets, said a software bug was affecting its internal hardware systems and causing transaction delays. The company was working to bring banking services back online.
Some Chase customers received a message that said, “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”
Were other banks affected?
In a sense, yes. Customers at Bank of America, Citigroup and other banks trying to transact with Chase may have seen their transactions slow, even though those banks were not having issues with their services.
“Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” explained Joe Evangelisti, a spokesperson for Chase.
What about Zelle?
Zelle was not directly affected by the Chase glitch. But customers at other banks may have experienced transaction delays while trying to send or receive Zelle payments involving a Chase customer.
Zelle is a rapid peer-to-peer payment system used by major U.S. banks. The platform is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.
A spokesperson for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational.
Was this a cyberattack?
Chase said that the technical problem was not the result of a cyberattack, stressing that it was an isolated incident and not related to anything other than a bug.
When might service be fully restored?
Chase said its customers still have access to their accounts and funds. The company expects the issue to be resolved by the end of day Monday.
Was this related to the Microsoft and air traffic disruptions last week?
No. While the disruptions took place just days apart, government officials and company leaders have said they were unrelated.
The major outage by Microsoft on Thursday that lasted for hours, severely impacting services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, was due to a technical issue that arose during an upgrade. The tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, such as a cyberattack or due to action by artificial intelligence agents.
Another outage that affected the nation’s air traffic control system Friday, grounding all U.S. flights for several hours and disrupting domestic air travel over the weekend, was caused by a router that malfunctioned and overwhelmed the aging air traffic control system.
___
Associated Press journalist Hannah Schoenbaum contributed from Salt Lake City.

title: Holy Spuds! Maine Ranks Among America's Top Potato Producers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Holy Spuds! Maine Ranks Among America’s Top Potato Producers
Let's play a little word association, shall we? I'll say a word, and you tell me the first thing that comes to mind. Ready? Here we go.
"Maine."
Let me guess. You immediately thought of lobster, didn't you? Or perhaps seafood in general. And who could blame you? Sure, Maine is famous for its rocky coastline, towering forests, and spectacular natural beauty. But when it comes to what truly defines the Pine Tree State, nothing quite compares to our favorite crustacean.
However, there’s another product that deserves more attention on a grand scale. It’s one that fills the farmland in the north. It’s a versatile crop that is among the most popular in the world. Yes, I’m talking about the potato.
Maine continues to be one of the top potato-producing states in the country. Whether it's the popular russet, a special hybrid developed for the Frito-Lay company, or one of the many other varieties, Maine is proud to be one of the country's true leaders in the market.
How Many Potatoes Does Maine Produce Annually?
But just how big a potato producer is Maine? Well, according to World Population Review, Maine was the eighth-highest potato-producing state last year. Hey, that's not too bad at all.
World Population Review used data from the Department of Agriculture to determine its rankings. Maine produced 17.4 million cwt (hundredweight, a unit of weight equal to 100 pounds, commonly used to measure agricultural products) in 2025. That's a heck of a lot of spuds, folks. This total put Maine just behind Michigan (20.7 million) and ahead of Minnesota (16.7 million).
The majority of Maine's potato farms can be found up north in Aroostook County, where the climate is just right. According to Visit Aroostook, Maine was even the highest-producing potato state in the nation at one point. Of course, that was back in the 1940s, and times have changed just slightly.
Visit Aroostook also points out that the most popular uses for Maine's potato crop are french fry processing, potato chips (hello, Frito-Lay), seed potatoes, and home consumption. I'd say Maine potatoes are quite versatile.
What State is Number 1 in Potato Production?
Producing nearly 18 million cwt a year certainly seems like a ton of spuds. However, it's nothing compared to what Idaho, the country's top potato producer, is pumping out. The Gem State produced a whopping 138 million cwt last year. It was the only state in America to surpass the 100 million mark. I guess that's why they call it the Potato State.
READ MORE: This Portland Taco Joint Was Just Named the Best in Maine
But Maine is still holding its own when it comes to spuds, and it's great to see. So don't forget to keep supporting Maine's potato growers. The backbone of our agricultural community deserves it.

title: How to talk with older family members about driving
text:
(Aging Untold) — Families can start conversations with older loved ones about driving before it becomes a problem, according to Amy O’Rourke, an Aging Untold expert.
For many older adults, driving means independence. As people age, their health changes, and families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving.
Starting the conversation
O’Rourke suggests asking a loved one questions before driving becomes a problem.
“Do you mind if I bring this up, Dad?” O’Rourke said.
How would you feel if I brought up the car? I’m not telling you, I’m not talking about that, but I want to be prepared for when I think you might need some evaluation. I don’t want to be blindsided and I don’t want to be talking to you in a crisis,” she said.
“Start before it’s a problem and just start lobbing some questions and make it part of a routine check-in,” O’Rourke said.
Red flags to watch for
Experts say these are some of the red flags families can watch for:
- Delayed responses
- Getting lost or disoriented easily
- Increased close calls
- Difficulty seeing pedestrians, objects or other vehicles
- Dents or scrapes on the car or on surrounding objects where the person drives and parks at home
Where to find help
Families also can talk with a doctor about any health issues or medications that can affect driving.
The state DMV can provide information on driver evaluations and restrictions. Local agencies on aging can help families find transportation options.

title: Patriots’ Drake Maye reportedly sidelined indefinitely with an ankle injury
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye has a right ankle injury that will sideline him indefinitely, a person with knowledge of the injury told The Associated Press on Monday.
The Patriots are trying to determine whether Maye will require surgery on his ankle, according to the person who spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity because the team hasn’t addressed the severity of the injury.
Maye stayed in Germany and did not travel back with the team following its loss to Detroit on Sunday for what coach Mike Vrabel said was a decision made “out of caution.”
Losers of two straight games and three of their last four, New England has a bye this week and won’t play again until Nov. 29 when it visits the Los Angeles Chargers.
During his news conference on Monday, Vrabel wouldn’t confirm or deny that Maye will be out for an extended period. But he did say he would miss more time.
“I wouldn’t imagine him being available when we come out of the bye,” Vrabel said.
Maye injured his ankle on a sack by Aidan Hutchinson in the first quarter of the Patriots’ 35-10 loss and didn’t return. Vrabel said after the game that Maye would get tests done once home to determine the severity of the injury.
“He’ll be traveling back here shortly, but (the team) just wanted to make sure that everything was good for him to travel back and safely,” Vrabel said earlier Monday during his regularly scheduled radio interview with Boston’s WEEI on the “Greg Hill Show.”
“And it seems like he is.”
The coach said Sunday that he didn’t consider the sack that injured Maye to be improper — Hutchinson had caught up to Maye and pulled him down from behind.
“I’m not going to assume there was something there,” Vrabel said. “However it happened, I don’t think it was anything intentional. I’m sure that it wasn’t. That’s part of the game.”
Backup quarterback Tommy DeVito completed 12 of 24 for 81 yards with one interception and a fourth-quarter touchdown pass to Lan Larison for New England after replacing Maye.
The Patriots managed just 151 total yards on the day, a season low. The only other quarterback on the roster is Behren Morton, who is on the practice squad.
“We never got to establish who we were,” DeVito said. “Kind of felt like we were playing on their terms, and I think that’s just not our style of football. That’s not our offense. That’s not how we want to play. That’s not what we preach.”
DeVito added that “it starts with me.”
“I just have to play better and sustain drives and get the thing going and stop feeling so lax,” he said.
Asked about the potential of starting should Maye be sidelined after the bye, DeVito said: “I’m going to continue the process I have been doing up to this point. As cliche as it sounds, you have to be prepared to be a starter.”
Wide receiver A.J. Brown and running back Rhamondre Stevenson were able to play — after being listed as questionable Friday — but neither was a factor. Brown had two catches for 27 yards before leaving in the second half with a hamstring problem. Stevenson rushed six times for 4 yards.

title: California sues OpenAI, seeking court-ordered changes after the Hugging Face hack
text:
California’s attorney general filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday in an effort to force the ChatGPT-maker to change its business practices over a July cybersecurity incident in which its artificial intelligence system hacked into another company on its own.
In the lawsuit filed in San Francisco Superior Court, Attorney General Rob Bonta alleges that OpenAI misled and endangered the public and users of its services by knowingly developing advanced AI models without necessary safeguards. He says the company’s actions could put critical infrastructure, institutions and the public at risk, which makes it a “public nuisance” under state law. Bonta says OpenAI is a public nuisance, and he wants a judge to order the company to change its ways and give up any profits generated by what he claims are the company’s risky business practices.
OpenAI announced an “ unprecedented cyber incident ” on July 21, when its AI agent hacked into another AI company, Hugging Face, after escaping from what was supposed to be an isolated testing environment known as a sandbox. OpenAI said its AI used stolen credentials and discovered a previously unknown vulnerability to access Hugging Face’s servers.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that has been identified by every major AI lab.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” Pusateri wrote in an email to The Associated Press. Those steps include publishing detailed technical and independent reports, strengthening safeguards, and creating a framework to identify when AI agents act in a way that doesn’t match the company’s instructions or goals, Pusateri said.
“We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry,” Pusateri wrote.
In the lawsuit, Bonta says OpenAI’s promises about safety and security are deceptive.
“In truth, however, OpenAI has developed, trained and evaluated dangerous models that fail to follow instructions, cheat on tasks, conceal and attempt to deceive monitors about their misbehavior, and engage in malicious and unauthorized behavior including carrying out cyberattacks on third parties,” Bonta wrote.
He also noted that early last month, OpenAI reported that it had discovered that internally deployed agents were able to suppress monitoring alerts and disable monitoring. A month later, the company published a research report finding that as AI models become more capable, they become more difficult to supervise, he wrote.
“Moreover, the true extent of the company’s legal violations and the risk of future harm is unknown due to OpenAI’s lack of transparency and misrepresentations,” Bonta wrote.
OpenAI was already being sued by at least eight states that say the company’s popular chatbot model is hurting children and deceiving adults by giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to kill themselves or hurt or kill others. The lawsuits contend the ChatGPT chatbots are pretending to be agreeable and compassionate while preying on the vulnerable and teenagers.
In a statement released last month in response to those lawsuits, OpenAI said it had built safety protections into ChatGPT for children and that it would continue to improve the model.

title: Ask ACE: I want to introduce technology that’s new to my industry. What are my options?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ACE advises: You may have more options than you think. Maine’s seven designated technology sectors are broader than their names suggest, and other funding programs aren’t necessarily tied to them.
The seven sectors. In 1999, the Maine Legislature designated seven sectors for technology investment: biotechnology; aquaculture and marine technology; composite materials; environmental technology; advanced technologies for forestry and agriculture; information technology; and precision manufacturing.
Lawmakers also created Maine Technology Institute to administer grants, loans and other funding for innovation in these sectors.
In 2023, an independent Camoin Associates report suggested adding an eighth category, “emerging technologies.” MTI recommended keeping the existing framework, arguing that its categories were flexible enough to embrace new technologies. But your question highlights a potential problem: businesses may overlook funding because they don’t recognize themselves in the list.
Here’s the trick: Instead of asking, “What industry am I in?” ask, “What technology am I introducing?”
A clothing manufacturer developing automated, made-to-measure production might fit under precision manufacturing. A retailer creating an innovative inventory system or a financial services firm developing new software might fit under information technology.
The key word is innovation. If you’re developing new technology rather than buying something off the shelf, explore MTI’s funding programs, even if your industry doesn’t fall within the seven sectors.
For equipment purchases and technology adoption, look into Efficiency Maine incentives for energy-saving upgrades, financing through the Finance Authority of Maine (FAME) and grants and incentives listed by Maine’s Department of Economic and Community Development.
Don’t let a sector label stop you. Focus on what your technology will accomplish, then find the funding program that fits.

title: Arkansas city of El Dorado uses travel spotlight to clear its name. Call us 'El Duh Ray Duh'
text:
LITTLE ROCK, Ark. (AP) — When a system failure grounded airplanes nationwide, led to thousands of flight cancellations and disrupted air travel worldwide, a little place called El Dorado suddenly found itself in the spotlight.
The southern Arkansas city of about 18,000 people gained unwanted attention when a radio communications site based there was identified as a possible source of the troubles.
While it may not be the attention they sought, the El Dorado-Union County Chamber of Commerce figured any attention is an opportunity to introduce the world to the town.
“While our community is not to blame for the outage, we want to take this time to point out that, as folks on cable television networks, podcasts, and other outlets talk about El Dorado, we want you to do it the right way,” the chamber of commerce said on Facebook, starting with the name.
The chamber posted a pronunciation guide: “Proper use: El Duh Ray Duh,” although “El Duh Ray Doe” is also acceptable. Calling the city “El Duh Rod Oh” is to be avoided.
“And while we’re at it — tell the masses that our community is growing, we are adding jobs, your children can get their college tuition covered through the El Duh Ray Duh Promise,” the chamber stated.
The chamber also referred readers to the city’s website, which promotes the city’s tourism and culture.
On Monday, Steven Jones, president of the El Dorado-Union County Chamber of Commerce, said that companies are also eyeing lithium reserves in the city.
Standard Lithium, a Canada-based lithium production company, is developing a project for the mineral’s extraction near El Dorado, according to its website.
“We just thought why not capitalize on the marketing and have a little fun,” Jones said Monday.

title: You can cut sodium without giving up flavor
text:
(Aging Untold) — For many older adults, watching sodium is part of managing blood pressure, heart health and other medical conditions.
If you think that means giving up favorite foods and flavors, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said it does not.
‘Smarter ways to make things healthier’
Rogers said people do not have to give up the foods and flavors they enjoy.
“Absolutely not,” Rogers said. “We just find smarter ways to make things healthier.”
Other spices can bring out the natural flavor of food.
“Other spices will bring out the natural flavor, because many times we’re hiding it,” Rogers said. “Many times we’re hiding it. We don’t even taste what that real food tastes like.”
She said people with high blood pressure or kidney issues may not want a lot of sodium.
“The sodium is going to make you absorb water and hold on to it,” Rogers said.
High insulin can also make the body hold on to sodium and water, she added.
“You just have to learn how to blend the spices and things like that to make your food taste actually just as well, or better,” Rogers said.
Cooking and seasoning at home
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said her husband follows a low-sodium diet. She cooks vegetables, such as carrots, for a long time to bring out their flavor, though not until they are mushy.
“I also toast and warm spices like cumin and paprika, and that brings out the flavor also,” O’Rourke said. “The less we season the food, the more you can taste the actual food.”
She said she reads labels because bread, pastries, processed foods and canned foods can contain a lot of sodium. When her husband started the diet, she looked up how much he should have.
“It’s 2,300 mg, which is a teaspoon,” O’Rourke said. “So it’s very, very little.”
Reading labels and finding hidden sodium
Rogers said some people make their own seasonings, such as garlic powder instead of salt. She also brought up the recommended daily allowance on food labels.
“If you see 5% or less, that’s a really low sodium,” Rogers said. “You start seeing 20% or higher, that’s pretty high in content.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said the biggest source of sodium is not the salt shaker.
“The most dangerous salt shaker there is isn’t even the one that’s on the table or the one that you use,” she said. “It’s what’s already in the food that you’re eating.”
The body still needs sodium
Cradduck said the body needs sodium.
“That’s what makes our nerves work. It’s what makes our muscles contract. It maintains blood pressure, normal fluid balances,” Cradduck said.
She said low sodium can be an issue in older adults, especially for people who take a diuretic or have heart failure or kidney disease.
“One is nutritional, one is metabolic, and you need to find the balance,” Cradduck said.
Sea salt, sports drinks and potassium substitutes
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said people hear that sea salt, Himalayan salt and pink salt are good for them. She said some fitness trainers recommend a certain amount of salt each day, while a low-sodium diet calls for less. She named lunch meat, fast food, canned goods and energy drinks as sources of sodium.
“I think it’s going to be individualized,” Rogers said. “You have to look at who’s getting what and who needs what.”
She said replacing sodium with potassium may not be a good idea, depending on a person’s medical conditions.
Butter and nutritional yeast
When using butter as a seasoning, check whether it is salted or unsalted, Cradduck said.
“Don’t think, ‘Oh, I’m going to get rid of the salt and I’m just going to season with butter,’ and then you use butter that’s full of salt,” Cradduck said.
Rogers also mentioned nutritional yeast, which can give a cheesy flavor.
“There’s a lot of different things that you can use that really enhance the flavors and actually taste better,” she said.
Key takeaways
- Sodium can hide in packaged foods and raise blood pressure
- Swap salt for flavor. Zest, herb blends and nutritional yeast can bring out the natural flavor of food
- Check labels to protect your heart without losing flavor

title: Lindsay Clancy to face second trial in deaths of her 3 children
text:
Lindsay Clancy to face second trial in deaths of her 3 children
Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of strangling her three children in 2023, will face a second trial next year.
Prosecutors announced their decision during a hearing on Monday, and the court set a date of March 29, 2027, for the start of jury selection.
Clancy, whose first trial ended with a hung jury in September, was previously denied attempts to block a second trial on double jeopardy grounds and the alleged misconduct involving one holdout juror from the first case.
Live updates from Hearst Television sister station WCVB below:
"I think you can read between the lines when they say the case is going to require a jury that it is an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments," defense attorney Kevin Reddington said.
Monday's hearing follows last week's rulings in which Judge William Sullivan denied a series of motions from both sides, and district attorney Tim Cruz's prior statement that he would “be talking more” at Monday's hearing.
Clancy, 36, was on trial over the summer for the deaths of 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan at their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023. Her defense argued she was not criminally responsible for murder because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings.
The jury was ultimately deadlocked, with a reported 11-1 split in favor of acquittal after seven days of deliberations. A mistrial was declared.
At the last hearing, when Sullivan asked the prosecutors whether they were planning to pursue another trial, Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague replied, "We're not at that point yet."
Cruz said his office was conducting a thorough review of the case.
Defense attorney Kevin Reddington, however, was more direct.
"I want a trial, and I want it with you, and I want it this spring," he told the judge.
Last week, Sullivan denied three significant motions in the case:
- Sullivan denied without prejudice the prosecution's motion for a gag order, which would have blocked attorneys from speaking to the press about the case. He allowed the prosecution to renew the request "if circumstances change and it can demonstrate that a prior restraint is necessary."
- Sullivan denied a defense motion to dismiss the case on the grounds that retrying Clancy would constitute double jeopardy. He rejected the defense's argument that the lone holdout on the jury should have been replaced before a mistrial was declared.
- Sullivan also denied the defense request for an inquiry into the holdout juror, including allegations of lying on his questionnaire and using a cellphone while in the jury room. "Because Clancy has failed to demonstrate that the requested evidence is relevant and material to her defense at any retrial of the murder indictment, the Court declines to exercise its discretion to order production," Sullivan wrote. "Nor can the Court perceive any valid justification for examining Juror Doe under oath at this point in the proceedings."

title: What to know before using gamified credit card rewards
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Some new “gamified” credit cards turn every swipe into a spin of the wheel, with random cashback amounts and surprise payoffs.
Sara Rathner of NerdWallet looked at the trend and said some of these cards now encourage cardholders to take certain actions.
Rathner said the effect depends on what the card asks cardholders to do.
“It could be positive. It could be nudging you to contribute every month to your savings account or pay your bills on time. It could be educational, completing financial literacy courses to unlock certain prizes. And it could also encourage you to spend just to try to game the system and earn just a little bit more rewards. And that’s a slippery slope,” Rathner said.
Rathner said cardholders could end up overspending just to try for a small chance of winning a prize. She also found that the average payout can be much lower than first advertised, and that in some cases the rules can change hour by hour.
“There are lots of examples of gamification that are good, but it’s when you introduce uncertainty and sweepstakes and the potential to win, but you have to spend, spend, spend to up your odds of winning. That’s when it gets dangerous,” Rathner said.
Rathner said anyone using gamification with a financial product should stick to games that are educational and positive and that encourage more saving, not more spending. She said cardholders should not have to engage in something risky just to benefit.

title: Fewer students are traveling from abroad to study at US universities, report shows
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Fewer international students are studying at U.S. universities as the Trump administration cracks down on immigration and reshapes higher education, data released Monday shows.
Overall, U.S. campuses saw a 9% decrease in international enrollment this fall compared with last year, according to a survey from the Institute of International Education. And the number of new students entering the United States for the first time fell by 15%.
“No one aspires to send their kids to get educated in the U.S.,” said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, whose father traveled from India to attend Tuskegee University, then the Tuskegee Institute, in the late 1960s on a student visa.
“It feels like an unsafe place. That’s the message that the Trump administration has been sending to families all over the world and they’re listening.”
Last year, the enrollment decreases were partially offset by large numbers of students who stayed in the U.S. for temporary work after graduating. But after months of speculation, the Department of Homeland Security proposed requiring schools to pay a $70,000 fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training program.
Although the rule hasn’t been finalized, participation in the program, known as OPT for short, dropped 6% this fall, according the survey.
International students facing political headwinds
The proposed rule, which is expected to face legal challenges, is part of wider DHS efforts that include terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, along with detaining and deporting many of them.
And this summer, the administration finalized a rule that will prevent international students from staying in the U.S. for more than four years without approval from the federal government, although a judge has temporarily blocked it.
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the changes were intended to crack down on loopholes that international students were exploiting by extending their studies.
Although the U.S. remains the top destination for international students globally, the changes are having an affect, college leaders told the IIE.
Among more than 800 U.S. colleges and universities surveyed this fall, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions for the enrollment drops. And if OPT options are limited, 95% of schools predicted that international students would likely look to another country, according to the survey, which offers an early look at trends before full data is released next year.
Politics aren’t the only reason students are looking elsewhere, said Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning for the institute. Its survey found more global competition for international students and the rising cost of a U.S. degree also contributed.
Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education, said students also are worried about research funding. Last year, the Trump administration began dismantling the federal grant-giving process and attempting to exert more political influence over what projects get funded.
“They’re saying to themselves, ‘Too much uncertainty in the United States. It’s too difficult, and you know, more importantly, we have many more choices today than we did 10 years ago. Why subject ourselves to this?’” Aw said, noting that students are going to places like China.
NAFSA, in partnership with the international education technology company JB International, found that amid the enrollment decline, international students’ contributions to the U.S. economy dropped by $2.4 billion this fall.
Colleges see budgets squeezed
American colleges and universities heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue. So the drops have punched big holes in tuition revenue at some schools.
At Cleveland State University, international enrollment has dropped by 46% in two years, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall. And fewer than 50 new international students started this fall, said Provost Nigamanth Sridhar, who estimated that the budgetary impact ranges from $2 million to $4 million.
Decades ago, he arrived in the U.S. on an F1 student visa and participated in OPT. Eventually, he went through the process to became a naturalized citizen.
“I am here in this position, in this job, because I had the opportunity to come to the United States as an international graduate student and then decided to stay here and build a career,” said Sridhar, who is from India. “So international education is personal to me.”
The biggest drops were at the graduate level. This fall’s data shows a 15% drop in international graduate enrollment, compared to a 3% decrease at the undergraduate level. The report also found declines in international students from India, which sends more students to the U.S. to study than any other country.
Midterms raise questions about the future
Sarah Spreitzer, vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents, said substantial immigration bills are unlikely while Trump remains president. But she said congressional oversight might halt new policies targeted at international students.
“Those types of things could provide more certainty for our international students that there’s not just going to be these sudden or unexplainable changes,” Spreitzer said.

title: Letter to the Editor: Public trust requires equal standards
Overnight warming shelter is open, 15 available beds
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - The only overnight warming shelter in Aroostook County opened Sunday, adding 15 beds for people who may face sleeping outside this winter.
Outreach to people sleeping outside
In October, News Source 8 reported that the city of Presque Isle was aware of and working with seven people who were still sleeping outside. Kari Bradstreet, executive director of Homeless Services of Aroostook, said she hopes the warming shelter can convince them to come inside.
“The individuals that are sleeping outside, hopefully will come in and utilize that service. It’s just overnight and they can go and do what they want during the day. But hopefully, we can get them under the roof where it’s warm and they can get showers and stuff,” Bradstreet said.
Warming shelter and warming center
Other locations open their doors for daytime warming centers. Homeless Services of Aroostook offers the only overnight warming shelter. Bradstreet said the difference is big.
“There is a difference between a warming center and a warming shelter. Warming centers, they’re not allowed to lay down and sleep. So we are a sleeping shelter overnight,” Bradstreet said.
Shelter serves as entry point
The shelter also provides a place to shower and a hot meal. Bradstreet said it is an entry point.
“Typically the warming is our entry point through the winter months. We’re able to get them in here quickly with minimal paperwork. So at least they’re safe,” Bradstreet said.
On the warming shelter’s first night open for the season, Bradstreet said staff started paperwork for one person. The next morning, that person was transferred to a permanent bed in the shelter.
How to help
The shelter is asking for donations and warm meals. More information on how to get involved is available at www.aroostookhomeless.org/
