title: These doctors had a history of being disciplined. Prison officials hired them anyway
text:
KANKAKEE, Ill. — (InvestigateTV)
When John Paris married his wife, Vikki, in 2008 he took the vow to see her through sickness and in health, for better or for worse. Even before saying those words, he knew what would be required – given his new bride was serving time behind bars in an Illinois prison.
“We loved each other deeply and didn’t care what anybody else thought,” he said.
Their relationship would be tested again a decade later, when Vikki – a bladder cancer survivor – had testing done that revealed potential warning signs the disease could be making a return.
A year went by before Vikki was finally seen and got the diagnosis they’d been dreading. It was bladder cancer.
But by then, it was too late – the disease had already spread to her lungs and kidneys.
Within months, Vikki was dead. Her husband claimed in a civil lawsuit that prison doctors were negligent and delayed Vikki’s care - leaving him without his best friend.
“Just basically took everything from me,” he said. “She deserved a lot better.”
But what John learned later from InvestigateTV added to his dread. Several of the physicians involved in Vikki’s case had histories of providing inadequate care, according to an InvestigateTV analysis of state medical board records.
Their disciplinary histories show sanctions for failures to diagnose, follow-up and notify patients about important medical issues.
But the issue is not isolated to Illinois. InvestigateTV spent months analyzing personnel records from state correctional agencies nationwide and searching for matches in state medical board disciplinary records. We found dozens of doctors with disciplinary histories practicing behind bars.
Those physicians, InvestigateTV’s research uncovered, had records that included medical license suspensions, restrictions that limited what procedures they could do and who they could treat, as well as medical license revocations.
In a small number of cases, InvestigateTV even found doctors whose histories showed their licenses had at one point been limited to practicing only within a correctional setting.
And these doctors - paid by tax dollars - were, with the full knowledge of state officials, hired or allowed to remain on the prison medical staff to treat men and women who can’t choose their own doctors.
“I don’t know if it’s widely known that these health care providers, some of whom have quite serious histories of misconduct, are essentially being foisted upon a captive population who has no choice,” said David Fathi, the director of the ACLU’S National Prison Project.
Andrea Armstrong, a professor of law at Loyola University New Orleans College of Law said, “if it’s your brother, if it’s your uncle, if it’s your cousin, if it’s your neighbor. You know, these are things that matter.”
Many prisons keep doctors’ names secret
Many prison officials refused to turn over names of physicians working behind bars for a variety of reasons, even though their positions are paid with tax dollars.
InvestigateTV filed public records requests with the correctional agencies in all 50 states.
Michigan estimated that it would need $800 in payment from InvestigateTV to fill the request. Nebraska wanted as much as $4,500 for the 140 hours of staff time the state claimed would be needed to respond.
Others, including Tennessee and North Carolina, delayed responding for months despite repeated attempts to follow up and gain access to records.
Eighteen other states either denied InvestigateTV’s requests, said they had no responsive records, or referred us to private contractors that provide medical care in state prisons. Idaho redacted provider names as “trade secrets” and Vermont shielded physicians from disclosure, saying the release of contracted names is exempt “due to privacy concerns”.
“We, as taxpayers and residents – we have the right to understand what the government is doing in our names and with our tax dollars. So, the failure to provide records is bewildering,” said Armstrong.
When unable to obtain information about providers through public records requests, InvestigateTV used salary databases made available online by individual state governments to track down some physicians working in state prison systems.
Ultimately, InvestigateTV was able to obtain the names of prison doctors employed in prison systems from 25 states, some dating as far back as 2020.
Doctors of ‘last resort’
After obtaining the names of prison providers, InvestigateTV used publicly searchable records from state medical boards to determine if doctors working in correctional settings had disciplinary histories.
Our team spent six months reviewing records for nearly 1,500 doctors from across the nation - finding at least 120 physicians in 17 states had at some point been disciplined by medical boards. While all had active licenses at the time of employment, some physicians had multiple actions against them, including discipline handed down after criminal convictions.
At least 30 had faced suspensions in the past.
Other physicians had practice restrictions, and some had surrendered their licenses or had them revoked – including some doctors who had been employed as Medical Directors in correctional settings.
“When somebody’s been disciplined, especially when their license has been restricted, that means that a colleague has expressed doubts about their ability to safely deliver care,” said Armstrong. “Just like in the real world, people make mistakes. They’re disciplined for those. And we as consumers of health care have an opportunity to choose our doctors. But that looks radically different behind bars because there is no choice.”
The conduct that resulted in discipline included drug and alcohol abuse, criminal convictions for drug offenses, DUI and fraud, sexual misconduct, missed diagnoses, improper prescribing, involvement in pill mills, drug diversion and inadequate care, records showed.
“What we know is that most of these systems are using doctors of, in some ways, last resort,” Armstrong said. “These are people who cannot practice anywhere else. And so, if they want to earn a living with the degree that they earned, then it only happens behind bars.”
Some doctors themselves had served time in prison. Some could see patients only with a chaperone, and some were barred from treating female patients. A few were even restricted at some point to practicing solely in prison settings.
“There should be no double standard,” Fathi said. “Doctors found unqualified to treat people in the community should not treat incarcerated patients.”
Yet that’s what happened in a South Carolina case settled in August that involved a physician with multiple license suspensions in his history in multiple states following incidents of self-prescribing, substandard care as well as a conviction for domestic violence.
Court filings in that civil lawsuit claim the doctor was working on behalf of a contractor that provides prison healthcare in several states and had been hired despite egregious conduct in his history. The suit claims negligent care led to the 2023 death of a young man who was being held in a county jail.
While the doctor died last year - before his death, records showed, his license had been limited, with the state medical board saying he “must work only at sites within the South Carolina Department of Corrections.”
The South Carolina Board of Medical Examiners told InvestigateTV the physician applied for and was offered a position in a correctional setting, which the board approved. They said he was not mandated to work in a correctional institution and was free to petition the board to remove the restriction or request approval to change employment – which did not happen before his death.
The South Carolina Department of Corrections did not respond to requests for comment.
‘Incarcerated people pay, often with their health, and sometimes with their lives’
South Carolina isn’t the only state where families say a risky hire had real consequences.
The Paris case in Illinois is another example. Vikki Paris was convicted in Illinois in 2005 in the shooting death of her first husband. Multiple records said the shooting followed years of spousal abuse. She took a plea deal and was given 20 years in state prison.
Her husband, John Paris, says she ended up with a death sentence instead, because of delays in her care.
“Your Hippocratic oath does not say heal all except those in prison. No, no. Do no harm is the main thing. And by ignoring people, that’s the exact opposite of your oath,” he said.
In 2021, Paris filed a civil lawsuit against five of the doctors involved in his wife’s care as well as Wexford, the company contracted by the Illinois Department of Corrections and paid with tax dollars to provide medical services.
Despite Vikki Paris experiencing months of severe pain and repeatedly reporting blood in her urine, the suit claims prison doctors didn’t get a second opinion, order additional testing or refer her to a urologist – delaying her diagnosis until it was too late.
Wexford declined to comment, and the Illinois Department of Corrections never responded to repeated requests from InvestigateTV. Just days before securing a settlement, the physicians involved were dropped from the suit – none provided responses to questions sent by email.
But InvestigateTV found three of the doctors named as defendants had prior disciplinary records, including action taken because of problems with patient care. One of the physicians had been reprimanded by the Illinois State Medical Board just three years before Vikki’s cancer reemerged.
Records show that disciplinary action followed settlement in a case that resulted from an “an alleged failure to timely diagnose breast cancer leading to a delay in treatment and poor prognosis” in a different patient.
That physician, InvestigateTV found, is still listed as an independent contractor in the Illinois prison system.
David Fathi said he was disturbed but not surprised by the discovery.
Second chances for problem providers
Dr. Keith Ivens, a Tennessee-based physician who oversaw prison health care for his own company and private contractors in states nationwide before retiring, said hiring for medical jobs in prisons can be challenging.
Lower paying salaries, the often-remote location of prison facilities and the complexity of the patient population are key reasons he said correctional institutions struggle to consistently hire top providers into the industry.
“If I had a university professor who wanted to work in my facility versus somebody with a fraud or sexual crime history, I want to hire the university professor,” Ivens said. “University professors are not lining up to take my jobs. I have to get medical providers into these institutions.”
Ivens admitted hiring doctors with serious discipline in their history does involve risk, but he said employers can and must monitor those with difficult histories. In his experience, he said some doctors with a dark past have performed “extraordinarily well” when given an opportunity to return to medicine through work in a correctional setting.
David Fathi with the ACLU doesn’t see it that way.
“If an airline is having trouble hiring enough pilots, they don’t get to say, well, we’ll just hire the person who lost their license for a while because they were flying while drunk. No, they have to hire someone who’s qualified, and the rule should be exactly the same when it comes to health care, which is every bit as much a matter of life and death,” he said.
‘Safe, competent care’ must be a priority
Until last month, Ivens chaired the National Commission on Correctional Health Care, a nonprofit that sets voluntary national quality standards for prison medicine. InvestigateTV sent the organization our findings.
The organization wouldn’t comment specifically but said in an emailed statement “Our mission is to improve correctional health care, not to defend inadequate practices or excuse shortcomings. Correctional facilities face significant challenges recruiting and retaining qualified health care professionals, reflecting broader workforce shortages across the country. However, staffing challenges do not justify compromising professional qualifications or standards of care. NCCHC’s position is that incarceration should never mean accepting a lower standard of health care. Ensuring that patients receive safe, competent care must always be the priority.”
The organization said its standards, which are voluntary, call for facilities to check providers’ licenses and credentials, including querying state licensing boards and a national repository of disciplinary information for any sanctions or disciplinary actions. The standards, the statement said, also prohibits clinicians from practicing under licenses that restrict their practice solely to correctional health care – in contrast to what InvestigateTV found in a few situations.
The commission emphasized there’s an important distinction between a history of professional discipline and a current license restriction, writing, “Disciplinary actions vary in severity, and restrictions may subsequently be lifted. NCCHC standards require verification of disciplinary histories but do not automatically prohibit employment based solely on past disciplinary action.”
InvestigateTV contacted correctional agencies in the 17 states that our investigation found employed physicians with a disciplinary history – either directly or through a contractor – asking about specific provider conduct and overall policies related to the employment of previously sanctioned doctors.
Only a few including Kentucky, Louisiana, North Carolina, Oregon and Washington provided full responses – with states saying the disciplinary actions identified by the investigation had been resolved and that doctors, like the people in their care, deserve a second chance.
SEE FULL STATE RESPONSES BELOW
Improving care: ‘We have a long way to go’
Experts from industry and advocacy agree that there are solutions that could improve healthcare provided behind bars.
Fathi said staffing shortages can be addressed by offering higher pay, more vacation or flexible hours. When courts have required prison systems to increase medical staffing, he said, those systems have found a way to do so.
Dr. Ivens echoed the call for higher salaries to entice more desirable candidates and pointed to telemedicine as a way to get in-demand physicians into the system without requiring them to move to rural locations.
For her part, Armstrong suggested partnering with public health agencies already experienced in providing complex care to the wider population. But she and others said the real solution is drastically reducing the number of people in incarceration so that their care can be managed effectively.
“There has to be a level at which a prison can say, “No, I can’t safely take any more people into custody because I don’t have the staff to provide the constitutionally required services,’ and that’s on the prisons to alert the public that they cannot do what they’re obligated to do because of the numbers,” Armstrong said.
Until changes happen, the loved ones of people impacted by the care provided by problematic doctors believe the incarcerated will pay the price.
“You’re costing money and lives. That’s all there is to it,” John Paris said.
Paris fought tirelessly for his wife’s release after her diagnosis, successfully securing clemency from Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker in March 2020.
Vikki Paris was home just four days before she died from cancer that her lawsuit claims could have been treated if it was caught earlier.
“She said, ‘Don’t worry about it. I’ve made my peace. I’m home with you. You kept your promise. You’re not letting me die in prison’,” he said.
RESPONSES FROM STATE CORRECTIONAL AGENCIES TO QUESTIONS FROM INVESTIGATETV
CALIFORNIA: “California Correctional Health Care Services (CCHCS) is committed to providing safe, appropriate, and professional medical care to incarcerated patients. Because personnel records and peer review information are confidential, CCHCS cannot comment on specific employees, former employees, or allegations involving individual providers.”
IDAHO: “The Idaho Department of Correction follows the terms of our contract with Centurion regarding information they designate as confidential or proprietary. When Centurion marks information as a protected trade secret under Idaho Code 74‑107(1), IDOC is required to review and redact that information before release. For additional information about Centurion’s classification of provider identities, you may contact Centurion directly."
INDIANA: “Thank you again for your inquiry. Unfortunately, since the individuals whose names you’ve requested are employees of Centurion and not the State of Indiana, we need to direct you to Centurion’s media team.”
IOWA: “Sounds like you reached out to most of the States with this request. Please reach out to our Open Records staff at docopenrecords@iowa.gov if you are wanting more information.”
KENTUCKY: “The Kentucky Department of Corrections is committed to ensuring the safety and well-being of all individuals in state custody. The Department of Corrections has several contracts in place with a variety of medical providers. Currently, the Department contracts with Wellpath, an independent medical provider, to afford those in state custody access to medical care and treatment; Diamond Pharmaceuticals has the contract for all prescription medication; Mid-America has the contract for dental care. These vendors are responsible for employing qualified medical personnel and ensuring they meet applicable licensing and professional requirements. All employees providing services through these contracted vendors are employed by the vendor and not the state. For a list of medical providers/employees, you would need to contact the vendor directly. At any time, the Department is made aware of inappropriate behavior, misconduct, or actions not aligned with departmental policy, the vendor is immediately notified, and if warranted, the Department will request the employee not be allowed further admission to the prison. Thank you.”
LOUISIANA: “The Louisiana Department of Public Safety & Corrections takes all allegations of professional misconduct seriously and recognizes its responsibility to ensure that individuals employed in medical positions are qualified to perform their duties and provide appropriate care to those in our custody.
The Department thoroughly reviews matters brought to its attention and considers relevant circumstances, professional qualifications, licensure status, and applicable employment requirements when making hiring and personnel decisions. A history of disciplinary action or criminal involvement does not necessarily constitute an automatic disqualification from employment, provided an individual meets the legal and professional requirements of the position.
As an agency that emphasizes rehabilitation, reentry, and second chances for the individuals in our custody, we believe those principles should extend beyond the walls of our correctional facilities. It would be inconsistent with our mission to advocate for second chances while categorically denying employment opportunities to qualified individuals who have taken the necessary steps to move forward from past mistakes.
Our responsibility is to evaluate individuals based on their qualifications, their ability to fulfill the essential duties of their positions, and their adherence to the professional and ethical standards expected of Department employees. We remain committed to maintaining those standards while recognizing that past mistakes do not necessarily define an individual’s ability to contribute meaningfully to our workforce."
NEVADA: “Medical contractors are reviewed before being hired. We can’t release personnel information, but we can say any disciplinary cases were closed before hire.”
NORTH CAROLINA: “The Department of Adult Correction takes seriously its responsibility to provide health care services to the incarcerated population by providing care that is consistent with standards of care that would be received in the community.
The people on the list you provided are all currently employed with the NC Department of Adult Correction. For the five you highlighted, we are aware of the past actions by the NC Medical Board.
Those physicians are fully licensed to practice medicine in North Carolina with unrestricted licenses. They have resolved their past issues—none of which involved criminal allegations or charges—to the full satisfaction of the medical board.
All NCDAC employees undergo a thorough criminal background check before employment. With all our medical professionals, we monitor all licensure actions and review in detail every two years with re-credentialing.”
OREGON: “The health and well-being of those in our care is a high priority. Too often the people coming into our prison system have complex medical conditions, high mental health needs, substance use disorders, and co-occurring disorders. It’s also an aging population with approximately 1,400 adults in custody age 60 years or older. We recognize the challenges facing correctional healthcare in Oregon, and as an agency we are dedicated to addressing them with innovation and process improvement. Patient-centered care must be central to what we do, and I am grateful for the dedication and hard work of our healthcare staff. As we move forward, I am committed to a transparent process of change in our Health Services Division to ensure we have the leadership, resources, and support needed to provide the highest standard of care.”
SOUTH CAROLINA: “The SC Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation issues medical licenses and determines whether someone is eligible to practice medicine in South Carolina. Those licenses are necessary for employment. If someone has a valid medical license in SC, they are eligible to be considered for employment. Also, SCDC believes in second chances. Every day we ask employers and community members to give inmates second chances. A previous act does not always define a person’s current reality.”
TEXAS: “The agency partners with University of Texas Medical Branch and Texas Tech to conduct medical care. Thus, these individuals would be employees of those institutions. Please reach out to them.”
VERMONT: “Our medical provider is WellPath.”
WASHINGTON: “DOC holds its medical professionals to high standards. Before being hired, they are subjected to background checks through the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) and under the Prison Rape Elimination Act (PREA). We also seek board certifications, where appropriate, and confirm that candidates have an active license.
If a current employee is accused of misconduct that violates their license, the alleged violation is reported to the Department of Health and DOC also conducts its own investigation. If the allegations are substantiated and the individual loses their license, they are terminated.
Incarcerated individuals in our care and custody deserve excellent health care. The agency has made significant strides in recent years to improve the level of care we offer. Our Health Services division has transitioned to a model centered on the patient and focused on prevention to improve outcomes. We implemented a fatality review process that examines each unexpected death in our facilities to determine if anything could have been done differently. DOC is currently implementing a much-needed electronic health records system that will replace an antiquated and inefficient paper system.”
RESPONSES FROM PRISON MEDICINE CONTRACTORS TO QUESTIONS FROM INVESTIGATETV
THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS MEDICAL BRANCH: “The University of Texas Medical Branch is committed to providing patients in the Texas Department of Criminal Justice system with safe, high-quality care. Everyone UTMB hires for Correctional Managed Care must go through TDCJ’s clearance process before they start. When we hire licensed clinicians, UTMB reviews their licensure and board history. After that, they are required to report any change in license status to UTMB. Any exception is reviewed on a case-by-case basis and approved by TDCJ. As a matter of policy, UTMB does not comment on individual personnel matters.”
Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center: “Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center is committed to providing safe, high-quality healthcare to the patients we serve, including those in the Texas Department of Criminal Justice (TDCJ) system. TTUHSC maintains rigorous standards for clinical quality, patient safety and professional accountability.
Prior to employment, all physicians undergo a comprehensive credentialing process that includes verification of licensure, training, qualifications, professional history and review of any disciplinary actions or restrictions associated with their medical license. When appropriate, other specialists, including representatives from human resources, compliance and legal, may provide input on a pending application. Physicians hired to provide care through TTUHSC’s correctional healthcare programs must also complete the TDCJ’s clearance process before beginning employment.
Following employment, concerns related to patient care or professional conduct are evaluated through established peer review processes and may result in corrective action, termination, and, when appropriate, reporting to the Texas Medical Board.
As a matter of policy, TTUHSC does not comment on individual personnel matters."
WEXFORD: “Wexford Health appreciates your inquiry, but we do not have any comment or response at this time.”

title: A spectacular November week ahead
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Strong high pressure over the Ohio Valley will control the pattern over the next week or so and bring with it unseasonably warm temperatures and sun splashed skies. We do remain in a fairly severe drought here in Maine but there will not be a hint of precip over the next week and temperatures may reach as much as 15-20 degrees above normal by Friday with highs near or above 60. Lows will remain more seasonable with the clear skies ahead but the days will be noticeably warm for this time of year.
Tonight: Mainly clear and chilly
Lows will drop into the 20s tonight, a few degrees colder than last night with clear skies. Winds W 5-10 mph.
Tomorrow: Warming up
Temps will continue to climb tomorrow with abundant sunshine and highs in the middle 50s with a few colder spots staying in the 40s. Winds NW 5-10 mph.
Tuesday night: Seasonable lows and clear
Lows will drop to right around 30 or so for most with the usual cold spots in the 20s. Light winds.
Wednesday: Warming trend continues
Clear skies will continue for most with a few clouds possible up north and temps will continue to climb to the upper 50s for most.
Wednesday night and beyond: Typical lows for November but much above average highs
While lows will be quite typical, right around freezing or a bit below, the highs will most certainly be not. Highs later in the week may reach above 60 for some and provide a downright balmy week for mid November in Maine. The next chance for rain likely isn’t until late in the weekend into next week, but that is way too far away to know how that will pan out.
Monday night: Mostly clear with lows in the 20s and 30s. Light winds.
Tuesday: Warming up with highs in the upper 40s to mid 50s. Winds light.
Tuesday night: Clear with lows in the 20s and 30s. Winds light.
Wednesday: The warmup continues with highs in the middle to upper 50s. Light winds.
Thursday: Very warm with highs near 60. Winds light.

title: A guide to Maine’s expanded property tax break for veterans
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine veterans who never served during a war will be eligible for a special property tax break for the first time starting April 1, and veterans with serious service-connected disabilities will see far larger exemptions.
The change was included in Gov. Janet Mills’ last state budget, which folds the state’s homestead, veterans and blind exemptions into one program. It is based on a bill from state Rep. Benjamin Hymes, R-Waldo, a retired Navy veteran.
Here’s what to know.
What’s changing?
Veterans now get a $6,000 exemption on their home’s value if they served during a federally recognized war period and are 62 or older, or if they get a federal total disability pension. Hymes told lawmakers that works out to roughly $100 a year in savings, an amount he said was too small to be meaningful.
Starting with the tax year that begins April 1, 2027, the wartime requirement is gone. Every eligible veteran gets an added exemption on top of the $25,000 homestead exemption for all in-state homeowners.
Who is eligible, and for how much?
You must meet homestead exemption requirements by living in the home and owning it for the previous 12 months. The law defines a veteran as someone honorably discharged after active duty.
Veterans with no VA service-connected disability rating, or a rating below 60%, get an extra $5,000 if they are younger than 62 and $6,000 if they are 62 or older.
Veterans rated 60% or higher get more. The extra exemption is $10,000 at a 60% rating and rises by $10,000 for each 10 percentage points, reaching $50,000 at 100%.
How much will it save me?
That depends on your town’s tax rate and your exemption level. At the statewide average of about $12.80 per $1,000 of value, the $5,000 exemption is modest at about $64 a year. But a 100% disabled veteran would save about $640, or $960 counting the homestead exemption.
The savings will first show up on 2027 property tax bills.
How do I apply?
Veterans who already get an exemption do not need to reapply unless they qualify for a larger one under the new tiers, according to Maine Revenue Services. Everyone else must apply to their local assessor by April 1, while veterans in the Unorganized Territory apply to Maine Revenue Services.
But you can’t apply yet, because the state’s current application was written for the old law. Hymes said the state plans to use the weeks before the deadline to get updated forms to towns. They should be there by the spring.
Veterans will need a DD-214 discharge form or a U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs benefit summary letter. For the disability tiers, they will need a VA letter showing their rating.
What about surviving family?
An unremarried surviving spouse or minor child of a dead veteran can claim the exemption the veteran would have gotten, as can some parents.
Who pays for it?
The state will reimburse cities and towns for 76% of lost revenue, costing nearly $5.1 million in the 2027-28 budget year and almost $6 million the year after, according to the Legislature’s fiscal office.
The Maine Municipal Association opposed the change, warning the state could later cut its share. That’s a common position for the advocacy group on measures that could increase costs for member cities and towns.

title: Study estimates how much pollution data centers produce
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Study estimates how much pollution data centers produce
The 400 largest data centers in the United States put more heat-trapping gas in the air in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did, and that was before the artificial intelligence boom really got going, according to a Harvard University study published Monday.
Meanwhile, negotiators at the United Nations COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, launched a voluntary pledge Monday for companies and countries to power the world's data centers with clean energy and be more open about their power and water consumption and emissions.
“We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet-heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow,” United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said Monday during the launch of the pledge. “Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now, making climate disasters even worse.”
The pledge also calls for focusing the power of artificial intelligence on solving the challenging problem of climate change and reflects concerns about AI's ever-expanding environmental footprint. The political backlash has played out in U.S. elections and major local objections to new sites.
The explosion of new and planned data centers also has prompted a push for new sources of power generation that has the biggest tech companies failing to reach their climate goals, with their electricity consumption rising 240% between 2022 and 2025, according to a new report by the advocacy group Climate Action Against Disinformation.
Study quantifies how much big data centers pollute
Harvard researchers looked at 403 of the largest U.S. data centers between May 2024 and April 2025 using available data and modeling to analyze their electricity use and emissions. They estimated electricity use by the centers produced around 28.3 million tons of carbon dioxide, according to a study in Monday's Nature Sustainability.
More than half of their 82 terawatt hours of electricity use — enough to power nearly 7 million homes for a year — came from fossil fuels, which are the primary cause of global warming, the researchers found.
The emissions estimate is two to three times what previous studies had shown, said study senior author Francesca Dominici, a Harvard biostatistics professor.
“It is the equivalent to the CO2 emission of an entire state like Michigan or a small European country,” Dominici said, adding that plans for 2,000 more data centers make that quantity more worrisome for the future. “We are going backwards toward the goal of controlling CO2 emissions.”
Several outside experts in climate, energy and artificial intelligence said Monday’s study made sense and reached realistic conclusions, finding the use of modeling reasonable because companies aren’t open about power consumption and pollution.
“We cannot manage environmental impacts effectively without reliable measurements and disclosure,” said Fengqi You, a Cornell University energy systems scientist who wasn’t part of the study. “Ultimately, the environmental footprint of AI is not fixed. It depends on where we build data centers, how efficiently they operate, and how we supply their electricity.”
A voluntary pledge proposed at climate talks
The “Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge,” launched by U.N. climate talks host Turkey and the International Telecommunication Union, says data centers should use clean power and efficient energy and water systems.
The pledge also calls for AI systems to be designed and managed responsibly, using environmental standards and reusing or recycling infrastructure and hardware. It says the environmental impacts of data centers should be assessed and shared and signatories should support using artificial intelligence as a climate solution.
COP31 President Murat Kurum has said world leaders at the talks must openly discuss AI’s growing energy consumption and start setting the terms.
AI produces pollution but also offers hope
One of the biggest climate fighters, former U.S. Vice President Al Gore, said while it is essential that data centers are powered by carbon-free energy, he is less concerned about the emissions from AI than others. And he is hopeful that its computing power can find novel ways of fighting climate change.
In an Associated Press interview, Gore quoted a study by prominent British economist and climate advocate Nicholas Stern, who predicted by 2030 “we will see 6 to 9% reduction in emissions of greenhouse gases because of the use of advanced AI in finding new ways to be far more efficient in the use of materials and energy.”
Caleb Max, president of the National Artificial Intelligence Association, said, “AI will solve not only the energy usage issues that data centers face, but unlock numerous currently unknown advances in science and technology that will address climate change and make lives better for humanity. I respect the concerns about energy and water consumption from data centers, but the fears may be overblown.”
But Climate Action Against Disinformation spokesman Philip Newell was skeptical.
“We have hope in one hand and then harms in the other,” Newell said. “They’re selling us hope while hiding the harms from us.”
Could we use the heat from data centers?
The computing equipment in data centers generates a lot of waste heat that is vented into the atmosphere. One approach to reducing data centers' environmental impact is to capture heat that can be used for nearby homes and businesses.
The Danish engineering and manufacturing company Danfoss said waste heat is “the world’s largest untapped energy source,” and reusing it can replace natural gas as a heat source. It identified data centers as a significant source of constant heat, particularly as their power consumption grows.
The International Energy Agency estimates data centers could provide enough heat for around 10% of European homes by 2030, if that heat were fully integrated into district systems that supply heat and hot water to residents.
In remarks broadcast during COP31, European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jørgensen said Europe must replace imported fossil fuels by capturing heat that is going to waste and tapping into geothermal.
In another example of this approach, industrial development firm BaRupOn is building an advanced manufacturing campus in Texas that plans to use recaptured heat to generate additional electricity on site, CEO Balaji Tammabattula said. In North Dakota, the company is planning a data center that could feed heat to the community.
University of Colorado Boulder Professor Gregor Henze said it's a perfect marriage because modern data centers that rely on liquid rather than air cooling are a fairly constant source of heat at the right temperature for thermal energy networks.

title: Questions swirl around FAA's new SMART AI system, though officials say no link to ground stop
text:
Questions swirl around FAA's new SMART AI system, though officials say no link to ground stop
The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA's new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology.
But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration's SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems.
Officials say no connection to ground stop
The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there’s no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system, and the top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday.
Related video: What caused the nationwide ground stop and where does the investigation stand?
The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn’t caused by “the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”
But lawmakers and outside groups raised questions about the SMART system before Friday's ground stop. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails.
“Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” the Oct. 13 letter said. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.”
SMART, however, is not — at least not yet — set up for AI to be in charge of flight control. Rather, it is making recommendations to humans who do so.
What is the SMART system?
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a “cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics — into one platform.” SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories. 
The system's AI-supported engine synthesizes the data systems and shows a “comprehensive visualization” of where planes are going, how much traffic the system can handle and where congestion or weather could cause problems, according to the announcement. The idea is for specialists to then use the platform to fix problems before they arise.
The FAA says that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system's recommendations.
So SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers. That was three days before the ground stop.
According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested. The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals.
SMART is also supposed to help with weather-related issues faster.
Currently, the FAA blocks off portions of airspace affected by weather as “large, rectangular boxes,” according to the fact sheet, which doesn't reflect how weather actually looks, with quick-moving thunderstorms and storm systems that are “often irregular in shape, with narrow gaps or corridors that aircraft could safely fly through.”
To help with this, SMART gives the FAA and airspace operators a “clearer picture of how weather will affect air traffic over time,” allowing air traffic controllers to plan around storms and use available airspace instead of unnecessarily shutting down large areas.
No other country has a working AI air traffic tool like the SMART system, according to Michael McCormick, a former FAA airspace manager and an associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority, has a system in testing and several manufacturers are prototyping similar tools.
Concerns around relying on AI
While government officials and ASI, the company behind SMART, have stressed that its AI system is designed to assist humans and not run flight control, its deployment has raised concerns about relying on artificial intelligence when human lives are at stake, given that even the most advanced models are prone to hallucinations — when models fabricate false information and present it as fact.
Mike O’Donnell, a former top FAA official who worked for the agency for 17 years and now does aviation safety consulting work, said the agency “has got to make sure that this is just a tool in the toolbox and not the actual machine that’s doing the work.”
The FAA, he said, “cannot afford to be wrong on this.”
“It’s good to use it with the proper guardrails and backstops to ensure that they’re not giving wrong information to controllers based on what (AI) has come up with,” O’Donnell said. “There’s got to be a way to verify and validate what it’s doing to make sure that it’s not the wrong information.”
He cautioned against putting too much trust in AI “until we know for sure that it's proven itself time and time again. And that's going to take a while.”
The AI system's launch comes amid a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers around the country. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association has been raising concerns about this for more than a decade, telling Congress in 2015 that the shortage was at a crisis level. It said then that the FAA had missed its hiring targets for five years in a row. The union represents about 14,000 controllers, roughly 3,000 of them trainees. That said, experts say no AI system can replace the human air traffic controllers who spend years training for this highly demanding and stressful job.
In an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the SMART tool is designed for traffic managers who manage the entire U.S. airspace.
“The AI does the math, the AI does the computation,” Buckendorf told NPR, but it’s ultimately up to the human operator whether to take the system’s recommendation. “They make the decision, they are the decider, they are the judge.”

title: Conservationists are trying to save Louisiana’s cypress forests, here’s why
text:
ST. FRANCISVILLE, La. (InvestigateTV) — Sandy Couvillon of Alexandria was on a road trip with some friends when they spotted a sign for the Cat Island National Wildlife Refuge.
They made a quick detour for a ride down bumpy roads and a short hike down a walking trail for a look at the star attraction in this swamp, the largest tree east of the Sierra Nevada Mountains.
“It’s amazing, it’s worth the trip,” said Couvillon as she stood in the shadow of the National Champion Bald Cypress tree, 90 feet high, 17 feet in diameter and 50 feet around.
While no one knows its precise age, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service estimates the tree is 1,500 years old.
Will DeGravelles, director of land protection for the Nature Conservancy, said the tree’s size is difficult to capture.
“It really is hard to capture on camera and film and telling people. You kind of have to be here to really feel it,” DeGravelles said. “Cypress knees that are the height of people take hundreds of years to get that way.”
Why the giant survived
The tree survived logging in part because it was hollow and ill-shaped compared to other massive cypress trees, DeGravelles said.
The tree and others nearly as large thrive in one of few places where the Mississippi River remains connected to the landscape. Regular spring floods feed them fresh water and nutrients.
“A flood plain of this size that is connected naturally to its river and has a natural hydrology is very, very rare,” DeGravelles said.
Decades of loss
There were once 25 million acres of bottomland hardwood and swamps along the river, DeGravelles said. Many fell to logging. Along the coast, scientists say saltwater intrusion, a sinking delta, and sea-level rise remain threats.
“We’ve lost perhaps 50-75 percent of our bottomland hardwood and swamp forests across Louisiana,” DeGravelles said.
Replanting efforts
Each year, volunteers working with conservation groups plant thousands of young cypress trees.
“If we were to plant trees without the nutria protectors, even 20 years ago or today, we would see almost 100% mortality of those trees,” said Kristi Trail, who runs the Pontchartrain Conservancy.
“We need this storm surge buffer in these swamps to make sure those levees can do their job,” Trail said.
The Pontchartrain Conservancy says the success rate from the plantings now tops 95 percent.
MRGO closure key to success
The closure of the Mississippi River Gulf Outlet was key to the improved survival rate, Trail said.
The MRGO was built as a shortcut from the Port of New Orleans to the Gulf. During Hurricane Katrina, it funneled storm surge into St. Bernard and Orleans parishes. Scientists say the MRGO turned Lake Pontchartrain saltier and helped kill the cypress forests surrounding the lake.
“When MRGO was open, a lot of salt water was able to enter our basin, change the salinity of these soils, and a lot of these cypress trees died as a result,” Trail said.
Following Katrina, the Army Corps of Engineers installed a rock dam to close the waterway and later a surge barrier.
Scientists have been studying salinity levels to pinpoint areas that are now candidates for cypress plantings.
“We’ve been able to identify areas in the estuary like this, like the LaBranche Wetlands, that are now ready for reforestation,” said Pontchartrain Conservancy Chief Scientist Eva Hillman.
Results from earlier plantings
A planting roughly 15 years earlier on the east bank of the Mississippi River in Plaquemines Parish shows the potential. The trees now tower about 30 feet high.
The Caernarvon River diversion nearby feeds fresh water and nutrients into the area.
“Even just those few pulses of fresh water, with nutrients and sediments, increases the growth rate of the planted trees there,” Hillman said.
Conservation groups and a government program that pays farmers to convert marginal agricultural land back into forested wetlands have also contributed to restoration efforts. Some conversions last 30 years, some are permanent.
The Nature Conservancy says restoration efforts in the Mississippi River Valley recently hit 1 million acres.
“That’s a huge accomplishment and we have millions more acres to do,” DeGravelles said.
DeGravelles said Louisiana will never get back to 25 million acres of swamp, but the efforts are a start.
“We are not talking about restored forests. It will take decades for those to become fully mature forests like we’re standing in,” DeGravelles said.

title: Zoo monitoring Fiona the hippo after she ingested object ‘tossed’ by visitor
text:
CINCINNATI (WXIX/Gray News) — Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s hippopotamus, is being closely monitored after she ingested a knit cap that a visitor “accidentally tossed” into her habitat.
How the hat entered the habitat
According to a zoo spokesperson, the hat was tossed into the air in front of Fiona’s habitat at Hippo Cove and got caught by a ceiling fan. The fan then “catapulted” the hat into the 1-foot opening above the viewing windows.
“We probably couldn’t make that happen again if we tried. It was clearly an accident,” the spokesperson said.
Fiona’s care
The zoo’s veterinary team and hippo care staff are watching Fiona around the clock to help her pass the hat safely.
“Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self,” the zoo wrote in a Facebook post.
Until then, Fiona will not make an appearance at the Hippo Cove habitat.
Zoo’s request to visitors
“Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately,” the zoo said.
Officials said they will keep people updated on Fiona’s health.

title: Outside Angus King’s Augusta office, protesters challenge his Schumer support
text:
AUGUSTA — Stacy Leafsong is frustrated with Sen. Angus King.
She helped organize a protest of about 50 Mainers on Monday in front of the Edmund S. Muskie Federal Building in Augusta, where King has an office, to demonstrate why: King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, is supporting New York Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.
Schumer has led Senate Democrats since 2016 and, Leafsong said, represents the old guard, the status quo. Voters told elected leaders on Nov. 3, in a sweeping “blue wave” election that took out even 30-year incumbent Sen. Susan Collins that the status quo won’t do anymore, Leafsong said.
“It’s consistent with the way that King has, I think, been leading the state of Maine as senator: milquetoast,” Leafsong, an organizer with the Maine Common Good Coalition, said of King’s support of Schumer.
Dozens on the sidewalk held signs demanding King support Schumer’s challenger for Senate majority leader, Sen. Chris Van Hollen. One sign said “Chuck Chuck.”
They later delivered a letter to King’s office, signed by the protesters, urging King to rescind his support of Schumer.
Van Hollen, a progressive from Maryland, said last week that he would challenge his party’s leader after being encouraged by several of his colleagues. Van Hollen has said his path to winning the leadership race is “wide open,” and that he has the support of more than 15 senators. He said on CNN’s “State of the Union” that his candidacy isn’t about Schumer, but about earning voters’ trust by “not going to business as usual, not going back to the status quo.”
Schumer, for his part, has already declared victory in the intraparty race for majority leader, telling The Associated Press last week that he was “going to win it.”
King’s soon-to-be junior counterpart, Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, meanwhile, said he would not support Schumer in the upcoming leadership election. He’s long aligned himself with the progressive wing of the party, led by Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders — one of Van Hollen’s earliest vocal supporters.
“Senator-Elect Jackson has already made clear that he believes it’s time for new leadership in the Senate,” Hilary Barrett, a transition team aide and Jackson’s campaign manager, said in a statement Friday. “He looks forward to speaking with Senator Van Hollen in the coming weeks. The next Senate majority leader needs to be ready to do what’s right for working families and the people of Maine. That’s where Senator-Elect Jackson’s focus remains.”
King made his support of Schumer public in a statement Thursday, saying “Schumer is one of the principal architects” of the Democrats’ biggest electoral win in decades. Plus, Schumer has the “experience and unique mastery of the Senate process” to take advantage of Democrats’ expansive majority, King said.
“Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?” King said in the statement.
A spokesperson for King declined to add to that statement Monday.
Schumer tried to influence the race for Collins’ seat, recruiting Gov. Janet Mills to run for Senate. But Mills floundered badly, and lost the June primary to the scandal-plagued Graham Platner, who later withdrew from the race — leaving the door open for Jackson.
The demonstration outside King’s Augusta office was a rare sight: King has not often caught the ire of protesters since he entered the Senate in 2013. He often polls as Maine’s most-liked politician, and he’s easily won reelection twice. But between his vote last year to end the federal government shutdown without concessions from Republicans on public health insurance and his recent support of Schumer, King has engendered recent criticism from the left flank of the Democratic Party.
Another progressive organization, People Powered Maine, also sent a text blast to supporters on Friday encouraging them to write to King about his decision to back Schumer.
Kay Mann, a Hallowell resident who held the “Chuck Chuck” sign, said King’s support of Schumer was unsurprising, if frustrating. Both represent Democratic leadership that, in her view, has failed to effectively check President Donald Trump during his second term.
Voters, she said, demand more.
“Everything gets watered down,” Evelyn Dean, a Democrat from Richmond, said on the Western Avenue sidewalk. “Healthcare, the war in Iran — he might take little steps, but he doesn’t really do anything.”
Dean said she thought King’s statement announcing his support of Schumer was tone-deaf: The whole system is broken, she said, and Schumer isn’t immune to accountability just because he is a Democrat.
“We voted with the idea that we don’t just want to stop something, but move forward to something better,” said Elizabeth Leonard, a retired Colby College professor and regular at these central Maine protests.
Leonard said she was surprised by just how early King declared his support for Schumer, with weeks before the majority leader election — scheduled for Dec. 1 — and before an open debate could take shape.
Leafsong said the same. It was disheartening to see King preempt that debate with “tone-deafness for the voice of the people,” she said. At age 82, King seems like he’s comfortable in his Senate seat and likely not worried about reelection, Leafsong said.
“He can either listen and show that he can attune to his constituents, or he’s going to just run the old party line,” she said.

title: Cony to play for state football title
text:
LEWISTON, Maine (WABI) - Cony blanked Fryeburg Academy, 28-0, to win Class B North on Friday at Lewiston High School.
The Rams return to the state title game with a reloaded roster after last year’s trip to the Gold Ball game.

title: Woman and her dog killed after being hit by car, police say
text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily/Gray News) — A woman and her dog died after being hit by a car in central Phoenix on Saturday evening, police said.
The crash happened near 7th Street and Indian School Road around 6:30 p.m., according to police.
Police said the woman was walking her dog across the street outside of a crosswalk when they were hit. Both were pronounced dead at the scene.
The driver stayed at the scene and is cooperating, police said. Police have not determined whether impairment was a factor.
Police closed the area around the crash scene while detectives with the vehicular crimes unit are investigating.

title: United Airlines says it resolved a technology issue that affected departing flights
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — United Airlines said Monday that it had resolved a technology issue that delayed departing flights, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop.
Chicago-based United said in a statement that while some flights were delayed because of the issue Monday afternoon, flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not impacted. It also said, “There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”
United apologized to customers for the inconvenience on social media.
A recording posted on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.
The flight tracking website FlightAware showed United with 418 delayed flights late Monday afternoon.
The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days.
Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem.
On Friday, the FAA ordered every flight grounded because a new router that was installed malfunctioned and overwhelmed the aging air traffic control system. And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored.

In an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the SMART tool is designed for traffic managers who manage the entire U.S. airspace.
“The AI does the math, the AI does the computation,” Buckendorf told NPR, but it’s ultimately up to the human operator whether to take the system’s recommendation. “They make the decision, they are the decider, they are the judge.”

title: Phil Collins inducted into Rock & Roll Hall of Fame for 2nd time; speaks on health
text:
Phil Collins inducted into Rock & Roll Hall of Fame for 2nd time; speaks on health
Music legend Phil Collins made a rare public appearance this weekend for his second induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.
The 75-year-old singer was originally inducted in 2010 as part of Genesis, but is now being honored for his career as a solo artist.
Collins has dealt with a number of health issues over recent years, beginning with a neck injury in 2007 that left him with nerve damage.
When Collins took the stage to accept his honor over the weekend, he joked with the crowd, saying, "Thank you so much. Thank you. I'm really not as bad as it looks. I'm much better."
The "In the Air Tonight" singer said he was "a well man now," and even hinted that he may be working on new music.
Collins was forced to retire from performing in 2022 due to a myriad of health struggles on top of his nerve damage, including knee problems, kidney issues and type 2 diabetes.
"Everything started to go wrong," the drummer said. "So at one point I didn't think I'd live, let alone go on the road again. But just the other night I was talking to the kids about it, and everyone got excited, including myself, that it's not beyond the realm of possibility of doing some shows."
The singer had given a health update to the BBC in January, saying his health issues were an "ongoing thing."
"I've had challenges with my knee. I had everything that could go wrong with me, did go wrong with me," he said. "I got COVID in hospital. My kidneys started to back up. Everything seemed to converge at the same time … I can walk, albeit with assistance, you know, crutches or whatever."
During his Hall of Fame acceptance speech, Collins looked back at his career, expressing gratitude for everyone who has been by his side over the years, including his three ex-wives, whom he thanked for giving him "five great children."
He said he has "really been just very, very lucky" to find success in music.
"I grew up just wanting to play the drums," Collins said. "That's all I wanted to do. From the age of 5, that's all I've done. Everything else has been a really happy accident. I can't believe when I look back how life has gone, and I've got so many people to thank."

title: Supreme Court declines to hear challenge to Maryland 'sensitive places' gun law
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court declined Monday to consider a challenge to a Maryland law restricting where people can carry guns.
The law prohibits carrying concealed weapons into schools, mass transit, bars and other areas deemed sensitive places.
The high court declined the case without comment. But Justice Clarence Thomas wrote to say he’s skeptical about the law and others like it. He expressed support for weighing the issue again in a “more narrowly focused case.”
The refusal comes as the court prepares to hear arguments over state laws banning AR-15s and similar semiautomatic firearms, measures that are often called assault weapons bans.
The conservative-majority court has handed down several decisions backing Second Amendment rights, including a recent ruling striking down wide-ranging gun-carry restrictions in Hawaii.
The high court has upheld some gun restrictions, though, including a law aimed at protecting victims of domestic violence.

title: Portland Jetport back to normal operations after nationwide stop
text:
Flights to and from the Portland International Jetport have resumed after the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years canceled thousands of flights over the weekend.
Operations were mostly back to normal Monday morning, Assistant Airport Director Zachary Sundquist said.
On Friday, more than a dozen flights in and out the jetport were canceled and several were delayed. Effects from the stoppage lingered Saturday, as 23 flights were canceled and 14 were delayed, according to FlightAware.
Trump administration officials have said the nation’s air traffic control system was overloaded when new technology was added, causing gaps in communications and radar. The shutdown lasted more than four hours.
This story contains reporting from The Associated Press.

title: A Maine man took his friend into the woods for one final deer hunt
text:
This story was originally published in December 2022.
Jerry Galusha and his best friend, Doug Cooke, shared a friendship that dates back to 1984, when they were living in Rangeley and were introduced by mutual friends.
Over the years, they often went fishing or deer hunting, activities they both enjoyed immensely.
“The relationship that we have is just unbelievable,” Galusha said. “We’ve had some really amazing adventures.”
This fall, Galusha was confronted with a heart-wrenching task. He would take Cooke into the woods, one last time, in search of a big buck.
The difference was that this time they would not be walking the tote roads and trails together. Instead, Galusha would be carrying Cooke’s cremains in his backpack.
Cooke died on Sept. 5 at age 61 after a long struggle with renal failure. Galusha said after 40 years of dialysis or living with a transplanted kidney, Cooke opted to cease treatment and enter hospice care when his third transplant failed.
Doctors had originally told Cooke he would be lucky to celebrate his 30th birthday. Thus, he tried all his life to avoid getting too emotionally attached to people. He seldom asked anyone for favors.
Cooke and Galusha hadn’t seen each other much in recent years as Galusha focused on raising a family. But in late August, Cooke left a voicemail for Galusha explaining that he planned to enter hospice care.
Cooke told Galusha he didn’t need to do anything, but wanted him to know. He did not want to become a burden to anyone else.
“His body was telling him that he’s had enough,” Galusha said. “He couldn’t golf. He couldn’t play his guitar. He hadn’t been hunting in years.”
Galusha couldn’t let it end like that. In spite of Cooke’s reluctance to have his old friend see him in such poor health, he went to visit him.
But as Cooke faced his own mortality, he asked one favor of Galusha.
“He said, ‘Promise me one thing, could you please, just one time, take me in to Upper Dam to go fishing before you dump my ashes?’” Galusha said.
The dam separates Mooselookmeguntic (Cupsuptic) Lake and Richardson Lake north of Rangeley. It was a favorite spot of theirs, one Cooke introduced to Galusha, who grew up in New York.
“He really loved the wilderness and Rangeley,” Galusha said of Cooke, who was a Vermont native.
Galusha immediately said yes but, knowing how much Cooke also enjoyed hunting, he didn’t feel as though the fishing trip was enough to adequately honor his friend.
“I said, I’m going to take you for the whole deer season, every time I go,” Galusha said. “He looked at me and started crying and said, ‘That would be so awesome.’
“It was hard. We cried and hugged each other,” he said.
When Galusha went deer hunting near his home in Rangeley during the third week of November — a week the two buddies often spent together over the years — he tried his best to make it like old times.
Galusha spared no effort. He carried the cardboard urn containing Cooke’s cremains inside a camouflage can, which was wrapped with a photo showing Cooke posing with a nice buck he had harvested many years earlier.
He also packed Cooke’s blaze orange hat and vest, along with his grunt tube, compass, doe bleat can, deer scents and a set of rattling antlers.
Galusha chronicled the events of each hunting day by posting to Cooke’s Facebook page, complete with observations, recollections and photos.
Lots of deer were seen and there was one encounter with a buck, but after missing initially, Galusha refused to take a bad shot as the deer was partially obscured by undergrowth.
“I just did what Doug would have done. He’s not going to shoot and I wasn’t going to shoot,” Galusha said.
He spoke reverently about Cooke’s resilience through the years in the face of his constant battle with health problems, which included not only kidney failure, dialysis and transplants, but four hip replacements and, eventually, a heart attack.
The arrival of muzzleloader season provided one more week to hunt. On Friday, Dec. 2, Galusha walked more than 3 miles along a gated road to an area where he had seen deer a week earlier.
That got him off the beaten track, away from other potential hunters, something Cooke would have appreciated.
“He wasn’t afraid to go do stuff,” Galusha said. “It might take us a little bit longer, but he didn’t care.”
Galusha, who still often refers to Cooke in the present tense, said he vocalized some of his reflections while in the woods. He saw eagles, which he thought might be Cooke keeping an eye on him.
“I talked to him a lot,” Galusha said, who also enjoyed telling the handful of hunters he encountered that he was not out alone, rather with his friend.
He then explained the story of his promise to Cooke and reverently removed the urn from his pack to show them.
When Galusha finally saw the buck, it wasn’t quite close enough. He uses one of Cooke’s favorite tactics to coax the deer closer.
Galusha tried the grunt tube, and then the doe bleat can, but the deer didn’t seem to hear it. Then, he blew harder on the grunt tube and finally got the buck’s attention.
“I irked one right in, that’s what Doug would say,” said Galusha, recalling Cooke’s affection for using the alternating calls.
The spikehorn turned and walked directly at Galusha, who shot it.
“I cried,” he said of the moment, recalling that Cooke had been there when he shot his first antlered deer, also a spikehorn.
During the long drag back to his truck, Galusha had plenty of time to think about how much Cooke would have enjoyed the hunt — and watching him make the drag.
At one point, a crew of loggers had approached.
“I was pointing to the sky saying, ‘We got it done,’ shaking my hand,” Galusha said. “A guy came up behind me and said, ‘You all set?’ and I’m like, yup.”
Cooke and Galusha had lived together for 10 years at one point, but they also had gone long periods without talking with each other. Even so, whenever they were reunited it was as if they had never been apart.
The last few visits were difficult. Cooke’s health was failing, but Galusha just wanted to be there for his buddy.
“It was emotional,” said Galusha, who was present when Cooke died. “I held his hand to his last breath.”
Next spring, hopefully when the fish are biting and the bugs aren’t, Galusha will grant Cooke — who he described as a fabulous fisherman — his final wish by taking him fishing at Upper Dam, just like they used to do.
“I’m thinking maybe around his birthday [July 19]. It might be sooner, depending on how buggy it is,” said Galusha, who expects to make more than one excursion with Cooke.
Galusha said he will know when it’s time to say goodbye.
“I really don’t want to let him go, but I promised him I would, so I will,” he said.

title: Everybody sells insurance. What businesses need is a partner.
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How Paul White Company, Chalmers Insurance Group, and MEMIC worked together to strengthen safety and business performance.
“Everybody sells insurance.” That is how Paul White describes the workers’ compensation marketplace. “What we were looking for was a partner,” he says. “Someone who answers the phone. Someone who shows up. Someone who is invested in your success.”
For Paul White Company, that partnership has helped turn workplace safety into a shared business priority. Founded by White’s parents in 1970 as a tile contractor, the family company has grown to serve residential and commercial customers across Maine, New Hampshire, and other parts of New England.
The work is demanding. Flooring installation can be hard on backs, shoulders, and knees, while stone and quartz countertops require careful handling. White says the company has focused on removing hazardous steps, improving material handling, addressing trip risks, and strengthening protection around cutting tools and fabrication work.
The most meaningful change, he says, came from involving the people closest to the work. Rather than treating safety as a top-down directive, the company asked for input across roles and gave team members ownership of the solutions.
“What I am most proud of is the buy-in from the ground up,” White says. “It was not just an ownership-driven thing. It was a lot of stakeholders in the process.”
That commitment is supported by Chalmers Insurance Group and MEMIC. Luke Goodine, account executive at Chalmers, describes the relationship as a three-pillar risk management program: a client committed to improvement, a carrier with hands-on safety and claims resources, and an agency that keeps communication moving among everyone involved.
“When we need help, MEMIC is willing to do what needs to be done,” Goodine says. “The agency ties those pieces together and creates communication between Paul White Company and MEMIC.”
The partners meet quarterly to review claims, discuss changing risks, prepare for key experience-modification dates, and make sure open issues do not linger when a conversation could move them forward. MEMIC specialists have also visited the workplace, helped assess risks, shared training resources, and collaborated on practical improvements.
White says the approach felt supportive rather than restrictive. “It was very collaborative,” he says. “There was great dialogue about why things were being done a certain way, and then we came up with a quick path forward.”
That sustained effort has produced measurable results. Paul White Company’s experience modification factor improved from 1.37 to a projected 0.82. The data also showed fewer injuries, fewer incidents, and faster returns to work.
But the number is not the whole story. Better safety means people go home safely. When an injury does occur, the partnership helps the company respond quickly, keep the injured person connected, and build a plan for recovery and a safe return to work.
Both White and Goodine emphasize that safety has no finish line. Risks change as operations change, and progress can slip if attention fades. The answer is consistency: scheduled conversations, clear responsibility, an openness to feedback, and a plan for what happens when something goes wrong.
“It is not something we wished would happen,” White says. “It is something we actively made happen.”
Goodine encourages other businesses to take advantage of the expertise already available through their carrier and agent. Start with a conversation, invite a walkthrough, ask questions, and dedicate a group with the authority to act.
“Companies may not realize how much MEMIC wants to show up,” Goodine says. “It is in everyone’s best interest that people stay safe and no one has a claim.”
For Paul White Company, Chalmers, and MEMIC, the lesson is simple: workers’ compensation is more than a policy. It is an ongoing business strategy built on listening, shared accountability, and trusted partnership.

title: Live updates: The bottom half of the AP Top 25 may be in for a shakeup
text:
The top 10 teams in the AP Top 25 were undefeated this past weekend, but the rankings should still be in for a shuffle after losses by a whopping nine teams in the bottom half of the poll.
The rankings are coming a day later than usual because the national air traffic ground stoppage pushed the Mississippi-Oklahoma game to Sunday.
Leading off the losing column is No. 13 Kentucky, which suffered a narrow defeat at the hands of an unranked Florida team. No. 14 Houston, No. 19 Ole Miss, No. 20 South Carolina and No. 23 New Mexico also suffered blows from unranked teams.
Near the top of the poll, it wasn’t all easy. No. 2 Utah remained undefeated only after coming from behind three times in the second half to pull out a 40-39 win at No. 22 Arizona. Arch Manning drove No. 8 Texas to the go-ahead touchdown with three seconds left to vanquish No. 24 LSU’s playoff hopes in a 22-21 road win.
Stick around for poll projections, voter Q&A and live updates when the latest rankings drop at 2 p.m. EST.
Who decides the rankings?
By THE ASSOCIATED PRESS
AP Top 25 voters are writers and broadcasters who cover college football.
AP employees do not vote, but they do choose the voters, and they seek wide representation from all over the country. This season, there are 69 voters.
The focus begins with voter representation in states with a Bowl Subdivision school, and the total number of voters from each state increases with the number of FBS teams. There are also spots reserved for national voters.
The AP allows broad latitude for voters to determine their rankings. They are urged to base their votes on performance, not reputation or preseason speculation (except, of course, for the always provocative preseason poll); to avoid regional bias, for or against; to pay attention to head-to-head results; and to make significant changes if desired.
Another easy win for No. 1 Georgia
By MAURA CAREY
A ranked opponent has proven to be a manageable task for the top-ranked Bulldogs this season, and the team cruised to a 48-21 win against Mizzou (No. 22 CFP) on Saturday.
Georgia got off to another hot start, going on a 31-0 run in the first 1 1/2 quarters. Two of those touchdowns belonged to running back Nate Frazier, who finished the outing with 72 rushing yards and three touchdowns.
In Isiah Canion’s first game since September, the Georgia Tech transfer proved to be another deep threat for the Bulldogs, finishing the outing with 63 receiving yards and a touchdown.

The Portland store will replace Thos. Moser’s Freeport showroom, which will close later this year. Freeport employees will be offered positions in Portland.

title: South Portland city network outage prompts cybersecurity investigation
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND, Maine (WABI) - The city of South Portland is investigating a network disruption that has impacted municipal computer systems and services.
The city said initial information suggests the incident may involve “bad actors,” and it is coordinating its response with state and federal agencies.
According to officials, the duration of the outage is currently unknown.
City Hall, the Assessing Office and the South Portland Library are closed to the public Monday while staff work with the IT Department on restoring some services.
Other city buildings will remain open, although some services will be unavailable, including the city phone system, in-person credit card payments, online administrative portals, mapping services and printed materials such as receipts.
Separately, the city’s Citizen Self Service online bill payment system had been experiencing intermittent outages since late the previous week.
The city said that the vendor issue was not connected to the network disruption.
Due to the payment problems, the property tax deadline has been extended to Monday, Nov. 23. Residents are still allowed to leave payments in the secure drop boxes outside City Hall.
Vehicle registration renewals remain available through the state’s Rapid Renewal website, according to the city.
The city said it would provide further updates as its review progressed.
