title: Johnny Depp film ‘Ebenezer’ gets actor first No. 1 opening in 8 years
text:
(AP) - Johnny Depp is back at the top of the box office with his first studio movie in eight years, and since fallout from a contentious libel trial against ex-wife Amber Heard left his future in Hollywood in jeopardy.
But six years after he was asked to leave the “Fantastic Beasts” franchise, and three years after Depp said that he had “no further need for Hollywood,” “Ebenezer,” a Paramount Pictures release, opened in first place with about $19 million in ticket sales, according to studio estimates on Sunday. Paramount released it in 3,535 theaters.
While it might be a far cry from the heights of the “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchise, which twice opened over $100 million, or even the $62 million opening of “Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald” in 2018, it is a solid start for the film, which cost a reported $38 million to produce. Internationally, it made $23 million from 63 markets, adding up to a $42 million global debut.
Outside of his franchise fare, Depp more often had openings in the $20 million range (as with “Black Mass” and “Public Enemies”).
The audience for “Ebenezer” was about 52% female and 81% over the age of 25, according to PostTrak exit polls. About 65% of ticket buyers said they would “definitely” recommend the film to friends. Less than half, or 47%, of the “kid” demographic (ages 12 and under) said they would tell their friends they “must see it right away.”
The Charles Dickens-inspired tale is rated PG-13 and directed by Ti West, who is best known for the horror franchise X. Critics were not as warm as audiences about the film. It’s currently sitting at 52% on Rotten Tomatoes. Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin and Daisy Ridley also star.
The question still remains as to whether this marks a major comeback for Depp, but time might tell. In exit polls, 51% of moviegoers cited Depp as their reason for attending the film. Depp’s next film, a revenge thriller called “Day Drinker,” is set for a March release from Lionsgate.
“The personal lives of stars generally don’t impact the box office. It really comes down to the movie,” said Paul Dergarabedian, the head of marketplace trends for Rentrak. “The key now will be its long-term playability.”
Sony’s “Ghost Soldier” and Amazon MGM Studios’ “How to Rob a Bank” also opened this weekend to less fanfare. “Ghost Soldier,” an action film starring Jim Caviezel, debuted in sixth place with $5.2 million from 2,558 theaters. “How to Rob a Bank” landed in seventh place with just under $5.2 million from 2,810 theaters. Internationally, it made $5.1 million. The film from “The Fall Guy” director David Leitch had a reported net production budget of $40 million. Starring Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz and Pete Davidson, “How to Rob a Bank” did not receive good reviews.
“The Cat in the Hat” landed in second place in its second weekend in theaters with $11.4 million, followed by “Godzilla Minus Zero” in third place with $8.3 million (down a whopping 73% from its opening). Fourth place went to “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” also in its second weekend, with $5.5 million. And the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” rounded out the top five with just under $5.5 million, bringing its domestic total to $89 million.
“The ‘You Can See Everything’ phenomenon continues,” Dergarabedian said. “It has become the ‘have you seen’ movie of the moment.”
“Wild Horse Nine” also added 1,075 theaters in its second weekend, where it earned $4.6 million. Jordan Firstman’s “Club Kid” had one of the best limited expansions of the year with $756,060 on 27 screens. And James Gray’s acclaimed crime thriller “Paper Tiger” opened in six locations in New York and Los Angeles to $215,009 before it expands nationwide next week.
Overall it was a slower weekend than last with around $86 million in total ticket sales from North American theaters. Business should pick up next weekend, however, with the release of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”
Top 10 movies by domestic box office
With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak:
1. “Ebenezer,” $19 million.
2. “The Cat in the Hat,” $11.4 million.
3. “Godzilla Minus Zero,” $8.3 million.
4. “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” $5.5 million.
5. “You Can See Everything,” $5.5 million.
6. “Ghost Soldier,” $5.2 million.
7. “How to Rob a Bank,” $5.2 million.
8. “Wild Horse Nine,” $4.6 million.
9. “Wildwood,” $4.5 million.
10. “Clayface,” $3.7 million.

title: First look at Arkansas radio site possibly linked to FAA national ground stop
text:
A look at the Arkansas radio site with possible issue that led to an FAA national ground stop
We’re getting our first look at the radio site that may be partly to blame for last week’s nationwide ground stop.
The FAA is investigating a router upgrade at South Arkansas Regional Airport in El Dorado, which is in South Central Arkansas, near the state's border with Louisiana.
Workers at the airport pointed out the specific radio site the FAA has identified as a potential source of the disruption. The agency believes a new router upgrade inside a brick building at the site may have caused system-wide instability.
According to the FAA, crews were upgrading the radio communications site, replacing copper wires with fiber-optics and installing new routers. While these upgrades are routine, the FAA said legacy equipment became unstable Friday afternoon when data began flooding the network, disrupting aircraft communications and radar feeds.
The nationwide ground stop was issued out of an abundance of caution, leading to widespread travel delays. Buddy and Debbie McAdams, who were trying to return home to El Dorado from Florida, were among those affected.
"After about a five-hour hold Saturday night with American Airlines, we were told that it would probably be at the earliest to get back here Wednesday morning," Buddy McAdams said.
"I rather have a route to be here. I was not very happy being stranded. I like to have a plan," Debbie McAdams said.
The FAA said the router in question is being examined by the network provider. The agency is also investigating a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, that may be connected to the issue.

title: As some students rely on AI in college applications, admissions offices scramble to keep up
text:
As some students rely on AI in college applications, admissions offices scramble to keep up
The college admissions essay is in a very weird place. It’s impossible to say just how many of them are now written by AI, but at this point, experts agree that it’s a lot of them. And while colleges generally frown upon that practice, they’re using AI to evaluate the essays, too.
Video above: Massachusetts author asks: Would you read a novel written by AI?
It’s all adding up to a scramble to stay ahead when it comes to the future of who gets to go to the university of their choice.
Kate Gilbertson, who graduated from UC Berkeley in 2025 and edits college applications full-time, said that lately she’s received a lot of drafts that don’t have the usual quirks of teenage writing.
“Those little moments of flaw tell me that this is still a 17-year-old’s writing, right?” Gilbertson said.
It’s not just essays. Though ChatGPT has been out for just four years, AI has already reshaped the entire college admissions process from top to bottom.
Now, as the Jan. 1 deadline for the Common App approaches, more and more high schoolers are using AI in their college applications and even turning to chatbots instead of college counselors, who often charge thousands of dollars for their services.
Meanwhile, colleges are rushing to update their AI usage guidelines and rethink the future of the essay. Yet they are also testing out AI evaluations of their own to help sift through thousands, if not tens of thousands, of applications.
Students, meanwhile, see an obvious double standard: If some universities are using AI to grade essays, why can’t I? If everyone is using AI to get ahead, why should I get left behind?
Different rules for different schools
Admissions offices around the country are rushing to figure out guidelines for AI use in applications, and each one looks a little bit different.
But “students are moving faster than admissions offices” when it comes to AI, Ashley Pallie, California Institute of Technology’s dean of undergraduate admissions, said.
Caltech, which is at the forefront of AI research, takes a nuanced approach. Its admissions office whittled down thousands of applicants to fewer than 450 admitted students last year.
For Pallie, the process is much more art than science. She said an AI bot couldn’t replace the job of professional essay readers anytime soon.
While “replacing your unique voice and tone with AI generated content” is unethical, the school said that “generating questions or exercises to help kick start the brainstorming process” is okay.
The University of Pennsylvania warned against AI usage for letters of recommendation written by counselors and teachers.
Colleges are also differing in how they grade essays, with some using AI tools themselves.
“You actually can’t develop the perfect formula that’s going to choose the right students for you. You do need humans who are reading the humans who submitted their application,” Pallie said.
However, CalTech does use an AI that reads students’ scientific research and asks them questions that faculty later view.
Major public universities like Virginia Tech, which received a record 57,622 first-year applications for 2025, are testing out AI to keep up with the mass application volume.
That experimentation hasn’t always worked. UNC-Chapel Hill reversed its decision to auto-score application essays based on writing quality. The student newspaper reported that a university spokesperson said that “the widespread use of AI-assisted writing tools was the factor diminishing the usefulness of AI essay ratings.”
Is this the end of the college essay?
More colleges are dropping supplemental essays altogether for this application cycle.
Tulane said that it is no longer requiring a “Why Tulane?” essay. While spokesperson Michael Strecker told CNN the essay hasn’t been that important in the selection process in recent years, he “can confirm that concerns about AI did play a role in this decision.”
Sophie Sajnani, who graduated college in 2025, founded a boutique college consulting firm. Sajnani discourages her students from using AI to help brainstorm, but doesn’t mind when it writes for them.
When asked if there’s a concern that all the essays will sound the same, she said her students are AI-native and have trained their AI chatbots to sound like them. And she said there’s been a spike in enrollment in her firm’s AI literacy program.
“The reason we still have the admissions essay is to show a moment of growth. I think it’s less so about the writing and more so to show situations and how a student has grown from it,” Sajnani said.
Some students aren’t totally sold on AI writing, but see its benefits for other parts of the admissions process.
“I feel like when using AI, people want to think that you want to cheat the process,” Anisah Ali, a high school junior in Washington, told CNN. “I see it more as you want to open up ideas in your brain that you wouldn’t think about doing yourself.”
Pallie does see a distant future where college essays don’t play as big a role. But, in a way, the replacement is even more person-facing than the essay.
“In our ideal world, everyone would do an interview of some sort,” Pallie said. But the style of that interview? “Human.”
But not all uses of AI in the college application process are as controversial.
Leveling the playing field
The college admissions process begins with deciding which schools are the best fit. In this case, AI can help students who are putting together applications on their own or whose families can’t afford to spend thousands on private college consultants.
This year, ChatGPT launched a college planner for teens. OpenAI said the most popular prompts included “ask questions to develop my ideas,” “give feedback on my draft” and “help me check my evidence.”
“For a lot of students, AI is the college counselor they can’t afford,” Michael Koppenheffer, chief innovation officer of enrollment solutions at EAB, told CNN. “They can get more information and they get more detailed guidance than they ever could before.”
EAB found that AI plays an outsized role in influencing what schools students applied to, compared to resources like colleges' websites and search. Eighty-two percent of students surveyed in its AI report said they used ChatGPT when asked what AI tools they used in their college search.
Christine Wilson, who already utilizes AI to help run her marketing agency in Virginia, at first hired a college counselor for her son, Ronan, who “built a list for him of initial schools that then we ended up kind of redoing ourselves using AI.” She used Claude to make a spreadsheet of the 22 universities Ronan applied to last year.
The spreadsheet ran an analysis of the cost of attendance for each school, taking stats like income and potential aid into account. It saved Wilson “many, many hours of research,” she said.
Wilson and her son ran a separate analysis for colleges that had football, Greek life and prestigious business schools. (Ronan ended up committing to the University of Florida.)
Bunmi Emenanjo’s 17-year-old daughter has specific criteria for her future university: It has to be urban, offer merit aid and have a diverse student body.
While she hired a college counselor for her older son, this year they are relying on Claude.
“It’s just easier to use AI to search for that versus going through each school and digging up that information,” Emenanjo said. But for her family, the application itself will use more of the traditional methods — she said her daughter won’t be using AI for her essays.

title: Prince William and Princess Catherine arrive in India for 3-day visit
text:
Prince William and Princess Catherine arrive in India for 3-day visit
Prince William and Princess Catherine arrived in India on Monday for a three-day visit, the first overseas trip together since she was diagnosed with cancer in 2024.
The U.K. royal couple began their visit in Mumbai and will attend the Earthshot Prize awards ceremony on Tuesday. Founded by William, the annual environmental prize awards five winners $1.3 million each to expand solutions addressing climate change.
The ceremony, expected to be the biggest since the prize was established in 2020, will feature several prominent guests including Indian cricket great Sachin Tendulkar, actors Alia Bhatt and Rami Malek and British pop group Take That, which will make its debut performance in India.
Previous video: Princess Kate announces cancer diagnosis (2024)
“India has made an extraordinary contribution to Earthshot over the past six years and is home to more Earthshot finalists and winners than any other country,” William posted on social media.
Shortly after their arrival, the royal couple took part in a game of street cricket in an alley in Ballard Estate, a neighborhood in Mumbai. Street cricket, a common sight across the city, is an integral part of everyday life in Mumbai.
The couple also will attend events highlighting India’s cricket, fashion and film industries before traveling to New Delhi, where they were scheduled to meet with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday.
The couple met with Modi on their previous trip to India a decade ago before William, the eldest son of King Charles III, became the heir to the U.K. throne.
The trip marks a significant return to overseas royal engagements for the Princess of Wales, commonly known as Kate, who announced in March 2024 that she was undergoing treatment for cancer following major abdominal surgery. Kate disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission and has gradually resumed her public duties.
She traveled to Italy without William in May, marking her first overseas engagement since her diagnosis.

title: Millions could lose Medicaid coverage. Here's what states told us about delaying cuts
text:
Millions could lose Medicaid coverage. Here's what states told us about delaying cuts
The Trump administration is offering states an optional six-month extension to implement new Medicaid work requirements, which could affect millions of Americans starting next year.
Millions could lose Medicaid coverage. Here's what states told us about delaying cuts
The Trump administration is offering states an optional six-month extension to implement new Medicaid work requirements, which could affect millions of Americans starting next year.
The Trump administration is giving states a choice: take another six months before denying or ending Medicaid coverage for people who cannot demonstrate they meet the new work requirements or qualify for an exemption, or move forward with enforcement under the original timeline.
CMS has asked states planning to use the optional extension beginning in January to notify the agency by Dec. 11.
Under the Republican tax-and-spending law, certain Medicaid recipients ages 19 to 64 will have to demonstrate they're working or volunteering for generally 80 hours a month, attending school at least half-time, or meeting another qualifying standard, unless they qualify for an exemption.
The requirements begin Jan. 1, 2027. States that receive approval for the extension must still determine who meets the rules, but can hold off on certain coverage denials and terminations through June 30.
What states told Hearst Television
Hearst Television contacted Medicaid agencies across the country to find out whether they plan to take the extension and what they're doing to prevent eligible Americans from losing health insurance.
In Pennsylvania, the Department of Human Services said it is still reviewing federal guidance before deciding what to do.
The department estimates approximately 700,000 Pennsylvanians enrolled through Medicaid expansion will be subject to the new requirements. It also estimates roughly 300,000 residents could lose coverage throughout 2027 because of the broader changes, including work requirements and twice-yearly eligibility renewals.
Officials worry that additional paperwork could cost people their insurance even if they qualify.
In North Carolina, health officials also have not made a final decision.
The state's Department of Health and Human Services said approximately 740,000 Medicaid expansion adults could be affected.
Officials welcomed the administration's offer, saying the extra time could help counties improve their systems, verify eligibility using existing government records and train employees. If North Carolina takes the extension, affected recipients would not lose or be denied coverage solely for failing to demonstrate compliance with the work requirements during the six-month period.
Arkansas, meanwhile, says it remains committed to moving ahead with its Medicaid work requirements on Jan. 1.
"We are reviewing the details of CMS's decision to offer states an additional six months before enforcing new Medicaid work requirements but remain committed at this time to implement the ARHOME Community Engagement and Work Requirement on January 1, 2027," the Arkansas Department of Human Services said in a statement to Hearst Television.
In Kentucky, state officials pointed to House Bill 2, a law passed by the Republican-controlled legislature requiring Medicaid work requirements to begin Jan. 1. The law also restricts the state from seeking certain federal delays without lawmakers' approval. Officials did not say whether Kentucky would request the newly offered six-month extension before certain coverage denials and terminations.
The Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services warned that broader Medicaid cuts could cause 250,000 Kentuckians to lose health insurance and put 35 rural hospitals at risk of closing. The state currently provides Medicaid coverage to 1.4 million residents.
Kentucky officials are encouraging Medicaid recipients to visit the state's website for information about the changes, keep their contact information current in Kynect, and check their mail regularly.
Ohio also says its implementation remains on track for Jan. 1, but officials have not confirmed whether they intend to request the additional six months before denying or terminating coverage for failure to demonstrate compliance.
The Ohio Department of Medicaid said it is continuing to review federal guidance to determine an approach that works for the state's eligibility operations.
Missouri said its Department of Social Services is evaluating the new guidance and will provide more information as its review continues.
None of these responses establishes that the states have formally accepted or rejected the optional enforcement extension.
Why experts are concerned
Nebraska started enforcing the work requirements early.
According to the state's Department of Health and Human Services, 533 Medicaid expansion renewals were denied or closed in July and August.
Just 43 were attributed to people failing to meet the work requirements or qualify for an exemption.
The other 490 involved people who did not provide requested verification information.
Those numbers do not establish how many people were actually eligible for coverage, but they highlight concerns about how states verify compliance.
Jennifer Tolbert of KFF, a health policy research organization, warns that eligible Americans elsewhere could also lose coverage because of paperwork.
"And there is a real concern that eligible individuals will be denied or disenrolled from Medicaid, not because they're not meeting the requirements or because they don't qualify for an exclusion from the requirements, but simply because they can't navigate the process and provide the paperwork that is needed to verify that they are still eligible," Tolbert said.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services says the additional time will help states test their systems, prevent mistakes and avoid unnecessary interruptions in coverage.
CMS is encouraging states to use existing government records to verify eligibility automatically whenever possible, rather than requiring people to submit additional paperwork.
How many people could lose coverage?
The Urban Institute estimates that by 2028, between 4.9 million and 10.1 million fewer Americans could be enrolled in Medicaid expansion coverage because of the new work requirements and more frequent eligibility checks.
Those projections represent changes in average monthly enrollment compared with what would be expected without the new policies. They are not estimates of how many people will lose coverage immediately in January.
What Medicaid recipients should do
State officials are urging Medicaid recipients to keep their contact information current, watch their mail and respond to requests for paperwork. Pennsylvania officials also recommend updating addresses with the U.S. Postal Service.
Anyone unsure whether the new rules apply to them should contact their state's Medicaid agency.
And even if a state takes the additional six months, recipients must still complete their Medicaid renewals.

title: Trump’s handpicked party chair faces a rebellion after midterm losses test president’s grip on GOP
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A nascent rebellion is underway against President Donald Trump’s handpicked chairman at the Republican National Committee, and it’s already getting ugly.
Some members are calling for a forensic audit of spending decisions, including hair and makeup services for Trump and other officials, as well as the hiring of the daughter of Trump’s former chief of staff. Feuding Republicans are leaking emails and opposition research on rival factions. The White House is threatening to cut off fundraising assistance if the rebels don’t fall in line.
The emerging fight, which will shape the 2028 presidential nominating contest, represents a rare challenge to Trump’s dominance, even after the party’s worst midterm performance in a generation. Despite the broad losses, Republican leaders across Washington have shown little desire to move past Trump and have largely stood behind his most unpopular policies.
But inside the Republican National Committee, an organization of 168 members elected from every state who oversee the party’s national political operation, a small and growing collection of concerned Republicans are backing an attempt to depose Joe Gruters. Trump wants to keep him in charge.
The dissidents are rallying behind Kentucky’s KC Crosbie, the RNC’s second-in-command. She launched her bid just two days after the Nov. 3 election in a letter that drew the fury of both the White House and Gruters’ allies.
Crosbie remains a vocal Trump supporter who backs his “Make America Great Again” agenda, but her opponents view her gambit as a direct challenge to the president and his power.
“Our job is to elect Republicans broadly, not to support one man all the time,” said RNC member Oscar Brock of Tennessee, who is supporting Crosbie’s candidacy. He said that requires a change in leadership because “there’s so much frustration that Chairman Gruters didn’t pull his weight in this election.”
In her letter, Crosbie described the midterms as “a serious setback” and called for the RNC to provide “an honest account” of what went wrong.
Crosbie declined to be interviewed.
The leadership election will be held in January at the RNC’s winter meeting in Arizona.
Inside the rebellion against Gruters
Some would-be Crosbie supporters privately acknowledge they’re worried about a backlash from the White House, especially with Stephen Miller taking over as Trump’s chief of staff. Others believe in the committee’s tradition of having presidents pick their own party chiefs.
Gruters also has vocal backers.
Lauren LePage, an RNC member from Maine, praised Gruters’ leadership and efforts to help her father, Paul LePage, flip a congressional seat — a rare bright spot for Republicans this cycle.
“From my perspective, as chairman, he did his job,” she said, adding that Trump’s endorsement is “something that the committee should take very seriously.”
The Republicans who have lined up behind Crosbie insist a leadership change is needed to send a clear message that the party will do things differently after losses even in Republican strongholds like Texas, South Carolina and Mississippi.
Patti Lyman, an RNC member from Virginia, said it would be “catastrophic” and “insulting” to the party’s base “to keep the same leadership and pretend that we don’t need to do anything different, that we don’t need new players and a new plan.”
Sue Cienki, an RNC committee member from Rhode Island, predicted that Crosbie would have the backing of at least two members from 10 states — a total of 20 — at the committee’s January meeting. That’s the minimum required for a successful nomination.
Trump is furious with Crosbie
Trump and senior White House officials were livid about Crosbie’s Nov. 5 letter and the fact that they were given no heads-up. The president soon released a lengthy statement on his Truth Social social media platform hailing Gruters as a “MAGA Warrior” and giving him his “Complete and Total Endorsement.”
Trump is expected to play a central role in picking the party’s next presidential nominee.
The party’s future is at stake
Allies of Gruters say a leadership change now would put the RNC at a severe disadvantage heading into the next presidential cycle because a new team would need time to get up to speed. They say friction between the president and the committee’s leadership would curtail their ability to organize and raise money.
They also reject Crosbie’s call for a postelection review, which they said would do little more than consume six months rehashing the past and put all their grievances on paper.
Gruters spent much of this week holding private phone conversations with committee members. Those who participated in the calls said Gruters listened to their grievances, but said little about what he would do differently.
Spending faces scrutiny
The opposition to Gruters has focused on the RNC’s spending decisions under him. Republicans had a massive fundraising advantage and still had deep losses.
“There’s clearly a groundswell of support for a forensic audit,” said Brock, the RNC member from Tennessee.
In a letter to RNC members sent Thursday night and obtained by The Associated Press, Gruters acknowledged concerns about spending and other issues.
Gruters defended a $22,500 expenditure for hospitality space at the Presidents Cup, a golf event, saying the space was offered to major donors and “resulted in $2.5 million in renewed contributions to the RNC.”
He also addressed “a brief contract” between the RNC and Caroline Wiles, a longtime Republican consultant, who is the daughter of Susie Wiles, Trump’s former chief of staff. Gruters said she was hired by his predecessor at the committee, Michael Whatley.
“While I have no reason to doubt Caroline Wiles’s value to the RNC or Chairman Whatley’s reasons for bringing her on, this was a brief six-month engagement that ended when I was elected Chairman,” he wrote.
Gruters also defended the RNC’s decision to pay for “hair and make-up services” for senior White House officials, including Trump, Vice President JD Vance and former press secretary Karoline Leavitt.
“This was a request made of us so that the expense did not fall to taxpayers,” Gruters wrote, adding that the beneficiaries “generously gave so much of their limited time and energies to help the RNC this cycle” and “did not ask for much of us in return, so we felt this was a request we could accommodate.”

title: Man allegedly fled from Brewer police during drug raid
text:
A Brewer man was arrested Friday after he allegedly fled an apartment during a drug raid.
Christopher Beayon, 35, has been charged with possessing drugs, refusing to submit to arrest and violating his conditions of release, according to the Brewer Police Department.
Brewer police executed a search warrant at a Chamberlain Street apartment, and during that raid, Beayon allegedly fled from police but was quickly caught.
A search of the apartment turned up drugs, Brewer police said Monday.
Beayon was taken to the Penobscot County Jail in Bangor, where he remained early Monday afternoon, according to the jail’s website.

title: UMaine women’s hockey rallies past Holy Cross 4-1 in strong second period
text:
ORONO, Maine — The University of Maine women’s hockey team rallied from an early deficit to defeat the College of the Holy Cross 4-1 on Friday, Nov. 13. This improved its record to 6-6-1 on the season behind a three-goal second period and a 28-save performance from third-year goaltender Kiia Lahtinen.
The Black Bears entered the week ranked No. 27 in the NPI and tied for fifth in Hockey East with seven points. Maine was coming off a shootout victory over Boston University and a 3-0 win over Merrimack College, both on the road. Holy Cross entered the matchup with a 3-6-4 record, sitting No. 10 in Hockey East with four points.
Ahead of the matchup, Maine head coach Alex Gettens emphasized the team’s efforts to become more effective offensively, particularly when converting scoring opportunities.
“We’re really working at how we can continue to be more dangerous on our rush opportunities, how we can continue to be more dangerous on our power play,” said Gettens. “[And] how we can continue to take some of that zone time and opportunities and just make them a little bit more lethal.”
Holy Cross head coach Katie Lachapelle also stressed the importance of consistency heading into the game, recognizing the challenge of facing Maine.
“There are times where we do some really, really good things. And then we’ll take half a period where we’re maybe not being as consistent, and it starts to really affect the outcome of games,” said Lachapelle. “When we play a full 60 minutes, we can play with anybody.”
Despite the eventual result, the Crusaders got off to a strong start. Second-year forward Violet Carroll opened the scoring just over five minutes into the contest, converting on a power-play opportunity to give Holy Cross an early 1-0 lead.
Maine responded in the second period, with third-year forward Gracie Hanson finding the back of the net to even the score. The Black Bears took control from there, scoring twice more in the period. First-year forward Julie Jebousková put Maine ahead before first-year forward Tiani Makokis added another goal on the power play in the closing seconds to extend the lead.
Fourth-year forward Lily Fetch, who scored Maine’s opening goal against Boston University in the previous game, discussed the importance of establishing momentum early.
“It’s always nice to score in the first period. It sets the tone for the team, and a big message from the game before was trying to bury goals early,” said Fetch.
Holy Cross entered the final period looking to climb back into the contest, generating 11 shots on goal. However, Lahtinen turned aside all 11 attempts in the period, finishing with 28 saves on the night.
Maine added an insurance goal in the final minutes, as second-year defender Lulu Rucinski found the empty net to secure the 4-1 victory.
The Black Bears outshot the Crusaders 34-29 and held a slight advantage in the faceoff circle, winning 30 draws compared to Holy Cross’ 25. Maine’s second-period offensive surge and Lahtinen’s performance in net proved decisive.
The Black Bears are traveling for a two-game series against sixth-ranked Northeastern University on Nov. 18 and Nov. 19 before returning to Orono for the Border Battle against the University of New Hampshire.

title: A draconian decision by the board
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
To the Editor:
I was at the Bar Harbor Historical Society the evening of Friday, Oct. 23, the day before their last day of the season. I was there because they were producing a historical play of mine, "Lace Curtain Irish." About an hour before the show, Erin Cough, the executive director and Nikki Moser, the director of engagement, came downstairs. They were visibly upset. Nikki told me in a sentence that they had just been informed that the entire staff was being let go. Then, she shifted into the role of producer and hostess for the evening’s event. Tabling what must have been a storm of emotions, Nikki proceeded to set up the refreshments — most of which she had baked herself, greet the guests coming in, run support for the actor, introduce the show, and then stay behind to clean up. She did all of this with grace, poise, and warmth. At the end of the evening, she handed me a gluten-free lemon cake that she had baked specially for me and for the actor. This is Nikki.

title: A republic, if we can keep it
text:
History tells us that as Benjamin Franklin emerged from the Constitutional Convention, he was asked, “Well, Dr. Franklin, what have we got, a republic or a monarchy?”
Franklin’s reply was, “A republic, if you can keep it.”
A republic is a fragile form of democracy. It cannot survive on good intentions alone. It requires constant vigilance, active citizen participation and, above all, a functioning system of checks and balances. That brings us to the crisis we face today.
We have allowed our republic to drift dangerously toward authoritarian rule. One branch of government has accumulated an alarming share of power and increasingly uses that power to silence dissent — even to the point of seeking the arrest of those who challenge its authority.
I know I am not alone in fervently hoping we can reverse this deeply troubling course. It will not be easy. Our history offers too many examples of Americans tolerating the actions of the powerful and the self-serving for far too long. Too often, we have looked the other way rather than stand up for the principles we claim to cherish.
Nevertheless, we must act. The survival of our republic and the future of our democracy depend on it.
Let’s make our voices heard. Contact our elected representatives. Let them know that we are paying attention, that we expect accountability, and will not remain silent when our democratic institutions are threatened. We cannot afford to do less.
Howard Search
Brunswick

title: How schools decide when to call a snow day
text:
Every Maine student knows the magic of the words “snow day,” but few know what goes into the early morning decision of when to call one.
Behind those two words is a process most families never see, and since many of you have recently asked about it, I’d like to walk you through it.
It starts days before the storm
Deciding whether to cancel school involves much more than checking an hourly forecast. As soon as a storm shows up on the horizon, often several days out, I begin talking with our transportation director, facilities director, Brunswick town staff (Public Safety and Public Works), and superintendents in neighboring districts.
Those conversations with neighboring districts matter more than people might think. Brunswick, RSU 5, and SAD 75 all send students to Region 10, so one district’s decision affects students in the others. Many of our staff members also commute from towns where the roads may be in rougher shape than they are here in Brunswick. Talking with my colleagues pushes all of us to look beyond our own town lines.
The morning of
On a day with questionable weather, I’m up no later than 4 a.m., go straight to the coffee pot, and then the morning weather report. From there, I call our facilities crew, who are likely already at the schools clearing sidewalks and plowing parking lots. I then stay in close contact with Brunswick Public Works, which can tell me what the roads and sidewalks look like and what crews expect as the morning continues.
Next, I check in with Michelle Caron, our transportation director, who is also monitoring the weather and how it will impact our buses. The truth is, a bus navigates the road very differently from a passenger vehicle.
At the same time, I’m comparing notes in a group text with area superintendents. I review additional local forecasts, and I often circle back to our crews and Brunswick Public Works with follow-up questions.
The questions I ask myself
My goal is always to make a decision by 5 a.m.
- What are the roads like now, and what will they be like when buses are running, and families and students are on the road?
- Is this an all-snow event, or is sleet and freezing rain in the mix?
- Are conditions the same across all of Brunswick, or are some areas much worse?
- If we can get students to school safely, can we also get them home safely?
- What are neighboring districts, especially those whose weather usually matches ours, deciding?
It’s not a science
There’s no formula for this, because no two storms are alike. The final decision rests with me, and I won’t always get it right. Some mornings, hindsight will tell me a different call would have been better. But every decision I make comes back to one priority: the safety of our students and staff.
Getting the word out
Once I make the final call, I begin to notify families and staff as quickly as possible through Reach My Teach automated messages, social media, and local television and radio stations so the news reaches as many people as possible.
My promise to you
I know that not every call I make will please everyone. Some mornings, a snow day will feel unnecessary to some families, and on others, a regular school day will feel like the wrong choice. And with no two storms alike, I won’t always get it right.
Every decision I make, whether it’s a closure, a delay, or a regular school day, will be grounded in the safety of our students and staff. That is my promise to you.
Thank you for your patience, understanding, and trust as we head into another Maine winter. Stay safe and warm.
Phillip Potenziano is superintendent of Brunswick schools.

title: EU accuses Russia of stalling Ukraine peace talks to target power plants as winter nears
text:
EU accuses Russia of stalling Ukraine peace talks to target power plants as winter nears
European Union countries on Monday accused Russia of trying to drag out talks on ending the war in Ukraine while it bombs power plants and other infrastructure to make life even harder for civilians as winter closes in.
At talks in Brussels, EU foreign ministers said the priority should be to secure a ceasefire and then a real peace agreement. They said that Russia started the nearly five-year war and must back down, rather than make fresh demands of Ukraine and its Western backers.
“Let’s not blur the picture right now. What we need to see is a ceasefire,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said before chairing the meeting. “We don’t see it at the moment. We see that Russia is really escalating.”
Related video: Talks between Russia, Ukraine, U.S. with no breakthrough
After negotiations in Abu Dhabi last week, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe, suggesting that it might help bring peace.
But Europeans see that as a Russian attempt to weaken NATO by obliging the military alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward, similar to the way they were deployed before the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland joined in 1999.
Russia again accused of delaying tactics
That demand is “really absurd,” Kallas said. “If we look at the history, none of these countries has ever attacked Russia.” She said Russia’s tactic is always to demand more, even though “they started the war. They are the aggressor. And there’s one victim.”
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee, whose country currently holds the EU’s rotating presidency, said that despite the talks, “Russia has clearly not changed its position. It is continuing its attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure.”
McEntee said the EU will agree on more sanctions later Monday “trying to in particular attack the financial mechanism by which Russia is waging this war.” The ministers will also look at ways to help Ukraine endure the coming winter.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said: “Europe has a security architecture – we don’t need a new one, we just need respect from everyone for the existing security architecture.” He said that is "the foundation for any conceivable agreement, from the European point of view.”
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys also insisted that Europe does not need another security framework, saying that Russia cannot be trusted and has already broken past agreements anyway.
“It’s very clear that we don’t need another one. We already have one. Secure Ukraine, strong Europe, strong trans-Atlantic bond,” he told reporters. “It’s not about the rules. Rules are working. The problem is that Russia is breaking them.”
Little progress in US-led talks
U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have positioned themselves as mediators and have been talking to Russia and Ukraine for just over a year. In that time, no lasting ceasefire has been agreed, and little obvious progress has been made toward peace.
Major differences remain over the control of territory and future security arrangements.
European leaders and officials, including Kallas, have expressed skepticism about the talks. The only tangible progress has been exchanges of prisoners, which are often used by warring parties as a trust-building measure during peace talks.
At a summit in Dublin last week, EU leaders agreed that Europe should be represented in future talks by a team of security advisers from France, Germany, the U.K., Italy and Poland, as well as senior officials from the EU’s main institutions.
The Europeans concede that as Ukraine’s biggest backers they cannot also act as mediators. Their role will focus on security arrangements, reconstruction and Ukraine’s future. Only Ukraine itself can decide on matters involving its sovereignty, they said.
___
Associated Press writer Geir Moulson in Berlin contributed to this report.

Firefighters stop garage fire from spreading to nearby home in Turner
Crews responded to a vehicle fire inside a garage on Round Pond Road Sunday
Firefighters prevented a garage fire from spreading to a nearby residence in Turner on Sunday.
Turner Fire Rescue said crews responded to Round Pond Road for a reported vehicle fire inside a garage on Nov. 15.
When crews first arrived, the garage was fully engulfed in flames and was threatening a nearby residence.
Firefighters quickly worked to put out the flames and kept the fire from spreading to the home.
Crews remained at the scene for approximately two hours. Crews from neighboring departments assisted with the response.
The Maine State Fire Marshal's Office is investigating the cause of the fire.
